deleted_rows.name: North Buttress
gear: Cracks/off-width gear including a wide cam for the finishing crack
hazards: Remote wilderness approach.
Off-width finish requires wide gear.
deleted_rows.overview: A III, 5.9 line up the north face just east of Middle Finger Buttress, following obvious crack systems up good rock to a finishing overhanging off-width crack.
deleted_rows.beta: Grade III, 5.9. Lies just east of Middle Finger Buttress on the peak's broad north face; climbs a line on the right side, with obvious cracks leading up the center on good rock, finishing with an overhanging off-width crack.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a hard turnaround before you leave camp, and base it on weather rather than the clock alone. On a north-facing wall at 8,000 feet with 20 miles between you and the car, any building cumulus, graupel, or first thunder means retreat immediately — the summit plateau is a broad, exposed lightning target and the walk-off crosses open ground. If you are not established on the upper, easier pitches by the time convection starts building, back off. Also turn around if you find the crux pitch unprotectable, if the rock is wet, or if snow is still filling the descent gully, since the walk-off is the only sane way down.
deleted_rows.rappels: None — the standard descent is a walk-off. Carry a single rope for the climb; no rappel stations are documented on the buttress.
deleted_rows.face: North Face — Middle Finger Buttress (right side)
deleted_rows.comms: Assume no cell coverage. From the Thirtymile Trailhead onward you are inside the Pasayten Wilderness and roughly 20 trail miles from the nearest road, with the last dependable signal down in the Methow Valley near Winthrop. Carry a satellite messenger or PLB and leave a written itinerary with someone. Useful numbers to have written down before you lose service: Okanogan County Sheriff dispatch 509-422-7232 and the Methow Valley Ranger District 509-996-4000.
deleted_rows.descent: Walk off: hike east along the crest to the small col southwest of the North Ridge, then down a 3rd-class gully on the north slope back to the lake.

waypoints.name: Thirtymile Trailhead (Chewuch Trail #510)
waypoints.directions: From Winthrop, head north on West Chewuch Road (Okanogan County Road 1213), which turns into Forest Road 51, and stay on it about 29 miles of decent gravel to where the road ends at the Thirtymile Trailhead, 3,430 ft. Park with a Northwest Forest Pass and fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register.

waypoints.name: North Face buttresses above Upper Cathedral Lake (Middle Finger Buttress base area)
waypoints.directions: Take Chewuch Trail #510 up a gentle valley alongside the river for roughly 18 miles, mostly in lodgepole; the first five miles run through the 2001 burn, where standing snags make it a poor place to be in wind, and Chewuch Falls comes in around 2.5 miles. Keep going past the Tungsten Creek and Four Point junctions, then climb out of the valley into the Cathedral Lakes basin — about 19.9 miles and 4,900 ft of gain to camp at Upper Cathedral Lake, which nearly every party splits over two days at Four Point Lake or the meadows past Pocket Lake. Expect blowdown north of Four Point Creek left over from the 2017 Diamond Creek Fire. From camp on the lake's west side the north-wall buttresses rise straight above the water; 15 to 30 minutes of talus and heather puts you under Middle Finger Buttress, the biggest and most westerly, and traversing right along its northwest side brings you to a steep slab split by one thin vertical crack, which is the start.

waypoints.name: Amphitheater Mountain summit
waypoints.directions: Seven pitches of crack and corner climbing take the northwest side of the buttress: the thin-crack slab at 5.7, a short 5.9 crux on the third pitch, then easing ground on clean granite. The last pitch drops to 4th class and low fifth onto the top of the buttress and the broad summit plateau, where many parties unrope; the true summit is easy walking east along the crest from there.

timing.recommendedStart: No alpine start needed from a lake camp. Leave Upper Cathedral Lake around first light to early morning; the wall faces north and stays cold and shaded, so a slightly later start is often more pleasant, but you want to be off the summit plateau before afternoon convection builds. On the approach days, start early to get the valley miles done in the cool.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: The rack called for is simply a wide range of nuts and cams, which for a 1970s crack line of this character means a genuinely full standard rack rather than a specialised one. A practical kit: a full set of wired nuts (small brass through large), a single set of cams from about BD #0.3 to #3 with doubles in the #0.5 to #2 hand sizes that make up most of the climbing, and one #4 if you want security in the wider dihedral sections. Bring a dozen alpine draws — the cracks wander and the pitches are long, so extend generously to keep rope drag out of a seven-pitch day. Nuts and small cams also serve for gear anchors; there is no fixed gear on the route. A single 60 m rope is sufficient since there is no rappel descent.
what_to_bring: Backpacking kit for 4-6 days (this is a 20-mile wilderness approach)
Water filter or purifier — horse traffic contaminates some creeks
Bear-resistant food storage or hang kit
Insect repellent and head net for early-season mosquitoes
Northwest Forest Pass for the trailhead
Self-issue wilderness permit (fill in at the trailhead register)
Map and compass or GPS with the Pasayten quads
Puffy and hat — north-facing wall, cold shade until midday
Sunscreen and sunglasses for the open valley miles
pro_tips: Camp at Upper Cathedral Lake, not at Cathedral Pass — the buttresses rise straight out of the lake and every route on the north wall is a 15-30 minute walk from the west shore.
Middle Finger Buttress is the largest and most westerly buttress above the lake; identify it from the lakeshore the evening before, because from the talus at its base the formations all look alike.
The Right Side starts on a steep slab with a single thin vertical crack — that slab is the identifying feature, and starting too far left puts you on the Left Side chimney instead.
The wall faces north and stays cold and shaded well into the morning; there is no penalty for a leisurely start from camp, and the rock will be more pleasant for it.
Split the approach over two days in each direction. Twenty miles with a climbing pack is the crux of the trip, and parties consistently underestimate it.

Bring a second objective. Cathedral Peak's Southeast Buttress (5.9, 1,000 ft, ten pitches) is a short walk from the same camp and is one of the great moderate rock routes in the Cascades — nobody walks 20 miles for one climb.
Refill water often on the Chewuch — creeks are regular on the valley trail — but treat everything; there is documented horse-stock contamination near Fire Creek.
Late September gives you no bugs, larch colour, and usually the most stable weather of the year, at the cost of short days and cold shade on a north wall.
watch_out: The first five miles of Chewuch Trail #510 cross a 2001 burn full of standing snags — do not camp or linger there in wind.
Blowdown from the 2017 Diamond Creek Fire persists north of Four Point Creek; one party counted roughly 50 downed trees on that section, and clearing varies year to year.
This route is still catalogued as Aid, a leftover from the 1973 first ascent; the free grade is 5.9 but the route description is thin, and route-finding on the upper pitches is on you.
The descent gully is 3rd class but can hold snow into midsummer — check it from the lake before you commit to the walk-off.
Afternoon thunderstorms build fast over the crest in July and August, and the summit plateau is a broad, exposed target.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection is entirely natural and generally good where the cracks are clean, but this is a low-traffic alpine line, so expect lichen, dirt in placements, and the occasional runout on the easier ground between crack systems. The short crux on pitch three is the one place worth having exactly the right piece on the harness. Belays are built from gear.
deleted_rows.best_season: Jul-Sep, consistent with the peak's other rock routes.
deleted_rows.approach: From Winthrop, drive north on Okanogan County Road 1213 (West Chewuch Road), which becomes Forest Road 51, and follow it about 29 miles of good gravel to the Thirtymile Trailhead at road's end (3,430 ft). A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park; the free self-issue wilderness permit is at the register. Start up Chewuch Trail #510, a gentle valley trail that follows the Chewuch River for roughly 18 miles, mostly through lodgepole pine. The first five miles cross the 2001 burn — many standing snags, a bad place to be in wind — and Chewuch Falls comes at about 2.5 miles. Creek access is regular enough on the valley trail that you can refill every hour or two. Continue past the Tungsten Creek and Four Point junctions and climb out of the valley into the Cathedral Lakes basin. Car to camp at Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft) is about 19.9 miles with roughly 4,900 feet of gain — essentially every party splits it over two days, with common first camps at Four Point Lake (6,850 ft) or the meadows just past Pocket Lake. Note the trail north of Four Point Creek still carries blowdown from the 2017 Diamond Creek Fire; trail crews have cut hundreds of logs out of it but conditions vary year to year. From camp on the west side of Upper Cathedral Lake, the north-wall buttresses rise directly above the water. Middle Finger Buttress is the biggest, most westerly one; walk and scramble talus and heather 15-30 minutes to its base, then traverse right to the toe of the northwest side, where a steep slab with a single thin vertical crack marks the start. Alternative trailheads: Andrews Creek (23 miles from Winthrop on the same Chewuch River Road, about 21 miles to the lakes) and Cathedral Driveway from Loomis via Toats Coulee Road.
deleted_rows.descent_text: There is no rappel descent and none is needed. From the top of the buttress, walk east along the broad summit crest of Amphitheater until you reach a small col immediately southwest of the North Ridge. From that col, drop north into a 3rd-class gully and downclimb it on the north slope, which deposits you back on the bench above Upper Cathedral Lake and an easy walk to camp. Parties on the neighbouring buttress routes report roughly 45 minutes from topping out to being back at camp. A longer alternative, useful if the gully is snow-filled early in the season or if you have continued to the true summit, is to walk off southwest across the summit plateau and loop back around the mountain to the lake — considerably more distance but all easy ground. Do not descend the north wall directly: it is a continuous line of buttresses and gullies, and the only reasonable weakness is the col gully.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is straightforward but leaves gear. The route is a crack system throughout, so downclimbing and lowering off nuts or a cam is possible from anywhere on the lower pitches; with a single rope you can back off in 30-metre stages. Above the third-pitch crux, the angle eases enough that finishing to the plateau and walking off the col gully is usually faster and safer than retreating down the line. From the summit plateau, bailing is simply the walk-off. The real bail decision on this route is made days earlier: once you are at Upper Cathedral Lake you are 20 trail miles from the road, so a genuine emergency means either a satellite call for a helicopter or a very long carry-out.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the steep slab split by a thin vertical crack — this is the identifying feature of the Right Side. Follow the crack up the northwest face of the buttress.
Continue up the crack system on the northwest side, linking corners and cracks.
The crux pitch. The hard climbing is a short section only; protect it well and the rest of the route is well below the grade.
Cracks and dihedrals above the crux, easing in angle.
More moderate crack climbing on clean granite.
The buttress broadens and the climbing becomes intermittent; look for the cleanest crack line.
Easy final ground to the top of the buttress and the broad summit plateau; many parties unrope here and scramble the last section.

deleted_rows.itinerary: Day 1: drive from the Puget Sound region (about 5 hours / 216 miles from Seattle via I-5 and SR 20 to the Chewuch trailheads), then hike 5-8 miles up the Chewuch and camp in the valley — the meadow past Pocket Lake or Four Point Lake. Day 2: finish the approach, roughly 12-15 miles, to Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft) and set up base camp; scope the buttress from the lakeshore in evening light. Day 3: climb the Right Side, walk off, and swim. Day 4: a second climbing day — Middle Finger Buttress Left Side or Pilgrimage to Mecca — or tag Cathedral Peak's Southeast Buttress next door. Day 5: hike the 20 miles out, or split it with one more valley camp. Most parties budget 4-6 days car to car; the approach, not the climbing, sets the schedule.

access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Pasayten Wilderness (USFS)

road.name: Okanogan County Rd 1213 (West Chewuch Road) → Forest Road 51 to the Thirtymile Trailhead
road.status: Gravel, maintained, passenger-car passable; one party in 2021 described the road as being in 'unbelievably good condition'.
road.driveNote: From Winthrop, head north on West Chewuch Road (County Rd 1213), which becomes FR 51, and continue about 29 miles to road's end at the Thirtymile Trailhead (3,430 ft). Roughly 5 hours and 216 miles from Seattle via I-5 and SR 20. The Andrews Creek Trailhead is on the same road at about 23 miles from Winthrop. There are restrooms and picnic tables at Thirtymile but no potable water; parking accommodates about 15 vehicles plus horse trailers, with an unloading ramp, hitch rails, a bear-proof garbage can and a vault toilet.
road.seasonalGate: No locked seasonal gate is documented; access is limited by snow rather than by a gate, so the trailhead is effectively a late-spring-through-autumn road.

climate.fall: September is often the best month — cold nights, no bugs, stable high pressure, and larch and aspen colour along the Chewuch. Days shorten quickly and the first significant snow can arrive any time after mid-September.
climate.spring: Not a climbing season. Deep snow lingers in the Cathedral Lakes basin, the valley trail is a runoff and blowdown obstacle course, and the road-to-lake approach is impractical on foot.
climate.summer: The reliable window. Warm, dry, sunny days on the granite from mid-July onward. The trade-offs are afternoon convective thunderstorms building over the crest, heavy mosquito pressure in early July, and mid-to-late summer wildfire and smoke, which is a recurring feature of this drainage.
climate.winter: No practical climbing season. The upper Chewuch road is snowbound and the approach becomes 20 miles of unbroken valley travel to a north-facing alpine wall.
climate.typical: Pacific systems are lifted over the Cascade crest and drop most of their moisture on the west side, so Amphitheater — sitting east of the crest — is markedly drier and sunnier than the western North Cascades. Most precipitation falls as winter snow; summers are typically clear.
climate.forecastZone: East slopes of the North Cascades, Okanogan Range, Okanogan County — well east of the Cascade crest. NWAC issues no avalanche forecast specific to the Pasayten Wilderness; the nearest routine mountain-weather coverage is NWAC's East Slopes North product, and the Methow Valley Ranger District (509-996-4000) is the best source for on-the-ground trail and fire conditions.

emergency.notes: Aero Methow Rescue Service is the EMS provider for the Methow Valley. There is no cell coverage in the Cathedral Lakes basin, so a satellite messenger or PLB is the only realistic way to call for help; a ground evacuation from Upper Cathedral Lake means roughly 20 trail miles. Leave a detailed itinerary with a contact who knows when to call.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — 24 W Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862, 509-996-4000. This is the office to call for road, trail, fire and closure information.
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, 507 Hospital Way, Brewster, WA 98812 — 509-689-2517. It is the public hospital district serving the Methow Valley and south Okanogan County. Mid-Valley Hospital in Omak is a comparable-distance alternative. Confluence Health's Methow Valley Clinic in Winthrop (1116 WA-20) handles walk-in, non-emergency care only.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 in an emergency. Okanogan County Sheriff non-emergency dispatch: 509-422-7232, or 800-572-6604 when dialling from within the 509 area code. The Sheriff's Office coordinates search and rescue in the county.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to mid-September, once the north-facing cracks have dried and before cold nights chill the shaded wall

July.reason: The approach melts out and the buttress dries, though early in the month snow patches linger at its base and the high creeks run full.

June.reason: Snow still fills the Cathedral Lakes basin and the talus below the north wall, and the cracks on this shaded face run with meltwater.

August.reason: Dry, warm rock on a face that sees little sun; the main risks are afternoon thunderstorms and wildfire smoke or closures in the Pasayten.

October.reason: The first snows of the season usually arrive at 8,000 ft, glazing the north face, and a two-day approach leaves little margin for a storm.

September.reason: Settled weather and cooler approach days; by late month the shaded north wall gets cold for the off-width finish and nights drop below freezing.

deleted_rows.name: Chockstone Route
hazards: Crevassed glacier travel on the approach
Loose rock on the summit tower
deleted_rows.overview: A named II 5.2 rock line up Austera's summit tower via its signature chockstone chimney, reached by the same long multi-glacier approach used for the standard route; may represent the same summit-block crux described elsewhere as part of the Southwest Ridge finish, catalogued here as its own named route on record.
deleted_rows.beta: A short, moderate 2-3 pitch rock climb up easy rock scrambling that ends in the notorious chockstone chimney, rated 5.2 and about 60 ft long. Reached after a long approach and glacier traverse; can be descended by rappelling the route or by continuing on a loop past nearby summits.
deleted_rows.turnaround: As with any glaciated approach, begin early enough to cross snow/ice terrain before it softens in the afternoon sun, and be prepared to retreat if the chimney is wet or icy.
deleted_rows.rappels: Rappel the chockstone chimney/route to descend from the summit tower.
deleted_rows.descent: Rappel the route from the top of the chockstone chimney, then either reverse the glacier approach back to high camp or continue a larger loop over additional glaciers.

timing.recommendedStart: Early alpine start from high camp to cross the glacier approach before it softens.

pro_tips: Can be combined into a scenic loop from high camp taking in Deans Spire, Banada Spire, Eldorado Peak, and Dorado Needle.
watch_out: Loose rock typical of the peak's upper terrain
Long, glaciated approach with crevasse hazard before any technical climbing begins
deleted_rows.best_season: Likely climbable in the same window as the standard route (roughly late June through September, once Cascade River Road opens and the glacier approach has consolidated).
deleted_rows.approach: From the Cascade River Road trailhead, approximately 7 miles and 6,000 ft of elevation gain leads to an East Ridge of Eldorado high camp. From camp, cross the Inspiration, McAllister, and Klawatti Glaciers (forested trail, steep talus, and glacier travel) to reach the base of Austera's rock tower.
deleted_rows.descent_text: After topping out via the chockstone chimney, parties typically rappel back down the same feature to the base of the tower, then re-cross the Klawatti/McAllister/Inspiration Glacier system to high camp; alternatively, strong parties can extend into a larger loop touching other nearby summits (Deans Spire, Banada Spire, Eldorado Peak, Dorado Needle) before returning.

pitch_detail.notes: The route's signature feature: a chimney with a chockstone, roughly 60 ft long, described as the crux.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee for the backcountry camping permit.
access.permit: Backcountry permit required for overnight camping; obtained at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount or via recreation.gov.
access.closures: Cascade River Road closes seasonally each winter and typically reopens in late June.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (NPS)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park Complex wilderness permit — quota, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount; $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee.

road.name: Cascade River Road
road.status: Gravel; narrows past the Eldorado turnout, with steep drop-offs and possible washouts requiring high clearance.
road.driveNote: From Marblemount, follow Cascade River Road to the Cascade River Road trailhead used for the standard Eldorado approach.
road.seasonalGate: Typically opens by late June (weather/snow dependent) and closes for winter.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate; heavy winter snow, drier but changeable summer weather over exposed glacier terrain.

emergency.notes: No reliable cell coverage in this glacier basin; carry a PLB or satellite communicator.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park HQ / Wilderness Information Center: 360-854-7200, 810 State Route 20, Sedro-Woolley, WA 98284
emergency.nearestHospital: United General / Skagit Regional Health - Sedro-Woolley (nearest to Marblemount); Skagit Valley Hospital, Mount Vernon (Level III ED), 360-424-4111
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Skagit County Sheriff's Office: 360-336-9450 (911 also routes to the correct agency)

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Cascade River Road trailhead

bivy.name: Eldorado-Inspiration snow arm high camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the East Ridge and for anything out on the Inspiration Glacier, on the broad snow arm where the Eldorado and Inspiration ice meet. Because it is a snow camp rather than a fixed site, the exact ground shifts year to year with the snowpack — early season it is uniform snow, while a thin year opens moraine and rock that some parties prefer. Tent platforms need to be stamped or dug and walled, since there is nothing between the camp and the wind. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, and keep well back from meltwater channels.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; carry a stove and fuel budgeted for melting, and fill before leaving, since the next dependable running water on the descent is thousands of feet lower
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit, required year round for any overnight stay. The Eldorado cross-country zone is quota-managed: roughly 60% reservable through Recreation.gov (a March early-access lottery, then a general window in late April), about 40% held for walk-ups between mid-May and mid-October. Cascade River Road permits must be collected in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Not free — confirm current pricing when booking.
bivy.capacity: Very large — the flats above the col hold many parties, though the wilderness zone quota is what actually limits numbers

bivy.name: Klawatti Col camp
bivy.notes: Only parties staying out more than one night use this camp; it exists to put Klawatti, Austera and Dorado Needle within a day's reach, and it is the natural staging point for continuing east. Getting there means traversing the Inspiration Glacier from the Eldorado camp, so it is a roped, crevassed approach rather than a walk, and one section of the onward route to Klawatti involves negotiating a moat and a short rappel that varies enormously with the month. It is high, fully exposed and entirely on snow — build walls and expect the site to be somewhere slightly different from where the last party pitched.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only, with no running water at any point in the season; plan fuel for every litre
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit. Depending on how your itinerary is written this may fall in a different cross-country zone from Eldorado, so describe the whole traverse when you book or when you present the itinerary at the Wilderness Information Center rather than assuming one zone covers it.
bivy.capacity: Limited — snow benches near the col, suited to a small number of roped parties

bivy.name: Marble Creek Campground, Cascade River Road
bivy.notes: Roughly eight miles up the gravel Cascade River Road from Marblemount, this is the practical place to spend the night before if you cannot start walking the same day. Its value is logistical: the Wilderness Information Center wants your permit activated in person the day before, or before late morning on your start day, so staying nearby avoids a pre-dawn drive from the west. There is no cell coverage, and the road above it continues to deteriorate toward the trailhead, so check current road status before committing a low-clearance car.
bivy.water: No potable water supplied; treat creek water or bring your own
bivy.permit: Forest Service campground, NOT park wilderness — no backcountry permit and no bear canister needed here, but a nightly fee applies. It does not substitute for the wilderness permit you still have to collect at Marblemount for the climb itself.
bivy.capacity: 22 sites, a mix of reservable and first-come

bivy.name: Eldorado East Ridge rock bivies
bivy.notes: Where the snowpack has pulled back from the base of the East Ridge, flat rock takes bivy gear directly and gives a firmer, drier platform than the glacier. The site sits anywhere from roughly 7,500 to 7,800 ft, and the range is real rather than an error — how much rock is exposed, and therefore where you end up sleeping, depends on the year and the month. It is more sheltered than the open snow arm but far smaller, so arriving late on a busy weekend often means going back onto the ice.
bivy.water: Seasonal. A trickle sometimes runs among the rocks near the site or off the south side in the afternoon and evening, but it dries as the season advances and should not be counted on
bivy.permit: Same North Cascades wilderness permit and Eldorado cross-country zone quota as the snow camp; nothing about a rock bivy exempts it. Collect in person at Marblemount before the trip.
bivy.capacity: A handful of parties at most — a few flat rock patches, best suited to bivy sacks or one small tent apiece

bivy.name: Eldorado Basin camp
bivy.notes: The usual bail-out camp for parties who leave the trailhead late or find the boulder field slower than expected, reached after the talus and the short cliff band on the climbers' trail. It sits on vegetated ground rather than snow, so it is warmer and has real water, at the cost of adding a couple of thousand feet to summit day. Accounts describe usable ground from about 5,600 ft up through 6,200 ft, so treat the number as the middle of a band rather than a fixed site. Keep tents on durable ground, off the meadow, and 100 ft from water.
bivy.water: Reliable running water from basin streams through the climbing season; the first dependable water above the boulder fields
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit for the Eldorado cross-country zone, in person at Marblemount. A bear canister is required for camps below the glacier — the Wilderness Information Center loans them, but only in person, so factor that into the pickup stop.
bivy.capacity: Small — a scattering of level spots on the ridge and in the upper basin, enough for several parties spread out

bivy.name: Roush Creek Basin camp
bivy.notes: The neighbouring basin to the east offers an alternative low camp when Eldorado Basin is occupied, with usable ground reported roughly between 6,100 and 6,400 ft. It suits parties splitting the approach into a short first day, or skiers wanting a lower base. Like the Eldorado Basin option it costs you the height you did not gain on day one, and the boulder-field descent still has to be done in daylight on the way out.
bivy.water: Creek water and snowmelt, usually reliable early and mid season; later in a dry summer it can be reduced to snow patches
bivy.permit: North Cascades wilderness permit, Eldorado cross-country zone, in-person pickup at Marblemount. Bear canister required at this elevation, below the permanent snow.
bivy.capacity: Small — a few tent spots, generally quieter than Eldorado Basin

deleted_rows.name: North Ridge
gear: glacier travel kit (crampons, ice axe, harness)
light rock rack for class 4 rock
hazards: Talus and scree field approach — loose rock hazard, particularly on descent
Exposure on ridge sections — Class 3-4 scrambling with exposure on narrow sections
Weather development — afternoon thunderstorms common July-August
Stream crossings in approach canyon — high water in June-July
deleted_rows.overview: Bonanza Peak is the highest non-volcanic summit in Washington and the Chelan County highpoint, deep in the Glacier Peak Wilderness above Holden Village. This line is the peak's standard east-side route: roped travel up the Mary Green Glacier, then loose Class 3-4 scrambling through a gully/rib system to a notch on the upper northeast ridge and a short, exposed crest to the summit.
deleted_rows.beta: From Holden Village, hike the Railroad Creek and Holden Lake trails to camp at Holden Lake or Holden Pass. Cross the Mary Green Glacier to the rock, weave between the two gully/rib lines to the notch on the upper ridge, and follow the crest to the summit. Descend the same route.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Turn around if weather deteriorates rapidly or if adequate daylight remains for safe descent.
deleted_rows.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
deleted_rows.descent: Downclimb the same north/notch line back onto the Mary Green Glacier and retrace the ascent route to camp.

waypoints.name: Holden Village / Ballpark Campground
waypoints.directions: There is no road to Holden Village. Take the Lady of the Lake boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, then ride the Holden Village bus about 11 miles up FS Road 8301 to the village at about 3,300 ft; reserve the bus seat in advance. A free self-issued Glacier Peak Wilderness permit is required.

waypoints.name: Bonanza Peak (true summit)
waypoints.directions: From the west side of the village, hike the Railroad Creek Trail about 1 mile and turn right onto Holden Lake Trail #1251, climbing about 4 miles to Holden Lake. Continue toward Holden Pass, then take the climbers' path through slide alder to the Mary Green Glacier at about 7,300 ft. Climb its north edge past the bergschrund, scramble loose gullies and ribs to a notch on the upper ridge, and follow the exposed ridge to the true summit.

timing.recommendedStart: Alpine start from high camp, roughly 4:00-5:00am

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A single rope (or two thin ropes for full-length rappels) plus a standard glacier kit — harness, crampons, ice axe, a few pickets or screws, and prusiks/crevasse-rescue gear. A light rack of small-to-medium cams and nuts is useful for optional protection or a rappel anchor on the upper class 4 rock; helmet is essential given the loose orthogneiss.
what_to_bring: insect repellent (heavy mosquitoes/black flies near Holden Lake)
bivy/camp gear for Holden Lake or Holden Pass camp
pro_tips: Climb mid-summer, before the glacier breaks up too much to cross cleanly to the rock
Start very early (4-5am) to be off the summit rock before afternoon thunderstorms or softening snow
Expect to weave between two adjacent gully/rib lines near the top — if one looks too hard, traverse to the other
watch_out: Talus stability — disturbed talus creates rockfall hazard for parties below, move quickly through loose sections
Ridge traverse exposure — one slip on narrow sections could result in significant drop; helmets recommended
Afternoon electrical storms — summit by 1pm in summer; thunderstorm risk increases afternoon
Bergschrund and moat — the step from glacier to rock gets harder as the glacier breaks up later in summer; stay roped on the glacier.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and optional on most of the route (glacier travel plus unroped/simul class 3-4 scrambling), but carry a few small cams/nuts and slings for anchor-building on the upper rock in case of wet conditions or a forced rappel.
deleted_rows.best_season: July through October; snow lingers into June, making descent hazardous
deleted_rows.approach: From Ballpark Campground at Holden Village (~3,300 ft), take Railroad Creek Trail (#1240) about 1 mile to its junction with Holden Lake Trail (#1251); turn right (north) and hike roughly 4 miles to Holden Lake (5,278 ft). Continue past the lake toward Holden Pass (6,360 ft), where most parties establish high camp, or continue on a climbers' path through slide alder toward the base of the Mary Green Glacier (~7,300 ft).
deleted_rows.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb loose class 3-4 rock back to the notch on the upper ridge, then descend the gully/rib system used on the ascent to regain the glacier. Some parties rappel the wet, slabby upper section (a rap station has been reported just below the summit) rather than downclimb when the rock is wet or icy; parties have used 4-5 rappels off slung horns/blocks on a 60m half rope in these conditions. Re-cross the bergschrund/crevasse zone on the glacier with care, then descend to Holden Pass/Holden Lake camp.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is straightforward on clear terrain: downclimb to the notch and back onto the glacier, then to camp. In poor weather, turn around before committing to the upper rock band, since the route-finding through the gully/rib system becomes very difficult in fog or rain and the rock is notoriously loose and unpleasant when wet.

pitch_detail.notes: Ascend along the north edge of the Mary Green Glacier; watch for crevasses/bergschrund.
Loose, sustained scrambling; route-find between two gully/rib systems to a notch on the upper NE ridge.
Short exposed ridge scramble from the notch to the true summit.

deleted_rows.itinerary: Day 1: boat/bus to Holden Village, hike in to Holden Lake or Holden Pass camp (half day). Day 2: alpine start (4-5am), climb the glacier and upper rock to the summit (~4.5 hrs up), summit break, descend to camp (total climbing day ~8-9 hrs). Day 3: hike out to Holden Village for the return boat/bus.

access.fees: None — no climbing fee (National Forest wilderness, not Mount Rainier NP)
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 (people + stock combined) — same Glacier Peak Wilderness system that covers Glacier Peak itself (one contiguous wilderness spanning both Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie and Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forests).
access.permit: None required — free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead, no reservation.
access.closures: Holden Village and the only access road (FSR 8301) are closed to all hikers and vehicles under USFS order #06-17-05-26-04, in effect 28 January 2026 through 31 December 2027, after Dec 2025 flood/landslide damage; the Lucerne-Holden boat shuttle is also suspended. Confirm current Forest Service and Holden Village access alerts before planning this climb.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Wenatchee River Ranger District), Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chiwawa/Entiat Ranger Districts) — Glacier Peak Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at some trailheads (fee day-use sites) — $5/day or $30/year.
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass (trailhead parking, where applicable)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk (Phelps Creek, Trinity, Entiat River, or the Holden trailheads). Holden Village and its access road are closed to hikers through at least summer 2026.

road.name: Railroad Creek Road / Forest Service Road 8301
road.status: Closed
road.driveNote: FSR 8301, the only land route to Holden Village, was destroyed by flooding and landslides in December 2025. It is closed to all vehicle and hiker traffic under a closure order in effect January 28, 2026 through December 31, 2027 (subject to change), and repairs (est. ~$20M) cannot begin until damage assessment after spring snowmelt. Boat shuttle service between Lucerne and Holden Village is also currently suspended, so the standard approach to this route is not available for the 2026 season.

climate.fall: Shortening weather windows and increasing chance of early snow at elevation.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack on approach trails and the glacier; avalanche hazard on steeper slopes.
climate.summer: The main climbing season; the glacier is most passable in early-to-mid summer before late-season breakup.
climate.winter: Not a viable season for this route; deep snow, avalanche hazard, and no approach access.
climate.typical: Continental-influenced Cascade climate on the drier, east-slope side of the range; conditions on the loose upper rock deteriorate quickly and dangerously in rain.

emergency.notes: This is an extremely remote objective. With FSR 8301 and the Lucerne dock closed since January 28, 2026 (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-05-26-04, through December 31, 2027) and the Lucerne-Holden shuttle suspended, any rescue would likely require helicopter access; self-rescue capability and a satellite communicator are strongly advised.
emergency.rangerStation: Chelan Ranger District / Wenatchee River Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
emergency.nearestHospital: Lake Chelan Health Hospital, Chelan, WA (24-hr ER; EMS also stationed in Stehekin)
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Chelan County Sheriff's Office (911 for emergencies)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to August, when the Mary Green Glacier is still well bridged and the rock above the moat is dry

July.reason: The glacier is still well bridged and the moat easy, but high creek crossings and lingering snow on the rock slow early July.

June.reason: Heavy snow on the Holden Lake approach and the rock, high water at stream crossings, and hazardous snow on the descent.

August.reason: Crevasses open but easy to weave around and the upper rock is dry; watch for afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge.

October.reason: Bare glacier ice, a wide moat, early snow on the scramble, and short days for a long route from Holden Lake.

September.reason: Dry rock, but the glacier is at its most crevassed and the moat onto the rock gets harder to cross as the month goes on.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Holden Village (~3,300 ft) — reached by Lake Chelan ferry to Lucerne and the village shuttle — via the Railroad Creek Trail

deleted_rows.corrections: The given routeId/name 'North Ridge' does not correspond to a distinctly named, independently documented technical line in primary sources (Mountain Project, SummitPost, AAC, guidebook trip reports); those sources consistently describe this line as the 'Mary Green Glacier' route, finishing on the mountain's upper northeast ridge to a notch just north of the true summit. This entry documents that standard/easiest route under the given name. Elevation is best sourced as 9,511 ft (matches AAC and most trip-report sources); a Wikipedia infobox figure of 9,516 ft and a cited LIDAR re-survey figure of 9,503 ft also appear in circulation. The 1937 first ascent (James, James, Leuthold) approached via the Company Glacier on the north side, a different line than this east-side glacier route, so no route-specific FA is claimed here.

bivy.name: Holden Pass and the slab bivies above
bivy.notes: Holden Pass at about 6,400 ft is the higher option for Bonanza and cuts a serious amount off summit day compared with sleeping at the lake. Parties who want more push another five hundred feet to ledges below the waterfall slabs at roughly 6,900 ft, which is a genuine bivouac rather than a campsite and is worth scouting in daylight before committing to it in the dark. From either, the route makes a rising traverse west to the snowfield below the slabs, scrambles onto the northern edge of the Mary Green Glacier and works southwest under the northeast ridge. The trade is comfort and water for time: an early start off wet slabs in the dark from the pass is a very different proposition to the same ground at first light, so choose the higher camp only if the party is competent moving on that terrain unlit. Exposed to weather with nothing to hide behind.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and running water off the slabs early in the season; by late summer this can dry up entirely and you may have to carry water from Holden Lake
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit. No campfires at this elevation on bare ground and in fragile alpine terrain — carry a stove. Camp on rock, snow or existing bare ground rather than on the heather benches, which do not recover.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small pitches at the pass, and higher up only ledges — one or two tents at best above the pass, and parties frequently sleep two to a ledge

bivy.name: Holden Lake
bivy.notes: This is the standard base camp for Bonanza Peak and the natural place to sleep before the Mary Green Glacier, the Northeast Buttress or the North Ridge. The trail leaves the Railroad Creek valley at around 3,600 ft and climbs four miles of switchbacks to the lake, which puts most of the day's work behind you before the climbing starts. From here a typical Mary Green day is around eleven hours camp to camp with several thousand feet of gain, so parties either accept a long day from the lake or push a high camp higher. It is also the launching point for Martin Peak and for traverses toward Holden Pass. The whole basin is remote enough that self-rescue is the realistic plan — there is no road within a day of you, and the way out is a boat.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and its inlet streams, plus snowmelt high into the summer
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit, filled in at the trailhead. Camping and campfires are both prohibited within 200 feet of the lakeshore, which is enforced and is the reason the good sites sit back in the trees and benches. Group size limits apply. Getting here at all depends on the ferry, the bus and the Railroad Creek road being open.
bivy.capacity: Several established sites spread around the basin, enough for a few parties, but they are the obvious base for every Bonanza attempt so expect company in July and August

bivy.name: Holden Village
bivy.notes: This is the base for Bonanza, Copper, Dumbell's eastern side, and the Railroad Creek walk in to Hart and Lyman Lakes. Its unusual value to a climber is that you can sleep indoors and eat three meals at 3,200 ft the night before starting up a 9,500 ft peak, which no other approach in this zone offers. The catch is that the whole thing runs on a schedule you do not control: a passenger ferry roughly forty miles up Lake Chelan from Chelan or Fields Point Landing, then a bus about ten miles up a single forest road, with the bus historically running only on certain days. Miss a boat and you lose a day at each end, so the practical trip length is dictated by the sailing schedule rather than by the climb. As of the 2026 season the village is closed to all guests including hikers and the road up Railroad Creek is closed by order after December 2025 flooding and slides destroyed sections of it — using the Lucerne dock or travelling that road in any form is prohibited while the order stands, repairs are expensive and slow, and reopening may slip beyond 2026. Treat any Bonanza plan as unbookable until that order is lifted, and confirm directly rather than assuming a summer has reopened it.
bivy.water: Village water supply, hot showers, laundry — the only fully serviced lodging anywhere near these peaks
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit needed to sleep here, but a confirmed reservation is mandatory and so is a booked seat on both the Lake Chelan passenger boat to Lucerne and the shuttle bus up Railroad Creek. Rates are per person per night and include all meals, with a lower long-stay rate and a higher rate in the peak weeks of high summer. A wilderness permit and the usual campfire rules still apply the moment you leave the village on any trail.
bivy.capacity: Dormitory-style lodge rooms in the old mining town, tens of guests at a time; individual bookings and group bookings are handled separately and both fill for the summer months

bivy.name: Holden Ballpark Campground
bivy.notes: About a mile above the village on the way to the trailheads, this is the answer for a climbing party that wants the Holden approach without paying village rates or fitting into a meal schedule. Being an open field it is exposed and has no shelter, and with only a site or two you cannot count on it if another party arrived on the same boat. It sits at the practical start of the walk to Hart Lake, Holden Lake and Copper Basin, so it works as a first night after a late ferry and again as a last night waiting for a morning bus out. It is subject to exactly the same road closure as the village — while Railroad Creek road is closed by order there is no legal way to reach it.
bivy.water: Railroad Creek is close by and needs treating; the village's services are a mile back down the road and are not yours to use unless you are a paying guest
bivy.permit: Free national forest campground with no fee and no reservation, but a free self-issue wilderness permit is required for the trails above it. Reaching it at all depends on the ferry and the Railroad Creek road, so the ferry booking is the real constraint. Standard forest fire restrictions apply and are usually tightened to no open flame by late summer.
bivy.capacity: Tiny — one or two primitive tent sites in an open field, so it is a place to sleep rather than a place to stage a large party

deleted_rows.name: East Ridge (Non-Technical)
deleted_rows.fa: Elvin R. Johnson, Norma Johnson, William A. Long, and Kathy Long — August 11, 1948 (also the peak's first ascent)
hazards: Ridge exposure — 50-100 ft drops on both sides of ridge; significant falling risk if not careful
Loose rock — some sections include loose Class 3 scrambling; rockfall hazard for any party below
Weather on ridge — exposed ridge attracts electrical storms; summiting window is critical
deleted_rows.overview: Colchuck Peak is primarily known for its technical alpine routes and glaciated approaches, but the East Ridge provides a non-technical Class 2-3 scrambling alternative for parties seeking to reach the summit without technical climbing. This route is less traveled than the technical options.
deleted_rows.beta: Start from the Colchuck-Dragontail col, reached as for the Colchuck Glacier route; this is the base of the ridge. Follow the ridge crest, negotiating Class 2-3 scrambling terrain. Several sections require hands but no protection needed. The granite is generally solid with good friction. Descent retraces the ascent.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Turn around if Class 3 feels uncomfortable or if rope/protection appears necessary.
deleted_rows.rappels: None — descend via the same route (glacier and moraine back to Colchuck Lake)
deleted_rows.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.
deleted_rows.descent: Descend the same route back down the glacier, moraine, and trail to the trailhead.
obj_haz: Rockfall shed off Dragontail Peak's cliffs onto the glacier
Crevasse hazard on Colchuck Glacier, more evident late season
Icy glacier surface and firm 40° snow near the col in early morning

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road and then FR 7601 via Eightmile Road to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, where the Stuart Lake Trail starts.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.directions: From the trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail along Mountaineer Creek about 2.5 miles to the signed junction and take the Colchuck Lake Trail, which crosses the creek and switchbacks up through boulder fields for another 1.6 miles to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Follow the lakeshore trail to the boulder field at the lake's south end and climb the moraine and basin onto the Colchuck Glacier. Ascend the glacier, keeping climber's right away from rockfall off Dragontail, to the col between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail, then turn right and scramble the Class 2-3 ridge west to the summit.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Ice axe and crampons are the essential technical gear; a rope and light glacier-travel protection are optional given the glacier's generally minimal crevassing, but recommended later in the season.
what_to_bring: extra water for the long approach
pro_tips: Start pre-dawn (4-5 AM) to cross the glacier while snow is firm and before afternoon rockfall/wet-slide risk rises.
Stay climber's right (toward the lateral moraine) on the Colchuck Glacier to reduce exposure to rockfall off Dragontail Peak.
Late May-early July gives the best glacier travel conditions; by late summer it gets icy with crevasses opening climber's-right.
watch_out: Ridge exposure severe — one slip means significant drop; this is more exposed than lower-angle scrambles; proceed with caution
Loose rock sections — Class 3 sections include unstable rock; kick test all handholds and footholds
Electrical storm risk — exposed ridge; thunderstorm risk afternoon July-August; aim to summit by early afternoon
deleted_rows.best_season: June through September; early season the Colchuck Glacier gully to the col is still snow, which is the easiest going, while by late August it can be bare ice where crampons bite poorly. Snow persists longer on north slopes.
deleted_rows.approach: From Leavenworth, drive Icicle Road (FR 7601 via Eightmile Road) to the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft). Hike the Stuart Lake Trail roughly 2.5 miles (1,100 ft gain) to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, then switchback up another 1.6 miles (1,100 ft gain) to Colchuck Lake (~4.1 mi, ~2,200 ft total). Continue along the lake's west shore and across the boulder field at its south end to the base of the Colchuck Glacier.
deleted_rows.descent_text: From the summit, reverse the ascent: scramble back down to Colchuck Col, descend the Colchuck Glacier (staying climber's right to minimize exposure to Dragontail's rockfall), then follow the moraine and lake-shore boulder field back to Colchuck Lake and the trail out.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is straightforward at any point by reversing the ascent line back down the glacier to Colchuck Lake.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4.1 mi, ~2,200 ft gain via the Stuart Lake Trail junction and Colchuck Lake Trail switchbacks
Gain the lateral moraine crest beyond the lake's south end to avoid loose scree
~550 m gain up the glacier's east (left) lobe; crampons and axe; stay climber's right to avoid Dragontail rockfall
~100 ft of 40° snow, then sandy 3rd-class steps to the 8,500 ft summit plateau and on to the true summit

deleted_rows.itinerary: Typically a long single day (10-12 hours car-to-car) with a 4-5 AM start; some parties instead backpack in and camp at Colchuck Lake (Colchuck Zone permit required for overnight May 15-Oct 31) to make summit day shorter.

access.fees: Day-use: free. Overnight lottery: $6 non-refundable application fee, then $5/person/night if selected. (Some approaches — e.g. Mount Stuart via Ingalls Creek/Longs Pass — fall entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area and need only the free self-issue permit even overnight.)
access.notes: 2026 lottery application window Feb 15–Mar 1 (results after Mar 17, accept/pay by Mar 31). ~25% of overnight slots also released as a walk-up daily lottery the day before entry. Season requiring the overnight permit: May 15–Oct 31. A single-day ascent with no camp inside the boundary never needs the lottery.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.
access.permit: Day climbs: free self-issue day-use permit at the trailhead — no lottery needed. Overnight camping inside the Enchantment Permit Area boundary: Enchantments overnight lottery permit (Recreation.gov).
access.closures: FR 7601 access road closes seasonally each winter
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Wenatchee River Ranger District — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Stuart Lake, Eightmile, and Snow Lakes trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (overnight permit holders get a covering parking pass instead).
access.passRequired: Trailhead day-use fee (Recreation Pass/Scan & Pay) or Interagency pass equivalent

overnight_permit.what: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (lottery, not free) May 15 to Oct 31; self-issue at the trailhead the rest of the year
overnight_permit.where: Apply in the February advance lottery or the daily lottery on Recreation.gov. The permit names one zone (Core, Colchuck, Snow Lakes, Stuart, Eightmile/Caroline) and you camp only there, except a Core permit, which covers every zone.

road.name: Icicle Road to Eightmile Road/FR 7601
road.status: Gravel, steep and washboarded late-season; high-clearance recommended
road.driveNote: From Leavenworth: Icicle Road ~8.5 mi, left on Eightmile Road (FR 7600), then FR 7601 ~4 mi to the Stuart Lake Trailhead; parking is very limited, carpooling recommended
road.seasonalGate: FR 7601 closes to vehicles every winter to protect the roadbed; Icicle Road is plowed only to the Eightmile Road junction in winter

climate.fall: Shorter daylight, first snow possible, glacier more icy/crevassed.
climate.spring: Snow-covered approach trail and glacier; avalanche hazard on the moraine/glacier slopes.
climate.summer: Prime climbing season — generally dry, with afternoon thunderstorm potential.
climate.winter: Heavy snowpack; access road gated, approach requires skis/snowshoes from the winter closure point.
climate.typical: Pacific weather systems bring heavy winter snowfall to the Stuart Range with typically dry, clear summers under Pacific high pressure.

emergency.nearestHospital: Cascade Medical Center, Leavenworth (24/7 ED, ~20 mi from trailhead); Central Washington Hospital, Wenatchee, for higher-level trauma (~30 mi)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, while seasonal snow still covers the Colchuck Glacier to the col and before it melts to hard bare ice

July.reason: Continuous consolidated snow up the glacier to the col takes crampons well, and the Class 2-3 ridge above is mostly melted out.

June.reason: Snow still fills the glacier gully to the col, often the easiest going; carry axe and crampons and start early before wet slides on warm afternoons.

August.reason: Snow on the glacier thins and gets suncupped; patches of hard ice near the col become more likely late in the month, so crampons are essential.

October.reason: Fresh snow over bare glacier ice, short days and freezing temperatures make the glacier and col treacherous; the access road can close with the first heavy snow.

September.reason: Seasonal snow is often gone, leaving bare glacier ice at the 40-degree section below the col where crampons bite poorly and a slip is hard to stop.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR-7601 off Icicle Creek Road, ~3,400 ft), via the Colchuck Lake Trail

deleted_rows.corrections: The given name "East Ridge (Non-Technical)" does not match how any primary source names this route. Mountain Project lists it as "Colchuck Glacier"; SummitPost calls it the "East Route" (attributed to Fred Beckey) or "Colchuck Glacier Route." It is the peak's original 1948 first-ascent line and standard non-technical route — same physical route as implied by the given name — so it is kept under the given routeId with the corrected, source-backed name.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier to the col, then the ridge west to the summit
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at 3,400 ft, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about two and a half miles to the signed junction, fork left and switchback up to Colchuck Lake at about 5,570 ft — roughly four miles and 2,200 ft.

Follow the boot path round the lake and across the boulder field at its south end into the basin, then climb the Colchuck Glacier toward the col between Colchuck Peak and Dragontail. Keep climber's right on the glacier to reduce exposure to rockfall coming off Dragontail's north face.

From the col the route is the ridge running west to Colchuck's summit — Class 2-3, hands needed in places, no protection, generally solid granite with good friction.

Navigate from the glacier and the col rather than from a compass bearing off the lake: the peak lies south-west of Colchuck Lake and the col lies south-east of the summit.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep as a scramble; earlier the glacier is a snow climb and wants an axe and crampons
hazards: Rockfall onto the Colchuck Glacier from Dragontail's north face — stay climber's right
Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the glacier
Exposure on the ridge crest despite the easy grade
Wandering off the crest onto steeper flanking ground in poor visibility
Afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed ridge with no shelter
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The col is the base, and you know you are on it because the ground falls away behind you. Walking up the Colchuck Glacier you are in a closed basin; at the col the far side opens and drops south into the Ingalls Creek drainage. That change from enclosed to open is the arrival, and it happens whether or not you can see anything.

Then turn right. From the col, Colchuck Peak is west and Dragontail is east. The two peaks share this col, so a party that gains it in cloud and turns the wrong way is climbing a different mountain on a different route — and Dragontail's side of the col is not Class 2-3.

The hands test: this ridge is Class 2-3. You will use your hands in places, and you should never need protection or a rope. If you find yourself on ground where you want gear, you have left the crest onto the north or south flank, and the correct answer is to come back to the crest rather than to press on.

Confirmation underfoot: the granite here is solid with good friction, unlike the loose scree of the glacier basin below. Rambling on loose rubble means you are still below the ridge proper.

A warning worth carrying: this is also the standard descent for the harder routes on the peak's north side, so parties will be coming down it. Meeting people descending is not evidence you are on the wrong line — it is evidence you are on the right one.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

deleted_rows.name: Southeast Buttress
hazards: Overall route length can force a late, headlamp-assisted return, especially outside peak summer daylight.
deleted_rows.overview: A long, moderate alpine rock route up the buttress on the southeast side of Cutthroat Peak, notable for its overall length and remote basin approach rather than technical difficulty.
deleted_rows.beta: Grade III. Short approach from highway. Rock improves significantly higher on ridge. Fair granite in approach, improves on ridge. Moderate exposure. A long alpine day from the SR 20 pullout west of Washington Pass. Uncrowded route.

The climbers' track leaves the east end of the pullout. SR-20 over Washington Pass is closed in winter, typically from late fall until spring.

waypoints.name: Cutthroat Peak
waypoints.directions: Follow the cairned track from the east end of the pullout down through timber, cross State Creek, and climb the open slopes on the east side of the southeast-draining stream into the basin south of the peak. At the headwall, start up the right-hand of the twin gullies and traverse into the left-hand one to reach the notch at the base of the buttress, then climb near the buttress crest to the summit.

timing.recommendedStart: Early — the route's length rewards an early alpine start.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A light rack weighted toward larger protection (1-2 inch cams) is recommended; the route is not sustained enough to require a full double rack of small gear.
what_to_bring: extra water — long, sun-exposed approach and route
pro_tips: Move efficiently — the route's length, not its technical difficulty, is the main challenge.
Start in the right-hand approach gully and traverse into the left gully before the notch, per the standard beta.
watch_out: Moderate technical scrambling on good rock (southeast facing)
Exposed sections with 40-50 foot drops to either side
Route-finding moderately complex in upper sections

deleted_rows.approach:
Drop to the State Creek crossing as for the South Buttress: the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, then the cairned track from its east end down through timber to the creek.

From the creek, climb the open slopes on the east side of the southeast-draining stream, which brings you into the basin immediately south of the peak. At the headwall, look for twin gullies running up to a notch — that notch is the base of the Southeast Buttress. Start up the right-hand gully and traverse into the left-hand one before you reach the notch; taking them in the other order is the common mistake here.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Two options: reverse the Southeast Buttress with a mix of rappels and downclimbing, or descend via the West Ridge, which reportedly has looser rock and a higher potential for rockfall than the ascent line.
deleted_rows.bail: The twin-gully approach system below the notch and the large traversing ledge mid-route offer natural downclimb/retreat options in the lower two-thirds of the route.
deleted_rows.itinerary: A long day given the route's overall length — efficient movement is important to avoid a headlamp-lit return or an unplanned bivy, particularly later in the season as days shorten.

approach_variants.name: State Creek to the basin south of the peak, then the twin gullies
approach_variants.notes:
From the highway, drop to the State Creek crossing as for the South Buttress — the long pullout on the north side of SR-20 about a mile and a half west of Washington Pass, cairned track from its east end down through timber to the creek.

From the creek, climb the open slopes on the east side of the southeast-draining stream, which takes you into the basin immediately south of Cutthroat Peak. Reports put roughly an hour and a half to the foot of the gully system.

Continue up to the basin headwall.

State Creek crossing in high water

approach_variants.baseFinding: At the headwall look for twin gullies running up to a notch — that notch is the base of the Southeast Buttress and it is the target. The sequence that matters: start up the right-hand gully, and traverse across into the left-hand gully before you reach the notch. Getting that order backwards is the classic error, because from the basin the left gully looks like the direct line. Scramble the lower part of the gully, then rope up and pitch out the upper section to the notch. Above the notch the ground eases to scrambling before a short steep face, and from there you stay near the buttress crest.

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground to Washington Pass, on SR 20 along Early Winters Creek six or seven miles east of the pass, just past the turn for the Cutthroat Creek road. Because nothing here can be booked, arriving Friday evening in July or August is a gamble and the fallback is dispersed camping on a spur road. The season runs roughly May or June through September or October, entirely dependent on when the highway opens and when snow returns.
bivy.water: No drinking water at Lone Fir. Early Winters Creek runs through the campground and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: No reservations and no permit — first-come, first-served with a nightly fee. A Northwest Forest Pass is not needed to camp, only to park at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, tents and small RVs

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground, with Early Winters nearby
bivy.notes: Klipchuck sits about a quarter mile off SR 20 in fir and pine down-valley toward Mazama, low enough to be warm and dry when the passes are still wet. Early Winters Campground is further east, smaller at around a dozen tent sites, split by the highway near the Methow River, and fills quickly. Both are a longer drive to the trailhead than Lone Fir, which is the tradeoff for a better chance of finding a site on a busy weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water spigots in season; vault toilets. Water is turned off at the end of the season while the sites stay usable.
bivy.permit: First-come, first-served, nightly fee, no reservation and no permit required.
bivy.capacity: 46 sites, the largest campground on this stretch of highway

bivy.name: Cutthroat basin climbers' bivy, south side
bivy.notes: Serves every route reached through the basin south of the peak: the South and Complete South Buttress, the Southeast Buttress, the East Face lines over the rib, and the North Ridge by its usual approach, which bears right out of the same basin toward the North Ridge Notch. The way in starts from the long pullout on the north side of SR 20 about 1.5 miles west of Washington Pass, not from the Cutthroat Lake trail on the east side of the pass: a cairned track leaves the pullout's east end, drops through timber to cross State Creek, and climbs meadows into the bowl, roughly two hours with a pack. Parties camp here to take a long route in a single push rather than commit to a headlamp descent. Ground is a mix of heather bench and talus and the pads are small, so a large party will be split up. The meadows are thin and the basin sees enough traffic to show it.
bivy.water: A snow-fed stream runs through the basin and usually carries water through the climbing season, but it thins as the snow patches under the peak melt out, which is why State Creek, low on the approach, is the last water to count on. Fill there, and carry enough for a dry night late in a hot summer.
bivy.permit: None. Dispersed camping on national forest land needs no permit, no reservation and no quota — the opposite of the North Cascades park zones a few miles west.
bivy.capacity: Several scattered one- and two-tent pads in the meadows and among the boulders; no established camp, so parties spread out

Rockfall is a recurring, ranger-documented hazard on Dragontail Peak, particularly during heat waves -- climbers report rockfall on both sides of the standard snowfield route above Aasgard Pass (climber-right low, climber-left higher up), so route-finding choice matters as much as timing
deleted_rows.overview: Hidden Couloir is the entry gully of Dragontail's north-face ice and mixed complex — it is the first of the three couloirs linked by the popular Triple Couloirs route. It starts around 6,400 ft directly above the south end of Colchuck Lake and, true to its name, is hidden from view from the lake itself. The couloir climbs roughly 800 vertical feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice before joining broader terrain higher on the face; some parties climb just this lower section as a shorter half-day objective rather than continuing through the Runnels and upper couloirs to the true summit.
deleted_rows.beta: Named for being out of view from Colchuck Lake, this couloir starts at roughly 6,400 ft directly above the lake's south end and trends south for about 800 vertical feet at roughly 45°, typically holding good neve snow into mid-summer. Climbed alone, most parties top out at the steep rock band (the top of the Runnels crux) rather than continuing into the second and third couloirs.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Turn around before daytime warming loosens the snowpack or triggers rockfall from the band above; this is a short enough objective that there is little reason to push into deteriorating conditions.
deleted_rows.rappels: Rappel or downclimb on descent depending on conditions
deleted_rows.permit: Enchantment permit area: overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need the free self-issued day-use permit at the trailhead.

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, counter-clockwise to the north face talus
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at 3,400 ft, Stuart Lake Trail then Colchuck Lake Trail about four miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft.

From the lake go counter-clockwise around to the south side, then head uphill on talus and snow toward the base of Dragontail's north face, aiming a little east of the face's lowest point. The base of the couloir sits at roughly 6,400 ft.

hazards: Overhead rock and icefall on the apron below the north face
