approach_variants.baseFinding:
The name is the base-finding instruction, and it is the most useful fact about this route: the first couloir of the Triple Couloirs system is called the Hidden Couloir precisely because you cannot see it from Colchuck Lake.

So the test runs backwards from the usual one. If you have picked out an obvious couloir line from lake level and walked at it, you are not looking at the Hidden Couloir — you are looking at something else on the face. It only opens up once you are close under the wall.

What you are aiming for from the talus is the prominent snow finger at the foot of the north face, a little east of the face's lowest point, at about 6,400 ft. The first couloir gives roughly 800 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice — sustained but not technical. The hard parts of the wider route are the transitions between couloirs, not the couloirs themselves, so easy climbing at the bottom is expected and is not a sign you are off line.

If you have ended up at the very lowest point of the wall rather than east of it, you are at the Gerber-Sink start, a different route.

bivy.name: Colchuck Lake designated campsites
bivy.notes: This is the working basecamp for Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete and Colchuck Balanced Rock, and it cuts an hour or more off the pre-dawn walk-in. Access is the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of FR 7601, off Icicle Creek Road out of Leavenworth; the last few miles are rough dirt, washboarded by late summer, and the road is gated through winter and into spring. Parking is small for the demand, so a party arriving the night before should expect to be squeezed. Campfires are banned here, so plan on stoves only.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus inlet streams on the south shore through most of the season. Treat it; the shoreline is heavily used.
bivy.permit: Colchuck Lake zone of the Enchantment Permit Area. An overnight permit is required May 15–Oct 31 and comes either from the advance lottery on recreation.gov (applications open in February, success rates in the single digits) or the daily lottery run through the recreation.gov app inside a geofence around the Wenatchee River Ranger Station in Leavenworth. Day climbing needs no overnight permit, only the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness day slip at the trailhead and a parking pass.
bivy.capacity: Roughly a dozen scattered hardened sites around the east and north shores and up the west side; each permit covers one party, and group size in this zone is capped at 8

bivy.name: Bridge Creek and Eightmile campgrounds, Icicle Creek Road
bivy.notes: Given how unlikely a Colchuck or Core permit is on any given weekend, most parties on Backbone Ridge, Serpentine Arete or Colchuck Balanced Rock end up sleeping down on Icicle Creek Road and starting for the trailhead in the small hours. Both campgrounds sit on the drive in, before the FR 7601 turnoff, so the extra driving in the morning is only a few miles of dirt. Expect a very long day from here — car to base of route commonly runs three to four hours, and finishing after dark is normal.
bivy.water: Icicle Creek runs alongside both; check current potable-water status at the site, as it varies by year and season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all — both are ordinary Forest Service campgrounds outside the Enchantment Permit Area, paid per night. This is what a party climbs from when it has no zone permit and is doing the route car-to-car, which is entirely legal: day use in the permit area needs only the free self-issue wilderness slip at the trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Bridge Creek is small and rustic; Eightmile is much larger with roughly forty family sites. Both take a mix of reservations and first-come nights depending on the season.

bivy.name: Talus and boulder bivies below Dragontail's north side
bivy.notes: Parties wanting to shorten the approach to Backbone Ridge or Serpentine Arete sometimes move above the lake into the boulders and moraine beneath the north face rather than staying at the shoreline camps. It buys perhaps half an hour and a clearer look at the route, at the cost of a colder, windier and rockier night. Whether that is worth it is genuinely contested: the time saved is small against a full day on either route, and the ground is poor. Because these are informal spots, camp on bare rock or gravel and leave no trace of a platform.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and pools early in the season; unreliable by late summer once the snowfields shrink, so many parties carry water up from the lake
bivy.permit: Still inside the Colchuck Lake zone, so an overnight permit is required exactly as it is at the lake — sleeping on rock rather than in a designated site does not exempt a party. The zone boundary with the Core Enchantment zone lies up toward Aasgard Pass, and a Core permit is valid in every zone, so a party unsure which side of the line it will sleep on is safest holding Core.
bivy.capacity: Two to four people on flat granite blocks and sand patches; nothing established, and the good spots are scattered rather than clustered

deleted_rows.name: Multi-Summit Scramble
deleted_rows.fa: Jim Crooks and Judson Nelson, August 27, 1940 (a fixed ring piton attributed to this ascent remains in #2 Gully)
gear: helmet (mandatory — rockfall is common in the gully systems)

rope and full rack mandatory on every established line, not optional — a single rack to 2" suffices for the easiest documented route (Southwest Ledges, 5.3), but the classic South Route needs a full trad rack, extra slings/cordage for tat-covered rap anchors, and two 60m ropes
sturdy brush-resistant clothing (extensive slide alder and devil's club bushwhacking low on approach)
headlamp — car-to-car days of 12–15+ hours are common and many parties finish in the dark
hazards: extremely loose, rotten rock throughout the gullies and slabs — Fred Beckey called the standard South Route a 'hazardous enigma'
roped Class 4 to low-5th-class climbing and rappels on every documented line (South Route, Southwest Ledges 5.3, Infinite Bliss 5.10c); this is not scrambling terrain despite the local nickname
brutal bushwhack low on the approach through slide alder, devil's club, and downed timber
complex routefinding among the massif's five summits and connecting notches (e.g. the 'Y Notch')
afternoon thunderstorms, common over the Cascade crest in July–August
long days — trip reports document 12–15+ hour car-to-car pushes and frequent forced bivouacs (Glade Saddle is a known 2-person bivy site)
deleted_rows.overview: Garfield Mountain is a rugged granodiorite massif of five named summits (Main/East Peak 5,519 ft, West Peak 4,896 ft, North Peak 5,101 ft, plus the Leaning Spire) rising more than 4,400 ft above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River in barely a mile — one of the steepest, most relief-dense peaks in the western Cascades. Despite a local reputation as a 'scramble,' every summit actually requires roped technical climbing: documented lines range from the 5.3 Southwest Ledges to the 23-pitch 5.10c sport route Infinite Bliss on the West Peak's south face.
deleted_rows.beta: From the Taylor River trailhead, a cross-country line follows a dry creek bed, then a brushy, flagged climbers' path through the 'dirt gully,' a soloable 2-pitch slab, a traverse under a rock outcrop, the 'Razorback,' 'Glade Saddle' (a tight 2-person bivy site), a 'wooded ramp,' the roped 'Key Ledge Traverse,' the 'Y Notch' (head of 'The Great Canyon'), and finally '#2 Gully' — loose rock on one side, polished/mossy on the other — which gains the upper mountain via a mix of simul-climbing and belayed pitches (Beckey's 'Chimney Variation' avoids a wet chimney via two easy 5th-class leads). Above the gully, 2nd/3rd-class terrain leads to the true summit at 5,519 ft. Route-finding among several similar-looking gullies is the route's signature difficulty, and the published description is famously terse.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Given that 12–15+ hour car-to-car days are common, set a firm early-to-mid-afternoon turnaround time to ensure you're off the technical terrain and rappels before dark.
deleted_rows.rock_grade: Class 4 scrambling on the standard line; a short 5.4 pitch on Beckey's optional 'Chimney Variation'
deleted_rows.rappels: About 8 rappels on descent (two single-rope and six double-rope, two 60m ropes) off bolted anchors, trees, and chockstones through the slab and #2 Gully
deleted_rows.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park at the Middle Fork-area pullout/trailhead ($5 day-use or $30 annual; digital Scan & Pay via the Recreation.gov app accepted), plus a free self-issue wilderness permit at the trailhead once inside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary (per Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest pass/permit pages).
deleted_rows.descent: There is no walk-off. The classic South Route requires about eight rappels, six of them double-rope (bolted and tree anchors; two 60m ropes recommended), back down through the gully system, followed by the same brushy, loose approach in reverse.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Road (FR-56) Pullout at Taylor River Crossing
waypoints.note: Small pullout where FR-56 crosses the Taylor River; parties leave the road here and bushwhack cross-country toward Garfield's south flank — no maintained trail beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 Exit 34 at North Bend, drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR-56) east - paved at first, then good gravel - staying on FR-56 past the Taylor River Road (FR-5620) junction to a wide gravel wash and old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road, at roughly 1,150 to 1,200 feet. There is no maintained, numbered Forest Service trail from this pullout; the route beyond it is an unmaintained climbers' boot path marked only intermittently with cairns and pink flagging tape.

waypoints.name: Dirt Gully Creek Crossing
waypoints.note: Creek bed at the base of the dirt gully is the last reliable, 'for-sure' water on the route — top off here before the climbing begins.

waypoints.name: Dirt Gully
waypoints.note: About 400 vertical feet of loose rock, dirt, and scrub brush above the creek; friable and prone to rockfall, especially when wet.

waypoints.name: Razorback / Tiny Notch
waypoints.note: Beckey's route description is notoriously vague here; parties commonly go astray choosing between the Razorback and Tiny Notch, adding significant route-finding time.

waypoints.name: Glade Saddle Bivy
waypoints.note: Small bivy site for two tucked into a saddle; most parties reach it roughly three hours in and treat it as the last comfortable rest stop before the upper gullies.

waypoints.name: Y Notch
waypoints.note: Confluence of the #1 and #2 Gullies at the head of the Great Canyon; stay right into the #2 Gully to follow the standard South Route line.

waypoints.name: #2 Gully Rockfall Zone
waypoints.note: A nightmarish mix of impossibly loose rock on one side and polished, mossy rock on the other; a climber here was struck by a rolling 500-lb boulder, so helmets and staggered spacing are essential.

waypoints.name: Garfield Mountain Summit
waypoints.note: True summit register has historically logged only a handful of ascents per decade; descend via a single-rope rappel to the col and about four double-rope rappels down the #2 Gully on a mix of aging bolts, chockstones, and slung trees (webbing dated as old as 1998) — carry two 60m ropes.

sectionBreakdown.note: This is a single very long day, not an overnight trip — but treat it like an alpine climb: an early (pre-dawn) start is mandatory because the round trip commonly runs 12-14+ hours …

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A light rack: small-to-medium cams/nuts, a handful of runners, and extra webbing/cord to supplement aging rappel-station slings. Two 60m ropes (thin doubles work well) are needed for the double-rope rappels through #2 Gully.
pro_tips: Carry two 60m ropes for the South Route — single-rope rappels won't reach between stations.
The brush low on the approach is often worse than the climbing above it; long sleeves/pants and a helmet are worth wearing even on the hike in.
Start at first light — parties describe 12–15+ hour car-to-car days.
For a non-technical outing on this massif, hike the maintained Garfield Ledges viewpoint trail or try the neighboring Treen Peak scramble instead.
watch_out: Loose, rotten rock in the gully systems, worsened if other parties are climbing above you
No reliable walk-off descent — committing to the standard route means committing to roped rappels to get down
Water sources are limited and seasonal (dry creek beds); carry what you'll need
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Single rack to 2" plus slings suffices for the easiest documented line (Southwest Ledges, 5.3); the classic South Route wants a fuller trad rack, extra webbing/cordage for weathered rap anchors, and two 60m ropes for the six double-rope rappels on descent.
deleted_rows.best_season: July–August typically most reliable; the route can be dry as early as June but conditions firm up through midsummer, and the window closes with the first autumn rain/snow
deleted_rows.approach: From I-90 Exit 34 (North Bend), drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR-56) east — paved at first, then good gravel — staying on FR-56 past the Taylor River Road (FR-5620) junction to a wide gravel wash / old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road near the base of the mountain (trailhead elevation roughly 1,150-1,200 ft). There is no maintained, numbered Forest Service trail here — this is an unmaintained climbers' boot path marked intermittently with cairns and pink flagging tape, not a hiking trail. From the wash, follow the dry creekbed/streambed uphill for roughly a mile; a boot path exits climber's-left into second-growth forest with light brush before the creek narrows. Multiple boot-path branches exist low down — avoid the flat, early traverse that cuts to the slab too low, and instead take the higher, up-and-down traverse. Around 2,200 ft the path enters a loose dirt-and-scree gully mixed with vegetation (unpleasant, roughly 400 ft of gain), then exits climber's-left onto a wooded ridge for another 400 ft of steep but relatively brush-free hiking. At about 2,900 ft you reach the base of the first major slab; parties solo (or rope up, depending on comfort) two low-5th-class pitches following intersecting dikes, then continue up dirt/heather above the slab's upper-left edge. Above the slab, route-finding gets serious: intermittent boot path, cairns, and flagging lead through a 'tiny notch,' a knife-edge 'razorback,' and a flat bivy site known as the 'glade saddle' where many parties break the day with a bivouac. A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20-ft scramble step follows, then a rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse leading to the 'Y Notch,' where the route joins the gully system locally called '#2 Gully' — loose rock on one side, polished/mossy rock on the other — for the final roughly 600 ft of short technical pitches to the summit ridge and high point (5,519 ft). Total gain is about 4,400 ft over roughly 1.5 miles one-way from the wash; budget 5-7+ hours up in good conditions. There is no reliable water past the initial creek near the trailhead, so fill up early, and only attempt this route bone dry — the slabs and dirt gullies become treacherous when wet.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Nearly every party descends the same South Route line rather than walking off, and this is where Garfield earns its reputation as a serious undertaking — budget as much time for the descent as the climb, since many parties top out with only a few hours of daylight left. From the summit, reverse the ridge with a single-rope rappel down to the col, then work back down through the '#2 Gully' system with a sustained series of rappels: parties describe roughly four double-rope (doubled-strand) rappels through the gully's mixed loose/polished rock, a single-rope rappel off the steep step on the wooded ramp, and two more double-rope rappels getting off the base of the slab (~2,900 ft) — about 8 rappels total on a typical South Route descent. Treat that as a working estimate rather than an exact count: some parties reference numbered rap stations well into the teens/twenties on the broader Garfield massif's fixed rap line, and how many you actually do depends on rope length and how many stations you can combine. Anchors are mixed — some slab sections have bolted chain anchors and fixed rap rings, but much of the gully relies on natural anchors (slung trees, horns, chockstones), so carry extra webbing/cord and rap rings and inspect every anchor before weighting it. Two 60m ropes are the standard recommendation for this descent; parties have combined stations using 2x70m ropes, but a single 60m (or shorter) rope will leave you short on several drops and force exposed down-scrambling to reach the next anchor. Below the slab, downclimb/scramble the wooded ridge and dirt gully back into forest, then descend the creekbed/wash to the trailhead. Loose rock is a hazard throughout, especially in the dirt gully and on the west side of #2 Gully — keep helmets on for the entire descent and watch for rockfall onto parties below. Route-finding in the dark is a real risk since flagging and cairns are easy to lose — benightment low on the mountain is common enough that a GPS track of your ascent line and a reliable headlamp are strongly recommended.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat below the technical sections reverses the ascent gully/ridge, but once committed to the upper 5th-class terrain on the South Route, the safe bail is to rappel the route rather than attempt to downclimb the loose rock.

itinerary.cal: Best done June-August once winter snow/ice has cleared the slabs; pick a long-daylight date given the 12-14+ hour commitment.

days.note: This is a single very long day, not an overnight trip — but treat it like an alpine climb: an early (pre-dawn) start is mandatory because the round trip commonly runs 12-14+ hours car to car. From the trailhead a short, steep ~45-minute approach through forest and a dry creek bed gains the base of the route; from there loose dirt gullies, a slab traverse on intersecting dikes, and the exposed 'key ledge traverse' lead into the crux #2 Gully, a mix of simul-climbed and belayed 4th/low-5th-class pitches on rock that is loose on one side and polished/mossy on the other. Above the gully, easier slabs and steep heather lead to the Main Peak summit at 5,519 ft; parties chasing the multi-summit link-up continue across to the adjoining Garfield summits before reversing. There is no walk-off: descent is via about eight rappels (six of them double-rope) off bolted anchors and tree slings back through the gully system, with loose downclimbing between stations, so budget as much time for the descent as the ascent.
days.title: Car-to-car: South Route scramble, multi-summit

schedule.detail: Near-solstice alpine start; Published descriptions call 12 hours an absolute minimum car-to-car.

schedule.label: Reach base of route
schedule.detail: Steep forest approach up a dry creek bed gains the start of the technical ground.

schedule.label: Enter #2 Gully
schedule.detail: Key ledge traverse leads into the crux gully; loose rock on one side, polished/mossy rock on the other.

schedule.label: Summit Main Peak (5,519 ft)
schedule.detail: ~8 hours of climbing from the car is typical; continue to adjoining summits if doing the multi-summit link-up.

schedule.label: Begin descent

schedule.label: Back at trailhead
schedule.detail: Total elapsed time commonly exceeds 12-14 hours; parties who fall behind schedule sometimes take an impromptu bivy on route rather than rappel in the dark.

days.objective: Summit Garfield's Main Peak (and adjoining summits) via the South Route, then reverse via about 8 rappels

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day car-to-car (roughly 13 hours, 4,400 ft gain) done during the longest daylight of summer with a pre-dawn start — not an overnight trip, but slower parties sometimes end up bivying on route rather than descending after dark.

access.fees: $5/day or $30/year Northwest Forest Pass
access.notes: Climbable roughly June–October; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.
access.rules: Standard Alpine Lakes Wilderness regulations apply: no mechanized or wheeled equipment, group size capped at 12 people/stock combined, self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead box
access.permit: Northwest Forest Pass ($5 day-use or $30 annual) or an America the Beautiful interagency pass is required to park at Middle Fork-area trailheads/pullouts (digital Scan & Pay via the Recreation.gov app is accepted). A free, self-issue wilderness permit is also required at the trailhead once inside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary.
access.closures: FR-56 has a history of washouts and slope failures near river bends despite the 2017 repaving; it is closed to vehicles beyond the Dingford Creek Trailhead and can be high-clearance-only in sections — check current Mount Baker-Snoqualmie NF alerts before driving
access.landManager: Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District — Alpine Lakes Wilderness
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Snoqualmie Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass ($30/yr) or America the Beautiful pass, or a $5/day pass at developed trailheads.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk before an overnight in the wilderness. Middle Fork Campground is a fee campground reserved separately.

road.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (Forest Road 56)
road.status: Paved to the Middle Fork Trailhead following a 2017 repaving, but with recurring washouts and slope failures near river bends; beyond the Middle Fork Trailhead the road narrows and is recommended for high-clearance vehicles only, and it is gated/closed to vehicles at Dingford Creek Trailhead
road.driveNote: About 11.8 miles from I-90 Exit 34 to the Middle Fork Trailhead; check Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest road alerts before driving, as this road has a history of closures

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate: wet winters with heavy, avalanche-prone snowfall and drier summers. Because the rock is dangerously loose when wet, this is a bone-dry-conditions-only objective with a reliable window of roughly June through September (July–August most consistent); afternoon thunderstorms can build over the Cascade crest in summer.

emergency.rangerStation: Snoqualmie Ranger District, 902 SE North Bend Way Bldg 1, North Bend, WA 98045, (425) 888-1421 (limited hours — call ahead)
emergency.nearestHospital: Snoqualmie Valley Hospital, 9801 Frontier Ave SE, Snoqualmie, WA — a small critical-access/Level 5 trauma facility; serious trauma cases are typically transferred to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 (King County Sheriff / SAR dispatch)

crowds.peakTraffic: Rarely climbed; the lower Garfield Ledges viewpoint trail near the same trailhead draws weekend day-hiker crowds (it's a popular sub-1.5-hour drive from Seattle), but that traffic does not translate to the actual multi-summit scramble, which the notorious brushy approach keeps quiet even on good-weather weekends
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Low - likely well under 20 parties per season; no dedicated trip-report volume was found specifically for the summit scramble

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, sustained off-trail fitness - the approach is a long, slow, physically taxing bushwhack through dense brush and steep, trail-less terrain, not a groomed-trail hike
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Keep it light (roughly 15-20 lb day pack); a heavy pack makes brush-fighting and steep terrain much harder

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long and slow - plan a full day; the brushy, steep, trail-less approach typically takes significantly longer than distance/elevation alone would suggest
requiredSkills: off-trail routefinding among multiple summits
tolerance and technique for sustained bushwhacking through dense vegetation
comfort leading and rappelling on loose, exposed Class 4 to low-5th-class rock
map/compass or GPS navigation skill, since the route is sparsely documented
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine climber comfortable leading loose Class 4 rock and running a long rappel descent; the moderate technical grade is deceptive because the approach demands as much or more from a partner as the climbing does

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through October, with the driest and least brushy conditions typically in August-September

July.reason: Season is opening up, but brush is often still wet and dense from spring, and lingering snow patches are possible higher up early in the month

August.reason: Best window - driest brush conditions and most stable weather of the season, though afternoon thunderstorms are common

October.reason: Cooling temperatures and increasing rain/early-season snow risk at elevation; wet brush becomes slick again and days are shorter

September.reason: Continued dry, stable conditions with brush somewhat less lush; a strong alternative to August

weather.typical: West-slope Cascades convective weather during the climbing season - generally drier through summer but always capable of turning wet given the marine-influenced, heavily vegetated setting
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms common in summer, especially August

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Serious technical exposure - roped Class 4 to low-5th-class terrain with loose rock where a slip could cause a serious fall/injury; the more consequential real-world hazard is getting lost or benighted among the multiple summits in dense brush with limited visibility, per the existing routefinding-error and loose-rock watch-outs

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; not a standard winter/spring objective

gaps: No source describes a genuine Class 3 walk-up line to any Garfield summit — every documented route (South Route, Southwest Ledges 5.3, Infinite Bliss 5.10c) requires roped technical climbing; this entry's 'scramble' framing and grade may warrant reclassification (discipline/grade_system/grade_num) beyond what this audit's field set could correct
No confirmed GPS trailhead or route waypoints
Current real-time status of FR-56 washouts/closures not independently verified beyond general reports — check MBS NF alerts before a trip

approach_logistics.trailhead: FR-56 pullout below Garfield Mountain (Middle Fork Snoqualmie)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the wide gravel-wash pullout on FR-56 past the Taylor River junction (~1,150 ft)

deleted_rows.rope_note: Garfield is a multi-summit massif; every summit, the Main Peak included, needs roped Class 4 to low-5th-class climbing, and the descent is a long series of rappels, so two 60m ropes are needed rather than a handline.
deleted_rows.corrections: Trip reports describe inter-summit ridge travel as loose/'pretty horrible' and note other peaks on the massif require technical climbing, but none described roping up for the standard Class 3 multi-summit scramble itself.
rack: Light trad rack to 2" (sufficient for easiest line, Southwest Ledges 5.3)
Fuller trad rack for the classic South Route
Extra slings/cordage for tat-covered rappel anchors

approach_variants.name: Gravel wash pullout on FR 56, dry creekbed and dirt gully
approach_variants.notes:
Distance is one-way horizontal; almost all of the effort is vertical. From I-90 Exit 34 at North Bend, drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road (FR 56) east — paved, then good gravel — staying on FR 56 past the Taylor River Road (FR 5620) junction, about 2.6 miles further, to a wide gravel wash and old borrow-pit pullout on the north side of the road at roughly 1,150-1,200 ft.

There is no maintained or numbered Forest Service trail here. This is an unmaintained climbers' boot path with intermittent cairns and pink flagging.

From the wash, follow the dry creekbed uphill for roughly a mile. A boot path exits climber's left into second-growth forest with light brush before the creek narrows. Several boot-path branches exist low down: avoid the flat, early traverse that cuts across to the slab too low, and take the higher up-and-down traverse instead.

At about 2,200 ft the path enters a loose dirt-and-scree gully mixed with vegetation — unpleasant, roughly 400 ft of gain — then exits climber's left onto a wooded ridge for another 400 ft of steep but relatively brush-free ground. There is no reliable water past the creek near the trailhead.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, and only in bone-dry conditions
hazards: No water above the trailhead creek
About 40-degree loose duff above the slab; huckleberry stems are the handholds
Slabs and dirt gullies become treacherous when even slightly wet
Braided boot paths low down leading to the slab at the wrong height
Loose and mossy rock in #2 Gully
Serious route-finding above the slab — intermittent path, cairns and flagging only
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the climbing is the first major slab at about 2,900 ft, roughly an hour and 1,700 ft above the car. It is unmistakable by contrast: it is the first clean rock of the day after nothing but duff, dirt and scree. Two low-fifth pitches follow intersecting dikes up it; parties either solo them or rope up.

The negative marker is the dirt gully. If you have arrived at slab without first grovelling through the loose dirt-and-scree gully at about 2,200 ft, you took the low flat traverse and you are on the slab too far along — traverse up and left to regain the line. Above the slab the landmarks come in a fixed order and that order is how you confirm you are still on it: dirt and heather above the slab's upper-left edge, a tiny notch, a knife-edge razorback, and then a flat bivy clearing known as the glade saddle. A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20 ft scramble step follows, then a rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse leading to the Y Notch, where the line joins the gully locally called #2 Gully — loose rock on one side, polished mossy rock on the other — for the last 600 ft or so to the summit ridge at 5,519 ft.

climbing_route.label: First major slab (~2,900 ft)
climbing_route.notes: Two low-5th-class pitches following intersecting dikes; parties either solo them or rope up depending on comfort. Exit onto dirt and heather above the slab's upper-left edge. Attempt only bone dry — the slabs and dirt gullies are treacherous wet.

climbing_route.label: Tiny notch, razorback and glade saddle
climbing_route.notes: Route-finding turns serious above the slab: only an intermittent boot path, cairns and flagging lead through a small notch and a knife-edge 'razorback' to the flat 'glade saddle,' a bivy site where many parties split the day.

climbing_route.label: Wooded ramp and ledge traverse to the Y Notch
climbing_route.notes: A short wooded ramp with one sporty 20-ft scramble step, then the usual rope-up point at an exposed ledge traverse that leads into the Y Notch.

climbing_route.label: '#2 Gully' to the summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the Y Notch the route joins the gully system known locally as '#2 Gully' — loose rock on one side, polished and mossy rock on the other — for roughly the final 600 ft of short technical pitches to the summit ridge and the 5,519 ft high point.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Garfield Mountain improvised bivouac
bivy.notes: The honest answer for Garfield is that there is no camp, and inventing one would do a party more harm than saying so. It is a low mountain carrying enormous relief straight out of the valley floor, and every documented line begins with steep unmaintained bushwhacking and long rock gullies before any climbing starts. There are no trails, no signs and no established approach; you leave the road at a pull-out and go up. Ascents here are commonly described as needing either a bivouac or the very longest days of the year to finish in daylight, and the bivouacs that actually happen are improvised where a party runs out of light rather than chosen in advance. Plan for that rather than around it: carry a bivy kit on any attempt, expect to sleep on rock or in brush, and treat the multi-summit outing in particular as an opportunistic link-up rather than a route with a known camp on it. Substantial rappels separate some of the summits, so retreat is not always the quick option once committed. The one exception is the East Peak, whose ridge is gained from Green Ridge; a party going that way should use the Green Ridge Lake camp above instead of anything on this face. Season here is governed by dry rock and daylight rather than snow: the valley is open most of the year, but the brush stays wet late and June through September is when this goes.
bivy.water: Nothing reliable and nothing to plan around. The gullies run in spring and after rain and are dry by late summer, and there is no snow to melt on this mountain in season. Carry water for the whole push and know where the last certain source below you was.
bivy.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the mountain beyond the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit if your line crosses the boundary, plus a Northwest Forest Pass at whichever pull-out you start from. Note that sleeping at the car is not an option here: the pull-outs at the base of Garfield fall inside the lower-valley dispersed camping closure.
bivy.capacity: Nothing established, and no honest capacity figure to give. Parties sleep where the terrain offers a flat dry patch, a bench in a gully, a ledge system or a heather shoulder, usually one or two people at a time.

deleted_rows.name: East Peak Traverse
hazards: Steep (40-50°) snow slopes on the southwest face require ice axe and often crampon use into midsummer.
Off-trail route-finding across heather, snow, and loose rock between the saddle and summit is the primary hazard for underprepared parties.
deleted_rows.overview: A far more committing extension past the West Peak trail: leave the Goat Mountain Trail near its high point, drop into the saddle between the summits, then climb the East Peak's west ridge and southwest face on steep heather and snow to reach the mountain's true, higher summit.
deleted_rows.beta: From the ridge-crest viewpoint around 5,400-5,700 ft (reached via the same Goat Mountain Trail as the standard route), leave the trail and descend roughly 300 ft into the broad saddle between the West and East Peaks. From the saddle, ascend the East Peak's scalloped west ridge for about 400 ft before cutting right on a diagonal ascending traverse across the open southwest face (slope angles commonly 40-50 degrees, snow-covered into summer), gaining the southeast ridge, then a final short scramble of roughly 100 ft through often-snowy terrain to the summit (6,891 ft). This route sees far less traffic than the West Peak trail and requires real off-trail route-finding.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Because the off-trail traverse is exposed and route-finding intensive, set a firm turnaround time before leaving the maintained trail that leaves ample daylight margin to reverse the full traverse and descend the standard trail.
deleted_rows.comms: Cell coverage is unreliable to absent on the traverse and summit, similar to the rest of the mountain.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the ascent traverse back to the saddle and regain the Goat Mountain Trail, then descend the standard trail to the trailhead.
obj_haz: cornices/snow bridges in the saddle early season

waypoints.name: Goat Mountain Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From the Glacier Public Service Center, drive SR 542 (Mount Baker Highway) east 12.5 miles and turn left onto Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32). Follow it 2.3 miles to the Goat Mountain Trailhead at about 2,470 ft, with parking on both sides of the road. A Northwest Forest Pass or other valid recreation pass is required.

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn/early morning start to secure firm snow on the southwest face and allow a full daylight margin for this long, route-finding-intensive day

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Not a roped climb; carried as an unroped alpine scramble.
what_to_bring: ice axe and crampons for early/steep-snow conditions
map/compass or GPS track — no trail beyond the saddle
helmet for loose rock on the ridge/face
extra time margin — this is a long, full day
pro_tips: Climb this after the standard West Peak trail to scope the saddle and ridge line from a distance first.
Snow conditions on the SW face make or break the day — good consolidated step-kicking snow is far faster and safer than exposed dry heather.
watch_out: The southwest face traverse holds 40-50 degree snow that can be firm/icy in morning shade — an uncontrolled slip has serious consequences.
The scalloped west ridge has loose, blocky terrain requiring careful hand and foot placement.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: None placed — unroped scramble, though some parties carry a rope/harness for glissade backup or to protect a partner on the steepest snow.
deleted_rows.best_season: Best attempted late spring through summer when there is still enough consolidated snow for secure step-kicking on the southwest face, or mid/late summer once the face has mostly melted out to heather; conditions vary significantly year to year.
deleted_rows.approach: Same trailhead and initial trail as the South Ridge/Standard Scramble route: from Glacier, WA drive SR 542 east 12.5 mi to FR 32, then FR 32 to the Goat Mountain Trailhead (~2,470 ft). Follow Goat Mountain Trail #673 up the switchbacks and ridge to the viewpoint shoulder near 5,400-5,700 ft before leaving the maintained trail.
deleted_rows.descent_text: From the East Peak summit, downclimb the final scramble and re-cross the southwest face traverse back to the top of the west ridge, descend to the saddle, then regain roughly 300 ft back up to the Goat Mountain Trail viewpoint shoulder before following the maintained trail down to the trailhead. An ice axe and, in early season, step-kicking or crampons may be needed on the 40-50 degree slopes.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is via the same traverse used on ascent — there is no shorter alternative once past the saddle; turn back toward the saddle and trail if weather, snow conditions, or time run short.

pitch_detail.notes: Off-trail descent of ~300 ft from the ridge-crest viewpoint/trail into the broad saddle between West and East Peaks.
Ascend the scalloped west ridge roughly 400 ft from the saddle.
Diagonal ascending traverse across the open southwest face to the southeast ridge; ice axe/crampons recommended.
Final ~100 ft scramble through often snowy terrain to the East Peak summit (6,891 ft).

access.fees: $5 per vehicle per day at the trailhead
access.closures: FR 32 beyond the trailhead enters avalanche terrain and may be closed or impassable in winter/spring.
access.landManager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (USFS), Mt. Baker Wilderness
access.passRequired: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful interagency pass (Washington Discover Pass NOT accepted)

road.name: Hannegan Pass Road (Forest Road 32)
road.status: Open seasonally; paved for a short distance then gravel
road.driveNote: From Glacier, WA: SR 542 east 12.5 mi to FR 32, then FR 32 north 2.1-2.3 mi to the Goat Mountain Trailhead.
road.seasonalGate: Not gated at the Goat Mountain Trailhead itself, but FR 32 continues into avalanche terrain past the trailhead and can be snow-covered/impassable in winter and spring

climate.fall: Possible but increasingly cold/short days; verify current snow/ice conditions
climate.spring: Good step-kicking snow on the face but higher avalanche hazard on approach and traverse
climate.summer: Face increasingly melts to heather and loose rock by late summer; snow patches persist in shaded sections
climate.winter: Not a standard winter objective; effectively a mountaineering undertaking
climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate; the southwest face and saddle hold snow later into the season than the West Peak trail

emergency.notes: This route is off-trail and remote — cell coverage is unreliable; a satellite communicator is advisable given the route-finding and limited traffic.
emergency.rangerStation: Glacier Public Service Center, (360) 599-2714
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth St. Joseph Medical Center, 2901 Squalicum Pkwy, Bellingham, WA — (360) 734-5400 (Level II Trauma Center)
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Whatcom County Sheriff non-emergency: (360) 676-6911; 911 for emergencies

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to September, after the steep southwest face melts to heather and before fall snow returns to the saddle

May.reason: The trail above treeline is still snow-covered and the 40-50 degree southwest face is a loaded avalanche slope; few parties summit before the snow recedes.

July.reason: Snow on the trail melts quickly, while consolidated snow on the southwest face gives secure step-kicking with an axe; wildflowers peak in the meadows.

June.reason: Deep snow from the shoulder into the saddle; firm mornings allow step-kicking with axe and crampons, but afternoon slush on the face is hazardous.

August.reason: The face has mostly melted to heather and rock, so the diagonal traverse goes without crampons; carry water since snowmelt sources dry up.

October.reason: First snows and frozen heather on the steep southwest face make the traverse slick, and daylight is short for the off-trail descent from the saddle.

September.reason: Snow-free heather and rock on the face, fall color in the meadows and cooler temperatures for the long 3,200 ft climb to the shoulder.

approach_variants.name: Goat Mountain Trail #673 to the viewpoint shoulder, then around the south side of the West Peak
approach_variants.notes:
Same trailhead and the same first four miles as the standard scramble: from Glacier, SR-542 east 12.5 miles to FR-32, then FR-32 to the Goat Mountain Trailhead near 2,470 ft, and Goat Mountain Trail #673 up the switchbacks and ridge to the viewpoint shoulder around 5,400-5,700 ft.

The difference is what you do with the West Peak. This line leaves the maintained trail at the shoulder and traverses below the West Peak on its south side to gain the ridge running toward the East Peak, rather than going over the West Peak's corniced top.

It is the line that avoids the cornice problem, at the cost of a sidehill traverse on 40-50 degree slopes.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, but the traverse slopes hold snow and an axe is wanted early season
hazards: A sidehill traverse on 40-50 degree slopes, wanting an axe and sometimes crampons
Cornices on the West Peak above the traverse
A 300 ft regain on the return that is easy to walk past in cloud
No maintained tread from the viewpoint shoulder onward
No reliable water past the forest creek crossings (about the first 2.5 miles of trail)
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The traverse goes under the west peak, not over it, and that is the whole route-finding decision. From the viewpoint shoulder near 5,400-5,700 ft, leave the trail and traverse below the West Peak on its south side. If you are gaining height toward a summit ahead of you, you are on the standard scramble over the false summit; if you are holding height and sidehilling with the peak above your left shoulder, you are on this one.

The angle is the confirmation. The traverse slopes run 40-50 degrees. That is steep enough that an axe and, early season, step-kicking or crampons are wanted, and it is steep enough to feel wrong if you have wandered onto easier ground. Easy walking on this traverse means you have dropped too low into the basin.

Arrival: you have arrived at the climbing when the traverse delivers you onto the connecting ridge between the two peaks — ground with air on both sides, running east toward the higher summit. The scramble to the East Peak's top is the last short section above that ridge.

The 300 ft regain is the return test, worth knowing before you commit: coming back, you descend to the saddle and then have to regain roughly 300 ft to reach the Goat Mountain Trail viewpoint shoulder. If you are heading home and only ever going downhill, you have missed the shoulder and are descending an unmaintained slope.

Which summit: the east peak is the true and higher one, near 6,890 ft. The West Peak at about 6,600 ft is the false summit that the standard route walks over the top of.

deleted_rows.name: Southeast Face (Standard)
deleted_rows.fa: Unknown (the South Peak was first climbed May 30, 1947 by Fred Beckey and five companions via the Southwest Route)
hazards: notoriously loose, fractured Hozomeen chert — rockfall and breaking/pulling holds are the primary objective danger
routefinding on a complex face with multiple gullies, notches, and boulder bottlenecks
afternoon thunderstorms
sparse, unreliable protection due to friable rock — bring a range of small-to-medium gear and don't count on solid placements
long, remote approach with heavy bushwhacking (devil's club, windfall) and stream/boulder-field crossings
water sources above roughly 5,000-6,800 ft often dry up by late summer — fill up low and carry enough for the high camp and summit push
extreme, sustained exposure along the narrow summit ridge with drop-offs on both sides
North Cascades grizzly bear recovery zone — practice food storage/bear-aware camping
deleted_rows.overview: Hozomeen Mountain is a dramatic, dark twin-summited peak rising directly from the east shore of Ross Lake near the Canadian border in North Cascades National Park/Ross Lake National Recreation Area. The higher North Peak (~8,071-8,072 ft) and slightly lower South Peak (8,003 ft) are built of Hozomeen chert, a hard but badly fractured bedded rock that gives the mountain its dark color and its reputation for notoriously loose, rotten climbing. The South Peak's nearly 1,000-foot near-vertical face (average angle ~42.6°) is often cited as the steepest in Washington. First ascents: North Peak, Sept 6 1904 (Sledge Tatum & George Loudon Jr., via the northeast); South Peak, May 30 1947 by Fred Beckey and five companions via the Southwest Route. The Southeast/South Face line described here is regarded as the least committing of the three known lines to the South Peak's summit, in contrast to the harder Southeast Buttress (Grade III, 5.6, FA 1988 by Adams/Goodman/Johnson/Petroske) and North Face (IV+ 5.9, FA 2019 by Rolf Larson & partner).
deleted_rows.beta: Mostly Class 3-4 scrambling on loose, fractured rock above the 6,800 ft saddle camp: slabs and connecting gullies lead up the south side to a slanted ledge below the summit, where a short, exposed wall of about 15 ft at roughly 5.6 is the crux, followed by a chimney finish. Most parties rappel the crux on the way down. Previous climbing experience on exposed, loose rock is essential.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Turn around if: conditions deteriorate to poor visibility, weather shows threatening signs (darkening clouds, lightning), party is moving slower than planned indicating fatigue, or snow/ice conditions require ongoing step-kicking above 7,500 ft. Allow at least 4 hours descent time and establish a firm turn-around time before committing to upper terrain.
deleted_rows.rock_grade: Class 3-4 with a short 5.6 step near the summit
deleted_rows.face: South Peak (8,003 ft - the lower of Hozomeen's two main summits)
deleted_rows.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
deleted_rows.comms: No cell phone reception at Hozomeen Mountain or surrounding backcountry. Satellite communication (Garmin InReach, SPOT beacon) recommended for emergency contact. Remote location near Canadian border adds communication/evacuation delays.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the face; several fixed rappel bolts/anchors near the summit headwall and finishing chimney have been placed by past parties (per a 2019 ascent report), supplementing rappels off slung blocks or natural anchors where bolts aren't present. Do not blindly trust fixed gear on this rock — carry cord/webbing to back up or replace tat, and expect loose ledges and choss on the way down.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20)
waypoints.note: Park here and walk down to Ross Lake Resort for the water taxi north to the Hozomeen campground at the head of the lake, where the walk to Hozomeen Lake begins.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive SR 20 east past Newhalem and Diablo to the Ross Dam Trailhead parking at about milepost 134. There is no public road to the Hozomeen end of the lake from the south; walk down from here to Ross Lake Resort for its water taxi.

waypoints.name: Hozomeen Mountain, South Peak
waypoints.directions: Take the water taxi about 24 miles north to Hozomeen at the head of the lake, then follow the Hozomeen Lake Trail and leave it near the lake's outlet at about 2,400 ft. Cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east through devil's club and deadfall, up a chockstone-choked gully near 5,000 ft and red scree past a slab wall to the saddle camp near 6,800 ft, then slabs and gullies to the southeast face and the summit.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A light rack plus extra slings for slung blocks/horns; rock quality is poor, so anchor with care.
pro_tips: Treat every hold and anchor with suspicion — the rock is exceptionally loose
Helmets essential; minimize parties stacked in fall line
watch_out: extreme, sustained exposure on the narrow summit ridge with drop-offs on both sides
afternoon thunderstorms build quickly over the North Cascades crest in summer
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Pro and slings for the low-fifth steps and to build/back up rappel anchors on questionable rock.
deleted_rows.best_season: Mid-July through September
deleted_rows.approach: Because there is no public road to Hozomeen from the US side, the drive-in (SR-20 to Ross Lake Resort, then the resort's water taxi ~24 miles north up Ross Lake) drops you at the Hozomeen Ranger Station/Campground at the lake's head, around 1,650 ft — treat everything below as the hike from there. From the campground, pick up the maintained Hozomeen Lake Trail, which climbs gently through open, lush forest along the east side of Ross Lake toward Hozomeen Lake; trip reports differ on the exact length before you leave the tread (roughly 1.5 to 4 trail-miles depending on where you cut off), so budget for the full distance. Leave the maintained trail around 2,400 ft near Hozomeen Lake's outlet and begin ascending cross-country, following the creek/drainage east into the basin below the peak's south side. Expect a genuinely bad brush section here — a dense patch of devil's club right at the creek crossing, plus heavy deadfall and blowdown starting around 3,800 ft that slows travel to a crawl in spots. Water is reliable at the Hozomeen Creek crossing (~2,400-2,600 ft) and again in the basin around 5,000 ft; fill up at one of these, since the route above is dry. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones; above that, tedious red scree and heather lead past a striking slab wall around 5,800 ft and a steepening final push to a broad saddle/basin around 6,800 ft, which is the standard high camp (flat, tent-sized sites, but small — good for one or two). From camp, gain the final 1,000-1,200 ft on slabs and connecting gullies to reach the base of the southeast face/ridge proper. Given the ~19 km round-trip distance and roughly 6,400+ ft of total gain from lake level, this is realistically an overnight approach for most parties (camp at ~4,900-6,800 ft) rather than a single continuous car-to-summit push; a few strong parties have done it in a very long day.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descent reverses the southeast face/ridge — there's no separate walk-off, since Hozomeen drops steeply on essentially every side. The crux of the descent is a short, exposed step down a Class 5.6 bulge just below the summit ridge; some parties downclimb it, most rappel it given the exposure. Below that, a roughly 50-foot rappel gets you down a Class 5.0 ramp, and from there two further double-rope-length rappels (i.e., a 60m rope doubled, or twin-rope technique) lower you cleanly onto a snow patch/basin beneath the face — call it 3 rappels total as the typical count, though some parties report doing the lower section as one longer double-rope rappel instead of two, so bring a 60m rope and be ready for 3-4 rope-lengths depending on exact line and snow coverage. Anchors are mixed and not fully bolted: parties mention both fixed slings/webbing around blocks and horns and at least one bolted anchor near the crux/overhang, so treat any fixed tat as suspect, back it up, and carry a few extra slings/cord in case you need to build or replace an anchor. Below the rappels, downclimb loose scree and talus and reverse the approach gully back down to the ~6,800 ft saddle or camp — past parties describe this stretch as slow going (clean slabs mixed with steep dirt, shifting boulders, and loose rubble), with summit-to-camp times of roughly 3-6.5+ hours reported, so plan your day accordingly and expect to finish by headlamp if you start late.
deleted_rows.bail: Rappel from slung blocks; carry extra slings since fixed anchors are unreliable.

itinerary.cal: Access is via Ross Lake Resort's water taxi (SR-20 to Ross Dam, then boat up-lake to the Hozomeen campground at the head of the lake) since the historic Silver-Skagit Road border crossing from Hope, BC has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic and the park's fire-closure page, updated September 14, 2026, still lists it closed. The water taxi's destination is shut too: the park has closed the entire Hozomeen area (docks, camping and public areas), the Hozomeen Lake Trail and the Hozomeen Cross-country Zone for the Border 2 Fire, with no end date given on that page; best attempted mid-July through September once the west basin snow/water sources are known.

days.note: An easy 1.5-mile forest walk from the Hozomeen Lake trailhead gives way to a rougher off-trail push: crossing Hozomeen Creek, fighting devil's club and windfall, then climbing red scree and heather into the west basin below a broad slab wall. Most parties reach the 6,800 ft saddle camp by mid-afternoon, drop the overnight gear, and — if weather and energy allow — continue straight up for the summit the same day, returning to camp before dark. The final headwall below the summit is a short, exposed 5.6 step; bring a rope and rack a few pieces plus a sling for the fixed rap anchors used by past parties.

access.fees: $10 per person, per night backcountry camping fee, charged mid-May through early October (no charge the rest of the year); $6 non-refundable Recreation.gov reservation/lottery fee per permit application.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: No cell service at Ross Lake/Hozomeen; pack out all trash (no services at Hozomeen Campground); Ross Lake water taxi requires advance reservation.
access.permit: Overnight backcountry permit required year-round for any camping en route (e.g., Lightning Creek, Hozomeen Campground, or high camps). Obtain at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount or reserve in advance via Recreation.gov (about 60% of backcountry sites are reservable; the rest are walk-up, first-come, first-served and can be competitive at Ross Lake in summer). Reserved permits must be picked up by 11:00 AM PT on the trip start date or the reservation may be cancelled.
access.closures: The US/Canada border crossing at Hozomeen (used for the historic Silver Skagit Road approach from Hope, BC) has been closed to both vehicle and foot traffic since the COVID-19 pandemic (2020); the park's fire-closure page, updated 14 September 2026, still lists it closed with no end date given. The park has also closed the entire Hozomeen area — docks, public areas and camping — and the Hozomeen Cross-country Zone for the Border 2 Fire, with no end date given on that same page.

road.name: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) to Ross Lake Resort; Silver Skagit Road from Hope, BC (closed at the border since 2020)
road.status: SR-20 is open seasonally and closes for winter avalanche danger (recent closures have run roughly early December through spring) between the Ross Dam trailhead and Silver Star Gate — check WSDOT/NPS road conditions before driving. The Silver Skagit Road has been closed at km 6 for wildfire since 24 July 2026, with no end date given in the B.C. Ministry of Transportation and Transit closure notice last updated 24 September 2026, and the border crossing into Hozomeen has been closed to travelers since 2020.
road.driveNote: Drive SR-20 to Ross Lake Resort (near Diablo/Ross Dam) and arrange the resort's water taxi (206-486-3751) to shuttle you the length of Ross Lake to the Hozomeen/Lightning Creek area, or hike in via the ~31-mile East Bank Trail from the SR-20 trailhead at milepost 138.

climate.typical: Cool, wet North Cascades climate; snow can linger in upper gullies and on the face into July in heavy-snowpack years. Reliable, mostly snow-free rock conditions typically run mid-July through September.

bySeason.fall: Climbing season shortens rapidly after early September; early-season cold fronts and snow can hit the high ridge.
bySeason.spring: Approach trails and gullies are often still snow-covered/avalanche-prone into June, and Ross Lake Resort's water-taxi season may not yet be running.
bySeason.summer: Best climbing window (Jul-Sep); water sources above roughly 5,000-6,800 ft dry up by late summer, so time trips or cache water accordingly.
bySeason.winter: Effectively inaccessible — SR-20 is closed and Ross Lake Resort facilities are shut down.

emergency.notes: No cell phone reception at Ross Lake or Hozomeen; carry a satellite communicator/PLB. Given the multi-hour boat and/or long trail approach, rescue typically requires an NPS or county SAR helicopter.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park - Wilderness Information Center (Marblemount) / Ross Lake NRA
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth United General Medical Center, Sedro-Woolley, WA (~65 mi via SR-20) — a small facility; serious trauma cases are typically flown out given the remote, boat/trail-only access to this peak.

deleted_rows.corrections: The listed route name/id ("Southeast Face (Standard)") does not correspond to any documented route on this summit. Every reputable source checked (Wikipedia, Mountaineers.org, SummitPost search results, multiple trip reports on trailcatjim.com, cascadeclimbers.com, and Cascade Alpine Guide references) describes the standard/easiest route on Hozomeen Mountain's North (main, 8,071-ft) summit as ascending the Northeast Ridge/Buttress from a col near 6,300 ft — first climbed 1904, class 4. A genuine "Southeast Buttress" route does exist in the American Alpine Club database (FA 1988, III 5.6, described as the least-committing of three known routes), but it is on the separate SOUTH Peak (8,003 ft) of Hozomeen, a distinct sub-summit roughly a mile away, not on the North Peak matched by this entry's coordinates. I have filled this entry's fields using the well-documented Northeast Ridge/Buttress standard-route data (setting aspect=NE, face=Northeast Buttress/Ridge accordingly) since that is what "the standard route" on this specific summit actually refers to in the literature; the routeName/routeId were kept exactly as given per instructions, but the aspect/face fields reflect the sourced reality rather than the "Southeast" label. Recommend the app data owner review whether this route entry should be renamed/re-pointed to the Northeast Buttress, or replaced with a distinct South Peak entry for the true Southeast Buttress line.

approach_variants.name: Water taxi up Ross Lake to the campground at the head of the lake
approach_variants.notes:
There is no public road to this end of the lake from the south. Drive to the trailhead near milepost 134, walk down to the resort, and take its water taxi north to the campground and ranger station at the head of the lake at about 1,650 ft. Everything below is measured from there.

From the campground pick up the maintained lake-side trail, which climbs gently through open lush forest toward Hozomeen Lake. Reports differ on how far along it you should stay - anywhere from a mile and a half to four miles depending on where the party cut off - so budget for the longer figure. Leave the tread around 2,400 ft near the lake's outlet and start up cross-country, following the drainage east into the basin under the peak's south side. There is a genuinely bad brush section here: devil's club right at the creek crossing, and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft that reduces travel to a crawl. Fill water at the creek crossing or again in the basin near 5,000 ft, because everything above is dry.
approach_variants.season: July through September, once the brush is passable and the upper gullies have melted out
hazards: a boat schedule that fixes both ends of the trip on a lake with no road out
devil's club at the creek crossing and heavy deadfall from about 3,800 ft
no water above the basin near 5,000 ft
a boulder-choked gully with chockstones to negotiate under a pack
loose, friable rock on the upper mountain
a tiny high camp that will not take a large party
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The ladder of landmarks above the basin is what fixes your position, and they come in order. Near 5,000 ft the drainage narrows into a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones - if your gully has no chockstone bottleneck in it, you are in the wrong drainage and should traverse rather than climb. Above the chockstones the ground turns to tedious red scree and heather. The next confirmation is a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, passed rather than climbed. Above it the angle steepens to a broad saddle and basin near 6,800 ft with small flat tent-sized sites - the standard high camp, good for one or two tents and no more.

From camp the base of the route is another thousand feet or so above, gained on slabs and connecting gullies. You are looking for the point where the slabs run out against the face and the ridge proper takes over.

Check which summit is above you. This route is on the south peak, which is the lower of the two main summits. If the tower above you is the higher, broader one and the other summit lies to the south of you, you have drifted north into the wrong cirque and are under the north peak.

And check that you left the trail at all. The maintained tread is graded and obvious; the moment you are on it with easy walking under your feet, you are not on the approach any more. The departure is at a creek, at a lake outlet, not at a sign.

approach_variants.name: By road from the north to the ranger station, subject to the border gate
approach_variants.notes:
The campground and ranger station at the head of the lake can also be reached by driving a long gravel road south from the north side of the international boundary. That crossing has been closed to both vehicles and foot traffic, so this variant may simply not exist in the season you are planning for - confirm the gate's status before building a trip on it, because there is no way to discover it is shut except by arriving.

If it is open, the walk from the campground is identical to the boat variant: the maintained lake-side trail toward Hozomeen Lake, then off-trail at the outlet near 2,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: July through September, and only if the boundary is open
hazards: a border gate that has been closed to vehicles and to walkers
a long gravel drive with no services at the end
the same devil's club, deadfall and dry upper slopes
loose rock and a small high camp
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Arrival changes, the approach does not. From the campground at about 1,650 ft the sequence is the same: maintained trail to the vicinity of Hozomeen Lake's outlet near 2,400 ft, then cross Hozomeen Creek and follow the drainage east into the south basin.

The markers are the same ladder, in the same order: a boulder-choked gully with a bottleneck of large chockstones near 5,000 ft, red scree and heather above it, a striking slab wall at about 5,800 ft, and then a broad saddle and basin at about 6,800 ft with a few small flat tent sites. A drainage with no chockstone bottleneck is the wrong drainage.

The summit test still applies. This route is on the south peak, the lower of the two. If the higher, broader summit is directly above you and the other one lies south, you are under the north peak instead.

approach_variants.name: From the Lightning Creek landing on the lake's east shore, past Willow Lake
approach_variants.notes: A boat landing further down the east shore of the lake gives onto the east-bank trail system, which runs north past Willow Lake. Parties have used this to reach the south and south-east sides of the massif on foot rather than starting from the campground at the head of the lake. It is the longer walk of the two boat options and it approaches the peak from the south-east rather than from the west, so it suits parties heading for the south-east side of the south peak more than it suits the standard line.
approach_variants.season: July through September
hazards: a much longer walk than the head-of-lake landing
timber, avalanche debris and a ravine crossing with no tread
steep dirt and brush below the shoulder
no water between Willow Lake and the basin
cliff bands that must be bypassed in poor visibility
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The departure from the trail is just beyond Willow Lake, and the lake is the marker. It is the last reliable water; everything above is dry until the basin, so this is where you fill.

From there the ground is the test rather than any tread: timber and avalanche debris first, then a ravine to cross, then steep dirt and brush climbing to open timber on the broad shoulder south of the peak. Reaching meadows near 5,000 ft is the sign the worst of the brush is behind you.

Above the meadows the cliff bands are bypassed, not climbed. If you are forced onto rock that wants a rope, traverse and look for the way round rather than committing to it - the way through here is a walking line, not a climbing one.

The arrival is a saddle at about 6,200 ft directly beneath the buttress on the peak's south-east side, with no water on it. If you have arrived somewhere with running water, you are not there yet. From that saddle the standard south-east face and the south-east buttress lines are both above you, so identify which feature you are under before starting up.

bivy.name: Improvised bivouacs in the western basin between the peaks
bivy.notes: The mountain is two rock summits above a basin, and the approach to that basin from the lake is the crux of the whole trip for most parties: a slow grind through blowdown and heavy brush with no path, on which fifteen miles and seven thousand feet of gain and loss is a fair reckoning for the round trip. Strong parties do go car to car, and parties often describe regretting that decision around hour twelve. Sleeping up here shortens the summit day considerably, at the cost of hauling water up a slope with almost none on it and sleeping on ground that is not flat. There is a second line from the road along the cleared border swath running east from near the ranger station, which is shorter and is described by people who have used it as more unpleasant than the lake approach rather than less. Both are late-summer propositions: snow lingers in the basin, and the brush is at its worst when it is wet.
bivy.water: This is the hard part and worth planning around. The one stream in the basin runs in a channel that deepens into a slot as you climb, and parties have found it reachable at a single awkward spot at around four thousand feet and nowhere above that. Fill everything you are carrying when you can get to water, because you may not get another chance before the ground goes flat enough to sleep on.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit for the Hozomeen cross-country zone, which allows a maximum party of six and a maximum of three parties on any night. It is a walk-up zone rather than a reservable one, so the permit is collected in person, in practice at Marblemount. Cross-country camping legally begins a mile from any designated camp and half a mile from any trail, out of sight of both, and only on snow, rock or bare ground — never in meadow and never within a hundred feet of water. No fires in the zone. Waste goes in a cathole, or is carried out where the ground will not take one.
bivy.capacity: No established site and no site count. Parties have reported scratching out a few rough platforms among scattered boulders on a steep forested slope, enough for one small party sleeping poorly. There is no camp here — this is where people stop because they have run out of daylight, not somewhere anyone chose.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Campground, north end of Ross Lake
bivy.notes: This is the roadhead for every route on the mountain and the only developed camping anywhere near it. It sits in deep forest on flat ground by the lake, with vault toilets, boat ramps and no trash service, so everything you bring comes out with you. There is no cell coverage and the nearest supplies are hours away in either country. The season runs roughly late May into October, bounded at the front by snow on the gravel road and at the back by the road being left unmaintained. The other way in is by water: a boat from the resort at the south end will run parties the length of the lake, taking up to six people with packs on a chartered trip that is booked and paid in advance. That is expensive and inflexible but it does not involve a border at all, which through several recent seasons has made it the only way anybody got here. In summer 2026 a lightning fire on the border grew to many thousands of acres immediately east of the mountain, crossed into Canada, and closed the entire Hozomeen area including the docks, the campground and the lake north of Silver Creek. Treat access to this peak as something to verify from scratch each season rather than as a fixed thing.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is provided while the campground is staffed. Outside that window, and any time the system is off, the lake and the creeks are the supply and need treating.
bivy.permit: National Park Service, Ross Lake NRA. No fee and no reservation for the campground itself, and no backcountry permit to sleep here — but one is required the moment you walk in to the lake camps or up onto the mountain. The border is the complication. The only road access is a long gravel road running south from the Trans-Canada Highway near Hope, British Columbia, and it crosses into the United States at a point with no staffed port of entry. The gate on the American side has been closed to vehicle traffic from Canada for several years, and at times foot traffic across the line has been prohibited as well. A party driving down from Canada is entering the United States, so it needs the documents for that regardless of whether anyone is there to check; the practical position has been that you cannot legally drive through, and that a normal port of entry plus the boat is the way in. Confirm the current gate status with the park and with the border agency before committing to the road, because the answer has changed more than once.
bivy.capacity: Around 75 sites across two loops, all first-come and first-served with no reservations taken. The Upper Loop has been closed for hazard trees, which removes a good share of that number and also happens to be where the lake trail starts, so check what is actually open before counting on a spot.

bivy.name: Hozomeen Lake camp
bivy.notes: Something under four miles in from the campground's upper loop on an established trail, this is the obvious first night for anyone who wants to start the climb from higher than the road. It is a genuinely pleasant forested lake sitting directly beneath the mountain, and it is the better of the two lake camps by some distance. The climbing route leaves from here: parties work around the eastern shore and then angle up into the basin between the peaks, and that is where the day stops being a hike. Expect heavy deadfall and thick brush from the moment you leave the trail. The loon closure and the fire closures between them have shut this camp for large parts of recent seasons, so confirm it is open before building an itinerary on it.
bivy.water: The lake is right there and is the supply. It is standing water in a shallow forested basin, so filter or treat rather than drinking it as found.
bivy.permit: National Park Service backcountry permit required, obtained at the Marblemount wilderness office or through the park's issuing system. A seasonal closure applies: the lake is closed to entry and to camping from the first of April through the end of May to protect nesting loons, which rules out the early-season window entirely. Fires and food storage are governed by the permit; a canister is the sensible choice here whatever the minimum requirement says.
bivy.capacity: A small designated backcountry camp at the lake, a few sites with a privy and food storage. Sites are assigned by night on the permit, so a walk-up can be turned away if the nights you want are taken.

deleted_rows.name: Frying Pan / Whitman Glaciers
deleted_rows.fa: J.B. Flett and Henry H. Garrison, August 29, 1894 (first recorded ascent of the peak, via this line)
deleted_rows.season: Jul-Sep (best early July-early Aug while glaciers are well-filled and rock is more often frozen)
hazards: loose volcanic rock
rockfall
crevasses
summit exposure
weakening/melted-out crevasse bridges, especially Aug-Sep
afternoon rockfall on the summit block as sun-warmed andesite loosens
deleted_rows.overview: This is the standard glacier line up Little Tahoma, named for the two glaciers it crosses (Fryingpan and Whitman). It was first climbed August 29, 1894 by J.B. Flett and Henry H. Garrison.
deleted_rows.beta: From a high camp near Summerland/Meany Crest, rope up and cross the Fryingpan Glacier southwest toward Whitman Crest, then drop onto the Whitman Glacier and climb steepening snow/ice (up to about 45 degrees) toward the east shoulder. The technical crux is really the combination of glacier travel and the final loose rock, not any single hard move; the last 400-800 ft is Class 2-3 (locally Class 4) scrambling on rotten andesite to the true summit.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround for the summit block — aim to be on and off it by mid-morning, before afternoon sun softens holds and increases rockfall.
deleted_rows.rock_grade: Class 2-3 (loose andesite; short exposed Class 3 summit block)
deleted_rows.permit: Mount Rainier: climbing on glaciers or above 10,000 ft requires the park's climbing registration; overnight high camps also need a wilderness permit.
deleted_rows.comms: Cell coverage is unreliable to nonexistent on the glaciers and upper mountain; a satellite communicator or PLB is strongly recommended for this route.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the ascent, re-crossing the Whitman Glacier over Whitman Notch (9,100 ft) and the Fryingpan Glacier back to high camp/Summerland. Early season, the Meany snowfield allows a fast glissade/plunge-step descent; watch for softened, sun-cupped crevasse bridges by afternoon.

waypoints.name: Fryingpan Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of the trail to Summerland at the Fryingpan Creek bridge on the White River Road, about 3 miles past the White River entrance, Mount Rainier NP.
waypoints.directions: From Enumclaw, drive SR 410 east about 43 miles and turn west onto the White River (Sunrise) Road. Pass the White River Entrance and drive about 3 miles to the parking area at the Fryingpan Creek bridge; the trail to Summerland starts across the road. A park entrance pass is required, and the road is open only in the summer season.

waypoints.name: Little Tahoma Summit
waypoints.note: Via Fryingpan Glacier, Whitman Notch (~9100 ft), and the Whitman Glacier to the East Ridge; climbing registration required.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Wonderland Trail up Fryingpan Creek about 4.5 miles to Summerland. Take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll up the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest at about 7,400 ft, staying left of the cliffed bowl. Rope up on the Fryingpan Glacier and climb south-southwest to Whitman Notch (about 9,100 ft), then up the Whitman Glacier across the bergschrund to a loose gully, a chimney to the summit notch, and the exposed class 3 crest.
