An alpine start gets the team across the Fryingpan Glacier and over Whitman Notch (9,100 ft) before the snow softens, then up the Whitman Glacier and a picket-protected couloir to …
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Summit day and move to Summerland

sectionBreakdown.note: A short, easy morning hike back down through Summerland and the forest to the trailhead.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Typical glacier rope-team kit: one rope per 2-3 person team, harness, 2-3 snow pickets, crevasse-rescue kit (prusiks or mechanical ascenders, pulley, spare carabiners), ice axe, crampons; helmet essential for the full glacier-to-summit sequence.
what_to_bring: climbing registration and wilderness permit paperwork
pro_tips: Climb the summit block early while it's still cold/frozen to minimize rockfall risk.
Keep the group tight and avoid stacking multiple parties on the loose rock.
Early July into early August offers the best-bridged glaciers and most reliably frozen summit rock.
watch_out: The final summit block is loose, crumbly andesite prone to rockfall onto climbers below.
Crevasse bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers weaken through the season, especially by late summer.
Rainier's massif builds severe weather quickly; storms can arrive with little warning even on a clear-morning start.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Glacier travel and crevasse rescue protection (pickets, occasional ice screw) rather than rock protection; the summit scramble is typically soloed or simul-climbed unroped by competent parties.
deleted_rows.best_season: Early July into early August is the genuinely optimal window: the Fryingpan/Whitman glaciers are still well filled and crevasses well-bridged, and the loose summit block is more often frozen solid on an early-morning ascent. By late August-September the glaciers melt out, crevasse bridges weaken, and rockfall increases markedly.
deleted_rows.approach: Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead (~3,800-3,900 ft) on the Sunrise/White River Road, about 3 miles past the White River entrance station. The Fryingpan Creek Trailhead parking area and the spur trail from it close from late September 2026 for the length of the park's Fryingpan Creek Bridge project (construction planned for 2027-2029); while they are closed, park at White River Campground and take the Wonderland Trail to Summerland. Follow the signed Fryingpan Creek Trail, which climbs gently along Fryingpan Creek through old-growth forest. At roughly 3.2 miles / ~1,400 ft of gain (about 2-2.5 hrs from the car) the trail reaches an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek - the main water source and a spot that can require careful footing in high runoff. Continue up-trail toward Summerland, reaching that popular alpine backcountry camp (patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, wilderness permit required to camp) at about 4.5 miles and roughly 2,500 ft gain (~5,900 ft elevation) - this is the last reliable running water before the climb proper. From Summerland, leave the maintained trail and pick up the climbers' 'spring route' path that heads northwest of the campground knoll, ascending steep tundra/snow up the Meany Snowfield toward Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft that serves as the standard high camp (flat tent sites, stone wind breaks). This band between Summerland and Meany Crest is where route-finding matters most: parties that contour too far climber's right have gotten cliffed out in a bowl below rock bands, so stick to the cairned/bootpacked line. Above Meany Crest, gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier - rope up here, as this begins sustained glacier travel with real crevasse hazard - and climb generally south/southwest across the lower glacier apron to the broad notch separating the Fryingpan and Whitman Glaciers (~9,000-9,100 ft, commonly called Whitman Notch). From the notch, traverse and climb the upper Whitman Glacier, crossing a bergschrund (usually a straightforward step-across early season, wider and trickier late season) up moderate glacier slopes to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to a loose rock-and-scree gully. Climb the gully to a short (~6 ft) headwall step, then a gully-chimney to the summit notch, finishing with an exposed, loose Class 3 scramble (roughly 30-100 ft) along a narrow, crumbly andesite ridge crest to the 11,138 ft summit - there is major exposure here, with a roughly 2,000 ft drop to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. Additional hazards along the whole approach: avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft/early-season conditions, and afternoon whiteout or thunderstorm activity common on Rainier's flanks.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line and involves no rappelling - this is a glacier/snow scramble route, not a technical rock route, so plan on downclimbing and plunge-stepping/glissading rather than roped rappels. From the summit, downclimb the exposed Class 3 ridge scramble and the gully-chimney/headwall back onto the upper Whitman Glacier, re-crossing the bergschrund, then descend the Whitman Glacier back through Whitman Notch onto the Fryingpan Glacier and down to Meany Crest. In good afternoon conditions most parties plunge-step or glissade the moderate glacier and snowfield slopes below the notch, which goes considerably faster than the ascent - but glissade routes need to be chosen with the ascent's crevasse locations in mind, since crevasses often widen and soften as the day warms. From Meany Crest, reverse the descent to Summerland (watch for the same cliff-band route-finding trap above Summerland - don't drift climber's right into the bowl), then follow the Fryingpan Creek Trail back to the footlog crossing and out to the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead. Key descent hazards: softening crevasse bridges and increased fall-through risk in the afternoon, loose rock in the summit gully, and deteriorating weather (rain/hail/whiteout/thunderstorms are a recurring theme in trip reports on this peak). No fixed anchors, bolted stations, or rappel gear are used on the standard Fryingpan/Whitman route; a rope, pickets, and a few ice screws/pickets for running belays on the steeper glacier sections are the extent of the technical gear needed.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is a straightforward reversal of the route from any point on the glaciers or shoulder; don't push for the summit block if you won't reach it while it's still cold.

pitch_detail.pitch: Fryingpan/Whitman glacier crossing and steep snow to the east shoulder

pitch_detail.notes: Loose, exposed scrambling to the true summit; significant rockfall potential

itinerary.cal: Best climbed June-August while the Fryingpan/Whitman glaciers hold consolidated snow; the road past the Fryingpan Creek trailhead usually opens by late May, and crevasses/moats open up more by late summer.

days.note: Hike the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead through old-growth forest, cross Fryingpan Creek, and climb through the Summerland meadows before leaving trail to work up scree/snow to a rocky camp overlooking the Fryingpan Glacier at roughly 7,350 ft.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach a high camp near Meany Crest on the Fryingpan Glacier moraine

days.note: An alpine start gets the team across the Fryingpan Glacier and over Whitman Notch (9,100 ft) before the snow softens, then up the Whitman Glacier and a picket-protected couloir to a short Class 3-4 rock finish on the summit block. After descending back to camp, most parties drop further to the Summerland shelter that evening to shorten day 3.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, 2-night trip is the standard club/party pace: ~14 mi round trip with ~7,600 ft of gain/loss, split between a moderate approach day, a long alpine-start glacier summit day, and a short exit.

access.fees: $82/person climbing registration, required year-round for any travel above 10,000 ft or onto a glacier, plus a $12/person/night wilderness permit for overnight camping (May 1-Sep 15); park entrance is $30/vehicle for 7 days.
access.notes: Inside the national park, so a Northwest Forest Pass does not apply; the park entrance fee does. Climbing registration and the per-person climbing fee are required before going onto a glacier or above 10,000 ft.
access.rules: Blue bags required for human waste above high camp — pack out and deposit only in barrels marked "Human Waste" at Camp Muir or the trailhead; do not cache on-route. Check-out is required after every climb.
access.permit: Climbing registration required for all travel above 10,000 ft or on any glacier; a separate wilderness permit is required for overnight camping at Summerland or high camp.
access.closures: The road is usually open past the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead to the White River Campground lot by mid-to-late May; the upper road to Sunrise stays snow-gated until late June-early July and closes for the season by mid-October. Mount Rainier National Park is closing the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead parking area and the Summerland spur trail for the Fryingpan Creek Bridge replacement from late September 2026 (September 27 on its construction page updated September 24, 2026; other park pages give September 28 or October 1) through the end of the project, with construction planned for 2027-2029. Summerland stays open by the Wonderland Trail from White River Campground, which has limited parking.

access.land_manager: National Park Service
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful / interagency annual pass covers only the $30 vehicle entrance fee, not the separate $82 climbing registration fee.

climate.typical: Alpine climate on the east side of the Rainier massif: cold nights even in midsummer, rapid cloud buildup, and afternoon thunderstorms are common.
climate.forecastZone: Not covered by NWAC avalanche forecasts (below ~8,000 ft and Nov-Apr only); use the NWS Seattle mountain/zone forecast and recent trip reports.

approach_variants.name: Fryingpan Creek, Summerland and Meany Crest to Whitman Notch
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Fryingpan Creek Trailhead near 3,800-3,900 ft on the Sunrise and White River Road, a few miles past the White River entrance station. Follow the signed trail up through old-growth beside Fryingpan Creek.

At roughly 3.2 miles and about 1,400 ft of gain there is an established footlog crossing of Fryingpan Creek — the main water and a spot that needs care in high runoff. Continue to Summerland at about 4.5 miles and roughly 5,900 ft: patrol cabin, pit toilet, bear wires, and the last reliable running water.

From Summerland leave maintained trail and take the climbers' path northwest of the campground knoll, up steep tundra and snow on the Meany Snowfield to Meany Crest, a rock outcrop at roughly 7,350-7,500 ft with flat sites and stone wind breaks. This is the standard high camp.

Above Meany Crest gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up. Climb south and southwest across the lower apron to the broad notch between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers at about 9,000-9,100 ft, then traverse and climb the upper Whitman across a bergschrund to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to rock.

The basin holds heavy snow and the approach slopes can be avalanche terrain in soft early-season conditions. Afternoon whiteout and thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun through Aug, best early July to early August — firm morning snow, drier rock, and bridges not yet melted out
hazards: Loose volcanic rock and rockfall on the summit gully and crest, worsening through the day
Crevasses and weakening bridges on the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, worst in August and September
A bergschrund that is a step-across early season and a problem late
Cliff-out potential between Summerland and Meany Crest if the line drifts climber's right
Avalanche potential on the Meany Snowfield in soft or early-season conditions
Major exposure on the final crest, with about 2,000 ft to the Emmons on the north side
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Whitman Notch at about 9,100 ft is the arrival, and you know it by what becomes visible rather than by the altimeter: it is the first place the Whitman Glacier comes into view. Until you can see a second glacier on the far side, you have not reached the notch.

The base of the climbing proper is higher still, and it is a change of surface: at about 10,500-11,000 ft the snow ends and a loose rock-and-scree gully begins. That transition is the base. The sequence above it is countable and in this order: gully, a short step of about 6 ft, a gully-chimney, the summit notch, then an exposed scramble along the crest.

The route-finding trap is low, not high, and it is the one thing on this climb that regularly commits parties to bad ground: between Summerland and Meany Crest, if you find yourself contouring climber's right into a bowl under rock bands, you are cliffed out and off the line. The cairned and boot-packed line stays left of that bowl. Fix this by going back to the last cairn, not by traversing further.

The summit-crest test is a negative and it is unambiguous: the last 30 to 100 ft is a narrow crumbling andesite crest with roughly 2,000 ft dropping away to the Emmons Glacier on the north side. If the ground is not falling away on both sides of you, you have not reached the true summit — you are on the notch or a subsidiary block below it.

Timing as a finding: the andesite loosens as the sun works on it, and the crevasse bridges soften through the day. Being at the notch early is not tidiness, it is the whole plan.

climbing_route.label: Fryingpan Glacier to Whitman Notch
climbing_route.notes: Above Meany Crest, gain the toe of the Fryingpan Glacier and rope up here — this begins sustained glacier travel with real crevasse hazard. Climb generally south/southwest across the lower glacier apron to the broad notch separating the Fryingpan and Whitman Glaciers (~9,000-9,100 ft, commonly called Whitman Notch).

climbing_route.label: Upper Whitman Glacier
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, traverse and climb the upper Whitman Glacier, crossing a bergschrund — usually a straightforward step-across early season, wider and trickier late season — up moderate glacier slopes to about 10,500-11,000 ft, where snow gives way to a loose rock-and-scree gully.

climbing_route.label: Gully, headwall step and gully-chimney
climbing_route.notes: Climb the loose rock-and-scree gully to a short (~6 ft) headwall step, then a gully-chimney to the summit notch.

climbing_route.label: Summit ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: An exposed, loose scramble of roughly 30-100 ft along a narrow, crumbly andesite ridge crest to the 11,138 ft summit. There is major exposure here, with a roughly 2,000 ft drop to the Emmons Glacier on the north side; afternoon whiteout or thunderstorm activity is common on Rainier's flanks.

bivy.name: Meany Crest
bivy.notes: The standard high camp for Little Tahoma, and the one that makes the climb reasonable. It is a large flat area within the cliff band directly above Summerland, gained by the climbers' path and scrambling out of the basin, and it also serves Whitman Crest and the spires on that shoulder. From here the Fryingpan Glacier lies immediately ahead and the summit is a manageable morning rather than an epic. It is exposed — the shelf catches wind off the mountain and there is nothing to hide behind — so build walls if the forecast is doubtful and site the tent where a rockfall from the band above cannot reach it. Getting a permit for the zone is generally far easier than getting one of Summerland's few designated sites, which is a second, practical reason to camp high.
bivy.water: Meltwater runnels and small falls at the edge of the snow through most of the season — parties routinely find running water a short walk from camp. Late in a dry summer it thins out, so carry a stove and be prepared to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit issued for the cross-country zone rather than a named site, obtained the same way and at the same per-person nightly rate as an established camp. Zone rules govern the pitch: well back from trails, at least a hundred feet from water, and on snow, rock or bare durable ground — never on the meadow. The climbing cost-recovery fee applies to this trip regardless of where you sleep, since the route crosses glaciers. There is no toilet, so human waste must be packed out; the park's blue bag system exists for exactly this and is the expected practice on any glaciated route here.
bivy.capacity: A broad, flat rock and snow shelf with room for several tents; no designated sites, no numbers, and no facilities

bivy.name: Summerland Camp
bivy.notes: The subalpine meadow basin that everything on this side of the mountain stages from, a little over four miles up the Wonderland Trail from the Fryingpan Creek bridge. For Little Tahoma it is the lower of the two realistic camps and much the more comfortable one — running water, a toilet, a stone shelter to cook under in bad weather, and a designated pitch. The catch is the site count and the competition: these are among the most sought-after backcountry sites in the park and they book out for midsummer weekends, with Wonderland Trail through-hikers taking most of them. Early season, before the Wonderland traffic builds, is when a climbing party can most easily get in. Camping here rather than higher costs you roughly 1,600 feet and a cliff band on summit morning, which turns Little Tahoma into a genuinely long day, so most parties treat Summerland as a staging night rather than a high camp.
bivy.water: Fryingpan Creek runs through the meadow just below the shelter and is reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness permit, required for every overnight. In 2026 that is roughly twelve dollars per person per night for anyone sixteen and over, plus a per-trip application fee, booked through the federal reservation system with about two thirds of capacity reservable in advance and the rest held for walk-ups; walk-up permits are issued in person at the White River Wilderness Information Center on this side of the park, or at Longmire or Carbon River. The park's separate climbing cost-recovery fee — about eighty-two dollars a head — is NOT triggered by camping here, but IS triggered the moment you step onto the Fryingpan or Whitman Glacier, or go above 10,000 feet, which every route on Little Tahoma does. Pay it online before you arrive and bring proof; a climbing permit will not be issued to a team until every member has paid.
bivy.capacity: A handful of designated individual sites — around five — plus a stone shelter built by the Civilian Conservation Corps a little below them, and a backcountry toilet

bivy.name: Toe of the Fryingpan Glacier
bivy.notes: A slightly higher and more committed alternative to Meany Crest, on the moraine and snow where the Fryingpan Glacier begins. It shaves a little more off summit morning and puts you on the ice within minutes of leaving the tent, which is worth something on a route where the Whitman Glacier softens badly through the day and the descent is best done before it does. The ground is rubble and old ice rather than a shelf, so expect to build a platform, and expect the good spots to have moved since whatever description you read. The glacier here has been retreating steadily, which is the honest caveat: this camp is described differently in accounts a decade apart, and its condition should be treated as a current-season question rather than settled.
bivy.water: Glacial meltwater at the snout in warm weather, silty and worth settling before filtering, or snow to melt. Carry fuel on the assumption you will be melting
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, same as Meany Crest. The climbing cost-recovery fee is unavoidable at this point — you are camping at the edge of a glacier. Pack out all human waste; there are no facilities above Summerland at all.
bivy.capacity: A small number of parties on moraine and snow at the glacier's lower edge; informal, and the usable ground shifts as the ice recedes

bivy.name: Whitman Glacier notch camp
bivy.notes: The highest of the three camps, in the prominent gap on the crest between the Fryingpan and Whitman glaciers, just under the base of the peak itself. It reduces summit day to a short glacier walk and the East Shoulder scramble, which is its whole justification. Everything else about it is a cost: it is cold, wind-hammered, waterless, and small enough that a third party arriving has nowhere to go. Little Tahoma's summit block is notoriously loose volcanic rock and the peak is the site of one of the largest rockfalls recorded in the range, so where you site a tent relative to the slopes above matters more here than anywhere lower on the route. Sound judgement is to camp high only if the freezing level is low enough to keep the mountain frozen overnight.
bivy.water: Snow only. No running water at this elevation — carry all fuel for the bivouac and for summit day
bivy.permit: Cross-country zone wilderness permit, plus the climbing cost-recovery fee, which is mandatory here in every sense. Registration for the climb is completed in person at a wilderness information center before you start, and the climbing rangers' account of current glacier and rockfall conditions is worth treating as part of the plan rather than a formality. Blue bags for all waste.
bivy.capacity: Two or three tents in the gap, dug into snow; very limited and fully exposed

deleted_rows.name: South Ridge
deleted_rows.fa: Bill Cox and Will F. Thompson, September 1938 — widely credited as the peak's first ascent, via this standard Luna Col/south ridge line
gear: crampons or microspikes for lingering snow/ice in the approach gullies and on Luna Col (persists into July)
optional light rack (a few slings/small cams) and a 30–35m rope for parties wanting a running belay across the false-to-true-summit traverse — not needed by most parties in normal summer conditions
hazards: extreme remoteness and a multi-day, largely off-trail approach shared with the Southeast Slopes route (Access Creek brush, cold creek fords, sparse cairns — see that route for detail)
lingering snow/ice on Luna Col and the approach gullies, rated up to M1 by early-season parties
~4,000 ft of sustained exposure on the false-to-true-summit traverse
deleted_rows.overview: Effectively Luna Peak's standard technical line: from Luna Col/Luna Pass (reached via the Access Creek approach shared with the Southeast Slopes route), climb the broad south ridge on Class 2–3 talus to the false summit, then complete the exposed Class 3–4 traverse across the notch to the true (north) summit — the same crux described under the Southeast Slopes route. It is rated 4th class / 1 pitch, with an early-season ice/mixed component (M1) reflecting the snow and occasional verglas that can linger on the col and in the approach gullies into July.
deleted_rows.beta: From a high camp near Luna(-Fury) Col, climb the broad Class 2 talus ridge north for roughly 1,100 ft to the false (south) summit. From there the ridge narrows; stay on or just below the crest (typically on the east side) across a short, exposed Class 3-4 section of solid but loose rock to the true (north) summit, roughly 15-20 minutes of scrambling. Some parties rope up for this final section; in dry summer conditions it is regularly soloed. The route is reached only after a full day (or more) of approach hiking and off-trail travel — the technical climbing is brief, the logistics are not.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before leaving high camp based on your slowest team member's pace on the approach gullies and ridge scramble — this is a long, physically demanding day with route-finding challenges, and descending the loose gully system or the exposed summit ridge in the dark or in deteriorating weather meaningfully raises the accident risk. Build in a safety margin for the multi-hour, multi-mile hike back to camp.
deleted_rows.face: South ridge (Luna Col to the true summit)
deleted_rows.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
deleted_rows.comms: No reliable cell service in the Big Beaver/Access Creek drainages or on Luna Peak itself; this is deep, remote North Cascades National Park backcountry. A satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is strongly recommended given the multi-day approach and lack of any quick bailout.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the south ridge to Luna Col/Luna Pass, then retrace the Access Creek basin and Access Col approach back to the Big Beaver Trail.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trail / Ross Lake access
waypoints.note: Access to Luna Peak via Ross Lake (ferry or lakeshore trail) to Big Beaver Trail, then bushwhack up Access Creek.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Ross Lake Trailhead near Ross Dam, at milepost 134. From there, most parties take the seasonal Ross Lake Resort water taxi across the reservoir to the Big Beaver Trailhead, skipping roughly seven miles of lakeshore hiking; without the taxi, hike the Ross Lake East Bank trail north to the same point. The water taxi typically runs late May through early October. A North Cascades National Park backcountry wilderness permit is required to camp at the Access Creek basecamp used for this climb.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: No fixed protection or bolted anchors exist on the route. Most parties climb it unroped as a scramble; a light rack (a few slings, a couple of small-to-mid cams/nuts, and a 30 m rope) is a reasonable option for parties wanting to protect the exposed Class 4 step between the false and true summits, but it is not standard practice in dry summer conditions.
what_to_bring: Bear spray / awareness (bear activity reported near Luna Pass/Access Creek)
Insect repellent and head net (mosquitoes/biting flies in the lower valleys)
Water treatment (running water available below Luna Col, less reliable above)
Extra socks / footwear for repeated creek fords
Sun protection for the exposed upper basin and ridge
pro_tips: Camp at or near Luna(-Fury) Col if possible — it sets up a much shorter, earlier summit push than camping lower in the Access Creek basin.
Of the three gullies leading to the SE shoulder, the middle one is the most commonly used — narrower and steeper on the right, broader and mellower on the left.
A water-taxi shuttle from Ross Lake Resort across Ross Lake meaningfully cuts the approach mileage and is worth arranging in advance.
The Class 3-4 traverse between the false and true summits is easier than it looks from below — there are good ledges for feet and handholds, but stay alert to loose blocks.
watch_out: Loose, blocky rock on the summit ridge and in the access gullies — parties below other climbers are at rockfall risk.
Firm, steep snow can persist in the access gullies well into summer, especially in the morning before it softens.
Access Creek and Big Beaver Creek fords can be knee-deep or higher and are more serious after rain or during peak snowmelt.
Dense slide-alder brush on the upper approach is disorienting; route-finding through it is a common source of delay.
Weather can close in quickly on the exposed upper basin and ridge, with no quick escape once committed.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection needs are minimal and situational — mainly for the short, exposed Class 3-4 ridge traverse near the true summit, where loose rock and exposure (not sustained difficulty) are the main concerns.
deleted_rows.best_season: July through September; The early-season ice/mixed (M1) rating reflects conditions before Luna Col and the approach gullies melt out, which is typically not before mid-to-late July.
deleted_rows.approach: Start at the Ross Lake Trailhead off Hwy 20 near Ross Dam. Most parties take the seasonal Ross Lake Resort water taxi across the reservoir to the Big Beaver Trailhead (~1,600 ft) to skip roughly 7 rolling lakeshore miles; without the taxi, hike the Ross Lake East Bank trail north to the same point. From Big Beaver Trailhead, follow the NPS-maintained Big Beaver Trail — a mellow, mostly flat old-growth forest walk with water at creek crossings — about 8 miles to Luna Camp, the standard backcountry-permit basecamp. Continue north on trail roughly another 1.5 miles; watch on the left (west) for a boot path near where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek, and cross Big Beaver Creek there (a log crossing is sometimes usable; otherwise wade). This is where the maintained trail ends. Follow a surprisingly well-defined boot path along the north (true right) bank of Access Creek through semi-open forest; near roughly 3,700 ft the brush turns thick with slide alder, so cross to the creek's south bank around 3,800 ft — several trip reports specifically warn that skipping this crossing leads to a miserable bushwhack, so don't put it off. From the south bank, cairns and a fainter climbers' path link talus benches that dodge most of the remaining brush and lead into the open upper basin at the Access Creek headwaters (roughly 4,400–5,800 ft depending on exact camp spot), which has reliable creek water and is the usual basecamp for the peak. From camp, ascend the Access Couloir/gully system above the basin — steep, loose scree and talus with lingering snow patches in early season, and a notably loose upper section of dirt and heather clumps — gaining roughly 1,500–2,000 ft to Access Col (~6,300 ft). From the col, a faint climbers' path traverses west across heather and talus, angling up snow and talus on Luna's southeast flank to Luna Pass (Luna–McMillan Col, ~7,200 ft). From Luna Pass, this South Ridge route turns directly up the broad south ridge on Class 2 talus (roughly 1,000–1,100 ft of gain) straight to Luna's false (south) summit, rather than continuing the southeast-snowfield traverse used by the standard Southeast Slopes line. Key hazards throughout: swift, sometimes-swollen crossings of Big Beaver and Access Creek; heavy slide-alder bushwhacking and genuine route-finding difficulty in the Access Creek drainage (multiple parties report initially following the wrong drainage); loose rock in the Access Couloir and on the south ridge itself, with real rockfall risk onto climbers below; and lingering snow/possible avalanche exposure on the couloir and southeast snowfields in early season. This is a remote, multi-day approach — the recorded ~77 km round-trip distance reflects the long lakeshore/Big Beaver Trail miles plus off-trail basin approach, and an NPS wilderness permit is required for camping in North Cascades National Park.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line and involves no rappelling. From the false (south) summit, down-climb the broad south ridge on the same Class 2 talus, moving carefully and staying alert for loose rock kicked down onto anyone below, back to Luna Pass. From the pass, retrace the heather-and-talus traverse east to Access Col, then descend the Access Couloir — loose scree/talus that many parties find faster (or even glissade-able on lingering snow) heading down than it was to climb, but still a rockfall hazard, especially with any party below on the same fall line. Continue down into the Access Creek basin to reclaim camp/gear. From there, follow the climbers' path back down Access Creek, recrossing to the north (true right) bank around 3,800 ft, continue through the brush and forest to the Access Creek/Big Beaver Creek confluence, cross Big Beaver Creek, and rejoin the maintained Big Beaver Trail back to Luna Camp and on to the Big Beaver Trailhead for the water-taxi pickup or the lakeshore walk-out. The South Ridge route as described (turning back at or near the false summit rather than continuing to Luna's true summit) is a walk/scramble the entire way — no fixed anchors, bolts, or rope work are needed or reported for this line. Parties who instead continue past the false summit toward Luna's true summit face a separate, distinct Class 3–4 exposed ledge traverse across the notch between the two summits, where some parties use a rope and running belays for protection rather than rappelling; that traverse is not part of this South Ridge route as scoped here.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is a straightforward reversal of the ascent line at any point; there is no shorter bailout given the peak's remoteness. The Class 3-4 step between the false and true summits is easily downclimbed, or a short handline/rappel can be rigged from a horn for less confident parties. Below Luna Col, the only way out is back down the access gullies to Access Creek and the Big Beaver Trail.

pitch_detail.notes: Broad talus ridge, roughly 1,100 ft of gain; some loose rock underfoot.
Narrow, exposed ridge traverse (~15-20 min), staying on or just below the crest, typically on the east side; solid rock but with loose blocks — the crux of the route.

itinerary.cal: North Cascades NP requires a backcountry wilderness permit for the Access Creek camp; Ross Lake Resort's water taxi, which saves ~6 miles of lakeshore hiking, typically runs late May through early October.

days.note: A long approach day: drop to Ross Lake and take the water taxi (or walk the lakeshore trail) to the Big Beaver trailhead, then follow the Big Beaver Trail roughly 10-11 miles past Luna Camp before leaving maintained trail to bushwhack and boulder-hop up the brushy Access Creek drainage to a high camp near 4,300-4,500 ft.

Round trip from camp runs 10-13 hours including rope work.

itinerary.totalNote: Shares the same remote 3-day Access Creek approach as the standard route, but the final link between the false and true summit is treated as a short roped pitch on the South Ridge rather than free-scrambled, adding time and gear to summit day.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee for advance backcountry reservations (walk-up permits carry no fee). No park entrance fee. The Ross Lake Resort water taxi is a separate optional paid service, charged per boat trip rather than per person - $110 to Big Beaver, carrying up to six passengers with standard backpacking gear.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: A bear canister or approved food storage is required where a proper hang isn't possible; free loaner canisters are available at the Wilderness Information Center. Practice Leave No Trace; off-trail cross-country travel is legal in this zone but stay on rock/snow/durable surfaces where possible to protect fragile heather meadows.
access.permit: A backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay, year-round. Reserve in advance on Recreation.gov (the general on-sale window opens around 7 a.m. Pacific in late April) or apply for a walk-up permit; permits must be picked up in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount. The Access Creek/Luna Camp zones carry limited nightly quotas and fill for summer weekends.
access.closures: SR 20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam Trailhead gate (MP 134) and the Silver Star/Early Winters gate (roughly MP 171–178), typically early December through mid-April, cutting off road access to the trailhead itself. The Ross Lake Resort water taxi runs seasonally, roughly June through October. Luna Fire closure (as of mid-September 2026): the Big Beaver Trail is closed from Big Beaver Stock Camp to Stillwell Camp, and Luna Camp, Beaver Pass Camp (with its stock and group camps) and 39 Mile Camp (with 39 Mile Stock) are closed; cross-country zone access from closed trails is prohibited. The closure moves - check current park fire closures before a trip.

road.name: Ross Lake Trailhead (off SR-20 near Ross Dam), then Ross Lake Resort water taxi
road.status: SR-20 to the Ross Lake Trailhead is paved; most parties take the seasonal Ross Lake Resort water taxi across the reservoir rather than hiking around, then a multi-day approach follows.
road.driveNote: Roughly 3 hours from Seattle via SR-20 to Ross Dam, plus the water taxi crossing and a multi-day wilderness approach.
road.seasonalGate: SR 20 is gated and closed roughly late November through early May each year (exact dates vary with snowpack).

climate.fall: Dry, stable stretches possible into October on south-facing terrain, but shortening days and the first snow can arrive with little warning.
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack in the approach gullies and on the ridge; stream fords are at their highest.
climate.summer: The main climbing window (Jul-Sep); still subject to sudden North Cascades convective storms and afternoon buildups.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible — SR-20 is gated and the approach is a serious winter mountaineering undertaking.
climate.typical: Wet, maritime-influenced North Cascades climate with a short, drier climbing window in mid-to-late summer; the range generates its own weather and cirques like Luna's hold snow late.
climate.forecastZone: NWS zone WAZ567 (West Slopes North Cascades and Passes); NWAC's West Slopes North zone is the nearest avalanche-forecast reference, though the Pickets themselves are outside NWAC's core forecast area

emergency.notes: Extremely remote wilderness with unreliable cell/satellite coverage per NPS guidance; expect a slow, likely helicopter-dependent rescue timeline given the multi-day, off-trail approach.

approach_variants.name: Access Creek to Access Col and Luna Pass, then straight up the broad south ridge
approach_variants.notes:
From the Ross Lake Trailhead off Hwy 20 near Ross Dam, most parties take the seasonal water taxi across the reservoir to the Big Beaver Trailhead at about 1,600 ft, skipping roughly 7 rolling lakeshore miles. From there the maintained Big Beaver Trail runs about 8 miles to Luna Camp, the standard permit basecamp, then roughly another 1.5 miles north.

Watch on the left, the west, for a boot path near where Access Creek enters Big Beaver Creek, and cross Big Beaver Creek there. A log crossing is sometimes usable, otherwise wade. That is where maintained trail ends.

Follow a surprisingly well-defined boot path along the north bank of Access Creek through semi-open forest. Near 3,700 ft the brush turns thick with slide alder, so cross to the south bank around 3,800 ft; several trip reports warn specifically that skipping this crossing leads to a miserable bushwhack. From the south bank, cairns and a fainter path link talus benches into the open upper basin at the Access Creek headwaters, the usual basecamp, with reliable water.

From camp, the Access Couloir gains roughly 1,500-2,000 ft of steep loose scree and talus, with a notably loose upper section of dirt and heather clumps, to Access Col at about 6,300 ft. From the col a faint path traverses west across heather and talus to Luna Pass, the Luna-McMillan col at about 7,200 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: Swift, sometimes swollen crossings of Big Beaver and Access Creek
Heavy slide-alder bushwhacking and genuine route-finding difficulty in Access Creek; multiple parties report following the wrong drainage
Loose rock in the Access Couloir and on the south ridge, with real rockfall risk onto climbers below
Lingering snow and possible avalanche exposure on the couloir and southeast snowfields in early season
No water above the Access Creek basin
approach_variants.baseFinding:
At Luna Pass the two routes on this peak part company, and the test is simple: this one goes straight up. From the pass, turn directly up the broad south ridge on class 2 talus, roughly 1,000-1,100 ft of gain, straight to Luna's false, southern summit. There is no traverse and no contour. If you are sidehilling across snowfields on Luna's southeast flank you are on the Southeast Slopes route, which is the other line from this same pass.

Arrival at the pass itself, which is the harder find: Luna Pass is the col between Luna Peak and a smaller tower to its left, at about 7,200 ft, reached by a faint traverse west from Access Col. It is a gap on a crest, not a shoulder. If the ground ahead of you keeps rising instead of dropping away on the far side, you have not reached it.

What going too far looks like, on the ridge: this route as scoped tops out at the false, southern summit. Continuing past it toward Luna's true summit means a separate exposed class 3-4 ledge traverse across the notch between the two summits, where some parties use a rope and running belays. That is beyond this route, and the notch is where you decide whether to take it on.

A named approach error, because multiple parties have made it: several report initially following the wrong drainage out of Big Beaver. Access Creek is the one with the boot path on its north bank and the 3,800 ft bank change; if there is no boot path, you are in the wrong creek.

bivy.name: Luna Col bivy, Luna cross-country zone
bivy.notes: Open bivy ground on the col above the Luna Cirque, reached by leaving the Big Beaver trail near Access Creek and climbing trackless ground to Access Col. It is the working high camp for Mount Fury's west peak and for Luna Peak, with no established site — you camp on rock, heather or snow and pack everything out. The brush on the Access Creek approach, which forces a bank change around 3,700 ft, is the part parties consistently underestimate.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and small tarns only; expect to melt snow once the basin dries out late in the season
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit required for the Luna cross-country zone. Walk-up only — this zone cannot be reserved in advance, so it is claimed in person at Marblemount. A party that has already driven and boated in can still be turned away if the night's slots are gone; carry a fallback itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Party limit 6; up to 6 parties per night in the Luna zone

bivy.name: Luna Camp, Big Beaver Trail
bivy.notes: The standard staging camp for the Access Creek side of the Northern Pickets — Mount Fury's west peak and the Luna Cirque generally. Most parties take the Ross Lake water taxi to the Big Beaver landing near 1,600 ft and then walk eight to ten miles of nearly flat old-growth trail, so it functions as a first night rather than a destination. The climbers' path leaves the maintained trail roughly a mile and a half beyond and crosses Big Beaver Creek near the Access Creek confluence; whether that crossing is a log or a wade varies year to year and with runoff.
bivy.water: Big Beaver Creek runs beside camp — reliable all season
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center; trail-corridor camp, reservable on Recreation.gov or walk-up. Closed under the Luna Fire closure as of the park's August 2026 list — confirm current status before building a trip around it.
bivy.capacity: Two 4-person sites; party limit 4; pit toilet, food hang

deleted_rows.name: South Face (2001 Variation)
deleted_rows.overview: Begins near the low-center of the south face at an obvious layback hand-crack (5.10, can be wet). Climb up and left to gain a rising ramp, then exit rightward in the upper section on fun 5.7-5.8 rock, topping out on the west ridge near the summit.

sectionBreakdown.note: Same approach as the West Ridge, but continue to the base of Lundin's south face instead of the couloir. Climb a crux layback hand-crack (5.10) low on the face, follow a left-trend…

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Small-to-medium alpine rock protection up to 3+ inches, plus runners.
deleted_rows.approach: The approach is essentially the same as the standard South Face route: from the Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead (I-90 Exit 52, ~3,000 ft), follow the PCT north about 2.5 miles to the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction and follow it into Commonwealth Basin. Shortly after crossing Commonwealth Creek (the last water on the approach), this line stays briefly on the climbers' path along the base of Red Mountain's flank before cutting left (northwest) off-trail into upper Commonwealth Basin to reach the base of Lundin's south face. The variation starts near the center and lowest point of the face, at an obvious layback, hand-sized crack - distinctly different from where the original South Face line starts, so look for the crack itself rather than following old route photos literally. Expect the same cross-country talus/boulder travel and lingering early-season snow in the basin as the standard South Face route.
deleted_rows.descent_text: No descent has been published specifically for the 2001 Variation, but since the route finishes up a left-trending ramp then breaks rightward near its top to join the West Ridge a short distance from the true summit, the natural way off is the same Southeast Ridge descent used for the standard South Face route: scramble the connecting ridge to the Southeast Ridge (Class 3-4) past its rock horns, with one roughly 25-meter rappel from a fixed natural (chockstone) anchor partway down to regain Class 2 ledges, then continue down to Commonwealth Basin and retrace the approach. Parties who'd rather not traverse back to the true summit could instead downclimb west along the West Ridge crest toward the Cave Ridge notch (Class 4, no fixed rappels reported on that side near the top), but that exits toward Alpental, a long way from the PCT-North trailhead, unless a shuttle is arranged.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the standard South Face approach. Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead (about 3,000 ft), PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles to the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction, then #1033 into Commonwealth Basin.

Shortly after the trail crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last water — leave the tread, either right there or after the path has begun to swing up onto Red Mountain's flank, and climb cross-country northwest into the upper basin beneath Lundin's south face.

Expect the same talus and boulder travel, and the same lingering early-season snow in the basin, as the standard route.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variation starts near the centre and lowest point of the face, at an obvious layback hand-sized crack. The crack is the identifier, not the position — look for the feature itself.

This matters more here than on most routes: the variation does not start where the original South Face line starts, so a party trying to match an old topo photo will be put in the wrong place. Find the layback crack near the low centre of the face and start there.

If you are on rock with no single obvious crack line, or the crack you have found is off toward one edge of the face rather than near its centre, keep looking along the base rather than committing.

deleted_rows.overview: Baring Mountain is the dramatic, steep-sided peak rising directly above the town of Baring on US-2, famous for its sheer north face. The standard south route is a notoriously brushy and steep climb with exposed scrambling to a small summit far harder than its elevation suggests.
deleted_rows.beta: A popular mountaineering route requiring moderate off-trail navigation skills. A fairly well-used climber's trail ascends approximately one mile to the ridge, then continues east to the notch between north and south peaks. Pink tape and cairns occasionally mark sections but are unreliable. An ice axe is recommended in spring and summer. Navigation can be challenging in bad weather; GPX/map recommended.
deleted_rows.turnaround: This is a full-day objective. Establish a turnaround time in early afternoon to ensure descent before dark, especially on descents.
deleted_rows.rappels: 0-1, conditional on snowpack and party. Most parties downclimb the notch step; in higher-snow years, or when it is icy, some rig a short rappel off natural anchors. No bolted or fixed anchors exist on this route.
deleted_rows.permit: No wilderness permit or quota is required. Northwest Forest Pass at developed trailheads.
deleted_rows.comms: Cell service is unreliable in the Barclay Lake/Baring Mountain drainage; download maps and directions before leaving cell coverage.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the route with possible rappel
obj_haz: steep off-trail brush on the ridge approach
possible lingering snow/ice at the notch

waypoints.name: Barclay Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Parking for ~20 cars plus a privy; the Baring climbers' path begins behind the outhouse rather than on the signed Barclay Lake trail.
waypoints.directions: Drive FR-6024 (Barclay Creek Road) off US-2 at Baring to its end at roughly 2,200-2,300 ft; the last stretch is rough enough that high clearance helps. The lot is shared with Barclay Lake hikers and the Gunn Peak climbers' path, so it fills on summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Old road / climbers'-trail split
waypoints.note: Follow the overgrown logging road about 1/3 mile to a cairn marking where the unmarked, brushy climbers' path breaks off toward the ridge.
waypoints.directions: Go around the back of the privy and pick up the overgrown logging-road grade. Follow it about a third of a mile to the first creek crossing, where a cairn marks the climbers' path turning uphill. Nothing here is signed.

waypoints.name: Steep dirt-and-creek ascent gully
waypoints.note: Path climbs a steep, muddy/loose-dirt gully next to a small creek with repeated crossings; poorly marked and the crux of routefinding in fog or after rain.
waypoints.directions: From the cairn the path turns sharply uphill and stays that way — a steep, eroded dirt gully beside a small creek, crossing it repeatedly, with occasional pink tape and cairns that cannot be relied on. This is where most parties lose the route, it is slick after rain, and there is no reliable water above the creek.

waypoints.name: West ridge crest
waypoints.note: Boot path tops out on Baring's west ridge; follow the ridge crest roughly the next mile through slide alder and forest.
waypoints.directions: Keep grinding up the wooded slope, roughly 1,800 ft of gain in about a mile from the road, with a short heavily-eroded Class 3 step below the top, before the path crests Baring's west ridge.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band bypass gully
waypoints.note: Cliffs block the ridge crest — drop briefly into a wooded gully on the south side to get around them, then regain the ridge/basin above.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge crest east and southeast for about a mile through slide alder and timber; a 2022 burn on the south-facing side has left loose ash and dirt that hides the tread. Where cliffs block the crest, drop briefly into a wooded gully on the south side to get around them — staying high on the crest is the standard mistake and forces a downclimb back to the correct line.

waypoints.name: Summit basin
waypoints.note: Boulder- and heather-filled basin beneath the twin summit gap; flattish talus here is used as an informal bivy by parties splitting the day.
waypoints.directions: Regain the ridge above the cliff bands and follow the faint path into the boulder-and-heather basin under the twin summits, crossing it toward its east side. This basin holds snow late into the season.

waypoints.name: North/south summit saddle
waypoints.note: Ascend the talus/boulder gully to the notch between Baring's north and south summit humps, then go left (north) for the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Climb the main talus and boulder gully out of the basin to the notch between South Baring and the true summit. The step at the notch is the crux of the day and changes year to year with snowpack — a short, steep snow wall wanting an axe in a heavy year, mostly loose talus by late summer. Turn north (left) at the notch for the true summit.

waypoints.name: Baring Mountain summit (Class 3-4 finish)
waypoints.note: Final scramble is easy hiking on heather giving way to blocky Class 3-4 rock to the true (north) summit; reverse the same brushy route to descend, with an optional rappel off the summit block.
waypoints.directions: From the notch scramble up and right a short distance, break out onto an open slope, then trend north across Class 2-3 boulders and heather roughly a quarter mile to the base of the summit block. Take the block on its left (west) side on Class 3-4 rock. Loose rock throughout — helmets on from the boulder field upward.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, follow the old logging road then a climbers' path up the right side of the creek, alternating banks before gaining the ridge near 4,000 ft. Travers…

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: No technical rack is needed for typical dry-condition ascents. This is an unroped Class 3-4 scramble up a brushy climber's trail, a snow/talus gully, and heather/talus slopes to the north/south peak notch, then easy scrambling to the summit. In early season or after rain the gully holds snow (ice axe, plus crampons/microspikes if firm), and when the summit-block heather is wet some parties choose to rope up for the class-4 moves — in that case a short 30-40m single rope with a handful of slings/small nuts is enough; this is not a route with an established protection rack.
what_to_bring: microspikes or crampons if the gully is icy/firm
pro_tips: Far harder than its elevation suggests
Expect a long, brushy battle on the approach
watch_out: dense brush
exposure and loose rock near the top
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection is essentially optional here — the terrain is loose/brushy/vegetated rather than clean rock, so any gear carried is for psychological security on one or two exposed class-4 steps, not for sustained protection. Most parties climb it entirely unroped in dry summer conditions.
deleted_rows.best_season: August
deleted_rows.approach: Park at the Barclay Lake Trailhead (~2,200 ft, end of FS Road 6024/Barclay Creek Road, 4WD recommended for the last stretch), which is shared parking for the Barclay Lake hike and the unofficial Baring/Gunn Peak climbers' paths. From the trailhead, go around the outhouse/toilet and pick up an old, overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — this is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail (look for cairns and a boot path; it is not a maintained trail and is easy to lose). The tread is very steep and often slick from the first steps, with no reliable water past the initial creek crossing, so carry what you need from the trailhead. After roughly 1 mile and about 1,800 ft of gain, the path tops out on Baring's west ridge (~4,000 ft). Follow the ridge crest generally east/southeast; there is a 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope here, which adds loose ash and dirt underfoot and can obscure the tread — it is easy to stay too long on the crest and have to downclimb back to the correct line, so watch for where the path dips slightly below cliff bands into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge. The route then drops into a talus/boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully/talus slope up to the notch (~5,550 ft) between South Baring and the main (true) summit — this gully and basin hold snow late into the season, so an ice axe (and possibly crampons) are recommended into mid-summer; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the 'vertical snow wall,' and its difficulty varies year to year with snowpack. From the notch, scramble up and right a short distance, break out onto an open slope, then trend left/north across class 2-3 boulder and heather terrain toward the base of the summit block. Climb the summit block on its left (west) side via class 3-4 moves to reach the true 6,127 ft summit. A helmet is recommended from the boulder field onward given loose rock, and the whole outing is a long day (allow 8-12+ hours car-to-car).
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the summit block (some parties report a short, wet class-3 crux move here rejoining the main path), cross back down to the notch, and descend the gully and basin back toward the west ridge — tedious and loose but faster than the climb up. This is a walk-off/downclimb for most parties in typical late-summer conditions, when the gully is mostly talus and scree and can be down-climbed or plunge-stepped. However, in higher-snow years or when the notch's vertical snow-wall step is icy or awkward, parties do rig a short rappel rather than downclimb it: one spring party built a rappel off natural anchors — a small rappel to a tree, then a single-strand rappel — using a 30m rope, to get past the steepest part of the gully/notch step. Treat this as conditional and optional rather than mandatory: it depends on the year's snowpack and the party's comfort downclimbing steep snow/ice with an axe. If you bring a rope for this contingency, a 30m single-strand rope anchored to trees is reported to be sufficient; no bolted or fixed anchors exist on this route — expect natural gear (trees, boulders) only. Below the ridge, retrace the west-ridge trail back down the steep, eroded, occasionally ash-covered climbers' path to the Barclay Lake Trailhead, moving carefully on the loose, muddy tread, especially through the 2022 burn-scar section.
deleted_rows.bail: If conditions deteriorate or party is moving slowly, return down the same route before dark. There are no bailout routes on the ridge; commitment is required.

pitch_detail.notes: ~550 ft of exposed scrambling up ledges from the ~5,550-5,600 ft notch between the south and true summits to the 6,127-ft true summit; a firm snow/ice wall is often present at the notch in early season.

itinerary.cal: Snow can linger in the summit gully/notch into early summer - carry an ice axe through June.

days.note: From the Barclay Lake trailhead, follow the old logging road then a climbers' path up the right side of the creek, alternating banks before gaining the ridge near 4,000 ft. Traverse below cliff bands, drop into the upper basin, and scramble Class 3 terrain to the summit (a short rappel may be needed at the notch on descent if wet). Round trip is roughly 5.3 miles with about 3,847 ft of gain, done comfortably in a day by fit parties.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead at the end of FR-6024 off US-2 near Baring

deleted_rows.rope_note: Unprotected scramble; published descriptions list protection as 'None'. Crux is a short, exposed Class 3-4 step on the summit block, which parties climb without placing gear. Ice axe recommended for the snow-holding gully in spring/early summer.
deleted_rows.corrections: None — brushy, dirty Class 3-4 gully to south (true) summit; not a standalone recommended objective but gear needs confirmed via Mountain Project route page and multiple trip reports.

approach_variants.name: Climbers' path behind the Barclay Lake trailhead outhouse
approach_variants.notes: Barclay Lake trailhead at about 2,200-2,280 ft at the end of FR 6024 / Barclay Creek Road, shared parking with the Barclay Lake day hike. Go around the outhouse and pick up the old overgrown logging-road grade for a few hundred yards before it turns sharply uphill into a steep, muddy, eroded gully — that is the start of the unmaintained climbers' trail. Look for cairns and boot tread; this is not a maintained trail and is easy to lose. The tread is steep and often slick from the first steps, and there is no reliable water past the initial creek, so fill up at the car. After roughly a mile and 1,800 ft the path tops out on Baring's west ridge at about 4,000 ft.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; the basin and notch gully hold snow late
hazards: Steep, muddy, eroded unmaintained tread from the first steps
Cliffing out by holding the crest too long
Loose ash and obscured tread in the burn scar
Late snow in the basin and notch gully — axe and possibly crampons into mid-summer
Loose rock from the boulder field onward — helmet
No water above the trailhead creek
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The west ridge crest at about 4,000 ft is the handover point — the angle eases and the tread improves noticeably. Follow the crest generally east/southeast. Where the cliff bands appear, watch for the point where the path dips slightly below them into a wooded gully before regaining the ridge; staying too long on the crest is the recorded error and forces a downclimb back to the correct line. The 2022 burn scar on the south-facing slope adds loose ash and hides the tread here.

The route then drops into a talus and boulder basin, crosses it, and climbs the main gully up to the notch at about 5,550 ft between South Baring and the true summit. That gully and basin hold snow late; the step right at the notch is sometimes called the vertical snow wall and its difficulty varies year to year. From the notch scramble up and right a short way, break onto an open slope, then trend left/north over class 2-3 boulder and heather to the base of the summit block, which is climbed on its left (west) side at class 3-4 to reach 6,127 ft.

climbing_route.label: 'Vertical snow wall' step at the 5,550 ft notch
climbing_route.notes: The main gully/talus slope tops out at the notch (~5,550 ft) between South Baring and the main (true) summit; this gully and the basin below hold snow late into the season, so an ice axe (and possibly crampons) are recommended into mid-summer. The step right at the notch is sometimes called the 'vertical snow wall,' and its difficulty varies year to year with snowpack.

climbing_route.label: Boulder and heather to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, scramble up and right a short distance, break out onto an open slope, then trend left/north across class 2-3 boulder and heather terrain toward the base of the summit block. A helmet is recommended from the boulder field onward given loose rock.

climbing_route.label: Summit block, left (west) side
climbing_route.notes: Climb the summit block on its left (west) side via class 3-4 moves to reach the true 6,127 ft summit.

deleted_rows.name: Finger Traverse
hazards: highly exposed narrow ledge traverse (the 'Finger Traverse')
loose rock
commitment once committed to the traverse
thin, marginal footholds despite the continuous positive handhold crack — a slip could still be caught by the crack, but exposure below is severe
deleted_rows.overview: A rock alternative to the adjacent Terrible Traverse, encountered above the South Chute around 7,400-7,450 ft. Climbers cross an airy, narrow ledge with thin footholds by jamming fingers into a continuous horizontal crack/flake that runs the length of the traverse, giving good hands even though the feet are marginal. Because it doesn't depend on snow conditions, many parties prefer it over the Terrible Traverse once it's dry.
deleted_rows.beta: On the standard South Chute approach, the Finger Traverse is crossed on the way to the summit and again on the descent. From the summit ridge near the Terrible Traverse, locate the downsloping ledge on the eastern side. Place your fingers in the horizontal crack running along the top edge and traverse carefully. The slab below is steep and exposure is extreme—a fall would be fatal. The traverse exits to easier terrain and rejoins the descent route.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround; the traverse is time-consuming if belayed
deleted_rows.rock_grade: Class 3-4 (exposed finger-crack ledge; a few 4th-class moves on the summit block)
deleted_rows.face: Upper South Face (crux traverse), below the summit block
deleted_rows.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the route or descend via the standard North Chimney line

waypoints.name: Dosewallips Road washout parking
waypoints.note: Parking where the Dosewallips Road is closed at the washout. The Lake Constance climbers' trail leaves the closed road about 5 mi farther on, at roughly 1,450 ft.
waypoints.directions: From US-101 at Brinnon, turn west onto the Dosewallips Road and drive about 9 miles to its end, where the road is bermed off at the washout; park here at about 550 ft. No parking pass is needed, but camping at Lake Constance requires an Olympic National Park wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Lake Constance
waypoints.directions: Walk or bike the closed Dosewallips Road about 5 miles to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,450 ft. Climb the steep, unmaintained boot path, roughly 3,300 ft in about 2 miles with roots and rock steps that need hands, to Lake Constance, and follow its east shore to the camps at the north end.

waypoints.name: Mount Constance (true/main summit)
waypoints.directions: From the north-end camps go north up Avalanche Canyon about 0.6 mile and turn east up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears tower comes into view, to the notch beside it. Cross the saddle, drop about 150 ft, climb a second scree gully to a notch, and follow ledges marked by cairns and faded white paint to the Finger Traverse. Past it, cross the snow basin, climb the ramp and scree to the ridge, and take the summit tower from its north side.

deleted_rows.approach: From the Dosewallips River Road washout (~mile 1, roughly 550 ft) it's about a 5-mile road-walk or bike-in on the now-closed road to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at approximately 1,450 ft, crossing Constance Creek on a couple of wooden footbridges near the start. From there the real work begins: the boot path gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in only 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance (4,800 ft), one of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutally steep and eases only slightly as it enters denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps requiring hands; expect scramble-grade (class 2-3) tread throughout with no switchbacks and cairn/flagging-based route-finding in spots. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours to the lake with a full pack. Water is available at Constance Creek partway up and at the lake/outlet — treat everything. From Lake Constance the trail skirts the east shore to established campsites at the north end, cupped in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon; most parties camp here rather than going car-to-car. From camp, head up scree into the canyon's lower basin, bend east along a rib, and pick up the 'Cat Ears' rock landmark marking the turn east into the South Chute. The South Chute is a long, narrowing scree gully climbing about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft — loose underfoot and much better done on residual early-season snow, since bare scree here is notoriously miserable and can sluff rock onto parties below. Above the chute, cross a saddle, drop about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge; the route then threads gaps and ledges (marked in places by faded white-paint dots) to the base of the Finger Traverse itself — an exposed, downsloping class 3 ledge above a large cliff where climbers jam their fingers into a crack running along the top edge for balance. A rusty, decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along the ledge for parties who want to protect it, though most cross carefully unroped. Figure a full alpine day from camp: 5-6+ hours above the lake to the summit.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent line: back across the Finger Traverse (now angled downward and around a blind corner, which most parties find mentally harder than the way up), down through the ridge notches and gaps, and back down the South Chute scree to Avalanche Canyon and Lake Constance. Lower in the chute the scree turns to dirt/fine gravel and many parties plunge-step or 'dirt-glissade' the last stretch — fast, but hard on ankles and knees. There is no mandatory rappelling on the standard Finger Traverse line; it is a walk-off/downclimb route. The one technical wrinkle is the small class 3-4 summit block near the top: a fixed sling/rap anchor is in place there and some parties do a short ~20 ft rappel off it, but just as many simply downclimb the block instead, so treat any rappel here as optional rather than required — a single-strand lower or short rap on a 30-60m rope is more than enough if used. Below the lake, reverse the steep 3,300+ ft climbers' trail back to the Dosewallips Road washout; this descent is hard on the knees and, in the wet Olympic climate, roots and rock steps get slick, so many parties report the hike out taking nearly as long as the climb. Not counting the closed road walk, a round trip from the Lake Constance trail start to the summit and back runs about 8 miles with roughly 6,400 ft gained and lost.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat off the traverse before committing if conditions are poor; return to Lake Constance

pitch_detail.notes: From camp at the north end of Lake Constance, go north up Avalanche Canyon about 0.6 mile on talus, scree and old snow; cairns and a faint path help in places. Start up the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears come into view. That is the tower just north of the chute's top notch, and starting early skips much of the worst scree. In early season the canyon carries serious avalanche exposure.

Climb east up the broad chute, gaining about 1,200 ft, to the notch at the low point of the South Ridge (about 6,560 ft) beside the Cat Ears. Bare, it is tiring loose scree that sends rock onto anyone below. It is much better on firm early-season snow. The buttress beside the gully offers bigger rock, at the cost of a short 4th-class move over down-sloping slabs.

Cross to the east side of the ridge and traverse north about 200 yards below cliffs. Then climb a broad scree gully system to an obvious notch in a minor east–west ridge. Go through the notch and drop a short way to a scree or snow ledge. Early in the season that snow can be hard and steep, and parties sometimes use the moat along the rock.
pitch_detail.pitch: Scree gully to the east–west ridge notch

pitch_detail.notes: Contour north around a rock outcrop to a second notch; the Terrible Traverse line drops down a snow chute from here. For the Finger Traverse, make a rising traverse over gravel-strewn, sloping slab ledges on the east side of the ridge. Cairns and a couple of white painted marks show the line, so stay just above them. From here on there are cliffs below.

A narrowing ledge, then a down-sloping slab around a blind corner above a cliff of 1,000 ft or more. A continuous horizontal crack along the top takes the fingers. Feet are scarce for the last few steps, and the step from ledge onto slab is the crux. Old pitons at the start make an anchor. An alcove boulder halfway, a horn, a #1 cam and a rusty piton past the corner protect it. A 4th-class bypass goes around the west side. Treat it as far harder when wet.

Past the traverse, keep along the east side of the ridge and descend into the snow basin (a half-bowl) below the summit ridge. Climb scree and rock right of the cliffs to a diagonal, down-sloping ramp that cuts a large cliff face. Use the wall on its left for handholds and expect loose rock. The ramp tops out on an open scree slope below the summit.

Grind up the scree to a small headwall, then scramble roughly 100 ft onto the ridge. A deep gap separates the ridge from the summit tower, so follow the crest north past it and come back to where it connects. The standard way up the tower is on its north side, above a huge drop. A Class 3 line on the east side is also used.

itinerary.cal: Lake Constance camping needs an Olympic NP wilderness permit (limited nightly quota via recreation.gov in summer), and the Dosewallips Road, washed out in a January 2002 storm and still listed as washed out on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026, adds a several-mile bike/walk before the actual trailhead each way.

Camp on the north side of the lake (permit required).
