approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Dosewallips Road (FR-2610) washout parking near Brinnon

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
From the Dosewallips River Road washout at roughly 550 ft, about 5 miles of road-walk or bike on the closed road, crossing Constance Creek on wooden footbridges near the start, to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,450 ft.

The trail gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — one of the steepest approaches in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutal and eases only slightly into denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps needing hands. Expect scramble-grade tread with no switchbacks and cairn-and-flagging route-finding in places. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a full pack. Water at Constance Creek partway and at the lake outlet; treat everything.

The trail skirts the lake's east shore to established campsites at the north end, in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Most parties camp there rather than going car to car. From camp, head north up scree into the canyon's lower basin, then bend east along a rib.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Residual snow in the South Chute makes it a far better climb than bare scree does
hazards: The Finger Traverse is a highly exposed, downsloping narrow ledge; footholds are marginal even with the crack in hand
Reversing it on descent goes round a blind corner and most parties find that harder than the way up
1,900 ft of loose scree in the South Chute, which sluffs rock onto parties below
The fixed pitons on the traverse are decades old — do not trust them without inspection
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics; the descent takes many parties nearly as long as the climb
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is a tower called the Cat Ears, and the published instruction is a trigger rather than a description: begin climbing the South Chute as soon as the Cat Ears are visible. Follow Avalanche Canyon north from the lake — roughly 0.6 mile — and watch east. The Cat Ears is the tower standing just left of the notch you are aiming for at the top of the chute. The moment it comes into view, turn east and start up. Starting later means more scree; starting earlier puts you on the wrong ground.

In cloud, when the Cat Ears cannot be seen, the fallback is the chute's own shape. The South Chute is a long gully that narrows as it climbs, gaining about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft at the notch in the south ridge. It is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake. If the gully you are in is widening rather than narrowing, or if you are still walking north up the canyon bed after well over half a mile, you have passed it and are heading for the North Chute and the Terrible Traverse instead.

Second test, and it is what confirms you were right about the chute: above the notch you cross a saddle, drop about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge. A route that only ever goes up is not this one — the deliberate loss of height above the first notch is part of the line. From there the route threads gaps and ledges marked in places by faded white paint dots. Painted dots are man-made, they do not move, and they are visible at arm's length in fog; if you are seeing them you are on the line.

The finger traverse itself is a tactile test, which is the best kind here: a downsloping ledge above a large cliff with a horizontal crack running along its top edge, which you jam your fingers into for balance because the footholds are thin. A rusty decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along it. If there is no continuous crack at hand height above the ledge you are standing on, that is not the Finger Traverse.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail entirely. From the Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles, about 1.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off, to the old campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end. Take the Constance Pass Trail up through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft, then leave the trail and go cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and up to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif.

From Crystal Pass descend south into Avalanche Canyon on an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the north side of the canyon, and continue down the canyon toward the lake until the South Chute opens on your left (east).

This is considerably longer than the lake approach and it exists because the lake trail is brutally steep, unmaintained and blowdown-choked. Most parties on it are on a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Unmarked cross-country travel between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass, on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass beyond transient snowmelt
Every hazard on the Finger Traverse itself, reached at the end of a longer day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Entering the canyon from Crystal Pass puts the Cat Ears test the other way up: you must descend past the North Chute before the South Chute opens. The Cat Ears tower and the formation trip reports call the Thumb both sit in this stretch of canyon, and on this side you pass them going down rather than meeting them going up.

The reliable test on this side is the chute's top, not its bottom. The South Chute tops out at a notch in the south ridge at roughly 6,600 ft, with the Cat Ears tower standing just left of that notch. Coming down the canyon from Crystal Pass you can pick your entry by which notch the gully above you leads to: the one with a tower just left of it is the South Chute. The chute that leads straight toward the Terrible Traverse without a tower beside its notch is the North Chute.

Above the chute the tests are identical to the lake approach and they are the good ones: cross the saddle, lose about 150 ft, up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge, then gaps and ledges marked with faded white paint dots, then a downsloping ledge with a continuous horizontal finger crack along its top edge and old fixed pitons in it.

Honest limit: the track fades near Crystal Pass and the drop into the canyon is unmarked. This variant is longer and navigationally harder; it is chosen for the trail it avoids, not for the ground it crosses.

climbing_route.label: South Chute
climbing_route.notes: Turn east into the South Chute at the 'Cat Ears' rock landmark. A long, narrowing scree gully climbing about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft. Loose underfoot and much better done on residual early-season snow, since bare scree here is notoriously miserable and can sluff rock onto parties below.

climbing_route.label: Saddle and second scree gully to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Above the chute, cross a saddle, drop about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge.

climbing_route.label: Gaps and ledges to the traverse
climbing_route.notes: From the notch the route threads gaps and ledges, marked in places by faded white-paint dots, to the base of the Finger Traverse itself.

climbing_route.label: Finger Traverse
climbing_route.notes: An exposed, downsloping ledge above a large cliff, where climbers jam their fingers into a crack running along the top edge for balance. A rusty, decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along the ledge for parties who want to protect it, though most cross carefully unroped. Figure 5-6+ hours above the lake to the summit.

bivy.name: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute
bivy.notes: The base camp for essentially every ascent by the standard South Chute, reached by a savage climbers' path that gains roughly 3,300 to 3,400 ft in under two miles of hand-over-hand scrambling above the Dosewallips road. Published elevations for the lake vary between about 4,650 and 4,800 ft, a fair reflection of how imprecise everything about this approach is. From camp the route runs north into Avalanche Canyon and then up the chute toward the south ridge notch, so a summit day from here is short by Olympic standards. The 20-person ceiling is the real planning constraint — it is a basin, not a campground, and it is full most fine weekends.
bivy.water: Reliable at the lake itself. Constance Creek, which the climbers' trail follows, runs well early in the season and can be dry by late summer — carry water up rather than assuming you will find it on the climb.
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and Lake Constance is a named quota area. Reserve on Recreation.gov; the 20-person cap makes this one of the scarcest permits in the Olympics. Bear canisters required. Older write-ups describing a free self-issued permit at the trailhead are out of date.
bivy.capacity: Hard overnight quota of 20 people for the whole basin; roughly five individual sites plus one group site are commonly reported, and parties of seven or more must take the group site

deleted_rows.overview: The Terrible Traverse is the historic crux of the standard Mount Constance route: an exposed, steep snow traverse across a cirque above a sheer cliff, encountered around 7,400-7,450 ft while crossing from the South Chute notch toward the summit block — a fall here would likely be fatal, hence the name. When it still holds hard snow (common through June and into July in heavier-snow years), published descriptions recommend carrying and placing 2-3 pickets for protection; many parties instead take the parallel rock alternative, the Finger Traverse, once conditions allow.
deleted_rows.beta: The Terrible Traverse is crossed on the way up and again on the way down, unless the party descends by the Finger Traverse instead. Parties locate the Australia-shaped snowfield (exposed ridge line with precipitous drop below). The traverse crosses steep, exposed snow above a massive cliff. Early season parties must be equipped with ice axes and crampons; self-arrest techniques and belay skills are essential. Many climbers place pickets for protection or opt for the Finger Traverse bypass instead.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Treat the traverse as the decision point; turn around if conditions are poor
deleted_rows.rappels: Possible to rappel the traverse section if pickets are placed, though most parties downclimb or traverse carefully without rappelling.
deleted_rows.face: Upper South Face (crux traverse), ~7,435 ft, below the summit block
deleted_rows.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
deleted_rows.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.
obj_haz: A slip is essentially unrecoverable — the runout funnels to a ~500 ft cliff

waypoints.name: Dosewallips Road washout parking
waypoints.note: Same approach as Finger Traverse/North Chimney; Terrible Traverse is the original/harder crux crossing that Finger Traverse became the popular alternative to.
waypoints.directions: From US 101 at Brinnon, turn west onto Dosewallips Road (FR 2610) at milepost 306, just north of Dosewallips State Park, and drive about 8.5 miles to where the road is closed to vehicles at the washout; park along the roadside. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required to park.

waypoints.name: Lake Constance
waypoints.directions: Walk or bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed about 5 miles up the valley to the Lake Constance climbers' path at about 1,400 ft. The steep, unmaintained path gains about 3,300 ft in roughly 2 miles, past Half Acre Rock at 0.8 mile and over exposed rock ledges and short cliff bands above 1.3 miles, to the lake; camps are at its north end.

waypoints.name: Mount Constance (true/main summit)
waypoints.directions: Go up Avalanche Canyon past the Thumb and climb the South Chute, turning east as soon as the Cat Ears come into view, to the saddle near 6,600 ft. Drop a little, climb the second scree gully to the notch near 7,300 ft, then lose a little height and traverse north on ledges to cross the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft. Beyond it, follow the Key Ledge onto the upper scree slope and finish up the summit block.

deleted_rows.pro_needs: Limited pro on the traverse; many parties belay or use a running belay across it
deleted_rows.best_season: Mid-July through September (after the traverse melts out)
deleted_rows.approach: Same demanding approach as the standard route: roughly 5 miles of road-walking/biking up the washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail (~1,450 ft), then a punishing, unmaintained boot path gaining roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance (4,800 ft) — steep from the first half-mile, with exposed roots and rock steps requiring hands and no real switchbacks. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours and treat water at Constance Creek or the lake. From the established camps at the lake's north end, head up into Avalanche Canyon on scree/talus (firm snow, when present, makes this section far faster and safer than bare scree). Like the Finger Traverse, this route climbs the South Chute, a long, loose gully to a notch near 6,600 ft, then a second gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft. From there the route loses a little elevation and traverses north on ledges to reach the base of the Terrible Traverse itself at about 7,435 ft — a steep, exposed snow (or, late-season, bare rock ledge) crossing directly above a large cliff, where a fall would be unsurvivable. Conditions vary considerably by season: early-to-mid summer it's a hard, steep snow traverse best done with an ice axe and crampons; by late season it often melts back to a narrow but more secure rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above, which many parties find preferable. Some parties place running protection (pickets in snow) across the traverse given the consequences of a slip, though it is not a roped rappel move.
deleted_rows.descent_text: From the summit, the standard plan is to reverse the Terrible Traverse — but be aware parties often describe bypassing it on descent in poor visibility, wet snow, or softened afternoon conditions, instead going down via the Finger Traverse and South Chute, which many parties consider the safer late-day option. If you do reverse the Terrible Traverse, expect the same steep, exposed snow (or bare ledge, late season) crossing above the cliff, now with the added psychological weight of down-facing exposure. Below the traverse, return to the upper notch and drop back down the South Chute's loose scree/talus into Avalanche Canyon, retrace the canyon to Lake Constance, and descend the steep climbers' trail to the road. There is no mandatory rappelling on the Terrible Traverse or its connecting chute — it is a walk-off/downclimb descent. As with the other Constance summit routes, an optional short ~20 ft rappel off a fixed sling/anchor is available on the class 3-4 summit block for parties who don't want to downclimb it; treat this as optional, not required, and a single 30-60m rope is sufficient if used. A helmet is essential given the terrain — the chute and traverse are classic Olympic choss, and rockfall or sluffing snow from parties above is a real hazard.
deleted_rows.bail: Once committed to the traverse there is no easy retreat — downclimbing back across exposed, potentially icy terrain is often more dangerous than finishing the crossing, so assess snow conditions from the notch before starting across.

pitch_detail.notes: An unrelenting boot path gains about 3,300–3,400 ft in roughly 2 miles from the Dosewallips Road to Lake Constance. The lower part runs through an old burn. It is steep from the start, with roots and rock steps that need hands and a few exposed spots. Camps sit at the lake's north end; treat water from the creek or lake.

From the north end of the lake, head up Avalanche Canyon between Mount Constance and Inner Constance on boulders and talus, with snow patches into summer. Firm snow is faster and safer than bare scree. A climbers' path threads the talus in places. Start before dawn to be off the upper route before the snow softens.

Pass the Thumb and climb the long South Chute, marked by the Cat Ears, to a saddle near 6,600 ft with heather benches and bivy spots. It narrows and gets loose near the top. From the saddle drop about 175 ft, then turn left up a wide scree gully that narrows to a notch in the east–west ridge. A ledge up its left side is easier and safer. Rockfall between parties is constant, so keep close together.

From the notch, drop about 75 ft on steep snow or loose scree, then turn left and contour toward the north–south summit ridge. Here the line splits. The Finger Traverse is up and around a corner on an exposed ledge. The Terrible Traverse is reached by crossing hard-packed scree with a bad runout to a cairned ledge that leads north.

A steep snow cirque whose danger is the runout: a funnel into a cliff of roughly 500 ft. When it holds hard snow, pickets and front-pointing are standard. Late season it melts back to scree and rock-and-heather benches beneath it. The alternative Finger Traverse is a Class 3 but very exposed down-sloping ledge, with a crack at its top edge for the hands. It can be bypassed west of the crest via a short chockstone chimney.

Past the traverse, drop to talus on the east side and follow the Key Ledge, a broad sidewalk-like ledge along the foot of a vertical wall, onto the upper scree slope. Climb to the crest of the headwall and follow it east around to the southeast corner of the summit block. The pillow-basalt rock is fun but still loose in places.

Solid 4th-class rock on the block's southeast corner. A short Class 3 chimney leads to a couple of exposed 4th-class moves and the top. On the way down, many parties rappel the block from a fixed sling rather than downclimbing it. Inspect that sling before trusting it.

itinerary.cal: Lake Constance camping needs an Olympic NP wilderness permit (limited nightly quota via recreation.gov), and the Dosewallips Road washout adds a multi-mile bike/walk before the trailhead each way; the traverse often still holds snow well into summer, so an axe is commonly carried.

deleted_rows.corrections: Sources disagree on summit elevation: older guidebook/SummitPost/Mountaineers material cites 7,743 ft, while Wikipedia and PeakVisor give 7,756 ft; this record uses the higher, more recently-sourced figure. The 1922 first ascent (Schellin & Smith, via a southeast line) is the peak's first ascent, not a confirmed first ascent of today's specific South Chute/Terrible Traverse line, so it is listed here with that caveat rather than as a verified route FA. gainFt (6,356 ft) is computed from the sourced trailhead elevation (~1,400 ft) to the sourced summit elevation (7,756 ft); actual cumulative gain is higher once the washed-out road approach and terrain undulation are included, and will continue to shift as the Dosewallips Road washout evolves.

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail and Avalanche Canyon to the South Chute
approach_variants.notes:
Road-walk or bike about 5 miles up the washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at roughly 1,450 ft. The trail is unmaintained and gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — steep from the first half-mile, exposed roots and rock steps needing hands, no real switchbacks. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a pack. Camp at the lake's north end.

From camp, head up into Avalanche Canyon on scree and talus. Firm snow, when it is there, makes this whole section faster and safer than bare scree. This route takes the same South Chute as the Finger Traverse, then a second gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft. From there the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to reach the Terrible Traverse itself at about 7,435 ft.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Steep hard snow persists longer on the Terrible Traverse than on any other crux on this mountain, which is exactly the point of it
hazards: The Terrible Traverse crosses steep firm snow directly above a large cliff — an unprotected slip is very likely fatal
Hard, icy neve is common through June and early July; afternoon softening increases slip risk later in the day
Loose rock throughout the South Chute — classic Olympic choss, and rockfall from parties above is a real hazard
Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes, called out specifically for May-June conditions
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics, hard on the way down and slick when wet
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The test is the Cat Ears, and it is a trigger: start up the South Chute as soon as that tower comes into view. Walk north up Avalanche Canyon from the lake past the Thumb and watch east. The Cat Ears is a rock tower standing just left of the notch at the top of the South Chute; once you can see it, turn east and climb. If you are still walking up the canyon bed well after it appeared, you are heading for the North Chute instead.

In cloud, when the tower is hidden, use the chute's shape: the South Chute is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake, and it narrows as it climbs to the notch at about 6,600 ft.

Second test, above that notch: the line drops a little, climbs a second scree gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft, then loses height again and traverses north on ledges. Here the two crossings part company. The Finger Traverse goes up and around a corner on a ledge with a horizontal finger crack along its top; the Terrible Traverse is reached over hard-packed scree to a cairned ledge heading north, and you meet the crossing itself at about 7,435 ft. It is unmistakable when you arrive: a steep exposed snow slope directly above a large cliff, or in late season a narrow rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above it. It is called the Terrible Traverse because a slip there does not stop.

What the season changes: early to mid summer this is hard steep snow wanting an axe, crampons and, for many parties, pickets. Late season it often melts back to that rock ledge, which most parties find more secure. Neither is the wrong condition; they are different climbs.

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.notes:
The long way in, and the one parties choose to avoid the Lake Constance trail. From the same Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 1.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Published trail mileages differ by several miles depending on where the count starts, so none is quoted. The upper stretch is open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass descend into upper Avalanche Canyon — which is where this variant differs usefully from the lake approach, because it puts you in the canyon above the lake rather than below it.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow remnant below Crystal Pass is safe or gone
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and the descent into upper Avalanche Canyon is unmarked
Early-season snow remnant below Crystal Pass may want an axe and, for some parties, a rope
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt — carry it
All the Terrible Traverse hazards above, reached by a longer and more committing line
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming in from Crystal Pass you enter Avalanche Canyon from above, so you must descend past the North Chute before the South Chute opens. Dropping south into the canyon, the first couloir you meet on the Constance side is the North Chute; keep going down the canyon toward the lake.

The fixed landmarks on this stretch are the Cat Ears tower and the Thumb. The gully you want is the one whose top notch, at roughly 6,600 ft, has the Cat Ears tower standing just left of it: that is the South Chute. If you reach the lake you have gone below it.

Above the chute the test is the same as the lake approach: a short drop and a second gully to the upper notch near 7,300 ft, then the route loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft — a steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, or a narrow rock ledge in late season.

Honest limit: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and lingering snow with real route-finding. This variant trades a brutal trail for a navigation problem; in cloud it is the harder of the two.

climbing_route.label: South Chute
climbing_route.notes: The same South Chute used for the Finger Traverse — a long, loose gully to a notch near 6,600 ft, then a second scree gully to a higher notch near 7,300 ft. Firm snow, when present, makes the scree/talus below far faster and safer than bare scree.

climbing_route.label: Ledges north to the traverse
climbing_route.notes: From the upper notch the route loses a little elevation and traverses north on ledges to reach the base of the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft.

climbing_route.label: Terrible Traverse
climbing_route.notes: A steep, exposed snow (or, late-season, bare rock ledge) crossing directly above a large cliff, where a fall would be unsurvivable. Early-to-mid summer it is a hard, steep snow traverse best done with an ice axe and crampons; by late season it often melts back to a narrow but more secure rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above, which many parties find preferable. Some parties place running protection (pickets in snow) given the consequences of a slip, though it is not a roped rappel move.

bivy.name: Lake Constance — the standard base for the South Chute
bivy.notes: The base camp for essentially every ascent by the standard South Chute, reached by a savage climbers' path that gains roughly 3,300 to 3,400 ft in under two miles of hand-over-hand scrambling above the Dosewallips road. Published elevations for the lake vary between about 4,650 and 4,800 ft, a fair reflection of how imprecise everything about this approach is. From camp the route runs north into Avalanche Canyon and then up the chute toward the south ridge notch, so a summit day from here is short by Olympic standards. The 20-person ceiling is the real planning constraint — it is a basin, not a campground, and it is full most fine weekends.
bivy.water: Reliable at the lake itself. Constance Creek, which the climbers' trail follows, runs well early in the season and can be dry by late summer — carry water up rather than assuming you will find it on the climb.
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and Lake Constance is a named quota area. Reserve on Recreation.gov; the 20-person cap makes this one of the scarcest permits in the Olympics. Bear canisters required. Older write-ups describing a free self-issued permit at the trailhead are out of date.
bivy.capacity: Hard overnight quota of 20 people for the whole basin; roughly five individual sites plus one group site are commonly reported, and parties of seven or more must take the group site

deleted_rows.fa: 1907, L.A. Nelson and party (first ascent of Mount Olympus)
gear: Rope, harness, crampons, ice axe for the Blue Glacier approach and Snow Dome
1-2 ice screws for crevasse-rescue anchors — this is a standard glacier walk, not steep ice, so pickets are not needed
A few stoppers/nuts and a tricam or two, plus long runners — protects the exposed 5.4 moves on the chossy summit dihedral, which is described as pocket-and-edge terrain rather than crack terrain
Helmet — loose rock on the ramps and real rockfall exposure from parties above
hazards: Documented fatal accident, 1993: an unroped fall near Snow Dome.

Frequent whiteout conditions on the crevassed Snow Dome complicate route-finding.
deleted_rows.overview: This is the standard finish on the highest summit in the Olympics, reached after one of the longest approaches in the Lower 48. After miles of rainforest and a glacier crossing, the climb tops out by winding up a series of loose ramps on the east face of the summit pinnacle. The moves are moderate, but the rock is rotten and an exposed corner is best protected — a small, serious finale to a big wilderness peak.
deleted_rows.beta: From Glacier Meadows, descend to the Blue Glacier lateral moraine and rope up for glacier travel. Cross the Blue Glacier for approximately 1 mile with crevasse avoidance and careful snow bridge assessment. Ascend the broad Snow Dome to 6,600-7,000 feet. From Snow Dome, ascend toward Crystal Pass at 7,250 feet. After crossing Crystal Pass and traversing Five Fingers Ridge, encounter the false summit before the final push. The crux involves Class 4-5 scrambling on loose rocky ramps on the East Face, with one Class 5 step. The final 50-60 feet involves several Class 5.3-5.4 moves on mostly solid rock to reach the summit block belay ledge, then 50 feet of Class 5.3-5.4 rock to the true summit.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Be off the block and recrossing the Snow Dome by early afternoon; on busy weekends the block bottlenecks, so hold to the 2-3 AM start. Early season the ramps may be iced; late season a moat can block access to the east ledges.
deleted_rows.rappels: 1 rappel off the summit block, roughly 80 ft, from the summit anchor at the top of the block down the north side of the block.
deleted_rows.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
deleted_rows.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable throughout the Hoh River valley and Olympic backcountry. Service may be available at the trailhead but not in the wilderness. Satellite communicators (Garmin InReach, SPOT device) are highly recommended for emergency communication and tracking. Radio frequencies are not reliably available in the Olympics.
deleted_rows.descent: Rappel the summit block, reverse the Snow Dome and Blue Glacier to the moraine, then the Hoh River Trail.

waypoints.name: Hoh Ranger Station
waypoints.directions: From Forks, drive south on US 101 about 13 miles and turn east onto the Upper Hoh Road. Follow it about 18 miles to its end at the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center, where the Hoh River Trail begins. An Olympic National Park entrance pass is required, and overnight trips need a wilderness camping permit.

waypoints.name: Olympus Guard Station
waypoints.directions: Follow the Hoh River Trail east up the valley through flat old-growth rain forest, passing Five Mile Island, to the Olympus Guard Station near mile 9.

waypoints.name: Mount Olympus West Peak
waypoints.directions: From Snow Dome go up and over Crystal Pass, minding the large crevasse near it, then traverse below the south side of Five Fingers Ridge and over the false summit. Drop into the sharp saddle and climb the short steep snow slope to the flat platform at the foot of the 80 ft summit tower. Turn right around the corner onto the east face and climb the loose ramps angling across it to the final Class 4/5.4 step to the top.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: The summit block needs only a light rack: a few nuts and a tricam or two, or three or four small-to-medium cams (roughly 0.5-2 inches). Include 2-3 quickdraws, multiple slings (60 cm and 120 cm), and lockers for anchor building. The East Face ramps are often ascended with minimal protection due to poor rock quality; protection is intermittent and bomber placements are rare. Bring 2-3 ice screws (10 cm length) for ice/névé anchors on Snow Dome. Rappel anchors typically use natural rock features or pre-existing slings, but climbers should build solid anchors as backups.
what_to_bring: Ice axe (55-75 cm mountaineering axe with adze and pick)
Crampons (12-point steel with anti-balling plates for wet snow)
Alpine harness with adjustable leg loops
Helmet (mandatory for rockfall hazard on East Face)
Rope (40-60m, 8-9mm dynamic rope for glacier and summit block climbing)
Crevasse rescue kit: prusiks (120 cm and 240 cm cord), mechanical ascenders (Micro Traxion or Nano Traxion), locking carabiners (at least 4), ice screws
Small rock climbing rack: a few nuts and tricams or 3-4 small-to-medium cams, quickdraws, slings (various lengths), rappel anchors (cordellette)
Glacier glasses or goggles with UV protection and side shields
Map, compass, GPS device, and altimeter watch
Insulated water bottle (32 oz) with insulation to prevent freezing at altitude
Down jacket or synthetic insulation layer
Windproof and waterproof outer shell jacket and pants
Insulated, waterproof gloves and expedition mittens
Lightweight base layer (merino wool or synthetic)
Gaiters to keep crampons and snow out of boots
Emergency/repair kit: duct tape, cordage, knife, first aid supplies
Food: high-calorie snacks for 4-5 days (nuts, energy bars, dried fruit, electrolyte supplements)
Sleeping bag rated to at least 10F (-12C)
Tent with four-season rating for Olympic weather
Stove and fuel (canisters, or liquid fuel for cold temperatures)
Water treatment (tablets or filter for glacial meltwater)
Bear canister (required for all overnight camping)
Blue bags for human waste (required by NPS on Mount Olympus)
pro_tips: Start summit day in pre-dawn darkness (2-3 AM) to minimize rockfall exposure on the East Face and avoid afternoon thunderstorms
Carry a 60-meter rope late season (July-August onward) to avoid multiple rappel stations; 40-50m may require intermediate anchors and extra time
Use a small, lightweight alpine rack (a few nuts or small cams, slings, quickdraws); most teams climb the summit block with minimal gear and good footwork
The Snow Dome is a broad, gently sloping platform; in whiteout conditions, use a GPS waypoint or compass bearing to navigate toward Crystal Pass to avoid wandering
Acclimatize at Glacier Meadows for at least one full day before summit attempt; the 4,200-7,980 ft push in a single day is taxing
Bring extra layers and a windproof shell; the summit is severely exposed and weather can change in minutes
watch_out: Loose rock on the East Face ramps — many parties now prefer the NW-edge or N-face summit-block finishes for more solid rock
Crevasses on the Blue Glacier and Snow Dome, worst late season
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection is essential for the Class 5 pitches on the summit block, with solid rock only in sections. Expect variable protection quality due to loose or fractured stone. Place all protection carefully, test holds, and be prepared to retreat if protection opportunities are poor or nonexistent. The ramps offer minimal protection; many parties choose to simulclimb the East Face ramps.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late June through August most reliable; May ascents see firmer snow but colder, less settled weather
deleted_rows.approach: This is the same approach as the standard North Ridge/Blue Glacier route to the point where the routes diverge on the final summit pyramid. From the Hoh Ranger Station (578 ft), follow the Hoh River Trail roughly 17.2-17.5 miles and about 3,700 ft of gain to Glacier Meadows (4,200-4,300 ft), via Lewis Meadows (10.5 mi), the High Hoh Bridge (13.2 mi), and Elk Lake (15 mi); expect a fixed-rope ladder crossing a washout about 0.25 mile before camp, and steep early-season snow between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows requiring axe and crampons. From Glacier Meadows, a way trail climbs about 0.8 mile onto the lateral moraine crest, follows it roughly 0.2 mile, then descends onto the Blue Glacier (rockfall hazard on this descent). Rope up and cross the glacier, climbing through/around rock islands and staying left (south) of the largest rock buttress to reach the crest of Snow Dome (6,600 ft) — good camps exist in the rocks below and on top of Snow Dome near the Panic Peak weather station. From Snow Dome, head south-southeast through one of two passes flanking the five-fingered false summit east of the true summit, dropping into the sharp saddle between the false summit and the (now visible) true summit pyramid. This is where the East Face Ramps finish diverges from the more direct standard line: instead of the shortest line to the base of the summit rock, this variation climbs a series of ramps angling up and across the east face of the summit pyramid before joining the final Class 4/5.4 step to the top. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass, usually crossed on a snow bridge, is a key hazard on the glacier portion, and route-finding through the rock islands and false-summit passes is the crux of the upper mountain in flat light.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descend by reversing the East Face Ramps line back to the saddle below the false summit, or drop directly to the standard Snow Dome line once off the summit block — both funnel back into the same Blue Glacier/moraine descent. From the top, build/use the summit anchor at the base of the 80 ft summit rock and rappel the block's north side; this is described in route notes as a double-rope rappel, meaning either two ropes joined for one long rappel or a doubled single rope depending on party gear and season, generally wanting 50-60m of rope to comfortably reach the notch/belay ledge below as snow recedes over the summer. Anchor material is natural/fixed slings on rock features (not bolts) — some seasons have a thin fixed line in place, but back it up. From the base of the block, downclimb/glissade the snow slope (mind runout and any bergschrund) back to the Snow Dome plateau, re-rope for the glacier, retrace the moraine catwalk to Glacier Meadows, and follow the Hoh River Trail 17+ miles out, watching for the ladder/washout and any early-season snow between Elk Lake and Glacier Meadows.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat down the glacier to Glacier Meadows is straightforward from almost anywhere below the summit block.

pitch_detail.notes: East-face ramps on loose rock; one exposed corner worth a fixed line or belay; rockfall from above.

itinerary.cal: The 'Fourth of July' direct gully has been reported out/closed by bergschrund conditions in several recent seasons, making these east-side ramps the default line — check recent trip reports before relying on the direct finish.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center (about 578 ft) the Hoh River Trail runs east up the valley for roughly 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at about 4,300 ft, past Five Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station near mile 9, Lewis Meadow near mile 11 (the usual overnight if you split the walk in), the High Hoh Bridge near mile 13, and Elk Lake near mile 15. A washed-out cliffside stretch about a quarter mile below Glacier Meadows is crossed on a fixed ladder; rungs have been reported missing in recent seasons, so look at it before you commit weight. Water is frequent the whole way.

From Glacier Meadows a way path climbs about 0.8 mile to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine and follows it roughly 0.2 mile before dropping onto the ice. That drop is loose and rockfall-prone; some parties fix a short line. Rope up on the ice. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading the rock islands to the right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to the crest of Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft. Snow Dome is the standard high camp, a thousand feet below the summit.

From Snow Dome the standard line goes up to and over Crystal Pass, then traverses just south of and below Five Fingers Ridge and over a false summit to the summit pyramid. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is usually bridged through midsummer.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier and the trail above Elk Lake is steep snow; later and the moat at the base of the summit rock opens and the ramps go from snow-covered to loose
hazards: Crevasses on the Blue Glacier and a large one near Crystal Pass, usually snow-bridged and not always
Rockfall on the moraine descent onto the ice, and a fixed-ladder washout around mile 16 of the trail
Loose rock on the east-face ramps and rockfall from parties above on them
A developing moat at the base of the summit rock in warm or late-season conditions, forcing a committing step onto rock
Whiteout on Snow Dome — the crevassed plateau is where the 1993 fatal unroped fall happened
A 17-mile walk out with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: The arrival test is a flat top at the foot of an 80 ft tower, and it works in cloud because it is underfoot, not on the horizon. Off the false summit you drop into a sharp saddle, then climb a short steep snow slope with a clean runout. That slope ends flat. The moment the ground stops rising and you are standing on a small flat platform of snow with an 80 ft rock tower directly above you, you are at the base of the summit block, on its northeast side. There is nothing else on this mountain that is a flat snow top under an 80 ft tower. Second test, and it is the one that separates this finish from the two other routes on this same block: from that platform the East Face Ramps line goes right, around the corner onto the east face, and climbs a series of ramps angling up and across it before joining the last Class 4 / 5.4 step. If you are climbing straight up the face directly above the platform you are on the North Face Direct, and if you have walked round to the far side you are on the Northwest Edge. All three finish on the same 80 ft tower and all three start from this platform; the only thing that tells them apart is which way you turn. What going too far looks like: if you are still gaining height on snow with no rock tower over you, you are on the five-fingered false summit east of the true one and have not yet dropped into the saddle. If you can see the Blue Glacier below you on your right the whole way, you are still on the traverse and have not reached Crystal Pass. Honest limit: the ramps themselves are loose and the correct one is chosen by eye. A fog test can get you to the foot of the block; it cannot pick the ramp for you.

approach_variants.name: From the Bailey Range: Queets Basin, Blizzard Pass and the Humes Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach of parties already on the Bailey Range Traverse rather than a way anyone drives to. It comes at Olympus from the south instead of the north: from the High Divide out of Sol Duc, along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, then down into Queets Basin, and up over Blizzard Pass onto the Humes Glacier. From the Humes the summit massif is gained from the south side and the summit block is reached from the opposite direction to the Snow Dome line.

It is longer by days and it exists in the record because traverse parties use it, not because it is easier. A party carrying glacier gear can also run it the other way and exit down the Blue Glacier to the Hoh, which is how most traverses finish.

Nothing about the approach shortens the climb: the last five hundred feet, the false summit, the saddle and the summit block are the same ground the Hoh parties cross.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Bailey Range crest is walkable and the Humes is not avalanching
hazards: Multi-day committing wilderness travel with no bail options once on the Bailey crest
Crevasses and icefall on the Humes Glacier
Blizzard Pass holds steep snow and is named for what happens there
Route-finding on the Bailey crest in cloud, where the ridge is the only handrail
No resupply and no reliable rescue access; NPS has reported multiple helicopter rescues per season among permitted Bailey parties
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The arrival test is the same flat snow top under the 80 ft tower — the block does not care which side of the mountain you walked in from. What changes coming from the south is which way you meet the false summit: from the Humes side you are working up toward the summit ridge from below rather than dropping onto it from Crystal Pass, so the sharp saddle between the false summit and the true one is reached from the opposite end.

The test that you have not overshot on this side is Five Fingers Ridge. The standard line runs just south of and below it. If Five Fingers Ridge is below you rather than above you, you are on the crest itself and too high; drop back under it and keep the ridge on your uphill side until the false summit is passed and the saddle opens.

Honest limit: this approach is thinly documented as an approach — it is described in traverse accounts, which are about the traverse. Treat the Hoh variant as the one with detail and this one as the one that gets a traverse party to the same platform.

bivy.name: Glacier Meadows — the standard Blue Glacier base camp
bivy.notes: The standard base camp, roughly seventeen miles from the Hoh trailhead and the last established camp before the Blue Glacier — the park does not permit camping between here and the ice. From the meadows you climb the moraine, drop onto the glacier and work up past the Snow Dome to the summit rock, generally quoted as four to six miles and around 3,500 ft of gain each way, so most parties leave in the dark. accounts differ on the elevation, giving anything between about 4,200 and 4,400 ft, which matters only because published gain figures vary with it. A ranger station and pit toilets are here in season.
bivy.water: Reliable — meltwater creeks in the meadows; treat it, and expect it to run silty in hot weather
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, quota-limited, reserved on Recreation.gov. Bear canisters mandatory. Practically every party climbing Olympus wants this camp, so treat the permit as the crux of the trip rather than an afterthought.
bivy.capacity: A cluster of individual sites plus a group site, under a nightly quota; the single most contested permit on this approach

bivy.name: Lewis Meadows Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: The last low-elevation river camp on the Hoh before the trail leaves the valley floor, roughly ten miles in from the Hoh Rain Forest visitor centre. Climbers use it mainly to break the walk in when they cannot get a permit for Elk Lake or Glacier Meadows, or when a late start makes the full seventeen miles unrealistic. Because it sits at around a thousand feet in dense rainforest, it does nothing to shorten the climbing day — expect to still be four to five hours below the glacier the next morning. Pit toilet provided; bear canister required.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Hoh River runs alongside the camp all season
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required, reserved on Recreation.gov; this stretch of the Hoh is not one of the tightly capped camps, so it is usually easier to obtain than the two above it.
bivy.capacity: Several individual sites plus a designated group site; parties of seven or more must use the group site

bivy.name: Elk Lake Camp, Hoh River trail
bivy.notes: Elk Lake sits about fifteen miles up the Hoh, where the trail finally starts climbing hard, and it is the fallback base for parties who miss out on Glacier Meadows. From here the summit day is long — you still have the switchbacks to Glacier Meadows, the lateral moraine and the whole Blue Glacier ahead before any climbing starts. Some parties deliberately take Elk Lake on the walk in and Glacier Meadows on the walk out, which spreads the permit demand across two nights. Pit toilet provided; food must be in an approved canister.
bivy.water: Reliable — Elk Lake itself, plus creeks nearby; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic Wilderness Permit required and this is an explicitly quota-limited camp — reserve on Recreation.gov well ahead. Summer-season reservations open in mid-April and the popular Hoh camps can be gone the same morning.
bivy.capacity: A small handful of individual sites; it fills every summer night in season

bivy.name: Snow Dome / Caltech Rocks high bivy, on the Blue Glacier
bivy.notes: Strong parties skip the pre-dawn start from Glacier Meadows by carrying a light camp onto the ice, either into the rocks below the Snow Dome or onto the dome near the old weather station. It turns a brutal summit day into a short one and puts you above most of the morning cloud, at the cost of a much heavier pack up the moraine and a night with no liquid water. This is glacier camping — crevasse hazard, wind, and no shelter — so it suits parties already competent on the Blue Glacier rather than as a way of making the route easier. The exact spots shift year to year as the ice and moraine change, so no single elevation is recorded.
bivy.water: Snow and glacier melt only; you are melting or filtering meltwater, and there is no running source you can count on
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic Wilderness Permit, but note that camping is NOT allowed between Glacier Meadows and the Blue Glacier — these sites are on the glacier side of that closure. Human waste must be packed out in blue bags, and bear canisters still apply.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a scatter of tent platforms in the rock bands and on the dome itself; no designated sites and no facilities

deleted_rows.name: North Route
hazards: loose rock and cliff bands near Hester Lake
devil's club brush below ~4,000 ft
route-finding on an unmaintained trail and off-trail terrain
deleted_rows.overview: Mount Price is the solitary high point of a ridge system between the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Dingford Creek in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, dwarfed by neighboring Big Snow Mountain but standing out as a distinct summit when viewed from other Alpine Lakes peaks. The north route follows the mountain's north ridge, reached via a long, mostly off-trail approach past Hester Lake — a quiet, rarely-climbed objective.
deleted_rows.beta: accounts describe three commonly used lines up Mount Price: this North Route (Dingford Creek/Goat Creek drainage), a route via Hester Lake on the northeast side, and a southeast-slope route. The North Route follows the Dingford Creek Trail about 2.1 miles (4-5 creek crossings), then leaves the trail near Goat Creek (~2,570 ft), crosses Dingford Creek, and climbs cross-country on a bearing of roughly 130°, staying below cliff bands on an ascending traverse to the saddle northwest of Little Hester Lake, then follows the ridge south to the 5,587-5,592 ft summit. It is class 2-3 routefinding terrain with a short section of moss-covered boulder scrambling to gain the saddle.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting — the cross-country traverse below the cliff bands and the boulder moves to the saddle are far slower and more hazardous to navigate in the dark or if benighted; plan for a full day given the ~15.6 mile round trip and 4,100 ft of off-trail gain.

obj_haz: Loose talus/scree on the upper slopes

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 56/5620 in the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley; no parking pass is currently required, and a self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR 56/5620) from North Bend roughly 17-18 miles to the Dingford Creek Trailhead, at the end of the road at about 1,400 ft. No parking pass is currently required; the self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit is at the trailhead kiosk. Both the road and the creek crossings on the trail are best left until spring runoff has subsided, roughly July through October.

sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Car-to-car scramble via Hester Lake basin

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: No fixed rock gear is needed for the standard line. Most parties carry an ice axe and, depending on season, light traction for the upper ridge snow; a rope and a few slings could be carried for the ridge's single exposed move by less experienced scramblers, though most parties climb it unroped.
pro_tips: Genuinely remote — the unmaintained Hester Lake Trail and long off-trail sections mean solitude is close to guaranteed
Some lingering snow into early summer eases the devil's club brush low on the route but adds avalanche exposure higher up
watch_out: cliff bands and brush around the Hester Lake shoreline
loose rock on the upper north ridge
creek crossings on Dingford Creek
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Minimal to none — an unroped scramble; the exposed section is short and usually downclimbed or spotted rather than protected.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late July through August offers the best balance of snow-free travel on the ridge/cliff-band section and manageable (though still present) brush. Earlier-season parties (June–early July) trade thicker devil's club for firmer lingering snow that can ease travel through the brushy sections and allow glissading on descent — but add avalanche and stream-crossing considerations.
deleted_rows.approach: Drive Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR-56) from North Bend roughly 17-18 miles to the Dingford Creek / Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead. Hike Dingford Creek Trail about 3 miles, then follow the unmaintained Hester Lake Trail and off-trail terrain past Hester and Little Hester Lakes to reach the base of Mount Price's north ridge; a long day (roughly 15 miles round trip with 4,000+ ft gain) or overnight.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Reverse the north ridge and off-trail route back past Hester Lake to the Dingford Creek Trail and trailhead.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat by reversing the ridge to the saddle and the traverse below the cliff bands; the crux on the way down is staying on the correct traverse line, so mark or GPS-track it on the way up before continuing above it.

pitch_detail.notes: ~4,400-5,100 ft: ascend the obvious talus slope directly or along its west side to the East-West ridge crest.
~5,100-5,587 ft: turn west and follow the steep, forested north side of the ridge to the summit; the route's single tricky move is on this section once snow is off.

itinerary.cal: Dingford Creek Rd (FR 5620) and the trail's creek crossings are best done after spring snowmelt/high runoff subsides, roughly July–October; snow can linger on the upper ridge into early summer.

days.note: A long single-day scramble: hike the boggy Hester Lake Trail into the basin below Little Hester Lake, traverse below the cliff bands to the tarn on the north side, gain the 4,680 ft saddle NW of Little Hester Lake, then scramble the south ridge to the summit. Reverse the entire route to descend, watching the clock since the trail's stream crossings and brush are unpleasant in the dark.
days.title: Car-to-car scramble via Hester Lake basin

schedule.label: Leave Dingford Creek trailhead
schedule.detail: Cross the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and start up the Hester Lake Trail through forest and boggy meadow sections.

schedule.label: Reach the basin below Little Hester Lake
schedule.detail: Trail gives way to talus and open slopes; begin traversing below the cliff bands toward the tarn on the north side.

schedule.label: Gain the 4,680 ft saddle NW of Little Hester Lake
schedule.detail: This saddle is the key routefinding waypoint separating the approach from the summit ridge.

schedule.label: Scramble the south ridge to the summit
schedule.detail: Class 3ish terrain with some loose rock and minor cliff bands to bypass; stay right (west) of obstacles per most trip reports.

schedule.label: Summit (5,587 ft)
schedule.detail: Views of Big Snow Mountain, Chimney Rock, and Overcoat Peak; short break before reversing the route.

schedule.label: Descend to saddle, traverse, and drop to the trail
schedule.detail: Reverse the ridge, traverse, and saddle, then rejoin the Hester Lake Trail for the hike out, aiming to beat dark.

days.objective: Summit Mount Price (5,587 ft) and return to the Dingford Creek trailhead same day

itinerary.totalNote: A long single day: roughly 15.6 miles round trip with 4,100 ft of gain, typically 9–11 hours car-to-car for a reasonably fit party leaving at first light.

access.fees: No fee at the trailhead
access.notes: Climbable roughly June–October; heavy winter snowfall and frequent avalanche control closures on I-90 affect access the rest of the year.
access.rules: Standard Alpine Lakes Wilderness rules apply: no bikes or motorized use, group size limits, Leave No Trace, dogs permitted but should be under control on the brushy/cliff sections
access.permit: None required — free self-issue day-use permit at the trailhead (no quota for day use).
access.closures: Forest Road 56 (Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road) is gated and closed to vehicles beyond the Dutch Miller Gap/Dingford Creek trailhead; check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF road status before driving in, since the road is prone to washouts
access.landManager: Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District)
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Snoqualmie Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: None: no parking pass or fee is currently required at the Dingford Creek Trailhead.
access.passRequired: None currently — Dingford Creek Trailhead is a fee-free USFS site (no Northwest Forest Pass charged as of the current USFS trailhead listing)

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk before an overnight in the wilderness. Middle Fork Campground is a fee campground reserved separately.

road.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road (FR-56)
road.driveNote: From North Bend, take FR-56 (Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road) about 17-18 miles to the Dingford Creek / Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead; gravel forest road, can be rough in spots.

climate.typical: Wet maritime climate; clearest mid- to late summer.

bySeason.fall: Good clear window before autumn rains return
bySeason.spring: Lingering snow in the north-ridge gullies; brushy lower slopes still snow-covered
bySeason.summer: Best window, but devil's club brush below ~4,000 ft is thick once snow-free
bySeason.winter: Deep snow, long approach; avalanche terrain on upper slopes

emergency.notes: Remote and little-traveled: the approach uses an unmaintained trail plus multiple miles of off-trail terrain, with no reliable cell coverage. Carry a satellite communicator and expect a slow rescue response.
emergency.rangerStation: Snoqualmie Ranger District (North Bend Office)
emergency.nearestHospital: Snoqualmie Valley Hospital, Snoqualmie

crowds.peakTraffic: scattered weekend attempts July-September; negligible midweek and shoulder-season traffic
crowds.estimatePerSeason: low - likely a handful to low dozens of parties per season; the Dingford Creek Trail carries hikers bound for Hester and Myrtle Lakes, but very few leave the trail to continue up Mount Price's brushy north slopes to the summit

fitnessSpec.hiking: comfortable with a long day (~15.6 mi round trip, 4,000+ ft gain) including sustained slow off-trail travel
fitnessSpec.packWeight: light day pack (15-25 lb) - no technical rack needed, but bring layers, navigation tools, and a time buffer for brush

partner_requirements.approachTime: long - Dingford Creek and Hester Lake trail approach plus a slow, brush-heavy off-trail gain to the north slopes typically makes this a full car-to-car day (8-12+ hours depending on brush conditions and party pace)
requiredSkills: off-trail route-finding/navigation (map, compass, or GPS - maintained trail ends well below the summit)
comfort with sustained brush/devil's club bushwhacking on the approach
basic Class 2-3 scrambling on loose rock, talus, and short rock steps
turnaround/time discipline given the approach's unpredictable pace
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: intermediate scrambler comfortable with off-trail travel, brush-bashing, and unroped Class 2-3 rock; not a beginner objective despite the easy grade because of route-finding and bushwhacking demands

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August is peak conditions; mid-July through October is the viable window

July.reason: Season opens mid-July; lingering snow patches can ease travel on upper slopes early in the month, but brush lower down is often still wet and thick

August.reason: In season - driest, most reliable footing on the heather/talus/rock-step summit slopes; brush is fully leafed out but trail conditions are most predictable

October.reason: End of the listed season; early snow, wet brush, and reduced daylight increase route-finding difficulty and turn a long day even longer

September.reason: Stable dry-season conditions continue; shorter daylight requires an earlier start given the long brushy approach

weather.typical: Typical Washington Cascades summer/fall pattern - drier and warmer July-September, with increasing chance of early-season wet weather and possible snow showers by October
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are possible in late summer; October attempts carry rising odds of rain or early snow shortening the weather window

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Low to moderate - Class 2-3 terrain with loose scree and short rock steps near the summit; a slip on loose rock or scree could cause a fall, but the terrain is not sustained high-consequence exposure. The greater real-world hazard on this route is getting off-route in the brushy, trail-less approach

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer/fall scramble route; NWAC's Snoqualmie Pass zone covers this area in winter but the Mid-July-October season falls outside the snow-covered period this route is normally climbed in

gaps: No official guidebook (e.g., Beckey) route description located; figures are drawn from The Mountaineers' route page, WTA, and trip reports

Distance/gain figures vary noticeably by source (10 mi/4,100 ft for this direct Goat Creek/bearing route vs. 13.5–15.6 mi and ~4,500 ft for the longer approach via the maintained trail to Hester Lake) — these likely reflect two distinct approach variants to the same saddle, but this hasn't been confirmed against a single authoritative source
Exact technical rating (solid Class 3 vs. brief Class 4 moves) of the cliff-band bypass and boulder section is not confirmed by a formally rated source

Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Dingford Creek Trailhead (Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Road from North Bend

deleted_rows.rope_note: No route-specific gear beta is published for this line. At the stated Class 2-3 a rope is not standard, but note where this route's own hazard list puts the hard move: one exposed 3rd/4th-class step on the summit ridge once it is snow-free. That is the place a party might want a short rope or a hand line, and there is routefinding around cliff bands on the north-south spur before it.
deleted_rows.corrections: No dedicated trip report for Mount Price's North Route was located; inference drawn from regional-terrain descriptions only.

bivy.name: Hester Lake and Myrtle Lake basins
bivy.notes: This is the real base camp for Mount Price, and the only one. The Dingford Creek trail climbs steeply from the trailhead, passes the Myrtle Lake junction at a little over three miles, and reaches Hester Lake at around five and a half; beyond the junction the tread deteriorates noticeably and the crossings multiply. Price rises directly above Hester, and both the Hester Lake Route and the North Route stage out of this basin, so a party camping here is looking at their objective from the tent. Myrtle is the softer option if the day runs out early, but it puts you further from the peak. Snow lingers in these basins into June and the summit slopes hold it later, so July through early October is the window. With the road washout in place the whole trip is several miles longer each way, which pushes this from a fit party's long day firmly into an overnight.
bivy.water: Both lakes are reliable all season, and Dingford Creek runs the length of the approach. Filter or treat.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead: fill it in, drop the stub in the box, carry your copy. No parking pass is currently required at the trailhead. Group size is capped at twelve people. Campfires are prohibited above 4,000 ft on this side of the wilderness; both lakes sit just under that line so a fire is technically legal, but the ground is thin and the sites are heavily used, and stoves are the better answer. Seasonal fire bans override all of that and are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A few established, flat tent spots at Hester Lake, enough for two or three parties before it feels crowded. Myrtle Lake, at about 3,780 ft and a couple of miles nearer the road, has a smaller number of rougher sites.

bivy.name: Middle Fork Campground
bivy.notes: The only developed drive-in camping on the Middle Fork road, and the practical roadhead base for every peak in this zone. It sits at about road mile twelve, a few minutes below the Middle Fork trailhead, so a party sleeping here is already at the start of the Preacher Mountain approach and within a short drive of the Garfield pull-outs. The road to it is paved the whole way now, which is a recent change and makes this reachable in any car. Season is roughly mid-May to mid-September; outside those months the gate is shut and the valley has no legal developed option at all. Book ahead, because this is the closest forest campground to Seattle and summer weekends fill months in advance. For Mount Teneriffe parties it is the nearest legal camping of any kind, about twenty minutes' drive from that trailhead.
bivy.water: Potable water is provided from a solar-pumped system, but it has failed for stretches in recent seasons and been shut off mid-summer. Carry enough for the first night rather than counting on the tap. The river runs alongside the campground year-round and can be filtered.
bivy.permit: Standard campground fee, booked up to six months ahead through the federal reservation system or by phone; the adjacent day-use parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or a small daily fee. No wilderness permit applies at the campground itself. Forest-wide campfire bans are routine through late summer and one is in force at the time of writing, so confirm before planning a fire. A food storage order applies across the whole forest.
bivy.capacity: About 36 tent and trailer units plus a pair of group sites, no hookups, all reservable. Fourteen-day stay limit.

bivy.name: Middle Fork road pull-outs, Taylor River and Dingford Creek
bivy.notes: Worth reading before driving up with a plan to sleep in the back of the car, because the situation has changed and the change is not obvious on the ground. The lower valley is closed to dispersed camping, so the answer there is the campground or nothing. The Taylor River road is gated at the bridge at the end of the drivable road and its old roadbed is now the trail, so there is no driving in to a quieter spot. The upper road toward Dingford Creek is the one stretch still open to roadside camping, and it is cut by a washout at milepost 17.3 that closes vehicle access short of the Dingford Creek trailhead at 1,400 ft; the Forest Service's road-damage alert of June 30, 2026 lists it with no reopening date. That washout matters well beyond camping: with it in place the Mount Price approach and the Treen Peak path both gain several road miles on foot or bike each way, which turns two long days into overnight trips. Beyond the Dingford Creek trailhead the road has been gated to vehicles for years in any case. Road status in this valley changes year to year, so confirm the current state with the ranger district before committing; a party that discovers the washout at the barricade has lost the day.
bivy.water: The river and its side creeks are within a few minutes of the road the entire length of the valley and run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used corridor.
bivy.permit: This is the field that decides whether you can sleep here at all. A forest order closes dispersed camping along the road from the forest boundary up to the confluence of the Taylor and Middle Fork rivers, and along the Taylor River road out to the Snoqualmie Lake trailhead, including a quarter-mile strip on either side. That closure runs through the end of 2026 and covers essentially every pull-out parties used to use, including the ones nearest the Garfield approaches. Above the confluence, on the upper road toward Dingford Creek, roadside camping is not covered by the order. Trailhead parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or the interagency equivalent.
bivy.capacity: Informal gravel pull-outs only, a vehicle or two apiece, nothing signed, levelled or established.

deleted_rows.fa: Joe Hutton, Peggy Hutton, Roy Mason; 1955
gear: Ice axe and crampons for the glacier travel and summit snow slopes
A rope plus a light crevasse-rescue kit (pickets, prusiks) for crossing the glacier
Helmet for the ridge and loose approach terrain
Sturdy boots for the class 3 scrambling and the exposed, slippery step in Depot Creek where a fixed handline aids passage
hazards: crevasse fall on the glacier
exposed scrambling near the summit
long committing approach
loose, chossy rock in the standard summit gully
knife-edge snow arete crossing en route to the gully
wet, slippery rock step near Depot Creek Falls on the approach

deleted_rows.overview: Mount Rahm is a glaciated summit sitting essentially on the US-Canada border ridge on Custer Ridge, near Mount Custer and Mount Spickard, deep in the remote Chilliwack zone of North Cascades National Park. It's named for David Rahm, a Western Washington University geology professor, and the peak has its own small extinct caldera. Rahm is rarely climbed alone — most parties tag it as part of a 3-5 day trip that also bags Custer and/or Spickard/Redoubt from a shared camp at Ouzel Lake, reached via the cross-border Depot Creek approach.
deleted_rows.beta: Mount Rahm presents a challenging alpine climb requiring solid mountaineering skills, glacier travel competency, and rock scrambling ability. The standard route follows either the South Ridge approach from Ouzel Lake or the Maselpanik Creek approach, both converging on the mountain's upper basin before the final scramble to the west summit (8,485 ft). Class 3 rock climbing and glacier work are the primary technical elements.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Establish a firm turnaround time based on daylight available and your descent pace. Given the 6-7 hour timeline, plan to start by dawn to be off the glacier well before darkness. Do not attempt the glacier in marginal light conditions.
deleted_rows.rappels: None reported; this route is a scramble and is downclimbed rather than rappelled.
deleted_rows.face: South side - the standard gully dropping from the summit, reached from Ouzel Lake
deleted_rows.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).
deleted_rows.comms: Virtually no cellular coverage (Verizon, T-Mobile, AT&T) in the Mount Rahm area. A satellite messenger (Garmin inReach, Spot) or satellite phone (Iridium) is essential for emergency communication. Some iPhone 14+ models offer emergency satellite SOS, though coverage and reliability vary.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose 3rd class gully and its knife-edge snow arete back to the bench above Silver Lake, then contour back to Ouzel Lake camp. The gully channels waterfall runoff down its center and is chossy — pick a dry line and watch for rockfall from any party above.

waypoints.name: Depot Creek Road Trailhead
waypoints.note: Depot Creek Road trailhead off Chilliwack Lake Road, on the Canadian side of the border; the standard start for the cross-border approach to Rahm, Custer, Redoubt, and Spickard.
waypoints.directions: The standard approach starts on the Canadian side. From Chilliwack, BC, drive Chilliwack River Road about 31.7 miles to the narrow dirt Depot Creek Road, then follow that spur another 2.5 miles or so to a rough trailhead turnout at about 2,300 ft; high-clearance or 4WD is recommended for the spur. The route crosses the unmanned US/Canada border on foot, so carry a passport, and camping at Ouzel Lake requires a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Depot Creek Falls crossing
waypoints.note: 967-ft falls; the climbers' path crosses wet, exposed slabs here on fixed handlines — slick and consequential in the wet.

waypoints.name: Lake Ouzel (Ouzel Lake) camp
waypoints.note: Flat, sandy, treeless benches at the head of Depot Creek valley — the standard high camp for Spickard, Custer, Redoubt, and Rahm.

waypoints.name: Silver Lake basin / Custer's South Ridge traverse
waypoints.note: From camp, gain Custer's south ridge and traverse east high above the Silver Lake basin toward the Custer-Rahm connection, using snow coverage where present.

waypoints.name: Rahm's guard-rock band (crux gully)
waypoints.note: A short band of loose class 4 rock guards the final slopes; take one of the leftmost gullies (3rd/4th, easier with snow fingers) rather than the first, harder option encountered.

waypoints.name: Mount Rahm summit
waypoints.note: Rubbly, unassuming true summit less than 0.25 mi south of the Canadian border, at the NE end of Custer Ridge; on the descent, reverse this same loose gully and the knife-edge snow arete below it.

waypoints.name: Trailhead / border return
waypoints.note: Descent reverses the ascent back to the same Depot Creek Road trailhead.
