Reverse the approach, descending back to the car. Many parties extend the trip by one or two extra days at Ouzel Lake camp to also climb Custer, Redoubt, and/or Spickard before hik…

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Glacier kit (harness, prusiks, pickets, slings); minimal rock gear needed.
pro_tips: Most parties combine Rahm with Mount Custer and/or Mount Spickard/Redoubt as a 3-5 day trip based at Ouzel Lake (~5,700 ft) rather than climbing it alone.
Bring a passport or NEXUS card — the Depot Creek trail briefly crosses the international border away from any official port of entry.
Expect wet scrambling early in the approach: the Depot Creek Falls section has required an 8-ft slippery rock step/handline in recent trip reports.
watch_out: The standard gully carries waterfall runoff down its center — pick a dry line and watch for rockfall from parties above.
The border-crossing section of trail is easy to lose in poor visibility; carry a GPS track or detailed map.
Weather can close in fast on the exposed Custer Ridge approach terrain — have a bail plan back to Ouzel Lake.
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Roped glacier travel and snow with Class 3 scrambling to the summit; little to no rock protection.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late June through September is the reliable window, matching current data. Earlier in the season there's more snow underfoot (which can bury the exposed knife-edge arete but also hides crevasses on the glaciers used by parties combining Rahm with Custer/Redoubt/Spickard); later in the season glaciers turn icier and crevasses open up but become easier to see and avoid. Snow commonly lingers on the border-ridge approach into July.
deleted_rows.approach: Standard approach is via Depot Creek from the Canadian side: from Chilliwack, BC drive Chilliwack River Road ~31.7 mi to the narrow dirt Depot Creek Road, then (high-clearance/4WD recommended) another ~2.5 mi to a rough trailhead turnout. The unmaintained Depot Creek trail climbs the valley and passes a wet, misty waterfall section requiring an 8-ft slippery rock step (a fixed handline has been reported in recent trip years); a boot-track hugs the north edge of the valley up to Ouzel Lake (~5,700 ft), the standard base camp on flat, sandy, treeless benches. About 200 yards of trail crosses the international border, marked by an obelisk and trail register, before you're on North Cascades National Park land. From Ouzel Lake, sidehill east/northeast across the bench above Silver Lake toward Rahm's south side, then ascend one of three gullies dropping from the summit — the standard gully is loose 3rd class with an exposed knife-edge snow arete partway up — to a well-defined climbers' trail leading to the top.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the loose 3rd class gully and its knife-edge snow arete back to the bench above Silver Lake, then contour back to Ouzel Lake camp. The gully channels waterfall runoff down its center and is chossy — pick a dry line and watch for rockfall from any party above.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is straightforward by reversing the gully back down to the bench and Ouzel Lake; from camp the Depot Creek trail leads back out to the Canadian trailhead, so an early turnaround still gets you to a known, previously-traveled exit.

pitch_detail.notes: Lower gully approach with Class 3 scrambling on loose volcanic rock; short steps and sustained climbing on rock and snow features. Approximately 1,500 feet of elevation gain.

Upper gully section with sustained Class 3+ terrain and one short Class 4 sequence near the top where the gully walls lean back to a climbable face for ~100 feet. Snow finger or rock climbing depending on conditions; total 1,000+ feet of elevation.
Glacier crossing from the gully exit to the base of the summit finger. Rope-team travel recommended due to crevasse hazards. Approximately 800-1,000 feet of moderate-angle glacier.
Steep glacier finger ascending to the summit; schrund crossing at 7,700 feet (can climb through soft snow or bypass via rock). Final 600+ feet of climbing with increasing angle and exposure.

itinerary.cal: Depot Creek trailhead is reached via Chilliwack Lake Road in BC and the route crosses the unmanned US/Canada border, so bring a passport; Ouzel Lake camping requires a North Cascades NP backcountry permit.

days.note: Drive to the Depot Creek trailhead via Chilliwack Lake Road, BC (crossing the unmanned US/Canada border swath), then hike a brushy, poorly-maintained trail through devil's club and deadfall up to camp at Ouzel Lake below Custer Ridge. Most parties find this a full half-day-plus effort with overnight packs.
days.title: Approach to Ouzel Lake camp
days.objective: Establish base camp at Ouzel Lake (5,700 ft)

days.note: From camp, sidehill along the bench above Silver Lake, cross an exposed au-cheval snow arete to reach the base of a loose, chossy 3rd-class gully, then top out onto Rahm's southwest ridge and follow a well-defined climbers' trail to the summit. Many parties tag Custer the same day via the connecting ridge since it's 'on the way,' though the traverse has sketchy, loose, exposed sections that turn some groups around.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day trip for Rahm alone: ~6 mi/3,400 ft hike in to Ouzel Lake camp, a full day round-trip (~8 hrs, ~3,000 ft) to tag Rahm's loose SW gully and ridge, and a 6-mi hike back out — most parties stretch it to 4-6 days to also bag neighboring Custer, Redoubt, and Spickard from the same camp.

access.fees: NPS backcountry permit fee during the summer season (mid-May to early Oct) is $10 per person plus a $6 nonrefundable reservation fee; no charge the rest of the year (fee structure changed March 2024).
access.notes: 60% of sites (Boston Basin/Eldorado/Sulphide Glacier/etc.) are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: The Depot Creek trail crosses the international border away from any port of entry (~200 yards lies in Canada); bring a passport or NEXUS card. Canada's CBSA has been tightening remote-area border-crossing rules — it ended the remote-area permit program for PCT hikers in January 2025, so confirm current policy before relying on this crossing.
access.permit: An NPS wilderness/backcountry permit is required for any overnight stay once you're inside North Cascades National Park (covers Ouzel Lake and beyond) — reserve in advance on Recreation.gov or get a walk-up permit at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.closures: Depot Creek Road and trail are unmaintained; washouts, overgrowth, and creek crossings vary year to year — check recent trip reports rather than assuming the ~2.5-mi driving distance still holds.
access.landManager: North Cascades National Park (US) for the peak and Ouzel Lake camp; the Depot Creek trailhead and road are reached via Crown/private timber land in British Columbia, Canada
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — quota, paid reservation
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov (early-access lottery in March, then general on-sale at least 2 days ahead); about 40% of sites are held for walk-up permits issued in person up to 24 hours before the trip at a Wilderness Information Center.

road.name: Depot Creek Road (off Chilliwack River Road, BC)
road.status: Rough, narrow dirt road that grows increasingly overgrown; high-clearance 4WD recommended for the final ~2.5 mi, otherwise park in a large turnout and walk
road.driveNote: Reached entirely from the Canadian side via Chilliwack, BC — there is no direct US road access to this approach, only cross-border trail travel

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with high precipitation, especially heavy, wet snowfall in winter; the Chilliwacks catch some of the heaviest snowpack in the North Cascades, so approach terrain and the summit gully can hold snow into midsummer.

bySeason.summer: Late June-September is the practical climbing window; snow patches linger on the approach and in the summit gully into July.
bySeason.winter: Heavy wet snow loading makes this essentially inaccessible without expedition/ski-mountaineering-level commitment.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (Mount Baker zone) for avalanche and mountain weather forecasting

emergency.notes: No cell service in the Depot Creek valley or on Custer Ridge. This is one of the more remote objectives in the North Cascades — carry a satellite communicator and leave a trip plan with contacts on both sides of the border.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades National Park Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount; NPS Sedro-Woolley office, (360) 854-7200
emergency.nearestHospital: PeaceHealth St. Joseph Medical Center, Bellingham, WA — in practice this is a multi-day self-rescue given the cross-border approach and lack of any nearby US road access; Chilliwack General Hospital, BC is geographically closer but complicates medevac coordination across the border.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 (Whatcom County Sheriff/SAR dispatch)

crowds.peakTraffic: Rare even in July-August; essentially no traffic outside the short glacier-covered window, and most 'traffic' is peak-bagger parties targeting Custer/Spickard/Rahm together
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - likely under a dozen parties per season; one of the more obscure Bulger/Washington hundred-highest peaks

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong 2-day-capable fitness; car-to-summit is roughly 6-7 hours one way from Maselpanik Creek (per route beta) but is realistically done as a 2-day trip with a high camp given the approach and border-ridge terrain
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy overnight glacier-mountaineering pack (camp gear, rope, glacier kit, several days of food given the remote approach)

approach_variants.name: Depot Creek from the Canadian side and the Lake Ouzel high camp
approach_variants.notes: The approach starts north of the border and crosses on foot, so carry a passport. From Chilliwack River Road, turn onto the narrow dirt Depot Creek spur and follow it to a rough turnout where the driving ends; high clearance helps on the upper part. The unmaintained trail climbs the valley, crossing the international boundary at an obelisk and register about two hundred yards in on foot, and a park backcountry permit is required to camp beyond. Near the head of the valley the path crosses the base of a very large waterfall on wet, misty, exposed slabs, including a slippery step that fixed handlines have been rigged for; that crossing is consequential when the rock is wet. Above it a boot track hugs the north edge of the valley and climbs to Lake Ouzel, a flat, sandy, treeless bench that is the shared high camp for this whole group of peaks. From camp, sidehill east and northeast across the bench above the Silver Lake basin toward the peak's south side, using snow coverage where it helps.
approach_variants.season: Late June through September. Earlier there is more snow underfoot, which buries the exposed arete but also hides crevasses on the glaciers used by parties linking this peak with its neighbours. Later the ice turns harder and crevasses open but become easier to see.
hazards: loose, chossy rock in the summit gullies
an exposed knife-edge snow arete partway up the correct gully
crevasse fall on the glaciers used when this peak is combined with its neighbours
the wet, slippery rock step near the falls on the approach
a long, committing cross-border approach with no cell coverage and a multi-day carry-out
approach_variants.baseFinding: Three gullies drop off this summit, and the first one you meet is the wrong one. Coming across the bench toward the south side of the peak, a short band of loose rock guards the final slopes and three gullies come down through it from the summit. The one you reach first as you traverse is the hardest and steepest of the three; do not take it. Keep traversing and take one of the leftmost gullies instead, which go at loose third and fourth class and are easier still when a snow finger is filling them. Two things confirm you are in the right one. Partway up, the correct line crosses an exposed knife-edge snow arete — a genuine, memorable feature, not a snow patch — and above that the ground gives way to a well-defined climbers' path that runs to the top. So: if you are grinding up steep loose fourth class with no arete underfoot and no boot track visible above, back off and move left. If you top out of a gully and find no trodden path, you are on the wrong side of the summit block. The summit itself is rubbly and unassuming and sits a very short distance south of the border. On the way down, reverse the same gully and the same arete rather than improvising a line.

approach_variants.name: Maselpanik Creek from the north
approach_variants.notes: Reaches the north side of the mountain at the head of Maselpanik Creek, starting from old logging roads off the Silver-Skagit Road in Canada. It is the shortest way to the summit, but the roads can be gated and overgrown. A long single day is possible, though most parties take two. Carry a passport for the border.

approach_variants.name: Silver Creek to Silver Lake
approach_variants.notes: The one approach that stays in the United States, but it is longer and rougher. Follow Silver Creek up from Ross Lake to camp at Silver Lake, then climb to the peak from there.

climbing_route.label: Standard gully on the south side
climbing_route.notes: From Rahm's south side, ascend one of three gullies dropping from the summit; the standard gully is loose 3rd class with an exposed knife-edge snow arete partway up.

climbing_route.label: Climbers' trail to the top
climbing_route.notes: The gully leads to a well-defined climbers' trail leading to the top.

hazards: exposed scramble moves near the summit block

deleted_rows.overview: The standard route up Mount Stone, the highest point in Mason County. From the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels, a class 3 rock scramble of roughly 5,000 ft of gain over about 10 miles round trip gains the summit, with broad views of The Brothers, Mount Anderson, Mount Deception, Mount Constance, and Mount Olympus.
deleted_rows.beta: Putvin Trail is notorious for its steep pitch, gaining nearly 3,000 feet in less than 4 miles. The trail negotiates several short sections of Class 3 scrambling over wet rocks and tree roots before reaching the Lake of the Angels basin. This route is more direct than any traverse and is the most commonly used summer climbing route on Mount Stone.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time of 1:00 PM at the latest to ensure the summit is reached and a safe descent begun in daylight. If turnaround time passes before reaching the summit, descend to Lake of the Angels, rest, and descend Putvin Trail carefully.
deleted_rows.comms: Cell phone coverage is unreliable; do not depend on cellular service for emergencies. A satellite messenger (Garmin InReach, SPOT device) is strongly recommended. Inform someone of your expected return time before departing.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the scramble and the Putvin Trail back to the Hamma Hamma trailhead.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Helmets essential—the steep Putvin Trail corridor is narrow and rock hazard is real from other parties and from natural rockfall. Trekking poles dramatically improve safety and reduce knee strain on the brutal descent. Ice axe recommended for travel through lingering snow (June-July). Good boots with deep lugs are critical for traction on wet, loose terrain.
what_to_bring: Olympic NP wilderness permit if camping at Lake of the Angels
pro_tips: Camp at Lake of the Angels to break up the ~5,000 ft of gain
Save the class 3 summit moves for good visibility
Carry an axe if attempting before the snow clears

early-season snow
winter mixed crux
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Normally an unroped class 3 scramble; a short rope can help protect the summit-block moves or the winter mixed crux.
deleted_rows.best_season: July through September
deleted_rows.approach: Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813, ~1,565 ft) on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25) — note that in recent years a slide/washout near mile 10.5 has at times blocked the final ~1.2 miles of road, forcing an extra road-walk to the actual trailhead, so check current Forest Service status before you go. From the trailhead the Putvin Trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek for a few hundred feet, then launches into a long, unrelenting climbing traverse to the west — this trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles and does not ease up. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an old logging road (the tread is easy to lose here; look for the trail continuation slightly downhill) and enters the Mount Skokomish Wilderness; the Olympic National Park boundary comes at about 3 miles. Around 4,200 ft there is a short but notable headwall/rock step with an old hand-line (or a large exposed tree root used as a handhold) to surmount slick rock — the crux of the trail itself and a common turnaround point for unprepared hikers, especially wet. The maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles (~4,500 ft, sometimes called Frog/Fawn Pond), where a rougher way-trail continues up steep, rocky terrain to Lake of the Angels (~4,900 ft), reached around 4 miles in. Snow typically lingers on the north-facing basin above Lake of the Angels well into summer (consolidated snow reported from ~4,500 ft on), so an ice axe (and sometimes microspikes/crampons) is worth carrying into early-mid summer. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail and goes cross-country: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet of rocky, brushy ground, then traverses up beneath St. Peter's Gate (the pass southeast of the summit) and back west to a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge; from the notch, class 3 scrambling leads a couple of hundred feet to a shallow hanging basin, then continue through talus/boulder terrain toward the summit block. Total one-way distance is about 4.8 miles with roughly 5,053 ft of gain to the 6,618 ft high point. Hazards: reliable water is available along Boulder Creek and at Lake of the Angels but is scarce above the lake; the gully/rib terrain above the lake is loose and route-finding is nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow; the lower trail's root/rock headwall is genuinely exposed when wet.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb route with no rappelling. The final summit block (roughly 150-200 ft of terrain) is mostly class 3 but includes one well-documented 15-20 ft class 4 step (a shallow crack, often marked by a cairn) that parties downclimb facing in; no fixed rappel anchor has been reported here in any trip account reviewed, so treat this step as a careful downclimb or build a natural (gear/sling-around-block) rappel only if your party is uncomfortable reversing it. From the summit, retrace the class 2-3 talus/boulder terrain back down to the west-ridge notch, reverse the traverse beneath St. Peter's Gate, and return to Lake of the Angels. From the lake, pick the way-trail back down into the basin and rejoin the maintained Putvin Trail, reversing the hand-line/headwall section around 4,200 ft (the single trickiest spot on the descent when wet or in the afternoon sun on lingering snow) and then the long steep 4-mile descent to the trailhead. Parties on this route (rated S5/T5) log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car-to-car with breaks — budget a full day and start early since the lower trail is exposed and hot in the afternoon. A steep mossy/waterfall gully off-route looks like a descent shortcut but is far worse than reversing the ascent line — stick to the known up-track rather than improvising a shortcut.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat by reversing the scramble and trail; Lake of the Angels offers a natural turnaround/camp point.

pitch_detail.notes: The trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek briefly, then starts a relentless climbing traverse west. Around 1.3 mi it crosses an old logging road where the tread is easy to lose; the continuation is slightly downhill across the road.
Unrelenting steep tread through forest; the trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 mi overall and does not ease. Roots and loose dirt make it slow and hard on the knees, especially on the way down.

A short, exposed step of slick rock and roots with an old fixed line looped over a stump. The line has been rotten in past seasons, so test it before weighting it and be ready to climb the step on holds and roots; it is the usual turnaround point for parties when it is wet.

The maintained tread ends in a small basin; a rougher way trail climbs steep, rocky ground to Lake of the Angels (~4,900 ft) in its grassy cirque. The lake is the last reliable water; above it the route is cross-country.
pitch_detail.pitch: Park boundary to Lake of the Angels

pitch_detail.notes: Climb from the lake on a steep, loose boot path toward St. Peter's Gate, the obvious notch with cliffs on both sides. Snow lingers in this north-facing basin into summer, so carry an axe early season; an eroding path through vegetation next to the scree is better avoided in favour of the talus.
pitch_detail.pitch: Lake of the Angels to the cliff band

pitch_detail.notes: Short of the Gate, head left and follow a boot path along the base of the long cliff band on poor scree and loose rock, climbing up and around to a notch on the west ridge. The path goes up a couple of narrow chutes; in fog or fresh snow it is easy to lose, so note the line on the way up.
pitch_detail.pitch: Traverse under the cliffs to the west-ridge notch

pitch_detail.notes: From the notch an easy third-class chimney and a couple hundred feet of scrambling lead up the east side of the ridge into a shallow hanging basin below the summit. Traverse around the basin toward the rounded main summit mass.
pitch_detail.pitch: West-ridge notch to the hanging basin

pitch_detail.notes: The crux: a short crack system of about 15 ft on the summit block, rated anywhere from class 2-3 to class 4 depending on the line taken. It is exposed and has to be reversed on the descent; downclimb facing in, or rig a sling rappel if the party is not comfortable.

itinerary.cal: The ground above Lake of the Angels often holds snow into July, so many parties carry an ice axe even on the single-day version.

days.note: Standard way most parties climb Mount Stone: steep trail up to Lake of the Angels basin, then boots-and-axe along the base of the cliff band and on to the west-ridge terrain to the summit block, reversing the whole route to descend. Expect short Class 3 (and a Class 3-4 summit move) plus lingering snow above the lake into mid-summer.

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail #813 to Lake of the Angels, then the traverse under the cliff band
camps: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
approach_variants.notes: this route and the Lake of the Angels route appear to be the same climb entered twice. The variants here are written for the ground the route itself describes. Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813) at about 1,565 ft on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25). A slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles; check Forest Service status. The trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek a few hundred feet, then starts a long unrelenting climbing traverse west, gaining nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles without easing. Around 1.3 miles it crosses an old logging road, and the tread is easy to lose there — look for the continuation slightly downhill. Around 4,200 ft comes the short headwall with an old hand-line or a large exposed tree root as the handhold, the crux of the trail and a common turnaround point when wet. Maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles at about 4,500 ft, and a rougher way-trail continues up steep rocky ground to Lake of the Angels at about 4,900 ft near 4 miles.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Consolidated snow has been reported from about 4,500 ft up well into summer in the north-facing basin above the lake
hazards: Exposed scramble moves near the summit block and a 15-20 ft Class 4 crack step with no fixed anchor
Lingering steep snow in the north-facing basin above the lake into early-mid summer
Route-finding above Lake of the Angels is loose and nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow
The 4,200 ft headwall on the trail is greasy when wet and the hand-line is not maintained

approach_variants.baseFinding: The climb starts where the trail ends, and the arrival test is a cliff band, not a summit view. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet toward St. Peter's Gate, and short of the gate you turn left along the base of the long cliff band. Rock wall at your shoulder on one side and scree dropping away on the other is a check you can make in cloud without seeing anything further. Second test: along the cliff base, Class 2-3 ground and a couple of narrow chutes lead up toward a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge, below the feature called St. Peter's Gate. Below, not through. St. Peter's Gate is the notch in the southeast ridge and it belongs to the traverse from Lena Lake; the notch you want is on the west ridge and sits lower and to the south of it. If you have walked up to a notch that opens onto an entirely different basin to the east, that is the Gate and you are past your turn. Third test, on the summit block: the final 150 to 200 ft is mostly Class 3 but contains one well-documented 15 to 20 ft class 4 step up a shallow crack, often marked by a cairn. A cairn is man-made and does not move. If you have reached the top without meeting a short crack step, you are on a sub-summit — this mountain has three, and parties confuse them in fog. What the route's own timing says: Mountaineers reports for this line log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car to car. Caution from a trip report, and it is route-finding advice rather than a hazard note: at least one party took a steep mossy waterfall gully as a descent shortcut and found it far worse than reversing the ascent. Reverse the cliff-base traverse; do not improvise a line down the south side.

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the St. Peter's traverse, arriving at the Gate from the east

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

approachLogistics.trailhead: Lena Lake Trailhead (Hamma Hamma Road, FR-25)

approach_variants.notes:
The long way to the same mountain, kept here because it is a genuinely different approach rather than a variation of the Putvin walk. Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft and 6.5 miles. From there, off-trail west past Lena Tarn and Scout Lake to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake and round into Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above Ullin's Bathtubs, then a rising traverse to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending on loose moraine, and finally exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

Most parties then continue southwest about half a mile into the Lake of the Angels basin, which is where this approach rejoins the Putvin ground, and exit down the Putvin Trail — a different trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake, so plan a shuttle or a stashed bike.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: Extensive off-trail route-finding across Scout Pass, Scout Basin and Ullin's Pass on faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt slopes below St. Peter's Gate
Requires a car shuttle or stashed bike between two trailheads about 4 road miles apart
Fog on the upper mountain, where parties have repeatedly lost the route
Unbridged stream crossings on the way-trail sections
approach_variants.baseFinding: The arrival test is St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft: the traverse's high point, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge, reached up a steep snow-and-dirt ramp over loose moraine. Ground stops rising, notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens beyond. The test that puts you on this route's line rather than the gully line: from the Gate, continue southwest into the Lake of the Angels basin and pick the route up from there — the traverse left along the base of the cliff band, and Class 2-3 ground to the notch on the west ridge below the Gate. The alternative from the Gate is to drop about 300 ft directly to the base of a basalt cliff and take the south-face gully; that is the Lena Lake traverse route, a Class 3-4 gully, and a different climb. Above the west-ridge notch the test is the same: a short Class 4 step up a shallow crack, often cairned, in the last 150 to 200 ft, on a mountain with three summits. Honest limit: coming from the east adds a day and several passes of unmarked way-trail. It is chosen for the country, not for the climb.

climbing_route.label: Traverse under the cliff band above Lake of the Angels
climbing_route.notes: From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail and goes cross-country: a boot path climbs a couple of hundred feet of rocky ground toward St. Peter's Gate; short of the Gate, turn left and traverse along the base of the long cliff band up to a notch on the west ridge. The gully/rib terrain above the lake is loose and route-finding is nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow; snow typically lingers on the north-facing basin above the lake well into summer, so an ice axe (and sometimes microspikes/crampons) is worth carrying into early-mid summer. Water is scarce above the lake.

climbing_route.label: Notch on the west ridge below St. Peter's Gate
climbing_route.notes: Follow the terrain up toward a notch on Mount Stone's west ridge below the feature known as St. Peter's Gate.

climbing_route.label: Talus/boulder terrain to the summit block
climbing_route.notes: Continue through talus/boulder terrain toward the summit block; the 6,618 ft high point.

bivy.name: Lake of the Angels
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Skokomish and for the south side of Mount Stone, and one of the best-placed camps in the Olympics for a climber. About 3.5 miles and 3,400 ft from the Putvin trailhead, which understates it badly — the trail is notoriously steep, with hand-over-hand sections on rock and root where a slip has real consequence, and it is slow going with an overnight pack. From the basin the east slopes of Mount Skokomish are a straightforward scramble, and Mount Stone is gained by working north toward St. Peter's Gate, so a fit party can take both peaks in one day from these tents. The four sites and the meadow are the constraint: this is a fragile alpine basin that has been loved hard, so camp only on the designated ground and expect company. Best from mid-July, once the steep upper trail is clear of snow, through September. Early season the last pitch to the basin holds snow and the trail is genuinely hazardous when wet.
bivy.water: The lake, but read this one carefully. It is a shallow basin lake fed by snowmelt with no significant inlet, so it draws down through the summer and by a dry late season it can be low, warm and unappealing, and the meadow seeps around it disappear entirely. There is a good spring roughly two miles up the Putvin trail that is often the last dependable water on a dry year. Late-season parties should plan to carry water up from lower on the trail rather than count on finding it in the basin
bivy.permit: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required — the trail crosses the park boundary shortly before the final climb into the basin, having already passed through the Mount Skokomish Wilderness on Forest Service ground below. Book through Recreation.gov or obtain the permit from a park wilderness information office; per-person nightly fees apply. An animal-resistant food container is required. No campfires — the basin is far above the 3,500 ft fire limit and this is stove-only ground. No dogs. No Northwest Forest Pass or other parking pass is needed at the Putvin trailhead itself, which is unusual for this road and worth knowing
bivy.capacity: Four designated sites in the upper basin. Four. It is a small hanging meadow and there is no overflow ground that is acceptable to camp on

bivy.name: Hamma Hamma River road campgrounds — Lena Creek and Hamma Hamma
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging option for everything on the Hamma Hamma side: Lena Lake and The Brothers, the Putvin trail to Lake of the Angels for Mount Skokomish and Mount Stone, and the Jefferson Creek spur for Mount Pershing. Lena Creek is the more useful of the two because it sits essentially at the Lena Lake trailhead, so a party arriving late can sleep at the car and start walking at first light instead of driving the gravel in the dark. This is a contingency and staging site rather than the normal plan for anyone climbing here — the objectives are all hours above it — but it is the right answer for a party that arrives after dark, gets weathered off, or comes out late and does not want to drive home tired. Being at 700 ft it is usable long before the high camps melt out, which makes it the practical base for an early-season Brothers attempt.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground — this catches people out. The Hamma Hamma River runs alongside both and can be filtered, but bring drinking water from Hoodsport
bivy.permit: Modest per-night Forest Service fee with an extra vehicle charge, paid at the fee machine, which is cashless. No reservation system and no wilderness permit — this is developed Forest Service camping. Fire rings and picnic tables at each site, vault toilets, no hookups. Typically open from mid-May into late October and gated the rest of the year
bivy.capacity: Lena Creek has around thirteen well-spaced sites at the Lena Lake trailhead junction; Hamma Hamma has around fifteen a couple of miles further down the river. Both first come, first served, no reservations

deleted_rows.name_search: putvin trail trl lake lk of the angels scramble

deleted_rows.name: The Direct North Ridge w/ Gendarme
deleted_rows.fa: North Ridge (original line, bypassing the Great Gendarme): Don Claunch & John Rupley, September 9, 1956. Complete North Ridge, via the lower ridge's west side: Fred Beckey & Steve Marts, 1963. First ascent climbing directly over the Great Gendarme: James Wickwire & Fred Stanley, 1964. Direct lower-ridge start variation (from the true toe): Mead Hargis & Jay Ossiander, 1970
hazards: The gendarme-bypass gully (rappelling right/west at its base) is prone to rockfall on dirty rock and is not recommended; the upper mountain is almost always shaded and can be icy/cold on the crux pitches
Documented accident, July 2020: a climber was struck by rockfall near the top of the route, took a long fall, and required roughly 24 hours to rescue after failed helicopter extraction attempts.
deleted_rows.overview: The full-length version of the North Ridge, starting at the true toe rather than the notch, adding roughly 800 vertical feet and a sustained 5.9+ opening lieback before joining the standard North Ridge line up through the Great Gendarme.
deleted_rows.beta: Three opening pitches off a ledge ~150 ft above the toe — including an awkward 5.8 squeeze slot and a striking, sustained 5.9+ lieback crack — join the standard North Ridge; from there roughly 11 more pitches of exposed 4th-to-mid-5th ridge climbing on excellent granite lead to the Great Gendarme (two 5.9 pitches: a fingers/hands dihedral and an offwidth), then blocky 4th/low-5th terrain to the summit.
deleted_rows.turnaround: A full-value Grade IV outing — recorded ascents range from about 9 hours of pure climbing to 15-40 hours car-to-car including bivies. Set a firm turnaround before the Gendarme and carry bivy gear as a contingency.
deleted_rows.rappels: Walk off via the Cascadian Couloir, or the Sherpa Glacier or Sherpa Pass early in the season; there are no rappels on the descent. Parties who bypass the Great Gendarme instead of climbing it make one rappel of about 75 ft around it.
deleted_rows.face: North Ridge (complete, base to summit via the 1970 direct start)
deleted_rows.permit: Depends on the approach. Over Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead you are outside the Enchantment Permit Area: the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit covers day and overnight use, with no lottery. Via Mountaineer Creek from the Stuart Lake trailhead, camps are in the Enchantment Permit Area's Stuart Zone, where overnight stays May 15-Oct 31 require a quota permit (Recreation.gov advance lottery); day trips need only the free self-issued permit.
deleted_rows.comms: No reliable cell coverage on the ridge.
deleted_rows.descent: Cascadian Couloir (most common) or Sherpa Glacier/Sherpa Pass (faster, early season, north side)

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead (Eightmile Creek Rd #7601)
waypoints.note: Trail #1599 up Icicle/Eightmile Creek, then cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the base of the ridge.
waypoints.directions: This pin is the Icicle-side start, not the Teanaway one. Drive Eightmile Creek Road (FS 7601) to its end at the Stuart Lake Trailhead, about 3,400 ft, where Trail #1599 up Icicle/Eightmile Creek leaves the lot; the approach then goes cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the toe of the ridge. If you are coming at the ridge the other way, over Ingalls Pass and Goat Pass, that is a different drive to the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, so make sure you and your partner agree on the trailhead before you leave town.

waypoints.name: Base of North Ridge (glacier moat)
waypoints.note: Gain the ridge crest via the moat beside the Sherpa/Ice Cliff Glaciers; complete ridge route starts here.
waypoints.directions: Follow Trail #1599 past the Colchuck Lake fork (keep right). About a mile beyond, where the trail turns uphill and switchbacks right toward Stuart Lake, leave it and stay in the valley; cross Mountaineer Creek on logs and follow its south fork upstream, then climb steep talus into the hanging valley below Sherpa Peak. A faint path leads to the moraine; keep the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left to the lowest rock of the ridge.

waypoints.name: Mount Stuart summit
waypoints.note: Crux is the Great Gendarme (5.9 offwidth) about 500 ft below the summit; a short rappel bypasses it around the base.
waypoints.directions: Start from a big ledge with a small tree about 150 ft above the toe and climb the three hard opening pitches, then simul-climb up and right to the large notch at about 8,200 ft. Stay left of the crest, follow the exposed knife-edge to the Great Gendarme, climb its dihedral and offwidth, then traverse right back to the crest and finish up broken ground to the summit.

timing.recommendedStart: Very early alpine start (a recorded ascent left the trailhead at 5:24am)

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Cams 0.3-3in (doubles 0.4-2in, optional #4 for the Gendarme offwidth), one set of nuts (offsets recommended), 8-12 alpine draws; optional ice axe/crampons/helmet for approach snow.
what_to_bring: Extra food/water for a long day
pro_tips: The lower 3 pitches are a real technical crux (5.9+ sustained lieback) — don't underestimate them
Decide on the Gendarme bypass vs. direct finish before you're below it
deleted_rows.watch_out:
Loose rock and sometimes crumbly black lichen on rock at times
Alternative bypass gully NOT recommended - involves climbing dirty rock prone to rockfall
Gendarme section almost always in shade - can be very cold or even icy, creating hypothermia risk and icy climbing conditions
Significant complex terrain: parties have taken the wrong descent path by mistake - disorientation hazard
Seasonal constraints: snow patches affect water availability at notch (8,200 ft)
Multiple approach/descent options involve glacier travel (Sherpa, Stuart glaciers) that become too difficult to navigate as the season progresses
Route quality varies - some sections clean, others lichen-covered and unstable
20 pitches of mostly 5th class climbing with mixed terrain
Helmet essential due to rockfall concern
Complex terrain and poor visibility increase navigation challenges especially during descent
deleted_rows.pro_needs: A standard alpine rack sized up for the offwidth crux; natural pro (horns, slung blocks) supplements the rack on the long ridge sections.
deleted_rows.best_season: July through September; a lingering ice/snow patch in the gully below the Great Gendarme can persist into midsummer.
deleted_rows.approach: From the Esmeralda/Lake Ingalls Trailhead at the end of FS-9737, hike the Ingalls Way Trail up switchbacks past several waterfalls. For the Cascadian Couloir and South Headwall, turn right onto the Longs Pass Trail at the junction about 1.7 miles in, climb to Longs Pass (about 6,250 ft) near mile 2.9, and descend the rocky climbers' trail on the far side to Ingalls Creek, cross on a log bridge, and follow the climbers' path up the meadow into the base of the Cascadian Couloir (South Headwall lies further up-basin via the same drainage). For West Ridge, the North Ridge routes, and the South Face (Gorillas in the Mist / Gorillas Direct / King Kong), instead stay on the Ingalls Way Trail over Ingalls Pass (about 6,500 ft, roughly mile 3) and continue past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then follow the climbers' trail onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass (7,600 ft) — the South Face wall with the Gorillas routes sits in the amphitheater roughly midway between Stuart Pass and Goat Pass, while West Ridge and North Ridge climbers continue over or along Goat Pass toward their respective start points. Camping is common near Goat Pass or down at Ingalls Creek depending on the objective. The North Ridge routes can also be reached from the opposite (Mountaineer Creek) side.
deleted_rows.descent_text: The Cascadian Couloir is the most common descent — a long traverse south then a loose, sustained scree/talus descent to Ingalls Creek. On the north side, the Sherpa Glacier is quicker and more direct in early season for parties based at a Mountaineer Creek camp; alternatively descend 3rd-class terrain around the south side of Sherpa Peak to Sherpa Pass and glissade a snow slope. A West Ridge downclimb is reported as tedious and not recommended.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat is difficult once established above the first few pitches; the short rappel around the Great Gendarme is the main planned bail/bypass option below the final headwall.

pitch_detail.notes: Start from a big ledge about 150 ft above the true toe of the ridge. Climb easy ground and a lieback to a small pine, then continue into an awkward squeeze slot, 5.8 and considerably harder with a pack on. Pitch breaks vary between parties here; belay on the ledge above the slot.
Face climbing on good granite to a comfortable ledge at the foot of the long crack on the left. Moderate and well protected; it sets up the belay for the crux pitch.

The technical crux of the whole route: a striking, sustained lieback crack on the left that goes on for a long way, ending with a pull over a small roof to a belay ledge. Pumpy and insecure with alpine packs. Parties who cannot free it often aid through the crux.

A short pitch that finishes the steep lower buttress. Above it, the ridge eases and the simul-climbing begins. Take note of the terrain above before pulling the rope, since route-finding from here to the notch is by the cleanest path.

Long simul-climbing blocks of 3rd class to 5.6 up and right along the ridge to the large notch at about 8,200 ft, where the Stuart Glacier approach joins. Rock off the most-travelled line is loose and lichen-covered, so follow the cleanest path. The notch has bivy sites and, earlier in the season, water from snowmelt.

From the notch stay on the left (east) side, then follow an easy ramp to the crest. The ridge narrows to an exposed knife-edge, taken on its west side, with short 5.5 laybacks and one 5.7 move. A superb 5.5 slab split by a crack comes just before the Gendarme. Most parties simul-climb most of this upper ridge.

A steep fingers-and-hands dihedral with laybacks and underclings, with good rests between the harder sections, to the top of a pillar. Given grades range from 5.8 to 5.9. The Gendarme is almost always shaded and can be cold, wet or iced after bad weather. Bypass option: a bolted rappel down the west side, then a dirty, rockfall-prone gully; not recommended.

Traverse to the offwidth and climb it. It is steep and intimidating from below but has solid holds and fist jams inside; given grades range from 5.8+ to 5.9+. A 3.5–4 in cam is essential, and a second one makes it much safer. Belay above once the angle eases.

Above the Gendarme, trend right on an airy traverse back to the crest at a small saddle. Climb a short 5.7 hand crack (some parties find a 5.8 move), then lower-angle broken ground leads to the summit (9,415 ft). The descent is the Cascadian Couloir to the south, or the Sherpa Glacier for a north-side camp.

deleted_rows.itinerary: Typically done as a long single day by fast parties (simul-climbing) or over 2-3 days with a bivy on the ridge for parties pitching it out fully.

access.fees: None beyond the parking or entrance fee this route already lists.
access.rules: Overnight groups inside the permit boundary capped at 8 people, must camp together at one previously-impacted site, max 14 consecutive days, no re-entry same trip, permits non-transferable. Bear-resistant food storage mandatory forest-wide.

overnight_permit.where: Apply to the advance lottery on Recreation.gov in late February; leftover and daily permits are released on Recreation.gov after the lottery. No permit needed for a day climb or outside the season.

road.name: Teanaway River Road (FR-9737) to Longs Pass/Ingalls Creek approach, or Stuart Lake Trailhead (Icicle Creek Road) depending on route/face
road.status: Teanaway River Road: paved then gravel, generally passable to standard cars to the road-end parking (~4,243 ft) about 1 mile past DeRoux Campground. Stuart Lake TH access road (FS-7601 off Icicle Road) is steep/washboarded, high-clearance recommended.
road.driveNote: Roughly 2-2.5 hours from Seattle via I-90 to Cle Elum then Teanaway River Road (for Cascadian Couloir/south-side routes), or via US-2/Icicle Creek Road from Leavenworth (for north-side/Stuart Lake approaches).

climate.fall: Climbable into October in dry years
climate.spring: Approach and Gendarme moat still snow-covered
climate.typical: Dry, continental high-alpine climate; hot days, cold nights, afternoon-storm risk

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Esmeralda Basin Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737), via the Ingalls Way Trail

sling_rack.cams: 0.3-3, doubles 0.4-2, optional #4 for the Gendarme offwidth

deleted_rows.rope_note: Striking pitch-3 liebeck crack, Great Gendarme offwidth crux, 5.5 slab with a good crack up top. Rock is loose and lichen-covered in places.
deleted_rows.corrections: fa corrected to include the North Ridge's actual 1956 original ascent (Claunch & Rupley, bypassing the Great Gendarme), previously omitted. 1963 Beckey/Marts re-labeled as the first ascent climbing directly over the Gendarme rather than the route's original FA, per American Alpine Institute / SummitPost / Cascades climbing-history sources. Rest of the row's beta was pulled directly from Mountain Project and is unchanged.

approach_variants.name: Mountaineer Creek to the hanging valley, then straight to the toe of the ridge

bivy.name: Mountaineer Creek basin below the Sherpa Glacier
bivy.notes: The standard base for the north side of Mount Stuart. Leave the Stuart Lake trail before the final switchbacks, cross the creek and follow the climbers' path up the south fork of Mountaineer Creek to the flat valley below the Sherpa and Stuart glaciers.
bivy.water: Creek runs through the basin
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (Stuart zone) from May 15 to October 31
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites on flat ground in the basin

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

approach_variants.notes: From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road (about 3,400 ft), follow the trail past the Colchuck Lake fork and keep going. Roughly a mile beyond that fork the maintained trail turns uphill and switchbacks away to the right for Stuart Lake. Leave it there and stay flat in the valley with Mountaineer Creek. Cross the creek on logs — there is no canonical log and the crossing moves with the snowpack — then follow the south fork upstream. After a couple of miles the valley steepens; turn up a steep talus and boulder slope into the hanging valley beneath Sherpa Peak, where the bivy sites are. That flat ground under the glaciers is the arrival cue for camp. From the hanging valley the last leg is a faint climbers' path through trees and talus to the moraine, then up the edge of the moraine to rock. The Direct start is the same climb as the Complete North Ridge with a lower-ridge variation on its first pitches; if you are looking at an entry on this app for 'North Ridge (Complete)' as well, treat the approach as identical.
approach_variants.season: Jun-mid Jul; best early, while the Sherpa Glacier still gives a straightforward descent back to this side
hazards: Log crossings of Mountaineer Creek that shift year to year and are worse under early-season snow
Rockfall and icefall off the Ice Cliff Glacier while traversing the moraine beneath it
An open moat between snow and rock at the toe late in the season
Loose rock and crumbly black lichen on the lower pitches
A committing 20-pitch route with the Great Gendarme high on it and no easy retreat once above the lower ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Keep the Ice Cliff Glacier on your left and walk until the rock stops you. That single sentence is the whole test, and it works in cloud because it is about which side the ice is on rather than about seeing the summit. Climbing out of the hanging valley towards the mountain, the Ice Cliff Glacier must stay on your left the whole way. If it swings round to your right you have walked past the toe and out onto the Stuart Glacier side.

The toe itself is the lowest rock of the ridge, at roughly 6,600 ft, where the moraine runs into the buttress. You are at the correct place when there is nothing lower to climb — the ridge above you rises unbroken and the ground on either side falls away into a glacier.

Second test, and it is what tells the Direct start from a wander onto the flank: the first belay is off a big ledge about 150 ft above the base of the toe, with a small tree on it. If you have not passed a big ledge with a tree inside the first rope length, you are not on the line. The three opening pitches are the hardest on the whole route — an awkward squeeze slot and then a long, sustained lieback crack on the left. If your first pitches feel easy, you have started too high and joined the ordinary ridge.

What going too far looks like: the ridge you are standing under gains a deep notch with flat bivy ground in it. That notch is where the Upper North Ridge starts, and reaching it on foot means you have skipped the 1,200 ft this route exists for.

approach_variants.name: Ingalls Lake and Goat Pass, traversing east below the Stuart Glacier to the toe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, follow the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass and past Ingalls Lake toward Stuart Pass, then pick up the climbers' path onto the talus shoulder below Stuart's West Ridge and contour northwest to Goat Pass, about 7,600 ft — the col between Point 7893 and the West Ridge.

This is now the common way parties reach the ridge, and its advantage is that it puts you on the south side of the range where the descent also finishes, rather than committing you to a north-side camp you then have to walk back around to.

From Goat Pass, do not drop onto the glacier and go up. Traverse east below the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe.

Bivy sites exist at Goat Pass and at Stuart Pass. Published trailhead-to-base times for this variant vary widely enough that no figure is given here.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Ingalls Way trail is clear and the Stuart Glacier traverse is walkable
hazards: Crevasses and a soft afternoon snow surface on the Stuart Glacier traverse
Loose moraine and talus on the traverse below the glacier
Route-finding error at Goat Pass in cloud, where dropping onto the glacier feels natural and is wrong
A long committing route with the Great Gendarme high on it
No water between the last melt stream and the summit
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Stay above the moraine mound and keep traversing. Coming from Goat Pass the mistake is vertical, not horizontal: the ground invites you to drop down onto the glacier or to climb up onto the ridge crest early, and both put you on the route above its start.

The line is a rising traverse east, above the large moraine mound below the Stuart Glacier, all the way to the toe. If you find yourself walking down onto flat glacier ice you have dropped too low. If you find yourself scrambling onto ridge crest before you have gone round the end of the rock, you are on the west flank and above the toe.

Arrival: the toe is the point where the buttress runs out into the moraine and there is nothing below it to climb, at roughly 6,600 ft. Confirm it the same way the north-side party does — from the toe, the Ice Cliff Glacier is on the far (east) side of the ridge and the Stuart Glacier is behind you to the west. If both glaciers are on the same side of you, you are not at the toe.

And the same first-pitch check applies: the opening belay is a big ledge with a small tree roughly 150 ft up, and the first three pitches are the hardest of the route. Easy first pitches mean you started too high.

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

bivy.name: Mountaineer Creek basin below the Sherpa Glacier
bivy.notes: The standard base for the north side of Mount Stuart. Leave the Stuart Lake trail before the final switchbacks, cross the creek and follow the climbers' path up the south fork of Mountaineer Creek to the flat valley below the Sherpa and Stuart glaciers.
bivy.water: Creek runs through the basin
bivy.permit: Enchantment Permit Area overnight permit (Stuart zone) from May 15 to October 31
bivy.capacity: Several small tent sites on flat ground in the basin

bivy.name: North Ridge notch bivy
bivy.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
bivy.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
bivy.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
bivy.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route

deleted_rows.corrections: "The Gendarme" is not documented as an independent, separately-graded route on Mountain Project, SummitPost, or AAC Publications; all sources describe it strictly as the crux buttress on the North Ridge / Direct North Ridge routes. approach_variants.name: Climb the whole North Ridge from its toe
Climb the Upper North Ridge from the notch
Climb the Direct North Ridge
Reached only by climbing the North Ridge — the base is a point on the route, not a place you walk to
approach_variants.notes:
There is no independent approach to this feature. The Great Gendarme is a tower high on Mount Stuart's North Ridge and you arrive at its base having already climbed either the complete ridge from the toe near 6,600 ft or the upper ridge from the notch above the Stuart Glacier. Reckon on roughly eight or nine pitches of ridge above the notch, and considerably more from the toe.

What matters at the Gendarme is the decision made at its base, because the Gendarme is the one place on the ridge where there is a real choice and where a party that has not decided in advance loses time at 9,000 ft.

Both options are established. The tower goes in two pitches — a lieback, then the offwidth — and it can also be turned on ledges to the west, which is what the original 1956 ascent did and what most parties still do. The bypass is not an escape hatch invented by tired climbers; it is the older line.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, as for whichever North Ridge line you are on
hazards: Arriving at the tower late in the day with the summit still above and no quick way off the ridge
1,000+ ft of exposure on both sides of the crest
Rockfall from parties above on a popular ridge
Cold wind, and an unplanned bivy if the choice at the base costs too long
Retreat from above the Gendarme is awkward in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are at the base when the ridge stops being scrambling and stands up in front of you. Everything below is fourth to mid-fifth class on excellent granite that you have been moving together on. The Gendarme is where that ends: a steep tower blocking the crest, roughly 500 ft below the summit, and there is nothing else on the ridge it can be confused with.

The discriminator is whether you can walk round it. If a line of ledges leads off left (west) and lets you keep moving without roping up properly, you are at the bypass — the same place, and the decision point. If you are looking straight up at a clean lieback flake with an offwidth above it, you are at the climb.

So the test in fog is a negative one, and it is worth stating because parties do get this wrong on the way to the summit: if you are still on the ridge and have not yet had to make that choice, the Gendarme is ahead of you and the summit is not. If you have made it and are back on blocky fourth and low-fifth ground, the Gendarme is behind you and the summit is close.

A useful sanity check on the two pitches themselves: the second one has a reputation far worse than the climbing, and parties consistently report it going on good holds and jams with fixed gear in it. If the offwidth you are in feels desperate and unprotectable, look again at where you are — you may have entered the wrong crack on the tower.

deleted_rows.overview: Alpine rock climbing on the northeast-facing aspect of Mount Index, featuring Class 4-5 scrambling and mixed rock pitches on primarily solid granite.
deleted_rows.beta: This route is less frequently documented than other Index routes. The northeast face offers an intermediate alpine rock objective with mixed scrambling and roped pitches. Route quality and exact character are variable; climbing conditions greatly affect difficulty.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Turn around by 2 PM if not past halfway mark; summit must be reached by 3-4 PM for safe descent.
deleted_rows.rappels: Descend via rappels down the route line — a few single-rope near the top, most of them double-rope off trees; fixed slings/bolts exist but are reported worn or rockfall-damaged in places — inspect every anchor.

waypoints.directions: From US 2 about 7 miles east of Gold Bar (near milepost 35), just as the highway curves left toward the bridge over the Skykomish River, turn right (south) onto Mount Index Road. Follow the gravel road about a quarter mile, turn right at the sign for Lake Serene Trail 1068, and park in the lot about 500 ft ahead at roughly 600 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass is required.

waypoints.name: Lake Serene
waypoints.directions: Follow Lake Serene Trail #1068, first along an old road and then climbing through forest. At about 1.7 miles stay left where the signed Bridal Veil Falls spur branches right, cross the creek, and climb the final 1.5 miles on steps, roots and rock into the basin at the lake's north end, about 3.6 miles and 2,000 ft from the trailhead.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Single set of nuts (micronuts through size 1), single set of cams (size 0 through #2), 2-3 alpinedraws, slings. Light protection; most climbing is scrambling.
pro_tips: This is a less-visited route; expect minimal established anchors
Start very early for good light throughout the climb
Mark your route carefully on ascent for descent reference
Rope up for all Class 5 sections; ground-up protection-only ethics
Combining with traverse to North Peak is possible for strong parties

Loose rock common on less-traveled aspects
Limited protection on many pitches; exposure significant
Weather can change rapidly; mist frequently covers this face

Hike Lake Serene trail 3.6 miles to the lake (2,000 ft gain, 1.5-2 hours). Traverse the lake and approach the northeast-facing slopes from the east side. Route-finding to the base requires good terrain assessment.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Retrace the route or descend via adjacent gully systems to the talus. Most parties rappel the line: a few single-rope rappels, then a series of double-rope rappels off trees and old slings back to the base of the North Face bowl and below. Inspect every anchor.

Sustained brush-and-tree climbing on vegetated, sometimes rotten rock through the North Face bowl area; consistently slower and wetter than expected.

deleted_rows.corrections: Multiple naming/grade conflicts across sources for this same line: (1) Mountain Project titles the route "North Face"; the DB's given name "Northeast Buttress" matches how some older trip reports/guidebooks refer to it (also seen as "NE Rib") — same physical route. (2) Grade sources disagree: Mountain Project lists YDS 5.7 and Alpine Grade IV, while The Mountaineers, CascadeClimbers trip reports, and general guidebook commentary describe it as 5.6, Grade III — reported here as 5.6-5.7 / Grade III (IV per MP). (3) First-ascent history is genuinely disputed: some sources credit Lionel Chute and Victor Kaartinen in 1929, but an earlier partial ascent to a false summit by Chute and Frank Hill is documented for August 7, 1927, and the first edition of Beckey's Cascade Alpine Guide (1973) instead credits Chute, G. Tepley, and possibly a third companion in summer 1929 — the exact party has reportedly been uncertain for decades.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, on slab and talus. That spot sits close to the edge of the quarter-mile no-camping ring, probably just outside it but not by a comfortable margin, so sleep as high and as far from the shore as the ground allows and be ready to move if asked. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.

deleted_rows.overview: A long, serious alpine rock route up Sherpa's north ridge, broken into three sections by notches, with sustained loose rock and two 5.8 pitches guarding the top.
deleted_rows.beta: Considerably harder and more serious than its grade suggests. The route climbs the north crest in three sections divided by rappels into notches, mixing simul-climbed class 2-4 terrain (with a couple of unavoidable 5.6-5.8 pitches on the lower section) with scrambling around spires, then two sustained 5.8-ish pitches before a final low-5th romp to the summit. It's not possible to give a precise total pitch count because of simul-climbing, short pitches to manage rope drag, and route variations — totals run to roughly 13 rope-length sections over about 1,400 ft.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Given the route's length, loose rock, and complex descent, treat this as a two-day outing with a hard turnaround time on the ridge to avoid descending in the dark.
deleted_rows.rappels: On the descent: a short rappel of about 30 ft off the summit anchor plus an optional ~20 ft one, then a class 3 gully to the south/southwest using established stations. The rappel into the second notch is on the way UP, not down - the ridge is climbed by rappelling or downclimbing into that notch before the upper 5.8 pitches - and retreat from high on the route means rappelling back into those same notches.
deleted_rows.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Mountaineer Creek drainage or on the ridge.
deleted_rows.descent: Rappel southwest from the summit, then descend a gully system and scree slopes back to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin.
obj_haz: Difficult, sparse protection around loose blocks
Complex multi-notch route-finding and a long, tricky descent

timing.recommendedStart: Alpine start from a mid-route bivy or the Sherpa-Argonaut basin

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A single rack to 3 inches with doubled 0.5-1 inch cams and numerous long slings/runners; a 60m rope is ideal though a 40-50m rope can suffice.
what_to_bring: Bivy gear — often climbed as a 2-day route with a mid-route bivy ledge
Extra water for the unmaintained Mountaineer Creek approach
pro_tips: Stay just on the east side of the crest on the lower section to avoid inadvertently adding harder 5.6-5.8 variations
Bypass the large gendarme with the 'diving board' feature on its right side
Plan on 2 days with a bivy given the route's length and loose rock
watch_out: Large detached, loose blocks throughout — test every hold
Difficult, sparse protection on several pitches
A complex, tricky descent with a scree/scramble finish
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Protection is frequently difficult around detached and loose blocks; this route is explicitly noted by climbers as serious for its grade.
deleted_rows.best_season: Best climbed July through September in dry conditions; the unmaintained Mountaineer Creek approach is easiest once seasonal snow has cleared.
deleted_rows.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (end of FR 7601 off Icicle Creek Rd), hike the Stuart Lake Trail and break off onto an unmaintained climbers' path following Mountaineer Creek. Stay along the creek — do not follow cairns into the boulder field — until it forks; take the left fork to a flat area around 5,800 ft, then continue up toward the Sherpa-Argonaut basin/saddle to reach the base of the North Ridge. The unmaintained path is riddled with blowdown and can be hard to follow.
deleted_rows.descent_text: From the summit, make a short (~30 ft) rappel, with an optional additional ~20 ft rappel, then descend a class 3 gully to the south/southwest using established rappel stations. Traverse benches east toward the Sherpa-Argonaut Col and descend roughly 1,000 ft of loose, unstable scree/talus back to the basin.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat by rappelling/downclimbing back into the notches between the three ridge sections; the lower sections are far easier to reverse than the upper 5.8 pitches, so committing above the second notch should not be done lightly.

pitch_detail.notes: The lowest section of the north ridge is easy fourth- to low-fifth-class ground, often climbed tied in but with little or no gear. It ends at slings for a 25 m rappel into the first (lower) notch. Many parties skip it and start at that notch, contouring up from the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and scrambling easy slabs before roping up.

From the lower notch the ridge steepens and offers many options. Keep just left (east) of the crest; straying onto the crest at the wrong point adds harder 5.6-5.9 pitches. The section mixes class 2-4 ground with several 5.7-5.8 pitches and is usually simul-climbed. It ends on top of the large tower about two-thirds of the way up the ridge.

From the big tower walk down, then rappel 25 m from slings (or downclimb) into the second notch. It is also possible to drop about 60 ft and traverse around the tower to a large ledge with bivy space. Cross the narrow knife-edge bridge beyond (class 3-4), scramble around a couple of spires, and pass the big gendarme with the diving-board feature on its right.

The first of two short, steep pitches guarding the summit section. Large detached blocks and awkward protection are common on the pitches above low fifth class, so test holds and place gear with care.
The second short, steep pitch, reached across a stretch of class 2-3. Expect the same mix of solid cracks and loose, detached blocks as the pitch below.
Several blocky steps lead to the summit. Most are low fifth class, but a few are short, bouldery 5.8+ moves. Descent begins from the summit anchor with a short rappel to the southwest.

deleted_rows.itinerary: Day 1: approach via Stuart Lake Trail and Mountaineer Creek to the Sherpa-Argonaut basin; many parties use an established bivy ledge partway up the ridge. Day 2: continue up the ridge (roughly 13 rope-length sections mixing simul-climbing, scrambling, and two 5.8 pitches) to the summit, then descend via the southwest gully/scree to the basin and hike out.
