seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August to early September, when the Mountaineer Creek basin is snow-free and the north-side notches and rock are dry

July.reason: The basin and talus melt out through the month; early July can leave snow in the north-facing rappel notches and wet rock.

June.reason: The trailhead road is usually open, but snow buries the talus below the Sherpa-Argonaut col and fills the shaded notches between ridge sections.

August.reason: The approach talus and north crest are dry; long days suit the two-day climb, though wildfire smoke can blanket the Enchantments.

October.reason: Snow and ice collect on the shaded north ridge and in the notches, and short days make the blowdown-choked descent slow.

September.reason: Still dry, but the north-facing crest is cold, days shorten for a long simul-climbing day, and early storms can dust the ridge.

deleted_rows.name: Neve Glacier / West Ridge
deleted_rows.fa: William Degenhardt and Herbert Strandberg, August 1931
gear: Glacier rope and crevasse-rescue kit (pickets, prusiks)
Sturdy boots for talus and bushwhacking
Blue bags/WAG bags (no toilets in the Colonial/Snowfield zones)
Extra water capacity for a dry camp
hazards: Crevasses on the Neve and Colonial Glaciers, worse as the season progresses and snowbridges deteriorate
Steep, dry climbers' trail with no water between Pyramid Lake and the Colonial Glacier basin
Loose rock and occasional verglas/snow on the class 3-4 west-ridge finish
Routefinding in fog/whiteout on the glacier and ridge
Long, sustained approach (talus, brush, elevation gain) that outweighs the technical climbing in difficulty
deleted_rows.overview: The West Ridge is the line taken by the 1931 first ascent party and remains the natural finish most climbers use off the Neve Glacier: gain the crest just west of the summit and scramble class 3-4 on gneiss to the top. It isn't a distinct technical line so much as the standard glacier route's summit exit, but it's worth listing separately since older published descriptions treat it as the named route.
deleted_rows.beta: A moderate but serious glacier-and-scramble outing that climbs the peak via its easiest side. After crossing the Colonial Glacier and dropping into the Neve Glacier basin, climbers follow the broad West Ridge to a gully on climber's left, ascend nearly to its top, climb over a wall on the left side and downclimb roughly 60 ft to a ramp system, then traverse right below the summit into a final open gully to the top. A rope is useful for the airy step and standard for the glacier crossings, especially when the route holds snow or verglas.
deleted_rows.turnaround: As with any glaciated North Cascades objective, set a firm turnaround time before starting and honor it — afternoon thunderstorms, softening snowbridges, and rockfall risk on the summit gully all increase later in the day; do not push for the summit if the party can't be back across the Neve and Colonial Glaciers before conditions deteriorate.
deleted_rows.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Colonial/Neve glacier basin or on the summit ridge.
deleted_rows.descent: Downclimb the same gully/ramp system back to the Neve Glacier, re-climb to the Colonial-Neve col, and reverse the Colonial Glacier and climbers' trail back to Pyramid Lake and the highway.
obj_haz: Crevasses on the Neve Glacier approach to the ridge base
Verglas/rime ice on the ridge gully and ramp after storms
Loose rock and exposure on the airy ramp traverse

waypoints.name: Pyramid Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: North Cascades Highway (SR-20), 6.4mi east of Newhalem; brushy climbers trail up from Pyramid Lake to Pyramid-Colonial col.
waypoints.directions: From Newhalem, drive the North Cascades Highway (SR-20) east past Gorge Lake to the Pyramid Lake Trailhead at milepost 126.8. Park in the small lot on the north side of the highway; the signed trail starts across the road beside Pyramid Creek. No parking pass is needed, but overnight stays in the backcountry require a North Cascades National Park Complex backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Snowfield Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Hike the Pyramid Lake Trail 2.1 miles to Pyramid Lake (no camping there), then take the steep, brushy climbers' path from the lake onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge and south to camps by the Colonial Glacier moraine. Climb the Colonial Glacier to the col near 6,800 ft, drop onto the Neve Glacier and cross it roped to the northwest-facing gully that gains the west ridge, then scramble class 3-4 past a notch to the summit.

sectionBreakdown.note: Same approach as the standard Neve Glacier line: Pyramid Lake Trail (2.1 mi, 1,500 ft) from SR-20, then a brushy climbers' trail up the ridge above the lake to a treeline or on-sno…
From camp, cross the col, ascend the Colonial Glacier to the ~6,800 ft pass, and traverse the Neve Glacier to gain the ridge just west of the summit. The finish is a short, exposed…
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Summit via Colonial/Neve Glaciers and the West Ridge

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: No fixed rack is required in dry conditions beyond standard glacier travel gear; carry a rope, a few slings, and perhaps a small selection of nuts/cams for the short exposed step near the notch if the rock is wet, snowy, or verglassed.
what_to_bring: Full water carry for the dry approach
pro_tips: Camp at the Colonial Glacier toe (~6,100 ft) or push on to the Colonial-Neve col to shorten summit day
Early-season snow bridges the Neve Glacier's crevasses but can obscure the route; by late summer the glacier opens up more but the summit rock band can still hold verglas after storms
Often combined with Colonial Peak from the same high camp for an efficient two-summit trip
watch_out: Crevasses on both the Colonial and Neve Glaciers demand careful route-finding and roped travel
The class 3-4 gully/ramp/notch section can be iced or hold verglas well into summer after storms
Long, sustained elevation gain (~7,400 ft) from the highway with an overnight pack makes for a serious two-day outing
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Minimal fixed protection is placed on this route — it is climbed as a roped glacier crossing followed by a lightly protected or unprotected class 3-4 scramble; a rope is most valuable for crevasse rescue and for the short airy downclimb near the notch.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late July through September, once the Neve Glacier has settled enough for reliable snowbridges but before crevasses fully open late in the season; the rock finish is driest and easiest by August.
deleted_rows.approach: From the Pyramid Lake Trailhead (~1,150 ft) on SR-20 (milepost 126.8, just east of Gorge Lake, about 7 miles east of Newhalem), follow the maintained Pyramid Lake Trail 2.1 miles and ~1,500 ft of gain to Pyramid Lake. Camping is prohibited at the lake, so continue on the rougher climbers' path along its west side, which climbs steeply and directly — no water beyond this point — through talus and brush onto the east ridge of Pyramid Peak to treeline camps near 5,400 ft. From there, continue south to the Colonial Glacier terminal moraine or the Colonial-Neve col (roughly 6,000-6,800 ft), the usual base camp. Round trip is about 15-16 miles with roughly 7,200-7,500 ft of total gain — the approach, not the climbing, is the crux of the day.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Reverse the west-ridge scramble and Neve Glacier crossing back to the Colonial-Neve col, then descend the Colonial Glacier and climbers' trail to Pyramid Lake and the trailhead. No rappels are typically needed; downclimb the class 3-4 section (including the ~60 ft notch downclimb) carefully, especially with snow or verglas on the rock.
deleted_rows.bail: The route has no fixed rappel stations; retreat is by downclimbing the same gully/ramp/notch used on the ascent back to the Neve Glacier, then reversing the glacier crossings to the Colonial-Neve col and back to high camp. Turn back before committing to the notch/ramp step if the rock is verglassed or the party is moving too slowly to be off the glaciers and ridge before afternoon weather.

pitch_detail.notes: Descend roughly 200-300 ft from the Colonial-Neve col onto the Neve Glacier and cross to its southeast edge below the West Ridge; watch for crevasses.
Follow the broad ridge to a gully on the climber's left; ascend the gully nearly to its top.
Climb up and over the wall on the climber's left, then downclimb roughly 60 ft to a ramp system; can hold snow/verglas.
Traverse right about 50 ft below the summit into an open gully leading to the top.

days.note: Same approach as the standard Neve Glacier line: Pyramid Lake Trail (2.1 mi, 1,500 ft) from SR-20, then a brushy climbers' trail up the ridge above the lake to a treeline or on-snow camp around 5,400-5,900 ft, or Colonial Basin.
days.title: Approach to high camp
days.objective: Reach treeline/Colonial Basin camp (~5,800-6,000 ft)

days.note: From camp, cross the col, ascend the Colonial Glacier to the ~6,800 ft pass, and traverse the Neve Glacier to gain the ridge just west of the summit. The finish is a short, exposed scramble: traverse into a northwest-facing gully, work left onto the arete, then up and around a pinnacle via ledges to the final summit gully. Descend by reversing the ridge and glaciers, then hike out to the trailhead the same day.

approach_variants.name: Pyramid Lake trail and the Pyramid Peak east ridge to the Colonial Glacier moraine camp
approach_variants.notes: From the trailhead at about 1,150 ft on the highway, the maintained trail runs a little over two miles and fifteen hundred feet to the lake, where camping is prohibited. Continue on the rougher climbers' path along the lake's west side, which climbs steeply and directly - and with no water beyond this point - through talus and brush onto Pyramid Peak's east ridge and treeline camps near 5,400 ft. From there continue south to the terminal moraine of the Colonial Glacier, or to the col beyond it between about 6,000 and 6,800 ft, which is the usual base camp. The approach rather than the climbing is the crux of this route.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through September
hazards: a steep brushy climbers' path with no water above the lake
loose rock and short route-finding steps on the Pyramid east ridge crest
crevasses on the Colonial and Neve glaciers
a featureless crossing where the exit point must be identified by the gully rather than by position
one exposed rib crossing in the entry gully
an exposed notch traverse near the summit, reversed on the way down
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The west ridge is gained from the glacier by a gully, and the gully is the positive marker. From camp, climb the Colonial Glacier to the broad col near 6,840 ft - it carries a stream, so a dry saddle is the wrong one - then drop 150 to 250 ft onto the Neve and cross it roped.

Leave the ice on the peak's north-west side, near the prominent rock feature there around 7,700 ft. The entry is a class 3 gully with one exposed rib crossing in it, and it tops out on the ridge three to four hundred vertical feet below the summit.

The negative marker is the one that matters on a glacier with no landmarks: if you step off the ice onto rock that rises straight into the summit pyramid with no gully beside it, you have crossed too far and are under the face. Traverse back rather than committing upward - the face and the ridge are different propositions and the ridge is the easier ground.

The second check is that the ridge has air on both sides. Once out of the gully you should be on a crest, not on a flank. A line that keeps a wall on one hand the whole way is not the ridge.

Above that the finish is common to both lines: a long class 3 gully to a notch just below the true summit, a short exposed traverse onto the south side, and blocky scrambling with one move that can feel low class 4. That notch is downclimbed on the exit, so read it on the way past.

climbing_route.label: Neve Glacier crossing
climbing_route.notes: A short snow climb from camp gains the Colonial-Neve col, then the route crosses the broad Neve Glacier toward the ridge just west of the summit. Crevasses are generally modest in number but present and open more as the season goes on, so parties rope and carry glacier gear. It is a long crossing and the last of it is where the ice meets rock, which is where a moat or schrund forms late season.

climbing_route.label: Gully onto the west ridge
climbing_route.notes: Around 8,200 ft leave the snow and traverse left roughly 100 ft into an obvious northwest-facing gully, then scramble up it about 50 to 100 ft. This gully holds snow, rime and verglas well into early July, and parties have had to climb over its left edge and drop onto a ramp system that was also iced. It is the section where footing, not difficulty, decides how the day goes.

climbing_route.label: Arete and north-side ledges to the notch
climbing_route.notes: Traverse left onto an arete and climb it about 75 ft, traverse left again, then up the north side roughly 150 ft to the notch between a pinnacle and the summit. A couple of 4th class moves at the notch move out onto the south side directly above a deep gully — short, but the most exposed position on the peak. Short-roping through here is common when the ridge is airy or holding ice.

climbing_route.label: South-side summit gully
climbing_route.notes: From the notch, up the ridge about 20 ft, then traverse right on ledges to a gully on the south side of the summit; the gully is easy and about 150 ft to the top, and it downclimbs readily. Route-finding is the trap rather than the climbing: reports agree the last 100 vertical feet run class 3 to class 4 if you find the ledges and can be pushed to class 5 if you do not, and all options off the correct line look steeper and higher-consequence.

waypoints.name: Hairpin-curve pullout on Hwy 20
waypoints.note: Park at the 180-degree hairpin turn on SR-20, about a mile east of Washington Pass; Spire Gully starts here.
waypoints.directions: This is an alternate roadside start rather than somewhere you walk to from the Blue Lake lot: parties using it drive back east along the highway toward Washington Pass and park at the big 180-degree hairpin below the spires, which puts them straight into the bottom of Spire Gully. It cuts out the traverse in from the Blue Lake trail on the way up. The standard descent comes back out at Blue Lake, though, so plan on a shuttle or a hitch along the highway to close the loop.

waypoints.name: Blue Lake Trailhead, Hwy 20
waypoints.note: Alternate start and the usual way out: the Blue Lake Trail and the climbers' path on the west side of the spires. Northwest Forest Pass required to park.
waypoints.directions: Drive Highway 20 to the Blue Lake Trailhead, about 1 mile west of Washington Pass, and park in the small lot; a Northwest Forest Pass is required. Many East Buttress parties instead carry on east toward Washington Pass and park at the unmarked 180-degree hairpin pullout roughly a mile along, below the east faces of the spires, which drops you straight into the bottom of Spire Gully. The standard descent comes back out at Blue Lake, so if you leave the car at the hairpin, plan on a shuttle or a hitch along the highway to close the loop.

waypoints.name: NEWS-SEWS notch
waypoints.note: Gain the notch between the two spires, then traverse left (south) below South Early Winters Spire's east face to reach the buttress base.
waypoints.directions: Follow that gully up to the notch. It steepens and gets looser toward the top and holds snow late into the summer, so keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than climbing directly above one another.

waypoints.name: Base of East Buttress
waypoints.note: Rope up here for the climb up the buttress crest to the summit.
waypoints.directions: From the notch traverse left, southward, along ledges beneath the east face until you are under the crest of the buttress. It is only a short way along and barely above the notch, so treat it as a traverse rather than a climb, and rope up once you are there.

waypoints.name: South Early Winters Spire summit
waypoints.note: Highest summit of the Liberty Bell group; sweeping views of Liberty Bell, the Wine Spires, and North Early Winters Spire across the notch.
waypoints.directions: The standard line takes the easier lower-angle rock up the toe of the buttress rather than the steep dihedral system the Direct start uses, then follows cracks and broken ledges up the crest on clean granite, with the sustained crack-and-corner crux about a third of the way up. Higher pitches ease off and merge with the Direct's terrain, and the short final pitch to the top is often simul-climbed.

waypoints.name: South Arete downclimb/rappels
waypoints.note: Standard descent: downclimb the South Arete (mostly 3rd/4th class with a short exposed 5th-class step), then three single-rope raps from bolted anchors to the base before dropping back toward Blue Lake trail or hitching from the hairpin.
waypoints.directions: Do not reverse the buttress. The way off is the South Arete: mostly third and fourth class downclimbing with one short exposed fifth-class step, then three single-rope rappels from bolted anchors to the base. From there drop back toward the Blue Lake trail, or back into Spire Gully if a car was left at the hairpin.

sectionBreakdown.note: Approach to the base of the east buttress, climb 6 pitches to the summit, then downclimb the South Arete and make 3 rappels back to the base before hiking out.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Single rack through hand size with a set of nuts is sufficient for the moderate climbing.

Watch for parties above to manage rockfall.
Great moderate introduction to Washington Pass alpine rock.

deleted_rows.best_season: Summer into early fall for dry, warm granite.
deleted_rows.approach: From the SR-20 hairpin pullout, hike up Spire Gully below the col (occasional cairns) to the last large tree in the gully, traverse right across talus (or snow early season) to the gully leading to the NEWS-SEWS notch, then traverse left to the base of the east buttress.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descend the standard SEWS gully/rappels back toward Blue Lake.
deleted_rows.bail: Rappel the route; retreat is straightforward on this moderate line.

pitch_detail.notes: The standard, non-direct start climbs easier lower-angle rock up the toe of the buttress, avoiding the steep dihedral system taken by the Direct East Buttress lower on the wall.
Featured cracks and ledges work up the buttress crest on solid, clean granite with good gear throughout.
The route's crux pitch, a sustained crack-and-corner section on excellent golden Washington Pass granite; well protected with a standard rack.
Easier climbing merges toward similar terrain to the Direct East Buttress higher on the face, following cracks and broken ledges.
Rambling, well-featured rock leads up broken ledges and short walls toward the summit block.
A short, easy final pitch tops out at the true summit; many parties simul-climb this last section.

days.note: Approach to the base of the east buttress, climb 6 pitches to the summit, then downclimb the South Arete and make 3 rappels back to the base before hiking out.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington/Sedro-Woolley, then east on SR-20 over Rainy Pass and Washington Pass to the hairpin turn near milepost 163, east of the pass (5,160 ft); from Winthrop/Mazama it's a 20-30 minute drive west on SR-20.

rappel_detail.notes: Downclimb the south arete (3rd/4th class with a short exposed 5th-class section) to the first bolted rap station.
Second of three single-rope rappels down the south arete descent gully, with short sections of downclimbing between stations.
Final rappel to the base of the route; from there hike out via the Blue Lake Trail.

deleted_rows.rappel_count_note: Some parties downclimb more of the south arete and rappel less, so reports describe 2-3 single-rope rappels depending on conditions; 3 used as representative, based on beta for the closely related Direct East Buttress on the same feature/descent line.

approach_variants.name: Spire Gully from the SR-20 hairpin
approach_variants.notes:
The east-side approach, shared with the other East Buttress lines. Park at the dirt pullout at the hairpin turn on SR-20 beneath the east faces of the Early Winters Spires — not at the Blue Lake Trailhead, which serves the west side.

Go up Spire Gully, which breaches the first cliff band above the road, following occasional cairns. Continue to the last large tree standing in the centre of the gully. From there traverse right across talus, which brings you below the gully leading up to the notch between North and South Early Winters Spires, then traverse back left to the foot of the buttress.

Early season the traverse is on snow rather than talus and an axe and crampons are worth having.
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep
hazards: loose rock in Spire Gully
exposed traverse across talus or, early season, snow
no water on the approach
approach_variants.baseFinding: The reference feature is the gully dividing North from South Early Winters Spire. The buttress toe is the low point of the prow immediately left of that gully — locate the gully first, then step left. The last big tree in the middle of Spire Gully is the checkpoint that tells you where to leave the gully and start traversing right; reaching it is what confirms you are far enough up.

bivy.name: Blue Lake trailhead roadside bivy
bivy.notes: The usual answer for a car-to-car day on this group, and the start of every west-side approach, about a mile west of Washington Pass. Parties routinely sleep at the lot or at the highway hairpin rather than walking in, because the approaches are short enough that a high camp buys little. There are no facilities and no water; it is a place to sleep in or beside the car, not a campsite. Highway 20 is closed through the winter, so this is unavailable until the road reopens.
bivy.water: None at the trailhead. Carry what you need.
bivy.permit: Northwest Forest Pass required to park
bivy.capacity: Informal, at the parking area — no prepared sites

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground
bivy.notes: The closest developed campground, about a ten-minute drive east down the highway from the Blue Lake trailhead, in the trees along Early Winters Creek. No reservations, so it is a gamble on a summer weekend. Its season runs roughly from late spring into autumn and is decided by snow rather than by a date.
bivy.water: Early Winters Creek runs through the campground
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee
bivy.capacity: 27 sites, first come first served

bivy.name: Klipchuck Campground
bivy.notes: Further east and lower than Lone Fir, which means it opens earlier in the season when the higher options are still under snow — the practical choice for an early-season trip. It sits far enough off the highway to be quiet and has more plumbing than anything nearer the climbing. The trade is a longer drive to the trailhead each morning. Check current status before relying on it; the highway-corridor campgrounds take periodic maintenance closures.
bivy.water: Piped water, sinks and flush toilets
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee
bivy.capacity: First come first served

bivy.name: Liberty Bell basin dispersed sites
bivy.notes: Sites in the basin on the west side of the group, reached by following the Blue Lake trail and then the signed climbers' path that branches off it toward the group. Worth it if you want to be under the west-side routes at first light rather than walking up from the road. Note the separate restriction around Blue Lake itself, where overnight camping is not allowed within a quarter mile of the lake — the basin sites are the ones to aim for, not the lakeshore. Treat it as a basin camp below the spires rather than a fixed spot.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and seasonal runoff in the basin — unreliable once the snow has gone
bivy.permit: No permit for dispersed camping; this is national forest, not the national park
bivy.capacity: Scattered dispersed sites, small parties

deleted_rows.name: South Twin Sister Olivine Scramble
gear: Mountain bike (recommended for the logging-road approach)
hazards: Loose rock and talus on the south-side gully bypass
Seasonal snow/ice in the gullies below the summit notch
A very long, physically demanding approach that increases exposure to fatigue and afternoon weather
deleted_rows.overview: The standard non-technical line up South Twin Sister: follow the West Ridge approach to a high notch, then bypass the steep upper ridge crest, which has 5th-class moves, by traversing south across gullies and a seasonal snowfield to the summit, keeping the entire route to Class 2-3 on the range's namesake sticky olivine (dunite) rock.
deleted_rows.beta: Shares its approach with the West Ridge route: bike/hike logging roads from the gated Middle Fork Nooksack bridge around Dailey Prairie to Orsino Creek Basin, then ascend talus to a notch in the West Ridge near ~5,200 ft and follow the ridge (Class 2-3) to a high notch at about 6,600 ft, some 400 ft below the summit. Rather than following the steeper ridge crest above it, which has exposed 5th-class moves, traverse south onto gullies and a seasonal snowfield (present into mid-summer) to reach the summit at a sustained Class 2-3.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Given the very long approach (roughly 10-11 miles one-way) and full exposure on the upper talus and gullies, set a turnaround time that guarantees a daylight descent margin.
deleted_rows.face: Orsino Creek Basin / south-facing summit gullies
deleted_rows.permit: No climbing permit; the approach crosses private and DNR timberland - check current access, and carry a Discover Pass where parking on DNR land.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the same south-side gully/snowfield line back to the notch and down the approach talus and logging roads.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Gate/Bridge
waypoints.directions: From I-5 Exit 255, drive SR 542 east about 16.7 miles and turn right on Mosquito Lake Road. After 4.8 miles, just past Porter Creek, turn left on Middle Fork Road (FS Road 38), follow it 4.8 miles, and turn right at the junction that drops to the gated bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack at about 1,200 ft. Most parties bike the logging roads beyond the gate.

waypoints.name: South Twin Sister Summit
waypoints.directions: Bike the logging roads around Dailey Prairie into the basin between the Twins and follow the climbers' path through forest and talus, past old cabin ruins, to Orsino Creek Basin (last water). Climb the loose gully and talus to the 5,200-ft notch in the West Ridge, scramble the ridge east to the high notch near 6,600 ft, then traverse right across the snowfield or scree to the southern gullies and climb them to the summit.

Extra water — Orsino Creek is the last reliable source
pro_tips: Staying south of the ridge crest in the gullies avoids essentially all of the technical climbing on the standard line
An ice axe is worth carrying for the seasonal snowfield below the summit notch even in mid-summer
This variant is a good option for parties wanting the summit without the West Ridge's Class 4/5th exposure

deleted_rows.pro_needs: No technical protection is used on this variant; it is a non-technical Class 2-3 scramble throughout.
deleted_rows.best_season: Most reliably climbed July through September, once winter snowpack has cleared from the approach road; the seasonal snowfield in the summit gullies can persist into July and is easier with an ice axe.
deleted_rows.approach: Identical to the West Ridge approach: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR 38) to the gated bridge, then bike the logging roads around Dailey Prairie, hike a brushy climbers' path and talus to Orsino Creek Basin between North and South Twin. Orsino Creek is the last reliable water source.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Downclimb the south-side gullies and seasonal snowfield back to the high notch (about 6,600 ft), reverse the West Ridge to the ~5,200-ft notch, then retrace the talus slopes, climbers' path, and logging roads to the bike stash and gate. An ice axe is useful for the snowfield crossing even in mid-summer; loose rock in the gullies is the main hazard.
deleted_rows.bail: Simply reverse the gully/snowfield line back to the notch and descend the approach — there is no technical climbing to down-lead or rappel on this variant.

pitch_detail.notes: From the gated Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, bike the logging roads around Dailey Prairie into the basin between the Twin Sisters. A climbers' path runs through forest, bearing right to a talus slope that often holds snow late. It then traverses right up the talus, over a timbered rib and past old cabin ruins to Orsino Creek Basin. Orsino Creek is the last reliable water.

From the basin, climb a steep, loose dirt gully and then scree and talus to an obvious notch in the West Ridge at about 5,200 ft. Gaining the ridge this low is the easier choice and adds more time on good rock. The dirt and scree here are loose, so keep the party out of each other's fall line.

Follow the ridge east toward a high notch at about 6,600 ft, roughly two hours of Class 2-3 scrambling on grippy dunite. Use the crest or its south (right) side, which is solid, and avoid the north side, which is loose. Towers can be skirted on ledges. The line only reveals itself a few feet at a time, so allow for route-finding.
pitch_detail.pitch: West Ridge to the high notch

pitch_detail.notes: At the high notch, about 400 ft below the summit, the ridge steepens into exposed ground with 5th-class moves. Leave it and traverse right (south) across a seasonal snowfield or scree slope to a set of shallow gullies. An ice axe helps on the snowfield into midsummer. Parties that stay on the crest here meet high 4th- to 5th-class climbing with serious exposure.

Climb the southern gullies; the second major one is a good choice, and a large dihedral near 6,500 ft goes on ledges and cracks. The first high point reached may be a false summit. The true summit, with survey markers and a register, is a short way along the ridge at its southeast end. Loose rock remains, so test holds.

deleted_rows.itinerary: Typically a single very long car-to-car day; some parties camp high in Orsino Creek Basin to split the trip over two days.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July to mid-September, once the logging roads and Orsino Creek Basin melt out and the summit gully snow has shrunk

July.reason: The roads are usually bikeable to the basin; the snowfield in the summit gullies lingers and is easier with an ice axe early in the month.

June.reason: Upper logging roads and Orsino Creek Basin often still hold snow and the summit gullies are snow-filled; expect axe-and-crampon terrain and a very long day.

August.reason: Gullies mostly melted and the olivine is dry and grippy; in high fire danger the timberland owner can close the gated roads, so confirm access first.

October.reason: Autumn rain and early snow make the talus and gully slick, days are short for a long bike-and-hike, and fall hunting runs on the timberland roads.

September.reason: Cooler days on the long south-facing approach and dry rock, with the summit snowfield at its smallest; Orsino Creek is the last reliable water.

bivy.name: Orsino Creek Basin
bivy.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
bivy.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
bivy.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

bivy.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
bivy.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
bivy.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
bivy.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
bivy.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

bivy.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
bivy.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
bivy.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

bivy.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
bivy.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags

deleted_rows.name: Sawtooth Range Scramble
deleted_rows.fa: Harold Pinsch and Garry Tate, 1966 (Northeast Face)
gear: Standard trad rack to ~3" plus a few small pins/nuts for thin approach moves
Single 60m rope typical for the tower itself; parties continuing along the ridge often carry two ropes
Extra webbing/cord for rappel anchors — little to no fixed gear on Sawtooth Ridge
hazards: Loose, frost-shattered basalt ("choss") on upper faces and ledges, typical of Olympic rock
Moss-covered slabs when wet, common in this wet climate
Sparse fixed protection — rappel anchors are typically slung webbing/cord around horns or blocks, not bolts
Post-fire rockfall, treefall, and landslide hazard along the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire burn scar on the approach trail
Late-season unstable talus and a moat in the Needle Couloir / approach gullies
Route-finding among roughly a dozen similarly sized named towers along the ridge crest
deleted_rows.overview: The Fin is one of roughly a dozen named rock towers strung along Sawtooth Ridge, which runs from Mount Cruiser (6,104') southeast to Mount Lincoln above the Flapjack Lakes / Gladys Divide basin in the Skokomish-Duckabush divide of southeastern Olympic National Park. It sits on the ridge crest between the Castle Peaks and The Horn (5.5), a short distance southeast of Mount Cruiser. The tower is best known for a 5.4 route up its northeast face that finishes in what climbers describe as a "world class," unusually deep chimney on solid pillow basalt — among the better rock quality on the ridge.
deleted_rows.beta: The only documented established route to The Fin's summit is a single 120-ft pitch rated 5.4, known as 'The Fin--Northeast Face', first climbed by Harold Pinsch and Garry Tate in 1966. From the northeast side, angled bouldery moves gain a 'monster chimney' with good chockstones that feels more secure the deeper you go; an easy 3rd-class scramble from the top of the chimney reaches the true summit. Rock is pillow basalt — generally solid in the chimney but can be looser/chossier on the outer face, especially as the season progresses and snow melts off holds.
deleted_rows.turnaround: The approach alone is 7+ miles each way to Flapjack Lakes plus additional cross-country ridge travel to reach the route, and Olympic summers bring a real chance of afternoon thunderstorms; set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight to reverse the scramble/downclimb and hike all the way back out before dark.
deleted_rows.rappels: No fixed rappel station. The standard descent avoids reversing the pitch altogether via the 3rd-class scramble/east-face walk-off back to Sawtooth Pass; parties who prefer to rappel the chimney build a gear anchor or sling a chockstone/horn for a ~120 ft (37 m) rappel, which needs two ropes — a single 60 m rope doubled reaches only about 30 m.
deleted_rows.descent: Descend the east-face scramble back to Sawtooth Pass rather than reversing the chimney pitch.
obj_haz: Rockfall, especially late season once snow melts off the approach slope and scree
Off-route class 4 terrain if the class-3 line near the pass is lost
Steep snow on the approach slope early season (ice axe useful)
Water scarcity along the ridge crest
Dense brush (slide alder, devil's club) on the lower trail approach

waypoints.name: Staircase Ranger Station / North Fork Skokomish Trailhead
waypoints.note: Wilderness permit required, reserved in advance (no self-issue or walk-up permits for Flapjack Lakes); trail departs above the ranger station past the stock corral.
waypoints.directions: From Hoodsport, drive about 16 miles northwest past Lake Cushman on FR 24 to the Staircase Ranger Station and the North Fork Skokomish River Trailhead at roughly 785 feet. The trail leaves from above the ranger station, past the stock corral. A wilderness permit is required, and because Flapjack Lakes is a limited-use overnight zone you should reserve one on recreation.gov ahead of time.

waypoints.name: Spike Camp Junction
waypoints.note: North Fork Skokomish Trail continues straight toward First Divide; right fork switchbacks steeply to Flapjack Lakes — last reliable creek water is ~100 yds past Spike Camp.

waypoints.name: Flapjack Lakes
waypoints.note: Designated backcountry camp in a subalpine basin (bear wire, pit toilet); campfires banned above 3,500 ft and lake water must be treated.

waypoints.name: Gladys Divide
waypoints.note: High saddle overlooking the Sawtooth spires (Mt. Lincoln to the south, Mt. Cruiser southwest); trail turns primitive/unmaintained beyond here and snow can linger into July.

waypoints.name: Needle Pass
waypoints.note: Notch on the Sawtooth Ridge crest southeast of Gladys Divide used for the spires north of The Fin; this route does not cross it, turning off the Gladys Divide trail near 4,400 ft for Sawtooth Pass instead.

waypoints.name: Exposed ridge crest below the NE face
waypoints.note: Short exposed scrambling/downclimbing sections along the crest approaching The Fin — the same steps most parties rappel or downclimb on the descent.

waypoints.name: The Fin
waypoints.note: True summit (5.4); standard line face-climbs the northeast side through an unusually deep chimney to the top.

sectionBreakdown.note: From the Staircase Ranger Station, follow the North Fork Skokomish River trail 3.4 mi to the Spike Camp junction, then climb a steadily steepening trail another ~3.6 mi to Flapjack…
Day-climb from camp: continue east on the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400 ft near a small pond, then leave the trail and climb open snow/rock slopes southeast to Sawtooth Pass. …
sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Climb The Fin via Sawtooth Pass

sectionBreakdown.note: Break camp and retrace the North Fork Skokomish River trail back through Spike Camp to the Staircase trailhead, losing the elevation gained on day one.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A standard alpine trad rack to about 3 inches works for the single pitch, with a doubled set of mid-size cams useful for the chimney's chockstones; long runners/slings help manage rope drag through the corkscrewing chimney.
pro_tips: Reserve a Flapjack Lakes wilderness permit on recreation.gov well ahead of time — it's a small, reservation-limited camp and the standard base for Sawtooth Ridge climbs

Check current NPS 'Fire Conditions and Updates' and Olympic National Forest alerts before you go — Staircase itself reopened July 8, 2026, but the North Fork Skokomish River and Flapjack Lakes trails needed to reach The Fin remain closed after the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026
Carry a topo or route description — The Fin sits among a dozen-plus similarly sized named towers on the ridge and it's easy to end up on the wrong one
Pack extra webbing/cord — rappel anchors on Sawtooth Ridge are typically slung horns and blocks, not bolts
watch_out: Runout moves getting into the chimney; rock is better than average for the Olympics but still loose in spots
Many similar named and unnamed pinnacles nearby along the ridge — easy to end up on the wrong tower without a topo or description
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Medium trad rack (small to ~3"), a few small pins/nuts, and extra sling/cord material — anchors on Sawtooth Ridge are almost entirely slung horns and blocks rather than bolts or fixed rap rings.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late June/July through September in a normal year — snow can linger in the approach gullies (e.g. the Needle Couloir) into early July. Separate from seasonal timing, the North Fork Skokomish River and Flapjack Lakes trails have been closed since the July 2025 Bear Gulch Fire and remain closed, with no reopening date on the park's fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026, even though the Staircase trailhead itself reopened July 8, 2026; confirm the approach trail is reopened before planning around any specific month.
deleted_rows.approach: From Hoodsport, WA drive ~16 miles northwest to the Staircase Ranger Station / North Fork Skokomish River Trailhead. Hike the North Fork Skokomish River Trail ~3.4-3.7 mi to the Flapjack Lakes Trail junction, then climb ~3.6-3.8 mi more to Flapjack Lakes (~3,850-3,900'). From the lakes continue east on the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400' near a small pond, then leave the trail and climb open snow and rock slopes southeast to Sawtooth Pass, the narrow chute beside The Fin; the northeast face starts just east of the pass. About 17 miles round trip with roughly 5,500' of total gain to the base of the climbing.
deleted_rows.descent_text: After the NE-face pitch it's an easy 3rd-class scramble to the true summit. Most parties do NOT reverse the technical pitch — the standard descent is the east-face scramble/walk-off back down to Sawtooth Pass (the same terrain used on the Class 3-4 alternative), rather than rappelling. A party that prefers to rappel the chimney should carry extra webbing/cord, since anchors are typically slung around horns/chockstones rather than bolts.
deleted_rows.bail: There's no quicker bail off Sawtooth Ridge — reverse the approach: down from Sawtooth Pass to the Gladys Divide trail, then Flapjack Lakes and out the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase.

pitch_detail.notes: Angled bouldery moves up the face gain a deep, unusually good chimney with solid rock and chockstones, widely described as a 'world class' pitch; tops out at an easy 3rd-class scramble to the true summit.
pitch_detail.anchor: Gear anchor / slung chockstone typical — little to no fixed gear on Sawtooth Ridge

itinerary.cal: Flapjack Lakes is a limited-use overnight zone in Olympic NP — reserve a wilderness permit on recreation.gov ahead of time; the Sawtooth Pass slope and summit are best snow-free from roughly July through September.

days.note: From the Staircase Ranger Station, follow the North Fork Skokomish River trail 3.4 mi to the Spike Camp junction, then climb a steadily steepening trail another ~3.6 mi to Flapjack Lakes, tucked beneath the Sawtooth Range. Set up camp in one of the established sites near the lakes.
days.title: Backpack in to Flapjack Lakes
days.objective: Establish camp at Flapjack Lakes (3,850 ft)

days.note: Day-climb from camp: continue east on the Gladys Divide trail to about 4,400 ft near a small pond, then leave the trail and climb open snow/rock slopes southeast to Sawtooth Pass. From the pass, scramble the east-face line (parties on the technical route instead take the 5.4 face-and-chimney route on the NE side) to the summit, then reverse the same line back to camp.
days.title: Climb The Fin via Sawtooth Pass

schedule.label: Leave Flapjack Lakes camp
schedule.detail: Light day pack; early start for routefinding margin and to beat afternoon weather.

schedule.label: Leave the trail near 4,400 ft
schedule.detail: Just before the small pond, head southeast up open snow/rock slopes.

schedule.label: Summit The Fin
schedule.detail: Via the east-face scramble line, or the NE face/chimney for the technical 5.4 route.

schedule.label: Back at Sawtooth Pass
schedule.detail: Begin descent to Flapjack Lakes.

schedule.label: Return to camp
schedule.detail: Rest, refill water, second night at Flapjack Lakes.

days.objective: Reach the summit of The Fin and return to camp

days.note: Break camp and retrace the North Fork Skokomish River trail back through Spike Camp to the Staircase trailhead, losing the elevation gained on day one.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Staircase trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day, 2-night trip out of Staircase: an easy backpack in and out (about 7.5 mi / 3,050 ft each way to Flapjack Lakes camp) bracketing one long scramble day from camp over Sawtooth Pass to the summit of The Fin and back — roughly 17 mi and 5,500 ft round trip overall.

access.fees: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/private vehicle (7 days), $15/individual on foot or bike, $55 annual park pass. The park does not accept cash — card only.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters mandatory for all food and scented items at Flapjack Lakes; no campfires above 3,500'; no stock/pack animals on this trail; bury human waste 6-8" deep and 200'+ from water where no toilet is available; Leave No Trace.
access.permit: Wilderness camping permit required for any overnight stay — reserve via recreation.gov ($6 reservation fee plus $8/person/night). Flapjack Lakes is a small, reservation-limited designated camping zone; no camping off-site. Groups of 7+ must use the designated group site.
access.closures: The Bear Gulch Fire started July 6, 2025 near Lake Cushman and burned into the Staircase area. On July 8, 2026 the Staircase developed area, FS-24 access road, campground, and ranger station reopened. The actual approach to The Fin remains closed, however: the North Fork Skokomish River Trail is closed from its junction with the Staircase Rapids Loop to Home Sweet Home, and the Flapjack Lakes Trail is closed outright while crews complete hazard-tree removal and backcountry trail rehab, with no end date given as of the Olympic National Park fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026. Check NPS 'Fire Conditions and Updates' before planning a trip.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park (Wilderness); the access road and lower approach pass through Olympic National Forest near Lake Cushman
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Olympic National Park (Olympic Wilderness)
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: NPS park entrance pass at Staircase — not a WA Discover Pass or Northwest Forest Pass, since the trailhead sits inside Olympic National Park.

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, reserved in advance, per-night fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov before the trip; there are no same-day walk-up permits. Bear canisters are required at Flapjack Lakes, and the Staircase trails are closed after the Bear Gulch Fire, so check status first.

road.name: NF Road 24 (Lake Cushman Road) to the Staircase Ranger Station
road.status: FS-24 and the Staircase developed area (campground, ranger station, Rapids Loop Trail) reopened July 8, 2026 after a year-long Bear Gulch Fire closure. The wilderness trails beyond — including the North Fork Skokomish River Trail and Flapjack Lakes Trail needed for this approach — remain closed for hazard-tree removal and trail rehab, with no end date given as of the Olympic National Park fire-conditions page updated September 18, 2026.
road.driveNote: From Hoodsport, WA, drive ~16 miles northwest via WA-119/Lake Cushman Rd and NF-24 to the Staircase trailhead — the road itself reopened July 8, 2026, but the trail beyond the Staircase Rapids Loop remains closed, with no end date given as of September 18, 2026.
road.seasonalGate: FS-24 is frequently gated/closed by snow from roughly November through May.

climate.fall: Cooling temperatures and increasing rain by October; road access can close by late fall.
climate.spring: Deep snowpack persists on the approach and at the passes into June; trail can be snow-covered.
climate.summer: Warmest, driest window (Jul-Sep) and the standard climbing season; afternoon thunderstorms are possible.
climate.winter: Heavy snow; access road typically gated and the route effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Cool and wet much of the year like the rest of the Olympics; the approach trail and ridge are typically snow-free and climbable only from roughly late June/July through September.

bySeason.fall: Shorter days and building storm frequency after mid-September; rock gets slick fast in rain.
bySeason.spring: Snow lingers in approach gullies like the Needle Couloir into June/July; postholing and wet-slide hazard are common on the approach.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (Jul-Sep); still expect afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes on this exposed ridge near Hood Canal.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — heavy snow and avalanche terrain, on top of the current fire-related closure, rule this out.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Olympics' zone for avalanche/mountain weather; NWS Seattle forecast zone for the Hood Canal/Skokomish drainage.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage on the approach or ridge. The area is remote even by Olympic standards, and the current Bear Gulch Fire closure means the trail is less traveled and slower to reach help on — carry a satellite communicator/PLB.
emergency.rangerStation: Staircase Ranger Station (seasonal, at the trailhead) or Olympic NP Wilderness Information Center, Port Angeles, 360-565-3100.
emergency.nearestHospital: Mason General Hospital (Mason Health), 901 Mountain View Dr, Shelton, WA — roughly 25-30 miles / 45+ minutes drive from the Staircase trailhead.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Mason County Sheriff's Office (non-emergency 360-427-9670); dial 911 for SAR callout.

crowds.peakTraffic: The Flapjack Lakes / North Fork Skokomish approach sees moderate day-hiker and backpacker traffic July-September (it's a well-known, reservation-limited ONP destination), but very few of those hikers continue past Gladys Divide onto the Sawtooth Ridge scrambling/climbing terrain — traffic on The Fin's actual route is light and mostly limited to dedicated scramblers/climbers on summer weekends
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 10-25 parties per season attempt the scramble to The Fin itself (low confidence estimate)

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong backpacker — the Staircase approach is on-trail but long: ~7.5 mi and ~3,050 ft gain to Flapjack Lakes camp, then several more off-trail miles and ~2,450 ft up to Sawtooth Pass and the tower on scramble day; most parties backpack in and base-camp at Flapjack Lakes rather than attempt car-to-summit-to-car
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light scrambling/rack pack for the summit day (helmet, minimal rack/webbing for the optional 5.4 chimney pitch, food/water); overnight backpacking pack for the approach to Flapjack Lakes camp

partner_requirements.approachTime: A full day (~5-6 hrs) to backpack in to Flapjack Lakes camp, then a long (~8-9 hr) summit day via Sawtooth Pass to The Fin and back — most parties treat this as a 3-day, 2-night trip with a base camp at Flapjack Lakes rather than a single push
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling / exposed rock movement
loose rock and rockfall awareness (helmet mandatory, tight group spacing)
basic routefinding among the Sawtooth spires (limited beta, no marked route)
comfort self-arresting or downclimbing steep dirt/scree on the Sawtooth Pass approach
optional: short-rope/rappel skills if a party opts to protect any section
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Solid Class 3-4 scrambling experience with exposure; should be comfortable on loose, exposed rock with no fixed protection and able to reverse or downclimb committing terrain

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July through September — this is when the Sawtooth Pass slope and the Sawtooth scrambling are typically snow-free

July.reason: Early July often still has snow patches on the approach and shaded scramble terrain; conditions generally firm up to match the late July-September window by the back half of the month

June.reason: Lingering snowpack commonly covers the steep Sawtooth Pass slope and the rest of the approach into July in a normal year; snow travel skills and possibly an axe would be needed, and the scramble rock itself may still be snow-covered or wet

August.reason: Peak dry-rock conditions, longest daylight, and the most reliable weather window of the season for the exposed scrambling

October.reason: Outside the established best-season window; Olympic weather turns wet and unstable, and new snow can make the loose rock and exposed sections considerably more hazardous

September.reason: Still within the optimal window — generally dry and stable, though days are shorter and early-season snow/weather can arrive late in the month

weather.typical: Consistent with existing climate beta for the range — the Olympics catch heavy Pacific moisture, so weather can change fast even in summer; fog/cloud off Hood Canal and the Sound can sock in the high country with little warning
weather.probability: Afternoon buildups/thunderstorms are less frequent here than in the Cascades but do occur in July-August; any incoming Pacific frontal system can bring rain and reduce visibility on the already loose, routefinding-dependent scramble

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Significant — with loose rock, exposure and rockfall from above, the Class 3-4 spire scrambling on The Fin has real fall consequences with minimal protection, and rockfall risk to parties below is elevated given the loose rock quality typical of the Sawtooth Range

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route (falls within NWAC's broader 'Olympics' forecast zone, but that forecast is not really applicable to this dry-season Class 3-4 objective)

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on this route

gaps: Exact pitch count/belay sequence for the 5.4 route is sourced from Mountain Project's route page (1 pitch, ~120 ft) rather than a primary guidebook topo
Elevation (5,599') and prominence (219') on file could not be independently re-verified (Peakbagger blocked automated access)

No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

approach_logistics.trailhead: Staircase Trailhead (North Fork Skokomish, Olympic NP)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Staircase Ranger Station trailhead past Lake Cushman (FR-24)

deleted_rows.rope_note: NE Face route (5.4): angled bouldery moves into a deep 120ft chimney pitch with chockstones, then easy 3rd-class scrambling to the summit. 17-mile RT approach from Staircase via Flapjack Lakes.
deleted_rows.corrections: None; matches the documented NE Face route on Sawtooth Ridge (Olympics).
rack: A few small pitons for thin approach moves
4-5 shoulder-length runners plus extra webbing/cord for rappel anchors (slung horns/blocks)
Single 60m rope (parties continuing along the ridge often carry two)

approach_variants.name: Staircase and Flapjack Lakes to Sawtooth Pass
approach_variants.notes: The only practical way in is from the Staircase Ranger Station on the North Fork Skokomish: about 3.5 miles of river trail to the Spike Camp fork, then a steep 3.6 miles to Flapjack Lakes, then the trail on toward Gladys Divide, which you leave near a small pond at about 4,400 ft. Flapjack Lakes is a limited-entry overnight basin, so a reserved permit has to be sorted out long before you drive out, and almost nobody does this tower as a day trip from the road. From there it is off-trail on open snow and rock slopes up to Sawtooth Pass. Check with the park before committing: fire damage in the Skokomish corridor has closed the approach trails for extended periods even while the Staircase road itself was open, and the tower is unreachable without them.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September; snow lingers
hazards: Frost-shattered pillow basalt on the outer faces and ledges, better in the chimney than out of it
Moss-slick slabs and holds after rain, which is most of the year here
No fixed protection on the ridge — rappel anchors are slung around horns and chockstones, so carry spare webbing and cord
Loose snow or scree in the Sawtooth Pass chute, which gets chossier as the snow melts out late in the season
A dozen similar towers strung along one crest, so a wrong tower costs hours
Burn-scar rockfall and treefall along the lower approach corridor
approach_variants.baseFinding: Short of Gladys Divide, leave the trail and head southeast toward a narrow chute that cuts the ridge immediately beside a blade-shaped tower. That chute is Sawtooth Pass, and the tower beside it is The Fin. From the pass, step east onto the northeast side of the tower and look for angled, bouldery moves leading up the face into a chimney you can genuinely walk into — a deep, dark slot with wedged chockstones jammed in it, and the only feature of its kind on this whole crest. That chimney is the confirmation: nothing else along Sawtooth Ridge has one, and the deeper you look into it the more obviously it goes. The Castle Spires just before it are a cluster of blockier pinnacles with an obvious north arete and no chimney, and they are the decoy most parties stop under. If you reach a notch with no chute below it, under a steep tower whose sides are clean and unslotted, you have passed The Fin and are standing under The Horn — turn back northwest one tower.

bivy.name: Flapjack Lakes — the base camp for the whole Sawtooth Ridge
bivy.notes: This is the single most important site in the zone and everything on Sawtooth Ridge runs off it. It is about 7.5 miles and 3,100 ft from the Staircase trailhead, up the North Fork Skokomish valley to the junction near Spike Camp at roughly 3.4 miles, then right and steeply up beside Madeline Creek. Most parties take five to seven hours in with climbing gear. From camp, the trail continues east toward Gladys Divide, gaining about 1,100 ft in a mile to a pass around 5,000 ft directly beneath Mount Cruiser. Cruiser's standard line breaks off before the divide, up a steep snow couloir to Needle Pass and then along the crest — an ice axe and crampons are wanted there most of the season. The Fin and The Horn are reached by cutting east short of the divide to the narrow chute at Sawtooth Pass, and the spires south toward Mount Lincoln go by way of the Harniss Chute. Summit days are four to five hours up from the lakes for Cruiser and long full days for the traverse peaks, so parties routinely book two nights and climb on the middle day. There is no legal higher camp. Gladys Divide, Needle Pass and Sawtooth Pass are all inside the Flapjack quota area and none is a designated site, so the temptation to carry a bivy up to the divide and shorten the summit day is not an option here — you sleep at the lakes and you accept the 1,100 ft of morning warm-up. Camping lower costs you more: the valley camps below the junction add three or more miles and 2,000 ft to every summit day and effectively rule out a one-night trip. Season is late June through September. Snow lingers in the couloirs and on the divide into July, which is what most parties actually want for Cruiser, and by late September the couloirs turn to loose rock. There is a privy at the lakes and a bear wire, but bring the canister regardless.
bivy.water: Reliable all season at the lakes themselves. The climb up is the dry part — there is little water between the valley and the waterfall near the Black and White Lakes junction, roughly half a mile below the lakes, so fill at Madeline or Donahue Creek on the way through rather than counting on anything in the switchbacks.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required and Flapjack Lakes is a named quota area, limited year round, so this is the one booking in the zone that will actually stop your trip. Permits are issued only through the federal recreation booking site; the online reservation window for this camp runs mid-June to mid-October, and the whole summer season releases in one drop on April 15 at 7 a.m. Pacific. No sites are held as same-day walk-ups — the old half-reserved, half-first-come arrangement is gone, and availability now updates live, so cancellations are the only late route in. For dates outside the online window you have to arrange it directly with the park's wilderness information office. Fees are a non-refundable per-permit reservation charge plus a per-person nightly charge for anyone sixteen and over, with an annual wilderness pass available that covers the nightly half. Parties of seven or more must take the group site. Bear canisters are required. Campfires are prohibited — the lakes are above the 3,500 ft parkwide fire line. Camping is in designated sites only. Stock is not allowed on the Flapjack trail, and dogs are not allowed on park wilderness trails. A park entrance pass is needed for the drive in, and the access road up Lake Cushman is unpaved for its last stretch and closes for snow and weather. Weekday permits here are usually gettable; summer weekends are not.
bivy.capacity: A modest number of designated individual sites scattered around the two lakes, plus one designated group site for parties of seven to twelve. The park does not publish a fixed site count and the honest answer is that whatever the booking system shows as available for your dates IS the count; there is no dispersed camping to fall back on. Maximum party size is twelve.

bivy.name: Black and White Lakes — the fallback when Flapjack is booked out
bivy.notes: Reached by branching left across Donahue Creek about half a mile below Flapjack Lakes and climbing further, which puts it around 4,500 ft and some 3,800 ft above the trailhead. It is a fine camp with a big outlook and it is the practical answer when the Flapjack quota is gone, but be clear about what it costs you: it is on the wrong side of the ridge line for the Sawtooth spires, and every summit day has to drop back to the Flapjack trail and then reclimb toward Gladys Divide. Budget an extra hour and a few hundred feet each way against a Flapjack start. Its real strength is as a first night on a longer loop, or as a place to sit out an afternoon when you have come in late and want to be moving early. Snow-free later than the lakes below it, so early-season parties should expect drifts here into July.
bivy.water: The tarns and a small creek beside the sites, but this is the weak point — these are shallow high tarns and they can drop badly or go stagnant by late summer. Treat everything, and in a dry September carry water up or plan to drop back toward Flapjack for it.
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This sits inside the same high-demand Staircase country but is not the Flapjack quota area itself, so it is usually available when the lakes are not — check both when you book. Bear canisters are required, campfires are prohibited at this elevation, and the same reservation site, fees and party-size rules apply as for Flapjack Lakes.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites on the lower side of the tarns, with easy access to a small creek and the water. Rarely busy.

deleted_rows.name: South Ridge
deleted_rows.fa: Everett and Ida Darr, 1940 (first ascent of the peak)
gear: Helmet (loose rock/rockfall is a real hazard on the summit pyramid)
30 m rope for rappelling the crux and upper pyramid
Light rack (a few small cams/nuts) for optional protection on the crux
Sturdy brush pants/long sleeves and gaiters for the Bird Creek bushwhack
hazards: Loose, rockfall-prone gneiss on the summit pyramid — spontaneous rockfall has been reported even without climber contact
Brutal, largely trailless bushwhack (slide alder, blowdown) between the Devore Creek Trail and Bird Creek camp
Remote, multi-day approach far from help; no cell service in the Stehekin backcountry
Exposed class 4/low-5th climbing on a route most parties do without fixed protection
deleted_rows.overview: Tupshin Peak (8,347 ft) is one of the 'Stehekin Seven,' a knot of rarely visited summits above the Stehekin valley in the Glacier Peak Wilderness. The mountain is built of several rock turrets running south, east, and northwest from a central high point roughly 200 ft above its neighbors. First climbed in 1940 by Everett and Ida Darr, it's approached entirely by boat and trail (no road reaches the peak). The standard line climbs the broad south ridge/upper east face to a short, exposed, and notably loose class 4-to-low-5th crux through old gneiss just below the summit.
deleted_rows.beta: From Bird Creek Camp, climb NNE up open sub-alpine slope to a broad shoulder (~7,000 ft) on Tupshin's lower South Ridge, then traverse/descend slightly around cliff bands into the upper east basin (~7,500 ft) below the face — about one mile from Bird Creek to the base of the climbing. The basin is a talus fan, often snow-covered early season. From there, rambly Class 2-4 terrain and a short crux (5.2-5.4, on a flake/crack) lead through the face to Class 3-4 summit-pyramid scrambling and the top. Multiple parties describe this same basic line with minor route-finding variations near the crux.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Given the long, remote approach and a descent that is itself technical and routefinding-heavy, set a firm turnaround time from camp that leaves ample daylight to complete both the summit climb and the rappel/downclimb descent — at least one recorded ascent summited in the evening and did not finish descending until after midnight by headlamp.
deleted_rows.rappels: One short rappel reported near the summit (~30 m rope sufficient) off an old webbing anchor; back it up before weighting
deleted_rows.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota. Northwest Forest Pass at many trailheads.
deleted_rows.comms: No reliable cell coverage in the Devore Creek/Bird Creek drainage or on Tupshin's upper mountain. A satellite messenger (e.g., Garmin inReach) is strongly recommended — regional Chelan County SAR operations in this area have relied on inReach activations to trigger helicopter response.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb and rappel the loose summit pyramid and crux back to the south-ridge shoulder and Bird Creek basin.

waypoints.name: Stehekin River Trail TH (Harlequin Bridge / airstrip)
waypoints.note: Reached via Lady of the Lake ferry to Stehekin Landing then shuttle ~4.4 mi to Harlequin Bridge; trail starts at the south end of the Stehekin State Airstrip and drops into forest immediately.
waypoints.directions: No road reaches this trailhead from outside. Take the Lady of the Lake or Lady Express passenger ferry from Fields Point Landing up Lake Chelan to Stehekin Landing, then ride the Stehekin shuttle (or walk) about 4.4 miles up the valley road to Harlequin Bridge. Cross the bridge; the Stehekin River Trail starts at the south end of the airstrip. Plan around the boat schedule, since missing the last boat costs a night.

waypoints.name: Devore Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Devore Creek Trail splits off the Stehekin River Trail about a half-mile before Weaver Point Campground and switchbacks steeply up into the Glacier Peak Wilderness toward Bird Creek.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Stehekin River Trail down-valley through forest about 3 miles toward Weaver Point to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction, about half a mile before the campground.

waypoints.name: Bird Creek Camp
waypoints.note: Forested camp alongside Devore Creek Trail with creek water nearby; the trail is well-maintained to here but grows overgrown with blowdowns above.
waypoints.directions: Turn onto the Devore Creek Trail and switchback steeply up into the Glacier Peak Wilderness, continuing up the Devore Creek valley to Bird Creek Camp at about 4,200 ft, the only designated camp on this stretch. Above here the trail is brushy and can carry heavy blowdown.

waypoints.name: Bird Creek basin high camp
waypoints.note: Open subalpine basin (reported anywhere from ~5,400 to ~5,800 ft) reached by bushwhacking blueberry brush and slide alder off-trail; used as the launch point for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail and work up the ridge north of Bird Creek through steep brush, slide alder and blowdown, about 1,000 ft or more of gain with little open forest, to a camp with running water in the lower Bird Creek basin, roughly 5,400 to 5,800 ft.

waypoints.name: South ridge shoulder / skyline ridge
waypoints.note: Meadow slopes north out of the basin crest here on Tupshin's lower south ridge, giving the first clear view of the summit pyramid and east face.

waypoints.name: Talus basin and snow finger below the east face
waypoints.note: Loose talus basin with a persistent snow finger at the base of the cliff; early-season parties need an ice axe/crampons here and the rock underfoot is notoriously loose and prone to spontaneous rockfall.
waypoints.directions: Traverse around the cliff bands into the upper basin on the east side of the peak, to the talus fan at the foot of the continuous cliff band, marked by a snow finger at the bottom of the wall that lingers most summers. Carry an axe early in the season.

waypoints.name: Summit pyramid chimney pitch
waypoints.note: Low-5th-class (5.2-5.4) chimney/flake pitch past a small chockstone gains the loose, exposed summit block; wear a helmet and rappel single-strand on the descent due to rockfall risk.
waypoints.directions: Kick up the snow finger to the ramp system and scramble rambly, loose rock, including a short class 4 step of about 20 ft, up the summit pyramid to the low-fifth chimney and flake. Wear a helmet; the rock releases on its own.

waypoints.name: Tupshin Peak summit
waypoints.note: Tight, exposed true summit reached through a notch in the final rock band; recent LIDAR puts the elevation at 8,343-8,348 ft.
waypoints.directions: Climb the short 5.2-5.4 chimney/flake past a small chockstone on sparse protection, then scramble class 3-4 gully ground through a notch in the final rock band to the small, exposed true summit.

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A light rock rack is sufficient for the crux and any protected pitches: a set of small-to-mid cams, a few nuts, and several slings/draws, plus a 30 m rope for the crux pitch and the short descent rappel. Some parties have soloed sections in rock shoes; others have pitched out the crux and upper face with a full rack.
pro_tips: Bring a rope even if confident — the crux exposure justifies it
Budget extra time for the remote Stehekin approach and brush
watch_out: Ropes snag easily in the loose rock on rappel — a single-strand rappel is usually preferable to a doubled rope
Devore Creek Trail blowdown can turn the approach into a multi-hour bushwhack in bad years; check current trail conditions with the Chelan Ranger District first
deleted_rows.pro_needs: A short rope and a light rack are advisable for the exposed class 4 / low-5th crux; many parties belay the steepest step.
deleted_rows.best_season: Snow typically lingers in the Bird Creek basin and on the upper route into July, so mid-July through September is the reliable window; early-season parties should carry an ice axe for lingering snowfields, while late-season parties get drier but no less loose rock. Check regional Cascades snowpack/NWAC data before an early trip.
deleted_rows.approach: No road reaches the mountain. Take the Lady of the Lake or Lady Express passenger ferry from Fields Point Landing up Lake Chelan to Stehekin Landing, then ride the Stehekin shuttle bus (or walk) roughly 4.4 miles up-valley to Harlequin Bridge, cross it, and continue about 3 more miles on the Stehekin River Trail toward Weaver Point to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction (about a half mile before Weaver Point). Follow the Devore Creek Trail as it switchbacks up into the Glacier Peak Wilderness (Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest); it is brushy but generally passable toward Tenmile Pass, though blowdown has been significant in some years — check current trail conditions with the Chelan Ranger District before you go. Leave the maintained trail and work up the ridge north of Bird Creek through steep brush, slide alder, and blowdown (about 1,000 ft of gain with little real open forest) to a good camp with running water in the lower Bird Creek basin, roughly 5,400-5,800 ft. The boat-landing-to-camp day is reportedly around 10 miles and 5,000 ft of elevation gain.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Reverse the climb: rappel (single-strand preferred over doubled rope to avoid snagging in the loose rock) and downclimb the crux and upper pyramid back to the 7,000-ft shoulder, then descend through the talus and brush back to the Bird Creek basin camp. From camp, reverse the bushwhack to the Devore Creek Trail, then the Stehekin River Trail to Harlequin Bridge and Stehekin Landing for the return ferry — plan the trip around the ferry schedule, since missing the last boat means an extra night in Stehekin.
deleted_rows.bail: Retreat down the ascent route; rappel the crux.

pitch_detail.notes: Bird Creek Camp NNE up open sub-alpine slope to the broad shoulder (~7,000 ft) on the lower South Ridge, then a slightly descending traverse around cliff bands into the upper east basin (~7,500 ft).
~1 mile across a talus fan, often snow-covered in early season, to the base of the technical climbing.
Rambly, somewhat loose rock; a short (~20 ft) Class 4 step is a common first obstacle en route to the upper face.
Short crux section on a flake/crack system gaining the upper face; protection is sparse and 'dubious.'
Class 3-4 gully/scrambling for the final distance to the true summit.

itinerary.cal: Best conditions mid-July through September, once the approach and upper basin have largely melted out; verify current Lake Chelan boat schedule (Lady Express/Lady of the Lake) since your itinerary is built around its Fields Point <-> Stehekin timing.

Hike the Stehekin River Trail then the Devore Creek Trail past Bird Creek Camp, then leave the trail and push up through steep brush to a camp with running water in the lower Bird Creek basin.
