itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day car-to-car trip built around the Stehekin ferry: ~1 day hiking in, 1 long summit day (~10 hrs, 3,300 ft round trip from camp), 1 day hiking out — roughly 22-25 miles and 8,000+ ft total, matching the recorded 36 km round-trip distance once camp shuffling is counted.

access.fees: Round-trip Lady of the Lake/Lady Express passenger ferry fare from Fields Point Landing to Stehekin (check current rates at ladyofthelake.com); the in-valley Stehekin shuttle bus runs about $10/adult one-way (2026 rate, Stehekin Valley Adventures) if you don't walk from the Landing to Harlequin Bridge. The wilderness permit itself is free.
access.permit: Once past the NPS boundary, a free, self-issued Glacier Peak Wilderness permit (available at the trailhead, no reservation or fee) covers the climb and Bird Creek camp. If you camp overnight anywhere within the Lake Chelan NRA/Stehekin corridor before reaching the wilderness boundary, an NPS backcountry permit is required (reservable via recreation.gov or in person at the Golden West Visitor Center in Stehekin).
access.closures: Stehekin suffered major flooding and landslides in December 2025 — a levee failure sent the Stehekin River into Company Creek Road near Harlequin Bridge — with a further damaging flood event in March 2026; recovery work was still ongoing into summer 2026. As of June 2026 the Stehekin Valley Road was reported open from the Landing to Stehekin Valley Ranch, but check the NPS 'Stehekin Flood Response Update' page and the Chelan Ranger District before a trip, since the Harlequin Bridge/Devore Creek approach corridor was directly affected by the flood. Sisi Fire: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closure order 06-17-02-2026-35 (Sisi Fire), in effect August 22 through December 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner, closes Devore Creek Trail 1244 from where it enters the national forest to Hilgard Pass, the 4th of July Basin Trail 1244.1 and Company Creek Trail 1243. This approach cannot be used while the order stands. Chelan Ranger District: (509) 682-4900.
access.landManager: The lower approach (Stehekin River Trail near Harlequin Bridge and the Devore Creek trailhead) lies within the North Cascades National Park Service Complex — Lake Chelan National Recreation Area (NPS). The Devore Creek Trail then crosses into the Glacier Peak Wilderness on the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Chelan Ranger District) for the climb itself.
access.passRequired: No Northwest Forest Pass needed at this boat-in trailhead; wilderness permits (above) are the operative requirement.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit; an NPS backcountry permit for any night inside Lake Chelan NRA
overnight_permit.where: Bird Creek camps are in the Glacier Peak Wilderness: fill out the self-issue permit at the trail register. Nights in the Stehekin valley or at Weaver Point need an NPS permit, reserved on Recreation.gov or picked up in Stehekin.

road.name: Stehekin Valley Road (Stehekin Landing to High Bridge) — no public road reaches the peak itself
road.status: Reported open from Stehekin Landing to Stehekin Valley Ranch as of June 2026 following Dec 2025 flood damage; check the NPS Stehekin Flood Response Update before a trip
road.driveNote: There is no public road into Stehekin — access is only by passenger ferry (Lady of the Lake/Lady Express), chartered floatplane, or on foot over Cascade Pass. The Devore Creek trailhead is reached from Stehekin Landing by shuttle/walk plus trail, not by car.
road.seasonalGate: Ferry (Lady of the Lake/Lady Express) and floatplane service run a reduced or altered schedule outside the May-October main season

climate.fall: Often the most stable weather window (September), but with shorter daylight for the long summit day.
climate.spring: Significant snowpack persists on the approach and upper basin well into early summer; trail and off-trail travel can involve substantial snow into June.
climate.summer: Primary climbing season; hot at lake level in Stehekin, but snow/ice can still linger at the base of the face into July.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible for this route; ferry/floatplane service is reduced and the approach is snowbound.
climate.typical: Drier east-side Cascades climate; afternoon storms possible.

bySeason.fall: Stable but short days; boat schedule reduces.
bySeason.spring: Snow on upper peak; brushy wet approach.
bySeason.summer: Prime window; hot in the valley, cooler up high.
bySeason.winter: Full winter conditions; very limited access.

emergency.notes: There is essentially no cell coverage in Stehekin's backcountry (Bird Creek basin included); carry a satellite communicator. Medical evacuation from the Stehekin area typically requires a helicopter, historically staged out of Brewster, WA (roughly 30 minutes response time).
emergency.rangerStation: Chelan Ranger District, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest — 428 W. Woodin Ave, Chelan, WA 98816, (509) 682-4900
emergency.nearestHospital: Lake Chelan Health Hospital, Chelan, WA — 24-hour ER, (509) 682-2531
emergency.sheriffDispatch: RiverCom 911 (Chelan/Douglas County dispatch): 911 for emergencies, (509) 667-6851 non-emergency; search and rescue is coordinated by the Chelan County Sheriff's Office

crowds.peakTraffic: If any, clustered in the mid-July through August optimal window, tied to Stehekin boat/floatplane schedules and good-weather windows; effectively no shoulder-season traffic
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - likely single digits to ~15 parties per season based on the near-total absence of dedicated trip reports specific to this route (only a handful of general Tupshin ascent reports exist)

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong/advanced backcountry fitness - long brushy, off-trail valley approach from Stehekin followed by a steep basin-to-summit push; expect a multi-day carry
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day pack (roughly 30-40 lb) for the approach and camp, dropping to a light summit pack for the scramble day

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day: boat or floatplane access to Stehekin, then a long valley/brushy off-trail approach to a basin camp before a full summit day - not a single-day car-to-summit route
requiredSkills: Class 4 / low 5th unroped or lightly-roped scrambling
loose rock and rockfall management
off-trail navigation and bushwhacking through brush
wilderness/remote self-rescue judgment
basic rope/belay skills recommended for the crux in case a party member wants protection
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scramblers only - must be comfortable soloing or lightly protecting exposed Class 4 to low-5th terrain on loose rock, with solid off-trail routefinding judgment and wilderness self-sufficiency given the remote, rescue-unfriendly setting

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September

May.reason: Lingering snowpack on approach slopes and high, dangerous creek crossings in the Stehekin valley; not the intended window

July.reason: In the season window; brush has typically leafed out but approach is passable and rock is dry

June.reason: Snow patches likely still linger on upper approach and summit block; creek levels from snowmelt can still be elevated

August.reason: Peak dry-rock conditions for the Class 4/low-5th crux; most reliable creek crossings and driest approach brush

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snow and storms increasingly likely, and Stehekin seasonal access/services wind down

September.reason: Still within best-season window; stable weather common but shorter daylight and possible early-season snow late in the month

weather.typical: East-Cascades rain-shadow character - warmer and drier than the west-side Cascades, with the main risk being sudden mountain weather changes on an exposed ridge far from any bailout
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms/lightning are a plausible summer hazard on the exposed upper ridge and crux, as is typical for North Cascades summer alpine objectives

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained exposure through the Class 4/low-5th crux on loose rock; a slip or rockfall incident here is high-consequence given the long, brushy, remote approach from Stehekin and correspondingly slow/difficult rescue access

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route climbed well after snowmelt; this peak falls outside NWAC's standard published forecast zones for the Stehekin/Lake Chelan-Sawtooth area

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel on this route

deleted_rows.rope_note: South Ridge line bears NNE up sub-alpine slope to the ~7,000ft shoulder. Route is Class 4/low-5th with exposed scrambling; Tupshin reportedly has no easy route to the top.

approach_variants.name: Stehekin, Devore Creek and the Bird Creek basin
approach_variants.notes: No road reaches this mountain. A passenger ferry up Lake Chelan to the landing, then a shuttle or a walk up-valley to the bridge, then the river trail to the signed Devore Creek junction about half a mile short of the campground. The Devore Creek trail switchbacks up into the wilderness and is brushy but passable, though blowdown has made it a multi-hour fight in bad years, so check the current state before committing. Leave the maintained trail and work up the ridge north of Bird Creek through steep brush, slide alder and downed timber — roughly a thousand feet of gain with very little open forest — to a camp with running water in the lower basin somewhere between about 5,400 and 5,800 ft. Plan the whole trip around the boat schedule; missing the last one costs a night.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July to September; axe early
hazards: Loose, rockfall-prone gneiss on the summit pyramid, which releases spontaneously as well as under a boot
A brutal, largely trailless bushwhack between the maintained trail and the basin camp
A snow finger at the foot of the cliff that lingers unexpectedly late — carry an axe and consider crampons
Exposed class 4 and low-fifth climbing that most parties do with minimal protection
Ropes snag badly in the loose rock on rappel, so a single-strand rappel is usually preferable
Remote and multi-day with no cell service in the valley
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the basin camp climb north-northeast up open subalpine slope to the skyline shoulder at roughly 7,000 to 7,200 ft, where the summit pyramid comes fully into view for the first time — that view is the checkpoint, and if you cannot see a distinct pyramid you are not yet on the shoulder. From there traverse and drop slightly around the cliff bands into the upper basin on the east side, at about 7,500 to 7,600 ft. The base is the talus fan at the foot of a continuous cliff band that runs unbroken to the top, and it is marked by a snow finger that sits at the very bottom of the wall and survives most summers. Start the climbing from that fan. The common error here is drifting too far east across the basin and starting up loose ground well right of the line; if the rock is uniformly rotten and you are hugging the skyline on your right, work back left toward the east ridge to regain the route.

bivy.name: Bird Creek Camp, Devore Creek trail
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Devore Peak and Tupshin Peak, and it is worth being clear that these two are not a Sawtooth trip. They stand west of Lake Chelan on the long ridge dividing Company Creek and Hilgard Creek from Devore Creek, and everything about them - the wilderness, the permit system, the transport - is different from the Twisp River peaks. The usual way in is a ferry to the Stehekin landing, then the Company Creek road, with the Devore Creek trail reached from Weaver Point on the far side of the head of the lake; Bird Creek Camp sits about four miles up that trail at around 4,200 ft. From here Tupshin's South Ridge and Devore's Southeast Ridge are both reachable, and parties commonly climb both from the same base, either from this camp or from a higher bivouac around 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek basin. Both are steep, brushy and loose by reputation and neither is a walk-up. The season is roughly late July into early October; the approach is low, hot and overgrown early, and the upper slopes hold snow. This is the least forgiving logistics in the zone - a party that misses a boat or a bus loses a day at each end - so build slack into the itinerary and carry more food than the schedule strictly needs.
bivy.water: Bird Creek is immediately past the camp; the site sits about a hundred feet short of the crossing. Below here, Devore Creek is the last dependable water on the climb, so fill there if you are unsure. Parties going higher can camp near 5,800 ft in the Bird Creek drainage, where there is water in early and mid-season but which can dry out late.
bivy.permit: This is inside the Lake Chelan National Recreation Area, so a North Cascades backcountry permit is required year-round for the overnight, tied to a specific camp and itinerary. Peak-season demand is high enough that an early-access lottery governs the best dates and the odds are poor; plan around it rather than hoping. Open fires are banned at several camps in this unit and restricted to established pits elsewhere, and a total ban is normal by late summer. The ferry and the Stehekin shuttle are the other half of the planning: the boat must be booked, the shuttle up the valley runs a limited seasonal schedule, and the Company Creek road trailhead is several miles from the landing, so missing a bus costs you a half day on foot.
bivy.capacity: Three small tent openings and a fire ring - room for perhaps four small tents. Very small, and there is no overflow.

deleted_rows.name: Snow Lake / Unicorn Creek approach
deleted_rows.fa: USGS party, 1910 (first ascent of the peak)
hazards: Loose talus/scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out (usually by mid-to-late July)
Wet-slide and cornice hazard on the NW approach gully/bowl in late spring — notable slide paths off the cliffs above Snow Lake have been documented in trip reports
Exposed step near the top of the summit horn with real air below on the block's east/arete side
Afternoon thunderstorms possible in summer
Unreliable cell coverage in the Tatoosh backcountry
deleted_rows.overview: Unicorn Peak (6,971 ft) is the highest summit in the Tatoosh Range, a jagged sub-range of the Cascades immediately south of Mount Rainier and entirely within Mount Rainier National Park. Its distinctive rock horn — said to resemble a unicorn's head — was named by early park officials and formally adopted by the USBGN in 1913. The standard day climb follows the popular Snow Lake Trail, then leaves the trail to climb snow/talus into a bowl on the peak's NW side, tops out at the west saddle, and finishes with a short, low-fifth-class scramble up the summit horn. It's commonly combined with neighboring Foss Peak, The Castle, Plummer Peak, Pinnacle Peak and Eagle Peak on a longer Tatoosh traverse.
deleted_rows.beta: From Snow Lake, traverse west on a climbers trail and ascend a steep chute with talus (summer) or good snow (spring). Aim for the saddle on the west side above the basin. From there, hike east just south of the ridge crest to a sub-summit dome, then approach the summit pinnacle from the south side. Multiple route variations exist on the 50-70 foot summit tower, ranging from Class 4 (east side, exposed) to 5.6 (direct south face).
deleted_rows.turnaround: In early/mid-season, a reasonable turnaround time would be early afternoon (1-2 PM) to ensure adequate daylight for descent and rappel. Mid-summer conditions with significant talus may require even earlier turnaround to complete the descent before dark.
deleted_rows.rock_grade: 5.0-5.6 (depending on route variation; classic south face is 5.4)
deleted_rows.rappels: One rappel of about 50 ft off the summit block; a 30-35 m rope is enough.
deleted_rows.face: South face of summit horn; main ascent from south side
deleted_rows.permit: Inside Mount Rainier National Park: no permit for day climbs; overnight stays require a park wilderness permit.
deleted_rows.comms: No cell service expected on trail; service may exist in immediate Paradise developed area only (very limited extent into wilderness). Do not depend on cell coverage for safety; consider satellite messenger or GPS device for emergency communication.
deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the route; rappel or downclimb the summit block

waypoints.name: Snow Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road ~1.5 mi east of Reflection Lakes; room for only 15-20 cars, no amenities, Stevens Canyon Rd open only from about late May or early June to mid-October.
waypoints.directions: From the Nisqually Entrance on SR 706, follow the park road past Longmire about 15.4 miles and turn right onto Stevens Canyon Road just below Paradise. Drive about 3.6 miles east, past Reflection Lakes, to the small Snow Lake trailhead lot on the right; it holds only 15-20 cars. Stevens Canyon Road is open only in summer, and a park entrance pass is required.

waypoints.name: Snow Lake
waypoints.note: Cirque lake below Unicorn Peak reached via the Snow Lake Trail; skirt the west (left) shore to pick up the climbers' path leaving the maintained trail.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail through subalpine forest and meadow, passing the Bench Lake junction, about a mile with roughly 350 ft of up-and-down to Snow Lake, the last reliable water.

waypoints.name: NW bowl entrance
waypoints.note: Leave the lakeshore and enter the steep, unmaintained valley on Unicorn's NW side; follow it roughly 0.5 mi up into the large bowl below the west saddle.
waypoints.directions: Skirt the lake's west shore and leave the maintained tread where a climbers' path breaks off up the steep drainage on Unicorn's northwest side.

waypoints.name: West saddle
waypoints.note: Top of the bowl gains the saddle on the west side of the peak (same saddle skiers use to access the Unicorn Glacier side); this is where the route turns east toward the summit.
waypoints.directions: Climb the steep gully about half a mile into the large open bowl, staying in the main gully and avoiding the steep headwalls to its left, then climb the moraine beside the small basin snowfield to the saddle on the peak's west side. The gully often holds firm snow through July, so carry an axe.

waypoints.name: South-side talus traverse
waypoints.note: Exposed traverse across loose talus/scree below the summit block to reach its south (easiest) side; rockfall risk onto parties below, care on wet or icy scree.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle turn east and follow the traversing use trail below the summit cliffs onto the peak's south side, crossing loose talus and blocky class 2-3 ground.

waypoints.name: Summit block
waypoints.note: ~40 ft of 4th/low-5th-class rock to the true top; rope and runners recommended, natural gear anchors reported at the summit for a short rappel on descent.
waypoints.directions: Continue the traverse east and around to the base of the summit horn on its south side, about 50 ft below the top, where the roped climbing begins.

waypoints.name: Unicorn Peak summit
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Tatoosh Range; tight summit with limited standing room, expect to belay or hand-line the last move in a crowd.
waypoints.directions: Climb about 40-50 ft of 4th to low 5th class rock up the horn to the cramped summit; most parties rope up and rappel the south side on descent.

sectionBreakdown.fromTo: Snow Lake approach and scramble to the summit block

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: Light rack suggested: A few runners/slings for anchors at summit, single 30-60m rope, harness, rappel device (ATC or similar), locking carabiner. Ice axe and crampons recommended mid-summer for steep gully. Helmet strongly advised given objective rockfall hazard.
what_to_bring: Ice axe and light traction (microspikes) if snow is present in the approach gully
30-35 m rope plus a few slings/small rack for the summit block and rappel
Helmet — loose rock on the approach gully and near the summit horn
Map/compass or GPS — the off-trail bowl/gully route above Snow Lake is unmarked and easy to misjudge in poor visibility
pro_tips: A 30-35 m rope and a handful of slings/small rack is plenty for the summit block — no need for a full 60-70 m rope or big rack
Even on the 'easiest' Open Book line, most parties still rope up and rappel given the exposure and loose rock near the top
Combine with Foss Peak, The Castle, Plummer Peak, Pinnacle Peak and Eagle Peak for a full Tatoosh Range traverse day
Consider a May-June ascent for good corn-snow travel in the approach gully, avoiding the loose talus that shows up once it melts out
watch_out: Rockfall and old avalanche debris on the gully below the cliffs above Snow Lake, especially in spring
Post-melt scree/talus below the saddle is loose and slow going by mid-to-late summer
The summit horn is small and exposed — an early right-hand/arete step looks straight down the peak's north face on some lines
Cell service is unreliable; carry a PLB/satellite messenger for a serious incident
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Single 30-35m rope for the one short rappel; harness, rappel device, slings/runners for anchors, rock shoes recommended for leader on 5.4 pitch.
deleted_rows.best_season: Late June through September gives a mostly snow-free scramble with the driest rock on the summit horn. Many parties instead target May-June for a consolidated-snow approach that avoids the loose post-melt talus below the saddle, but that window carries wet-slab and cornice hazard on the gully below the cliffs above Snow Lake. Either way, access is gated by Stevens Canyon Road itself, which is typically snowed shut from roughly October to late May.
deleted_rows.approach: Start at the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes (roughly 20 minutes past the Stevens Canyon entrance station). The lot holds only ~15-20 cars and fills by 8am on summer weekends. Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail as it climbs through subalpine forest and meadow, passing the Bench Lake junction, to Snow Lake at about 1-1.25 miles in (only around 350 ft of up-and-down by here) — this is the last reliable water source. Skirt the lake's west/north shoreline, then leave the maintained tread where a boot-path/climber's trail breaks off and climbs a steep drainage for about half a mile into the large open bowl on Unicorn's northwest side, shared with neighboring Foss and West Unicorn peaks. This basin is loose talus and scree (locally infamous 'Cascadian scree') — expect sliding underfoot and some loose rock; through much of July the gully above the lake can still hold firm snow, so carry an ice axe (and crampons in early season) and be alert to the runout below. From the basin, climb to the saddle on the peak's west side, then traverse/scramble east and around to approach the summit pinnacle from its south side — this stretch is sustained Class 2-3 on talus and blocky rock. Total distance is about 2.4 miles one-way with 2,397 ft of gain, topping out at the base of the summit block itself, about 50 ft below the 6,971 ft summit, where the roped climbing begins.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Descend by reversing the scramble route: from the base of the summit block, downclimb/hike back to the west saddle, then drop through the upper basin and the steep gully back to Snow Lake, rejoining the maintained trail out to the trailhead (about 2.4 miles, losing the 2,397 ft gained on the way up). The one technical piece is the summit block itself — the horn of the 'unicorn.' Most parties rappel rather than downclimb its short, exposed 4th/low-5th-class pitch: a single-rope rappel of about 50 feet down the south side of the pinnacle. A 30m rope is sufficient for this (it's also enough to lead any of the ~40-50 ft summit-block routes on the way up). The traditional anchor was an aging, dead tree at the top of the block that should no longer be relied on; parties now sling a rock horn on the south-facing side of the summit, which already carries multiple slings and rap rings left by prior climbers. Either anchor is climber-built/natural rather than a maintained bolted station, so inspect existing tat and hardware before weighting it and back it up or replace it if it looks sun-rotted or worn. After the rappel, continue the reversed scramble/talus descent back to Snow Lake and the trailhead.
deleted_rows.bail: Early season: if snow conditions deteriorate or visibility becomes poor, retreat via the ascent gully before committing to the final climb. Mid-summer: if talus/scree becomes too difficult, consider bailing at the basin saddle and avoiding the final rock pitch. Late season: wet talus hazard may force retreat before reaching the basin.

pitch_detail.notes: Steep chute climbing from Snow Lake to the upper basin. In summer, talus travel; in spring/early summer, consolidated snow provides faster ascent. Main gully clearly visible; avoid steep headwalls to left.

40-50 feet of rock climbing on solid granite. Rock shoes recommended for leader. Right-side approach (adjacent variation) is easier Class 3-4 with generally solid rock and good handholds. Direct south face (5.4-5.6) is longer and more exposed. East side Class 4 option is quite exposed to north face (descent not recommended).

days.note: This is the standard hiking/scrambling approach shared by all of Unicorn's technical finishes: an easy mile to Snow Lake, then a steeper climb up the bowl to the saddle west of the peak and an exposed class 3-4 scramble around to the base of the final summit block. Reaching the true summit still requires a short 4th/low-5th class move or two, so most parties carry a rope even if they don't plan to "climb" formally.
days.title: Snow Lake approach and scramble to the summit block
days.objective: Hike and scramble to the base of Unicorn Peak's summit pinnacle via Snow Lake and the west col

itinerary.totalNote: A single day, ~7 hrs car-to-car, 4.8 mi round trip and 2,397 ft gain to the base of the summit block; the last few feet to the true summit are low 5th class.

access.fees: $30 per private vehicle (7-day pass), $25 per motorcycle, or $15 per person on foot/bike; America the Beautiful/Rainier annual passes accepted. No separate fee for climbing the Tatoosh peaks.
access.notes: Inside Mount Rainier National Park, but both summits are non-glaciated and well below the 10,000 ft/high-camp threshold that triggers Rainier’s climbing permit and $82 Climbing Cost Recovery Fee — neither applies here. Only the standard park entrance fee applies.
access.rules: Standard NPS wilderness rules apply: camp at the designated Snow Lake sites or in the cross-country zone higher in the basin (wilderness permit either way) if overnighting, pack out all waste, no campfires above treeline, and stay on durable surfaces (rock/snow) on the fragile Tatoosh talus and meadow terrain.
access.permit: No wilderness or climbing permit is required for a day ascent — NPS climbing permits only apply to travel above 10,000 ft or on glaciers, which doesn't include Unicorn Peak. A wilderness permit ($12/person/night plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee) is only needed if camping overnight, e.g. at the small Snow Lake backcountry camp (2 sites, bear pole, privy).
access.closures: Stevens Canyon Road, which serves the Snow Lake Trailhead, is gated and snowed-in roughly October through late May; it typically reopens around Memorial Day to early June depending on snowpack. Check the NPS road-status page before driving out.
access.landManager: National Park Service — Mount Rainier National Park
access.land_manager: National Park Service — Mount Rainier National Park
access.parking_pass: Standard Mount Rainier NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7 days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: Park entrance fee or America the Beautiful annual pass

overnight_permit.what: Mount Rainier National Park wilderness camping permit
overnight_permit.where: Reserve online via Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at a park Wilderness Information Center; required year-round for any overnight stay, including cross-country-zone camping below Unicorn Peak or The Castle.

road.name: Stevens Canyon Road
road.status: Seasonal — closed by snow roughly October through late May
road.driveNote: From Longmire/Paradise, the Snow Lake Trailhead pullout is on the south side of Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes (roughly 2.7 miles east of the Paradise road junction). Small unpaved pullout with room for ~15-20 cars and no amenities — arrive early on summer weekends.
road.seasonalGate: Typically opens around Memorial Day weekend/early June and closes at the first significant snowfall of the season, often in mid-October; a 2022-2024 rehabilitation project has since been completed and the road is fully open in season.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate typical of the south Cascades: heavy, wet winter snowfall (the Paradise/Tatoosh area is among the snowiest inhabited/measured places in the US), with a drier, more stable window from July through September.

bySeason.fall: Snow-free climbing can persist into early October in good years, but Stevens Canyon Road can close on short notice with the season's first storm.
bySeason.spring: Approach gully/bowl typically snow-covered into June; can offer good corn-snow travel but carries wet-slide and cornice hazard off the cliffs above Snow Lake.
bySeason.summer: Talus/scree below the saddle is exposed and loose once snow melts (usually by mid-to-late July); afternoon thunderstorms are possible, so plan to be off the summit horn before they build.
bySeason.winter: Road closed for the season; the peak becomes a serious ski-mountaineering/snowshoe objective only, requiring full avalanche gear and skills.

emergency.notes: Call 911 for active emergencies — Mount Rainier NP's own climbing rangers coordinate SAR within the park. Cell coverage in the Tatoosh backcountry is unreliable, so consider carrying a PLB or satellite messenger.
emergency.rangerStation: Longmire Wilderness Information Center (seasonal staffing); Mount Rainier NP non-emergency line (360) 569-6650.
emergency.nearestHospital: Arbor Health — Morton Hospital, 521 Adams Ave, Morton, WA; 24-hour ER, roughly 30 miles from the Nisqually entrance/Longmire.
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Lewis County Communications Center, (360) 740-1105 for non-emergency reports.

crowds.peakTraffic: Weekend mornings July-August at the trailhead/Snow Lake; the summit scramble itself sees far fewer parties than the lake trail
crowds.estimatePerSeason: No official visitor count is known. Snow Lake trailhead itself is a popular Mount Rainier NP hike (parking lot holds only ~15-20 cars, fills by 8am on summer weekends), but parties consistently describe the scramble beyond Snow Lake into the Unicorn Creek bowl as lightly traveled - some parties report having the summit to themselves, others encounter a guided group (e.g. The Mountaineers) or one or two other parties on a busy weekend day.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Moderate-to-strong hiking fitness for a roughly 5-mile round trip from the Snow Lake trailhead with sustained elevation gain plus off-trail talus/gully travel above Snow Lake
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day pack (day-trip; no overnight or glacier gear needed) - water, layers, helmet recommended for the rockfall-prone gully

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 2-3 hours from the Snow Lake trailhead to the base of the summit block (estimate)
requiredSkills: Class 3-4 scrambling with exposure
Comfortable making a short low-5th-class move to the true summit (roped or unroped per party preference)
Loose-rock/rockfall awareness and spacing technique in the talus gully
Basic route-finding off-trail from Snow Lake into the Unicorn Creek bowl
Turnaround discipline for afternoon thunderstorms on an exposed summit block
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate scrambler - needs prior experience on exposed Class 3-4 terrain and should be comfortable unroped (or with a quick handline) on a short low-5th-class move to tag the summit block; not a beginner objective given the loose rock and exposure

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July through September

July.reason: Within the best-season window; typical dry scrambling conditions, though afternoon thunderstorms are a known hazard

June.reason: Lingering snow in the approach gully and around the summit block; moats and snow bridges can complicate footing before full melt-out

August.reason: Peak of the best-season window; driest, most stable footing on the summit block, but also peak thunderstorm season

October.reason: Outside the best-season window; early snowfall, colder rock, and reduced daylight increase difficulty and hazard beyond what's documented for this route

September.reason: Tail of the best-season window; stable weather typical but shorter daylight and possible early-season snow late in the month

weather.typical: Typical Cascades alpine-summer pattern - clear, cool mornings with building daytime heating in the best-season window
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August; parties should be off the exposed summit block before storms build

seasonal_hazards.exposure: The final summit block is a short but genuinely exposed Class 3-4 (locally low-5th-class) move; the approach gully above Snow Lake is loose and steep with real rockfall risk onto parties below, especially with multiple groups present

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer scramble route; no NWAC forecast zone specifically covers the Tatoosh Range/Unicorn Peak, and the route is normally climbed in dry summer conditions

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel (the Tatoosh Range peaks, including Unicorn, are non-glaciated)

gaps: Round-trip distance/elevation gain figures vary meaningfully by source (WTA vs. AllTrails vs. willhiteweb) depending on where the 'summit' is measured to

Exact avalanche/rockfall history not tied to specific dates beyond individual trip reports

approach_logistics.trailhead: Snow Lake Trailhead (Stevens Canyon Road, Mount Rainier NP)
approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Snow Lake Trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road (~4,500 ft); Stevens Canyon Road closes in winter — winter parties typically start from Narada Falls

deleted_rows.rope_note: Standard approach: Snow Lake Trailhead, up into the upper basin, gully to the saddle west of the peak, then east and around to the south side of the summit block to a short (~50ft) Class 4-low 5th technical step. Competent parties take the easiest line unroped.
rack: A few runners/slings for summit anchors
Rock shoes recommended for the leader on the 5.4 pitch

approach_variants.name: Snow Lake, the northwest gully and Unicorn Col to the summit horn
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Snow Lake trailhead on Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.5 miles east of Reflection Lakes. The lot holds only about 15-20 cars and fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.

Follow the maintained Snow Lake Trail through subalpine forest and meadow, past the Bench Lake junction, to Snow Lake at about 1-1.25 miles — the last reliable water. Skirt the lake's west and north shore, then leave the maintained tread where a climbers' path breaks off and climbs a steep drainage about half a mile into the large open bowl on Unicorn's northwest side, shared with Foss and West Unicorn.

The basin is loose talus and scree; through much of July the gully above the lake can still hold firm snow, so carry an axe and, in early season, crampons.

From the basin, climb to the saddle on the peak's west side, then traverse and scramble east and around to approach the summit pinnacle from its south side — sustained class 2-3 on talus and blocky rock. About 2.4 miles one-way and 2,397 ft of gain to the base of the summit block, where the roped climbing starts.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep; the approach gully holds firm snow through much of July
hazards: Loose talus and scree below the west saddle once the approach gully melts out, usually mid-to-late July
Wet-slide and cornice hazard in the northwest gully and bowl in late spring, with documented slide paths off the cliffs above Snow Lake
An exposed step near the top of the summit horn with real air below on the east side
Climber-built rappel anchors of uncertain age, including a tree reported as no longer sound
Afternoon thunderstorms in summer and unreliable cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The horn is the point and the col is not. Unicorn Col, the saddle just west of the summit at about 6,400 ft, is where the route-finding stops feeling hard — but the summit is still a traverse away, east, and around onto the south side.

The test at the col is a shape: the summit block is a free-standing 50 to 70 ft horn, the thing the peak is named for. If nothing in front of you looks like a detached tower, you have not come far enough east.

The approach negative is in the gully and it is the one that puts parties on bad ground: aim for the main gully out of the basin above Snow Lake, and avoid the steep headwalls to its left. If the ground ahead gets steep and rocky rather than staying a talus or snow chute, you have drifted left. Go back down and across rather than pressing up.

The traverse negative is about height, not direction: the correct use trail traverses below the cliffs on the south side, and it is easier travel than the loose scree above and below it. If you are scrambling up onto the ridge crest instead of contouring underneath it, you are above the path and on worse rock.

And the thing that matters most at the foot of the horn: three separate lines start within about 70 ft of each other there, and they run from easy fifth class to 5.6. Left to right they are: the roof, the Classic Route, Open Book. All three finish at the same slung block, so the only place to get this right is at the bottom. Know which one you came for before you rope up.

Descent finding, decided before you start up: most parties rappel the horn rather than downclimb it — a single-rope rappel of about 50 ft down the south side. The traditional anchor is an aging tree at the top of the block; many parties instead sling the rock horn on the south side, which carries slings and rings left by others. Both are climber-built and neither is maintained: inspect and back up before weighting anything. There are two rappel lines off that horn and they land in different places, so confirm which you are on.

climbing_route.label: West saddle to the summit pinnacle
climbing_route.notes: From the basin climb to the saddle on the peak's west side, then traverse/scramble east and around to approach the summit pinnacle from its south side; sustained on talus and blocky rock, with loose rock and sliding scree. The described line tops out at the base of the summit block itself, about 50 ft below the 6,971 ft summit, where the roped climbing begins — the summit block climbing is not described.

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. Two sites is a hard ceiling, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the cross-country zone rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

deleted_rows.name: North Face (Ragged Edge)
deleted_rows.fa: Darin Berdinka and Gene Pires, August 18, 2013
hazards: Rockfall has occurred on the face; expect loose blocks
Steep, exposed snow traverse on the approach ledges in early season (June)
High exposure along the summit arête pitch
deleted_rows.overview: A 6-pitch 5.7 alpine rock route on the right side of Vesper Peak's north face, following shallow corners, flakes, and low-angle slabs before finishing along an exposed arête to the summit; established in 2013, it is one of the most popular moderate multi-pitch outings in the Mountain Loop Highway corridor.
deleted_rows.beta: Ragged Edge climbs the right (east) side of Vesper's north face on solid granite/quartz diorite, mixing crack, slab, and face climbing across 6 pitches (5.5-5.7). The route is accessed via a heather ledge system that traverses the north face at roughly 5,760-5,800 ft, reached from a col/saddle between Vesper and Wolf/Sperry peaks. It is frequently crowded even on weekdays and is often paired with, or used as an alternative to, the neighboring True Grit (5.8) route.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Because the descent is a walk-off (not a rappel line) and the approach traverses exposed heather ledges and talus that become hazardous in the dark or in a storm, parties should set a firm turnaround time based on remaining daylight, weather, and party pace so the ledge traverse and any snow sections are crossed while visibility and footing are good.
deleted_rows.permit: No climbing or wilderness permit required; Northwest Forest Pass (or day fee) to park at developed trailheads.
deleted_rows.descent: Walk off to the southeast/east side of Vesper Peak.
obj_haz: steep snow on approach ledges in early season
high exposure on the upper arête
crowding leading to rockfall/rope-management hazard from parties above

waypoints.name: Sunrise Mine Trailhead (Trail No. 707)
waypoints.directions: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east about 27 to 28 miles, then turn onto Sunrise Mine Road, Forest Road 4065. Follow roughly 2.3 to 2.5 miles of gravel to the road's end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead, around 2,400 feet, where Trail No. 707 starts. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and there is a pit toilet on site.

waypoints.name: Headlee Pass
waypoints.directions: Follow Sunrise Mine Trail No. 707 across the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs, a real obstacle in high runoff, then up through Wirtz Basin onto cairned talus and up the narrow, loose couloir to Headlee Pass at about 4,720 ft, roughly 2.7 miles in. Watch for rockfall from parties above.

waypoints.name: Saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak (cairned pass)
waypoints.directions: Continue past the pass into the lake basin between Sperry and Vesper and follow the main summit trail up talus and slabs to about 5,600 to 5,700 ft. Leave it there and head north-northwest across the slabs to the two large cairns on the saddle, with Copper Lake in view to the northwest.

waypoints.name: Ragged Edge route start (north face ledge)
waypoints.directions: Do not drop into the saddle floor. Climb third-class slabs about 30 ft above the cairns onto the heather-covered ledges of the north face and traverse them roughly 800 ft to the original start, gained by fourth-class moves on an up-then-right arch. In June expect steep snow on the ledges and carry an axe and crampons.

waypoints.name: Vesper Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb six pitches: traverse hard right on a grassy ledge to the white dike, up the bolted dike slab, the arete past old pins, stacked blocks, the airy traverse out the ragged east edge, and a long easy arete to the summit.

timing.recommendedStart: Early (predawn/first light) given crowding on the route and a 3+ hour approach

deleted_rows.detailed_rack: A single 60m rope is sufficient. Recommended rack: doubles of cams from about 0.5-1 in, singles of 0.2-0.4, 2, and 3 in, plus a set of small nuts; the route also has some fixed protection (bolts on the pitch 2 traverse, fixed pins on the pitch 3 arête). Several parties note a single standard cam rack is adequate and doubling up is not strictly necessary.
what_to_bring: approach shoes for the talus/heather approach
map/compass or GPS for the cairned col and ledge traverse
pro_tips: The route is popular and can be crowded even on weekdays; start early to beat other parties to the base
True Grit (5.8) on the same face is a good backup objective if Ragged Edge is occupied
A single standard rack of cams and nuts is enough; doubling up on cam sizes is not required by most parties
watch_out: The approach ledge traverse and 4th-class downclimb to the alternate start become sketchy/hazardous when wet
Pitch 4 has loose and semi-loose stacked blocks
Rockfall has been documented on the route (September 2024)
The final arête pitch has significant exposure despite its modest grade
deleted_rows.pro_needs: Moderate trad rack (small-to-mid cams and nuts) supplemented by a handful of fixed bolts and pins; belays are reported as sometimes marginal, so care in anchor building is warranted.
deleted_rows.best_season: Prime season is roughly June through September; the Mountain Loop Highway/Sunrise Mine Road typically opens after seasonal repairs in late spring (often around Memorial Day) and closes again with the first heavy snow in late fall. Early-season (June) ascents commonly encounter lingering steep snowfields on the approach ledges and just below the summit, requiring an ice axe and crampons; by mid-to-late summer the route and approach are typically snow-free.
deleted_rows.approach: From Granite Falls, drive the Mountain Loop Highway east approximately 27-28 miles, then turn onto Sunrise Mine Road (Forest Road 4065) and follow the gravel road about 2.3-2.5 miles to its end at the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (~2,400 ft, Trail No. 707; Northwest Forest Pass required, pit toilet on site). Hike the Sunrise Mine Trail about 2.7-3 miles, gaining roughly 2,600 ft, to Headlee Pass (4,720 ft). Continue on trail around Sperry Peak's south flank into the Vesper Creek/lake basin between Vesper and Sperry, then follow the main summit trail up talus and slabs to about 5,600-5,700 ft. From there head north/northwest across slabs to the saddle/col between Vesper and Wolf Peak (two large cairns mark the pass near 48.01375, -121.51451, with Copper Lake visible to the northwest). Third-class slabs about 30 ft above the cairns lead onto heather-covered ledges on Vesper's north face; traverse these ledges roughly 800 ft eastward to the original route start (approx. 48.01376, -121.51736), reached via 4th-class moves. An alternative start via a small notch/col overlooking the Vesper Glacier is also used. Allow 3+ hours for the approach; early-season parties (June) should expect steep snow on the ledge traverse requiring ice axe and crampons.
deleted_rows.descent_text: From the summit, descend via a walk-off down the southeast/east side of Vesper Peak, rejoining the standard hiking route back down through talus and slabs to the lake basin and Headlee Pass, then out the Sunrise Mine Trail to the trailhead. No rappels are required; parties report the descent to the car taking roughly 2 hours in good conditions (total car-to-car time for the route is commonly cited around 8-12 hours, with one trip report logging 11 hours).
deleted_rows.bail: The route can be escaped by walking off along easier terrain to climber's right/east toward the summit walk-off slopes rather than continuing up the arête; because the route follows low-angle ledge and slab terrain rather than a sustained wall, retreat by downclimbing or traversing off to easier ground is generally more practical than rappelling.

pitch_detail.notes: There are two ways to start. The preferred one makes an exposed 3rd-class traverse around the buttress toe to a clean layback flake, followed by a low-angle groove onto 3rd-class slabs. The original start instead scrambles up a gully past a big flake-chockstone. From either, move well right along grassy ledges to a gear belay beneath the faint white dike that splits the slab; this rightward traverse is the most common place to go off route.

Climb the thin white dike past three bolts to a narrow ledge, then traverse right and up a short gully to a fixed anchor on the skyline. Some parties rate this slab the crux of the route. Keep slings long on the traverse to manage rope drag, and watch for parties above in the gully.

Step right, then traverse left on positive edges toward the skyline past bolt protection. Go up the arête past old fixed pins through a short, fun dihedral, and belay on gear at a heather ledge. Back up the old pins rather than trusting them alone.

Climb steep stacked blocks, then easier zig-zag cracks to a fixed anchor. Loose rock is the hazard here: a large detached block sits on this ground and can take away gear options. Test holds, keep the rope off loose edges, and keep the belayer out of the fall line.

Often called the crux: an airy face traverse out along the ragged east edge of the north face. Pass two bolts, then traverse right about 50 ft to a fixed anchor on the skyline. The exposure is big but the rock takes gear well. Protect the traverse for the follower as well as the leader.

The finish: a long, easy romp up the arête to a last bit of heather and the summit, where there is a bolted anchor. From the top, walk off the southeast side to rejoin the standard route. No rappels are needed.

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Sunrise Mine Trailhead (~2,340 ft) at the end of FR-4065 off the Mountain Loop Highway, via Trail #707

approach_variants.name: Sunrise Mine Trail #707, Headlee Pass, Vesper-Wolf saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From Granite Falls drive the Mountain Loop Highway about 27-28 miles, turn onto Sunrise Mine Road (FR 4065) and follow roughly 2.3-2.5 miles of gravel to the Sunrise Mine trailhead at about 2,400 ft. Northwest Forest Pass; pit toilet on site.

Sunrise Mine Trail #707 runs about 2.7-3 miles and 2,600 ft to Headlee Pass at 4,720 ft, crossing the South Fork Stillaguamish on logs low down and passing through Wirtz Basin onto cairned talus. Past the pass the trail continues around Sperry Peak's south flank into the Vesper Creek and lake basin, then the main summit trail climbs talus and slabs to about 5,600-5,700 ft. Leave the trail there and head north/northwest across the slabs.
approach_variants.season: Jun-Sep; expect steep snow on the ledge traverse in June
hazards: Rockfall in the Headlee Pass couloir
Steep snow on the ledge traverse in June — ice axe and crampons
Wet heather on the traverse
Log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish
approach_variants.baseFinding: Two large cairns mark the saddle at roughly 5,700 ft, near 48.01375 -121.51451, with Copper Lake in view to the northwest — that is the marker, and it is what you look for in cloud. Third-class slabs about 30 ft above the cairns lead onto the heather-covered ledges of the north face. Traverse those ledges roughly 800 ft eastward to reach the original start near 48.01376 -121.51736, gained by fourth-class moves on an up-then-right arch. An alternative start uses a small notch overlooking the remnant Vesper Glacier. If you have dropped into the saddle rather than climbing 30 ft above it, you are below the ledge system and it will not go.

bivy.name: Vesper Creek basin and Lake Elan, beyond Headlee Pass
bivy.notes: The working base camp for Vesper Peak's north side and for Sperry, and it puts Morning Star within reach along the ridge. Getting here means the Sunrise Mine trail's ford of the South Fork Stillaguamish, then the switchbacked chute below Headlee Pass at roughly 4,700 ft, which is loose and known for rockfall — parties should not stack up in it. Snow lingers in the chute and on the pass long after the valley is clear, and it is the section most likely to turn an overnight around. Camp on the durable benches rather than the meadow closest to the water. No elevation is recorded; none was confidently sourced.
bivy.water: Reliable — the basin outlet stream runs all season and the lake itself is a backup, though it holds ice and snow cover well into July
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest but outside any wilderness — no permit of any kind to camp. Northwest Forest Pass required at the Sunrise Mine trailhead.
bivy.capacity: Several tents — grassy benches above the stream just past the pass, plus more spread around the lake basin

bivy.name: Verlot corridor campgrounds — Turlo, Verlot and Gold Basin
bivy.notes: These sit on the paved lower half of the loop and stay reachable when the gravel section above Barlow Pass is gated shut, which makes them the fallback base for Vesper, Morning Star, Sperry and the Big Four side of the valley. They are closer to the Sunrise Mine and Big Four trailheads than anything up-valley, at the cost of being low, wooded and busy with general campers rather than climbers. Weekend availability is genuinely tight in midsummer, so a reservation is worth having. Dispersed roadside pullouts along the corridor need no permit but are increasingly signed and patrolled.
bivy.water: Verlot and Gold Basin generally have drinking water in season; the Stillaguamish runs alongside as a backup
bivy.permit: Developed fee campgrounds, no permit. None are in wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is what you need for the trailheads up the road, not for the sites themselves.
bivy.capacity: Large by the standards of this valley — dozens of developed sites across the three, tables, toilets, some with potable water; fee sites, reservable in part

deleted_rows.overview: North Twin Sister (6,644 ft) is the second-highest and northernmost summit of the Twin Sisters Range, a massif of dunite (mantle-derived, olivine-rich rock) about 10 miles southwest of Mount Baker. This line follows the mountain's west ridge on solid, high-friction olivine to the north summit as an unroped scramble.
deleted_rows.beta: Expect sustained class 3 scrambling on exceptionally solid, high-friction rock, with short class 4 steps and multiple false summits near the top.
deleted_rows.turnaround: Set a firm, conservative turnaround time before starting given the long approach and exposed upper ridge, and honor it regardless of proximity to the summit.
deleted_rows.rock_grade: Class 3-4 (Class 2 where staying well south of the crest)
deleted_rows.face: West Ridge (right of the crest low, left of it near the false summits)
deleted_rows.permit: No climbing permit; the approach roads cross private timberland where the landowner's paid recreation permit is required for walk-in or bike entry - check current access before the trip.

deleted_rows.descent: Reverse the scramble.

waypoints.name: Gated Bridge Trailhead (FR 38 / Weyerhaeuser Rd 9000)
waypoints.note: Park at the yellow gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack (reached via Mosquito Lake Rd from Acme, then FR 38/Dailey Quarry Rd); gate is usually closed and the landowner (Hampton Family Forests) requires a paid recreation permit — bike or hike the logging roads from here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue on Forest Road 38. Park at the yellow gate just before the bridge, at around 1,200 feet — the gate is usually closed and the landowner (Hampton Family Forests) requires a paid recreation permit. The road beyond is private timberland and access can change from year to year, so confirm the gate status before your trip.

waypoints.name: Dailey Prairie road-to-trail transition
waypoints.note: Logging roads climb roughly 2,000 ft over the first 5 miles to Dailey Prairie, a wet clearcut-plateau meadow, where the singletrack climbers' trail for the West Ridge route branches off the road.
waypoints.directions: Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and climb the graded logging road, which most parties ride on mountain bikes. At the first major fork, about 2.5 miles up, stay right; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after a second, sturdier bridge, take the left fork and continue to around mile 5, where the road ends near a dirt mound and cairn.

waypoints.name: Fire ring / treeline
waypoints.note: Switchbacking trail through old logging spurs reaches treeline near 4,100 ft, marked by a firepit and cairn; bikes are left lower, where road riding ends around mile 5, and from here the path continues on foot up onto the ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: Leave the road for an old, overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut, where brush soaks clothing even on a dry day and there is no tread or cairns to follow in fog. Around mile 6.4 you reach the old fire ring.

waypoints.name: Katie Gap
waypoints.note: Notch where the cairned crest route dead-ends at cliffs; climbers drop through this gap to bypass the obstacle — the route's well-known routefinding crux, easy to miss in poor visibility.

waypoints.name: Summit headwall scramble
waypoints.note: Final stretch of sustained Class 3, locally Class 4, scrambling on grippy but exposed orange dunite (olivine); loose blocks and multiple false summits above this point.

waypoints.name: North Twin Sister summit
waypoints.note: True north summit of the Twin Sisters Range; broad views of Mount Baker, the San Juan Islands, and across the connecting ridge to South Twin (7,000+ ft).
waypoints.directions: Start the headwall on its left and stay climber's left; ground that looks easier to the right turns into loose, exposed Class 4-5. Climb straight over the false-summit crag on steep Class 3, then take the broken chimney or traverse right around a corner into a rock-and-gully system, scrambling Class 3-4 to the summit. Several false tops near the end are easy to mistake for it.

deleted_rows.pro_needs: Minimal — the scrambling line is unroped for essentially all parties; the technical M1b variation and any roped class 5 moves belong to the 'West Ridge' entry, not this scramble line.
deleted_rows.best_season: July-September is the reliable window. Earlier in summer lingering snow on the ridge and the north slope calls for an ice axe; the route itself crosses no glacier.
deleted_rows.approach: Drive Road 38 west from Mosquito Lake Road, cross Clearwater Creek at about 4.5 miles, and take the right fork down to the gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack. From the gate, the approach is entirely on old logging roads and then ridge/brush for roughly 7 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car-to-summit, one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble — most parties mountain-bike the road portion to save time and legs. Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and ascend the well-graded logging road for about 2.5 miles; at the first major fork stay right (the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry). About 0.2 miles later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the left branch here. Around the 5-mile mark, near a dirt mound and a cairn, leave the logging road proper and pick up an old, overgrown road spur that switchbacks up through a clearcut; this is the point where route-finding gets harder and the brush thickens noticeably (expect to get soaked in wet weather — the clearcut brush is notorious for saturating pants and boots even without rain). By about 6.4 miles you pass an old fire-ring in the clearcut and enter a final band of brush before reaching timber at the base of the west ridge; from there, follow the timbered ridge itself up to where it opens onto rock and the class 3 scrambling begins. There is no reliable water source once you leave the river at the trailhead, so carry what you need for the day. In low cloud/fog, which is common on the Twin Sisters, the clearcut and lower-ridge sections lack obvious cairns or a defined tread and route-finding can be genuinely difficult; parties should be comfortable navigating by map/GPS through brushy, featureless clearcut terrain. On the ridge proper, cairns mark a Class 3 line — the lower ridge goes on or just right (south) of the crest, but from the small headwall below the false summits stay left (climber's left); drifting right up there leads toward false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 terrain on loose, exposed rock.
deleted_rows.descent_text: Reverse the scramble down the ridge crest. In early season (roughly May-June), many parties instead glissade a snowfield on the north slope and traverse back to the West Ridge trail near 4,600 ft.
deleted_rows.bail: Descend the connecting ridge to the approach roads and walk out.

pitch_detail.notes: Climbers' trail and broken talus/boulder slopes from the end of the bike route up to the base of the ridge.

Sustained scrambling on orange-weathered dunite, keeping on or south (climber's right) of the crest low down and left of it at the headwall, through the 'Katie Gap' notch (~6,300 ft) that bypasses a cliff band.
Final scramble up blocky terrain to the summit.

itinerary.cal: Best done roughly July–September once the logging-road gate is snow-free; in early season the north-face snow slopes offer a faster glissade descent.

days.note: This is climbed in a single long day — no camp. Parties bike or hike ~5-6 miles of closed logging road to the base of the peak, then scramble roughly 1,500 vertical ft of sustained, well-featured Class 3-4 dunite (olivine) rock to the 6,644 ft summit before reversing the whole route.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Nooksack bridge gate, the logging roads to the cairn at mile 5, then the clearcut spur to the west ridge
approach_variants.notes:
This is a Twin Sisters approach, so start with the range check: the Twin Sisters here are the olivine peaks west of Mount Baker, reached off Mosquito Lake Road and the Middle Fork Nooksack. Every road name below belongs to that range and to no other Twin Sisters.

Drive Road 38 west from Mosquito Lake Road, cross Clearwater Creek, and take the right fork down to the gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack. From the gate it is roughly 7 miles and about 5,500 ft of gain car to summit, almost all of it on old logging road and then ridge — one of the longer approaches for a Washington scramble, and most parties mountain-bike the road.

Cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack and climb the well-graded logging road about 2.5 miles. At the first major fork stay right; the left branch dead-ends at an old quarry. About 0.2 mile later, after crossing a second, sturdier bridge, the road forks again — take the left branch.

Around mile 5 the road walking ends. From there an old overgrown spur switchbacks up through a clearcut, and by about mile 6.4 you pass an old fire ring and enter a final band of brush before timber at the base of the west ridge.

The roads are on private timberland; access status changes, so confirm before the trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep for the scramble. In May and June parties still get up it but the north-slope snowfield is in play
hazards: Route-finding through a featureless clearcut with no cairns and no tread, in the cloud that is normal here
Brush that saturates clothing and boots without rain
Drifting right near the false summits into unintended Class 4-5 on loose, exposed rock
Private timberland access that changes year to year
No water after the river at the gate
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The dirt mound and cairn at about mile 5 is the most important marker on this approach, because it is where the navigation gets hard. Up to there you are on graded logging road and the only decisions are two forks — right at the first major fork about 2.5 miles in, then left at the next fork 0.2 mile past the second bridge. At the mound and cairn near mile 5, leave the road for an old overgrown spur that switchbacks up through the clearcut.

The fire ring at about mile 6.4 is the second marker, and it confirms you took the right spur. Past it is a final band of brush and then timber at the base of the west ridge.

In low cloud, which is normal here, the clearcut is the hardest ground on the route and it is not the mountain. There are no cairns and no defined tread through the clearcut and lower ridge, and the terrain is genuinely featureless. Parties should be prepared to navigate this section by map and GPS. The brush will also soak you to the waist without any rain falling.

Arrival at the climbing: follow the timbered ridge up until it opens onto rock. Trees stop, rock starts, Class 3 begins. There is no bergschrund, no notch and no col to look for — the transition is vegetative.

The fog test for the ridge itself: low on the ridge the line runs on or just right of the crest; from the small headwall below the false summits, stay left — climber's left. Cairns mark a Class 3 line that way. Drifting right up there leads to false summits and unintentional Class 4-5 ground on loose, exposed rock. If the climbing has got harder than Class 3 and the rock has got worse, you have drifted right; traverse back left rather than pushing on.

The rock itself is a confirmation you are in the right range. The Twin Sisters are dunite — olivine-rich ultramafic rock, exceptionally grippy, commonly compared to coarse sandpaper. If the rock under your hands is ordinary Cascade granite or volcanic rubble, you are not on the Sisters.

approach_variants.name: FR-38 gate at the Middle Fork Nooksack bridge, then the Dailey Prairie roads to the West Ridge path
approach_variants.notes:
The same gate and ridge, described by road names with the Dailey Prairie road-end as the marker: via Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then Forest Road 38. Park at the gate near 1,200 ft and continue roughly 5-6 miles with about 2,000-2,500 ft of gain on private-timberland logging roads — commonly by mountain bike — to reach the West Ridge climbers' path, which climbs through timber onto the ridge crest.

Several forks and offshoots near Dailey Prairie make GPS or a GPX track genuinely useful here; wrong turns on this network are common and expensive.

The gate situation on this network changes year to year. Treat the drivable road-end as unverified until confirmed for your trip.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
hazards: An unsigned logging-road network around Dailey Prairie where wrong turns are common
Private-timberland gates whose status changes year to year
The same drift-right-into-Class-5 trap near the false summits
Brushy, wet climbers' path with no maintained tread
Long approach with no water above the road network
approach_variants.baseFinding: The road network is the crux and the mountain is not. Around Dailey Prairie the logging roads fork repeatedly with no signage, every branch looks like the main line, and a wrong turn costs miles. Carry a track. The end of rideable road is the marker, and on this network it is commonly identified by a large culvert pipe at the timber-road terminus. Stash bikes there and continue on foot. The climbers' path is brushy and wet and not hard to follow — that combination is itself the confirmation. It climbs through timber onto the ridge crest. Arrival: the same as the other variant, because it is the same ridge. Timber gives way to rock and Class 3 scrambling starts. Low on the ridge the line runs on or just right of the crest; from the headwall below the false summits stay climber's left, because drifting right there puts you on false summits and unintended Class 4-5 ground. Which Sister am I on? This matters because the same road network serves North Twin, South Twin, Little Sister, Cinderella and Skookum, and the peaks look alike. North Twin's west ridge tops out at 6,644 ft and is reached from the road network north of the range. South Twin's west ridge is gained at an obvious notch in the ridge crest around 5,200 ft above Orsino Creek Basin, and its summit is 7,004 ft. If your ridge started at a defined notch, you are on South Twin.

climbing_route.label: West ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: Where the timbered ridge opens onto rock, scramble past small scrub trees, keeping just right of the crest, to the top of a prominent crag on the crest that ends in a drop-off of about 30 ft. The false summit and an obelisk-like tower come into view from here. The rock is grippy, orange-weathered dunite.

climbing_route.label: Right of the crest to the small headwall
climbing_route.notes: Drop about 100 ft right of the crest and continue for roughly 800 ft past the drop-off crag, then climb back left on solid rock to a small headwall. Watch the pull to the right: ground that looks easier out there turns into loose, exposed class 4–5. The crest itself also runs class 4–5, so cairns and the obvious worn line are the guide.

climbing_route.label: Over the false summit
climbing_route.notes: Start the headwall on its left, pass the last clump of about seven trees on the crest, and climb straight over the false-summit crag on steep class 3 rock. This is the most sustained stretch; the exposure grows but the holds stay good.

climbing_route.label: Summit gully and final rocks
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the false summit, either climb a broken, exposed chimney or traverse right onto a ridge spur and around a corner into a rock-and-gully system. Steep rock with bucket holds leads to class 3–4 scrambling and the summit; several false tops near the end are easy to mistake for it.

bivy.name: Orsino Creek Basin
bivy.notes: This is the standard overnight camp for the west ridge of South Twin and the most useful water stop on the whole northwest approach. It is reached from the Dailey Prairie road system by crossing Orsino Creek and following a brushy old road that fades into a path through timber, then traversing up red talus past the ruins of an old cabin into the basin. From the camp a steep and thoroughly unpleasant slog up dirt, scree and talus gains an obvious notch on the west ridge at around five thousand two hundred feet. The ground is coarse and drains fast, so pitch on the flat gravel benches rather than hunting for soft ground. Fill everything here. Above this point the only water is snowmelt and glacier runoff, and in a dry August there may be none at all. Best from July through September; earlier the basin holds snow and the creek runs high and cold.
bivy.water: Orsino Creek, the most reliable water on the west side of the range. It is the last dependable source for the summits and for the higher camps, and it shrinks noticeably by late summer
bivy.permit: The basin sits close to the boundary between private timberland below and national forest wilderness above. Camping is legal on the forest side and not on the timber company side, and the line is not signed on the ground, so camp high in the basin rather than low. No overnight permit is currently required on the forest side; standard wilderness rules apply, including a party size limit of twelve. Campfires are a poor idea anywhere here and are banned outright on the private ground below; late summer fire restrictions are routine.
bivy.capacity: A handful of small dispersed sites among talus and heather; two to three tents

bivy.name: Dailey Prairie road end (staging and bike stash, not a camp)
bivy.notes: This old prairie is where the logging road system tops out and the climbers path to the west ridge of North Twin begins, roughly five miles and two thousand feet of road above the river bridge. Almost every party bikes to here and leaves the bike, which turns a brutal road walk into a fast coast on the way out. It reads like the obvious basecamp and it is not one: under the current landowner rules this ground is day use only, no camping and no fire, and vehicles must never block the road or the gate. Treat it as a staging point where you shoulder the pack for the last three thousand feet, and push on to the wilderness ground above if you want to sleep out. Snow lingers on the path above roughly four thousand feet well into early summer. The road is also subject to closure on short notice for active logging, quarry work or fire danger, and signs posting a closure have appeared with no warning.
bivy.water: None reliable at the prairie itself; carry what you need up from the valley
bivy.permit: Private industrial timberland. The gate at the Middle Fork river bridge is locked and keys are no longer issued for this northern entrance, so the road is foot and bicycle only. The landowner now runs a fee recreation permit covering this block of forestland, with a hard cap on the number of non-motorized permits issued, daylight-only entry of roughly an hour and a half either side of sunrise and sunset, no campfires at any time, and no camping. Ownership of these roads has changed hands more than once and the terms have changed with it, so confirm the current permit and gate situation with the landowner before you go rather than assuming older terms still apply.
bivy.capacity: Open ground with room for several parties, but overnight use is not permitted

bivy.name: Col between the Twins and the Sisters Glacier margin
bivy.notes: The saddle between North and South Twin sits at about five thousand eight hundred feet, with the Sisters Glacier, the largest ice in the range, on the northeast side of South Twin below it. Parties splitting the two Twins over two days camp in this area, and it is the natural high camp if you have come up from Orsino Creek Basin and want an early start on the traverse. The attraction is water: the glacier margin and the slabs below it carry running meltwater when nothing else on the crest does, and this is the last chance to fill before committing to the ridge south. It is a genuinely exposed spot with no shelter, and weather here can be far worse than in the valley. Later in the season the ice recedes, the slab runoff dries up, and the whole plan depends on melting snow instead. Check that there is still snow or ice water before relying on this camp in August or September.
bivy.water: Running water at the edge of the glacier and on the glacial slabs below the col in season. This is meltwater, so it flows on warm afternoons and can vanish on a cold morning or after the snow has gone
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness. Dispersed camping is legal with no overnight permit currently required, party size limited to twelve. Camp on rock, gravel or snow rather than on the thin heather, and pack out everything including waste. Campfires are inappropriate at this elevation and are usually prohibited under late season fire restrictions. A Northwest Forest Pass or an interagency pass is needed at the forest service trailheads on the southeast side.
bivy.capacity: Two or three small tents on gravel benches and slabs; exposed and windy

bivy.name: South Twin Sister summit bivies
bivy.notes: The highest summit in the range, somewhere between about six thousand nine hundred and seven thousand feet depending on which survey you believe, and the classic place to split the north to south traverse into two days. There are a number of flat gravel and rubble bivy spots scattered among the summit blocks, built up by parties over the years, and the view across to Mount Baker at dawn is the reason people do it. It is entirely waterless. The dunite the range is made of is dense and unfractured and sheds or swallows water rather than holding it, so there are no springs on the crest and no tarns near the summit; whatever you drink here you carried or melted. Exposed to everything, with no wind shelter beyond the blocks themselves. Reasonable from July into September once the snow has consolidated. Do not plan on finding snow to melt in a dry late summer.
bivy.water: None. Melt snow if there is any, otherwise carry every litre from Orsino Creek, the glacier margin or Green Creek
bivy.permit: National forest wilderness, dispersed camping legal, no overnight permit currently required, party size limit twelve. No fires. The whole approach to this summit crosses private timberland where the current landowner permit applies, so the camp itself is legal while the walk to it may not be without the right paperwork.
bivy.capacity: Several small hand-built gravel platforms among the summit blocks; one or two tents plus tarps or bags
